# THE PRINTER
## TO THE READERS
->Sends Heartiest Greetings<- <note>original: "S. P. D." for Salutem Plurimam Dicit, a standard formal greeting in Latin correspondence.</note>

Some years ago, friend **READER**, we published a fairly substantial volume containing various authors treating the subject of chemistry <note>original: "perichemeias" (Greek: περιχημείας), referring here to the art of alchemy and chemical transformations</note>, collected through the labor of **GUGLIELMO GRATAROLO**, the Physician. Since that venture turned out well for us, and we noticed it was pleasing to those devoted to this Philosophy <note>The "Hermetic Philosophy" or alchemy</note>, we applied our mind to further refining and illuminating that art to the best of our ability. Therefore, with the help of friends and learned men, we have gathered more works, and from those gathered, we have selected the better ones, as I believe. We have distributed them into these two volumes in a more convenient and less expensive format. We are even thinking of bringing to light even more excellent works, if God grants us the leisure and friends continue to help; by which men of this fore-

# PREFACE

-> <-

Those who are eager for this most excellent and useful art <note>The "art" referred to here is alchemy, the precursor to modern chemistry</note> may be able to use and enjoy it. But someone will say that I, through these editions of mine, bring more harm to the State than benefit, since the art is vain and is no true science: one which deals not with entirely certain matters, but with things uncertain and rarely happening—indeed, most rarely, or perhaps never, according to the opinions of many. For they claim that no one, in our own or in the previous century, has actually performed what the writers of this art so magnificently and manifoldly promise. Since, therefore, it lacks the intended end <note>The "end" or goal usually refers to the successful transmutation of metals or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>, and all things are done for the sake of an end, it follows that it is no art, nor any science, and that those who handle these matters, or believe idle impostors, are ridiculous and foolish.

To these critics, a sufficient and more than ample response has been given through certain demonstrations by excellent and most learned Philosophers, and the truth of this art has been proven—especially indeed by the most celebrated Philosopher **Pietro Bono of Ferrara** in his *Precious Pearl* <note>original: "Preciosa Margarita," a famous 14th-century alchemical treatise</note>, now for the first time edited by us in its entirety (and not as it was previously at Venice); and also by **Lorenzo Ventura of Venice**, in our own age, in his book dedicated to the most illustrious **Otto Henry**

->Count Palatine<- <note>Otto Henry (1502–1559) was a Prince-elector of the Palatinate and a famous patron of alchemy and the arts</note>

# -> P R E F A C E <-

Since the truth of the art has been vindicated in the work dedicated to the Palatine <note>original: "Palatinum"; likely referring to the Elector Palatine, a high-ranking prince of the Holy Roman Empire</note> and published by us—and the same was practiced in the past by almost countless philosophers—there is no need for a response from me. This is especially true since it is not my role to teach or to defend specific factions, but rather to bring the teachers of good literature and the arts <term>arts: "artes" here refers to the liberal arts and practical sciences</term> before the public for the common good. My goal is to set them against one another so that the truth may be struck out, just as fire is struck from the collision of flints.

In the meantime, however, I will say what seems right to me, unskilled as I may be. Opposition comes almost entirely from those who (even if they are otherwise highly learned) have never been practiced in this specific art. Indeed, no one acts or judges more recklessly than the ignorant and the unskilled. To the inexperienced, many things seem impossible which are nevertheless very easily accomplished through art and nature, as experience teaches everywhere in almost every kind of craft.

On the contrary, the skilled and experienced investigator—and, if I may say so, the co-helper—of most sagacious Nature is able to provide and effect, through genius and diligence, even those things which seem impossible to the ignorant and are beyond the grasp of the common people. As for what pertains to me, although I have never touched such things, nor am I one who could speak of so hidden a mystery...

# PREFACE

-><-

Although I am unable to judge anything with certainty, I cannot bring myself to believe that so many learned philosophers and men of great reputation—indeed, even illustrious kings who were the primary authors of this art, whose writings we now present—could have been deceived themselves or wished to deceive others. These men have achieved a most excellent name among all the learned for so many centuries: such as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century Persian polymath often called the "father of chemistry."</note>, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval medicine.</note>, Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, a Persian physician and chemist who discovered numerous compounds.</note>, Villanova <note>Arnald of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, Raymond <note>Raymond Lully, a Majorcan philosopher to whom many alchemical works were attributed.</note>, and almost infinite others, both ancient and modern, whose names we shall refrain from listing now. 

I do not doubt, however, that there are many today, and have been previously, who are notorious impostors; worthless men, utterly ignorant of letters and all good arts and morals, yet most skilled in every kind of wickedness. These men know absolutely nothing beyond Ceres and Bacchus <note>original: "Cererem & Bacchum" — metaphors for food/bread and wine/drunkenness.</note>, with whom they are so familiar that they bear their marks not only on their bodies, but prominently displayed on their faces and noses. Nevertheless, with magnificent words, they sell themselves to great lords as if they were new Gebers or Raymonds, only to boil away their patrons' purses <note>A play on words regarding alchemical "decoction" or boiling down.</note>, even though they cannot even produce "burning water" <term>aqua ardens: an early term for concentrated alcohol or ethanol produced by distillation</term> from wine—despite the fact that they drain entire vats of it every single day.

<summary>The author defends the integrity of historical alchemical masters like Geber and Avicenna while sharply criticizing the drunken frauds and "impostors" who trick nobility for money.</summary>

# PREFACE

...we provide: indeed, we present all things from manuscript copies <note>original: "manuscriptis exemplaribus"</note>, either never before published, or in better and more enlarged versions. The page following the title indicates what is contained within each individual Volume <note>original: "Tomis"</note>. Now we must pray that you look kindly upon these labors of ours, such as they are: you may perhaps receive better things from us in the future, if those who love this art—and especially those who love the truth—are willing to consult for the common good and communicate to us those things which might otherwise perish in their possession, to no benefit of their own and to the detriment of others. 

I would wish this said not only regarding this art or science <note>original: "scientia"</note>, but in all others as well. For if the ancients had been born only for themselves and had concealed the sciences and arts <note>original: "artes"</note> from us, how, I ask, would we differ from the rest of the living creatures <note>original: "animantibus"</note>? Therefore, enjoy these things with a grateful heart.

# PROPOSITIONS, OR
## MAXIMS OF THE
### CHEMICAL ART. <note>original: "Ars Chemica." In this context, it refers to Alchemy, the art of transmutation and purification.</note>

## PROPOSITION I.

*EVERYTHING pure and clean that is extracted from its ore and stones, as well as from foreign matters, without any preparation—which does not melt like wax—is unsuitable for this work. From this, it is concluded that all metals are excluded, as well as all species of Marcasite <note>A term used historically for various metallic sulfides, often iron pyrites</note>, glass, crystal, coral, and all pearls, which do not liquefy in the fire.*

## Propositio II.

*Everything capable of sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note>, which adheres to the sides of the vessel and prevents the viewing of foreign matter within the vessel, is remote from and unsuitable for this business. By this, all four principal spirits are especially excluded: namely, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," or mercury</note>, arsenic, sulfur, and every kind of tutty <note>zinc oxide deposits found in furnaces</note> and magnesia <note>likely referring to manganese ore or a similar mineral used in glassmaking, not modern magnesium</note>.*

## Propositio III.

*Every mineral, from which earth is not made, a-*

*...is foreign and hostile to this work. From this are excluded all things which proceed from animals, such as hair, blood, flesh, dung, eggs, and the like; and also all animals themselves, such as tortoises, snails <note>original: "caragdi," likely referring to land snails or similar shelled creatures</note>, moles, frogs, bees, and the like.*

## Proposition IV.

*Any animate thing, or anything proceeding from inanimate things <note>The author here distinguishes between "living" organic matter and the "mineral" life sought in alchemy</note>, is unsuitable for this greater art. From this proposition are especially excluded all superfluities of animals, and all vegetables, and those things which proceed from them, such as wine, "burning water" <term>aqua ardens: distilled alcohol or spirits</term>, oil, honey, urine, sperm, and things similar to these.*

## Proposition V.

*Everything which cannot be blackened, whitened, and reddened <note>These refer to the three main stages of the alchemical process: Nigredo, Albedo, and Rubedo</note> by fire within one hour of a natural day, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the masculine principle.*

*Everything which lacks red smoke when enclosed in a small vessel over a proper fire, does not enter into the composition of this work in the role of the femi-*

### Proposition VII.

No thing of a single number can complete a work of a higher order. From this it is especially gathered that the Philosopher's Stone <term>Lapis Philosophorum: the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</term> is made from two: namely, the male and the female; or from the red and the white.

### Proposition VIII.

Whatever cannot be completed in one vessel and in one number is unsuitable for this work. And by this, the use of multiple vessels is especially excluded.

### Proposition IX.

Whatever is not able to finish such a perfection and create gold and silver within a space of one hundred days at most is an enemy to this work. By this, the nine-month period is especially excluded, or it is gathered that the stone must be completed in its final perfection within one hundred days, up to and including the time of multiplication <term>Multiplication: the process of increasing the potency and quantity of the alchemical medicine</term>.

# PROPOSITIONS.

## Proposition X.

Anything which, during the first six days, when melted over the required fire in a physical vessel <note>The "physical vessel" or *vas physicum* refers to the specialized alchemical flask, often called a philosopher's egg.</note> within its necessary furnace, does not appear saffron-yellow; and in the next six days, red; and in the following [six] days, white with a perfect whiteness; and in the final thirty days, most ruby-red with a perfect redness—this is not according to the intention of this work. From this, the method of operating is chiefly drawn: namely, that the physical stone <note>The *lapis physicus* or Philosopher's Stone in its developmental stage.</note> must be placed in a glass vessel closed inviolably <note>Hermetically sealed.</note> in a physical furnace, and it must be melted over a slow fire. In that state of fusion, it must be held at a uniform fire for a space of eighteen days. In the first six days, the medicine <note>The alchemical substance being transformed.</note> will be saffron-yellow; in the next six days, it will be red; and in the [following] six, it will be black; and afterwards, it will be a red of the most intense redness. You shall maintain this for thirty days, during which you must nourish the said stone day and night with two lights <note>Likely referring to specific lamps or degrees of heat.</note> that are not very thick <note>original: "grossis"; likely meaning not too intense or smoky.</note> for the duration of the said thirty days. When these are finished, a saffron color will appear, which will cover all the red like a cloud. And that saffron color will cease within the space of eight days; afterwards, a perfect and clear whiteness will appear, like the star of Diana <note>A poetic term for the planet Venus or the Moon, signifying the "White Work" or *albedo*.</note>; and the medicine will be perfected for [making] Silver <note>original: "Lunam" (the Moon), the alchemical symbol for silver.</note> upon Mercury...

# THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
<note>original: "Turba Philosophorum"; a famous early Latin alchemical text, likely translated from Arabic, presented as a debate among ancient Greek philosophers.</note>

### REGARDING THE SECOND PHILOSOPHY, FAR DIFFERENT AND MORE COPIOUS

THE BEGINNING OF THE BOOK OF THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS, in which Arisleus <note>A legendary figure in alchemical literature, often identified as the narrator or compiler of these debates.</note> gathered the sayings of the wiser disciples, introducing Pythagoras the philosopher and master, and collecting the opinions from the disciples. This book is also called the Third Pythagorean Synod, inscribed "Concerning Hidden Wisdom." Pythagoras, moreover, commands the disciple Eximidius to begin the conversation and to discourse upon hidden wisdom, and then for the others to also deliver their opinions in order. And so, beginning:

EXIMIDIVS says: The beginning of all things is a certain nature, and that nature is perpetual, infinite, nourishing and ripening <term>coquentemque: "cooking" or "ripening," a central alchemical concept where heat matures matter toward perfection</term> all things. Moreover, the times of corruption and generation are like the boundaries of nature, by which that which universal nature nourishes and ripens is reached. Truly, since the stars and the heavenly bodies are fiery, they are by nature the source of ripening and nourishment. However, so that they might endure and perform their duty rightly, God established the air between them and the earth—and the things to be nourished and <unclear>ripened</unclear>—which would contain and restrain the stars, lest (especially the flame of the Sun, for I remain silent regarding the others, he says) it should burn up all existing things. # THE ASSEMBLY

<note>original: "TURBA" — referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>

...if the air did not breathe into them, the Sun would destroy all existing things with its heat. But water, too, would destroy everything with its coldness and moisture, were it not for the mediation of the air. Therefore, since the air is warm and moist <note>The Latin text says "calidus & siccus" (hot and dry), but the context of Aristotelian elements usually defines air as hot and moist; the author here argues for its role as a bridge.</note>, it so harmonizes the heat of the celestial fire and the stars with the watery coldness, so that a lasting friendship remains between them, and from this proceeds the nourishment and the benefit of the "decoction" <term>decoction: a process of heating or "cooking" substances to extract their essence</term> of all existing things.

**THE ASSEMBLY** said: You have described fire well; continue then.

He said: I magnify and honor the Air, because by it the Work is improved, as it thickens and thins, and as it grows hot and cold. Its thickness occurs when things are distinguished in the heavens due to the rising of the Sun. Its thinness occurs when the air is thinned and heated by the other Sun. When it thins, the Sun becomes near; and when it is near, heat reaches man and the creatures.

**ANAXAGORAS** <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher here cast as an alchemical authority.</note> said: You have described the air well. But know, O Assembly, that the thickness of the four interior things rests in the earth alone, because the thickness of fire falls into the air, and the thickness of the air—along with what is gathered from the thickness of fire—falls into the water. The thickness of the water also, and what is joined from the thickness of fire and air, rests in the earth. Thus the thickness of these four rests in the earth, and in it they are joined. Therefore, the earth itself is thicker than all the other elements, as is openly apparent and can be seen. Fire, however, is thinner than the others, and just as the earth, which is thicker, is lower, so fire is higher and more worthy. Air is less thin than fire, and water again is less thin than air. For everything cold and moist is of less thinness than that which is hot and moist. And the earth is of less thinness than water, because it is cold and dry; and everything cold and dry is less thin than that which is cold and moist.

**PYTHAGORAS** said: You have well fitted together, O sons of the doctrine, the descriptions of these natures from which God created all things. Therefore, continue.

To this **LUCAS** said: I notify you that from these four natures, God created all things, and all created things return into them; in these they are generated and they die in their own time, just as God has ordained.

### PHILOSOPHY

**Locastes** <note>original: "Locastes"; likely a corruption of a Greek name in the Latin tradition of the Turba</note> says: Know that the creation of the World was formed from two dense things and two rare things, and nothing of the dense things exists within the sublime <note>meaning the heavenly or celestial</note> creation. Therefore, it is rarer <note>less dense</note> than the Sun and all lower creatures.

**Pythagoras** says: I say that God existed before all things; and when He was alone, He created four simple things in number, which are the four elements, of the same essence—that is, of the same matter—yet of different forms, which are the simple qualities that are converted into one another. From these already created things, He thereafter created all things, both of the sublime and the lower realms, because it was necessary for creatures to be extracted from a certain root, from which they might be multiplied to inhabit the world. Therefore, before all things, God created the four elements, from which He afterwards created what He willed: namely, diverse natures, some of which He created from one element alone.

The **Assembly** <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the gathered group of philosophers</note> asks: What are those things, Master, which the sublime God created from only one?

And he replied: They are the Angels, whom God created from fire.

And the **Assembly** asked: Which things are created from two?

And he replied: Created from two are the Sun, Moon, and Stars; namely, from air and fire. Therefore, the Angels are brighter than the Sun, Moon, and stars, because they were created from one singular thing, which is the fourth and rarest of all; but the Sun, Moon, and stars were created from a composite of fire and air.

The **Assembly** said: And from what comes the creation of the heavens?

And he replied: God created the heaven from water and air; thus the heaven is also composed of two: namely, from one of the rarer things, air, and one of the dense things, water.

And they said: Master, complete your sayings and discourse upon the three.

And he replied: From three elements God created the winged creatures, the brute animals, and the vegetables; namely, from air, water, and earth.

The **Assembly** then said: Distinguish these, Master.

And he replied: Some were created from air and earth; others indeed from fire, air, and earth. Of the latter, the examples are the winged creatures and all things having a spirit; of the former, the examples are the vegetables. All brute animals are from earth, air, and fire; but vegetables are from water, earth, and air, and have nothing in common with fire.

> And they asked: Shall we say then that fire is also present in plants? <note>original: "vegetabilibus"</note>

> And he replied: You speak the truth: for from the heat of the air hidden within them—just as I have indicated that a subtle fire exists within the air—fire is present in them, because fire is in the air, and air is in the plants. However, speaking of elemental fire by itself, it is not present except in those things possessing spirit and soul. Furthermore, man was created from the four elements. Understand therefore, all of you, that everything which God created from a single essence does not perish or die, except on the Day of Judgment. For the definition of death is the dissolution of a composite thing; but for that which is not composite, there is no separation. However, in things composed of two, three, or four parts, it is necessary for each composite to be separated, and this separation is death. And know that whatever was created from simple and most subtle fire alone neither drinks, nor eats, nor sleeps; but that which was created from dense fire is otherwise.

**ARISLEUS** said: Master, because you have gathered us together for the benefit of posterity, nothing more useful than the knowledge of the elements could have come to our attention. But now we desire that words be spoken concerning the hidden wisdom <note>The "occulta sapientia" or alchemy</note>, for the investigation of which we have been called together.

> And he said: I have said before that God brought forth all things—that is, the four elements—from nothing, and then from these he brought forth all created things: the heavens, the thrones, the angels, the stars, the sea, and all things that are in them. And because we see those four elements are almost enemies to one another, the creatures are therefore diverse. For if all things had been created from the same element, they would be of one nature and would agree. Nevertheless, God has so united and coupled those four that they are obliged to observe a perpetual peace: thus the dry is often mixed with the moist, and the hot with the cold, and they come together fittingly, and from there creatures emerge, which are indeed most precious. Of those elements which come together, two are seen and touched; but two are neither seen nor touched. Because if only those which are seen and touched are joined, without a doubt the remaining ones are also mixed in, which are present within the first two: for Air, participating in Fire, also has something in common with Water; similarly also the Ear- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "terra" (Earth) to match the catchword for the next page.</note>

It was said above that this [the stone] embraces all these things within itself. If you mix our copper—which is earth—with water, you will achieve a great thing. For when our copper itself is placed with sea water and cooked, it reveals earth, drinking in the water and embracing the other two elements <note>The "other two" being air and fire, completing the four elements required for the Great Work</note> within itself. This is signified by the process of the work, namely the grinding and the coagulation of the stone, from which "coins" <note>original: "nummos"; here referring to the circular, metallic results of the transformation</note> are immediately made. But I shall hear what each of you will reconsider and say on this matter. In the meantime, begin your exposition so that it remains unrecognized by the foolish, yet not unknown to the sons of doctrine <note>A common alchemical term for initiated students of the art</note>. And you, Aristenes, speak first.

**ARISTENES** says: The key to this work is the art of the coins. Therefore, take the body that has been shown to you and fit it into thin plates. Then place them in the water of our sea, which, while it is being governed, is called "Permanent Water" <note>original: "Aqua permanens"; a specialized solvent in alchemy that does not wet the hands</note>. Afterward, place it over a light fire until the plates are broken apart and become water. Join this to the *Ethelia* <note>A term likely derived from the Greek 'aithale', referring to a vapor, spirit, or sublimated substance</note> and roast them together over a slow fire until it becomes a thick broth. Turn this into its own *Ethelia* until it coagulates and becomes a variegated coin, which we call the "Flower of the Sun" <note>original: "Solis florem"; often signifying a gold-like state or the red stage of the work</note>. Cook it thereafter until it is deprived of blackness and whiteness appears. Afterward, govern it and mix in the soul of gold, and cook it until it becomes a red *Ethelia*. Grind this with patience; do not let it weary you to moisten it with the water that came out of it—which is permanent—until it becomes red. For this is the "burnt copper," the "flower of gold," and the "leaven" <note>original: "fermentum"; the substance that triggers the transformation of base metals</note>. Direct this with the permanent water, then dry it until it becomes a powder and is deprived of all moisture.

**PARMENIDES** says: Know, wise men, that the envious <note>The "envious" are authors who intentionally obscured their recipes to hide secrets from the unworthy</note> have treated waters, broths, bodies, and metals in manifold ways to deceive you who seek knowledge. Therefore, dismiss all these things and cause gold and coins to be made from this, our copper. Take copper, or lead for its fatness or blackness, and tin for its liquefaction. Know that unless you fit the natures of truth and its compositions well together, and join kin to kin, you will accomplish nothing, because natures meet with their own natures, contain them, and rejoice in them. For they rot and are born because the nature which governs it also destroys it and turns it into powder...

**DARDANUS** said: It is now known to everyone through the Master Philosophers concerning the permanent water. Therefore, the student of this art should begin nothing unless the power of this water is understood. **BELUS** said: The Philosophers have called it permanent water and have mentioned it frequently; likewise, they have described making the white and the red in many ways and by various names. Yet, while the truth is manifest, they agree in hidden words regarding the ways in which the weights, compositions, and governance ought to be joined; all of this was done so that the foolish would not recognize the stone itself. For among the Philosophers, this is a high principle: that the stone is not a stone; to the ignorant and foolish, it is a useful but incredible thing. For who would believe that a stone could become water, or water a stone, when nothing is more different? Yet in truth, it is so. For the stone is this very permanent water, and while it is water, it is not a stone. In this way, this water has been assigned diverse names. **ZEUMON** says: The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. That which we seek is sold publicly for a very small price, and if it were known, the merchants would not sell even a tiny bit of it. # PHILOSOPHY
<note>Header: PHILOSOPH.</note>

...an impalpable spirit, you labor in vain. And for this reason the Sages <note>original: "Sapientes," referring to the ancient masters of alchemy</note> have said: unless you turn bodies into non-bodies, and make incorporeal things corporeal, you have not yet found the beginning of this work. Now, they become incorporeal when the *Ethelia* <term>Ethelia: a technical term for the volatile spirit or the "hidden" essence of the matter</term> is ground until it becomes dust; and this dust is not made except by the strongest decoction <note>boiling or heating in liquid</note> and continuous grinding, and it is done by fire, not by hands, with imbibition <note>soaking</note>, putrefaction <note>the stage of breaking down or "rotting" the matter to its base state</note>, and *Ethelia*. 

And when the Sages said regarding this art that nature is useful and is sold for a small price, they caused the common people to err in this. They also said that their nature is more precious than all other natures, and by this saying they also deceived many; and yet, they spoke the truth. For the Art requires two natures, because the precious is not made without the vile, nor the vile without the precious. 

Wherefore it behooves you to follow the sayings of the elders, who said: Nothing else is useful to you except to sublime <note>to purify by turning into vapor and then solidifying again</note> the water and the vapor. For when you see those two purified natures become water, and the whole body of *Magnesia* <term>Magnesia: here referring not to the modern chemical, but to the "primitive matter" or the "whole" of the alchemical substance</term> liquefied into water, then certainly all things are vapor. By right, then, the vapor contains its partner—that is, water contains water. 

For this reason, the Philosophers named both "vapor," because they are united together in putrefaction and decoction, and one contains the other so that it does not flee. Therefore, they become permanent. For the hidden nature is congealed in the body, and its color is changed; it strips off its own nature and is enslaved so that it does not flee. 

If blackness appears, it is from sickness, and it dies in putrefaction and becomes redness <note>original: "rubigo," literally rust or redness, marking a successful transition in the work</note>; and then by the law of nature it does not flee, because it has dismissed the servitude of flight and nature has been made free, following its spouse, adorning him with its color and beauty—not as it had done before, but having taken up the "golden coin," it brings him to life. And this nature the Philosophers have called "spirit" and "soul." 

Furthermore, they said that the moist spirit is black, yet lacking in defilement. And just as in man there is moisture and dryness, so in our work there is nothing else but vapor and water. Therefore the ancients said the work is made of two things, and some have called these two joined together a "composite," because those two are actually four: for there is dryness and moisture, spirit and vapor.

If, at the beginning of the cooking process, you have not reached the point where everything becomes water without the grinding of hands, you have not yet found the work. And know that sometimes they call the <term>bronze</term><note>Latin: *aes*; in alchemy, this refers to the base material or "body" being transformed, not necessarily literal bronze.</note> "sand," and at other times "stone," for the names vary throughout the entire governance of the process. Nevertheless, the nature and the moisture become water, and then a stone if they are well mixed: because that which is light and spiritual is sublimated <note>raised up by heat</note> upwards; but that which is heavy and thick remains at the bottom of the vessel. This, however, is the "grinding of the Philosophers," which is achieved by decoction <note>boiling or heating</note> and not by hand. And know that unless you turn everything into powder, you have not yet ground it. Therefore, cook it until it is worn down and becomes dust.

**AGADMON** said: Cook the bronze until it becomes a light and impalpable body, and place it in its vessel: then sublimate it five or seven times, until the water descends, knowing that when the water is dust, it has been diligently ground. If you doubt how water becomes dust, know that the intention of the Philosophers is that the body—which was not water before it fell—should be mixed together with the water, and the water with the water, until they become one. Furthermore, it must be known that unless you turn both into water, you will not arrive at the precious work. For it is necessary that the body, seized by the flame of fire, be broken down and become weak with the water in which it is, until it becomes entirely water. The ignorant, however, when they hear the name "water," think it is the water of the clouds; but if they read our books, they would surely know it to be the <term>permanent water</term><note>Latin: *aqua permanens*; a central alchemical concept referring to a transformative solvent that does not evaporate.</note>, which cannot be permanent without its partner with whom it has been made one. This, moreover, is the water which the Philosophers have called the "water of gold," the "fiery poison," the "good of many names," and the "sand" which **Hermes** <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> ordered to be washed many times so that the <term>blackness of the Sun</term><note>Latin: *Solis nigredo*; the "nigredo" or black stage of the work, representing the death/putrefaction of the matter before rebirth.</note> might be deleted, which it had taken on during the dissolution of the body. And know that unless you take this body of mine which lacks a spirit, you will by no means achieve what you desire, because nothing foreign enters the work, nor anything except that which is sincere <note>pure</note>. Therefore, dismiss all plurality: for nature is content with one thing, and he who is ignorant of it will perish.

**AFFLICTES** said: Sons of the Doctrine, know that the whole work and governance is not done except by water, with which you must mix the body of <term>Magnesia</term><note>In this context, Magnesia is not the modern chemical, but a cryptic term for the "mother" or primal matter of the stone.</note>, and place it in its vessel, and [seal] the mouth diligently...

CRANSES <note>Likely a corruption of a name like Crates or another legendary alchemical authority.</note> says: Wise men, take our bronze and, with the first part of the water, place it in its vessel and cook it for forty days, and cleanse it from all impurity, and cook it until the days are completed and it becomes a stone without moisture. The Philosophers called this compound, when turned into blackness, **SUFFICIENTLY BLACK**, and they said: Rule it with vinegar and nitre. But that which remains, if it is whitened, they called **SUFFICIENTLY WHITE**, and they ordered that it be ruled by permanent water; that which they called **SUFFICIENTLY RED**, they ordered to be ruled by water and fire until it becomes red. They called it by this name for that reason, because of the variety of colors. For in the work there is no variety of things, nor multitude, nor contrariety, but it is only necessary to make the black bronze white, and then red. The true Philosophers had no other intention, nor did they teach anything else—

**EFISTES** says: Pay attention, sons of the doctrine, to how **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, the head of the Philosophers, spoke when he taught how to mix the natures. # PHILOSOPHY

<margin>Signature: b 4</margin>

They seem to bring harm to those who read our writings only once, twice, or thrice; for, frustrated in their understanding and all their zeal, they also (which is worst of all) lose their wealth, labor, and the time they have spent on this art. However, he who bends his back to read our books and devotes himself studiously to them—applying and sharpening both memory and mind, not entangled in vain thoughts, and praying to God for the granting of wisdom (as Solomon did) rather than for riches—he shall reign as a king in our kingdom without ceasing until he dies. Therefore, fear God, O seekers! For that which you seek is by no means of small price. You seek the greatest treasure and the most excellent gift of God.

And know, O seekers, that which the Philosophers long ago intimated when they said that the right path is only discerned through error, and nothing generates more grief in the heart than an error in this art and work. For while one thinks he has succeeded and possesses the world, he finds nothing in his hands. However, although the Philosophers have composed the work and the matter itself under various names, the truth is always in their writings. For they said: mix, cook, whiten, grind, roast, coagulate, and dissolve the <term>Ethelia</term> <note>original: "Etheliam"; likely referring to the volatile spirit or "vapor" of the substance</note>, and produce the redness. The words are many, yet the <term>regimen</term> <note>The systematic method or "rule" of the chemical process</note> is one.

If, therefore, you wish to find the truth, there is no need for that division of labor; instead, take care only of this: adjust the temperament <note>The "complexion" or balance of qualities</note>, then cook gently for a long time. Do not let the boiling and the soaking weary you, until you see the <term>Yxir</term> <note>The Elixir</note> adorned in Tyrian and royal clothing <note>A metaphor for the deep purple or red color signifying the completion of the work</note>. Although these words are dead, life is within them for those who understand. Therefore, read them frequently and meditate upon them always; may wisdom come to you.

It is necessary, therefore, for you to mix that thick substance with fiery poison, and to putrefy and diligently grind it until the spirit is formed within the other hidden spirit, and then the tincture is made, which tints everything you desire.

**PLATO** says: O you masters of the work, take care when you dissolve the bodies that you do not also burn them; for it is necessary to wash them by cooking in sea-water until all their salt is turned into sweetness, and it becomes clear and attains its goal. Therefore, once the spirit has been separated from the body and hidden within another spirit, both are made fleeting <note>original: "fugiens"; referring to volatile substances that evaporate or escape when heated</note>. The Sages have expressed this in these words: "Fly, and open the door to that which does not fly." For by converting the sulfurous nature into a spirit similar to itself, both become fleeting. However, those that do not fly are created in a similar way: because through the mediation of fire, they embrace and contain one another. Therefore, take those things which do not fly and join them; wash the body with the bodiless, and with that which lacks a body, make the body solid, until you turn it into a body among non-fleeing bodies. Turn earth into water, water into fire, and fire into air. Hide the fire in the depths of the water, and the earth in the belly of the air; mix the hot with the moist, and the dry with the cold. For Nature overcomes nature; then Nature rejoices in nature; and finally, Nature contains nature <note>This is a famous alchemical axiom: "Natura naturam vincit, natura naturam laetatur, natura naturam continet."</note>. But the container of all things is the earth. For when the four natures <note>The four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> have ascended into heaven, they finally descend again, so that fire falls into air, air into water, and water into earth. Thus, the end of the entire work is dust and ashes.

**ACTOMANUS** said: The Philosophers have very frequently discussed "rust" <note>original: "rubigo"; often used as a code for the red stage of the alchemical process or a specific oxidation</note>. However, "rust" is a made-up name, not a true one. I tell you that rust belongs to the "second work," which is made from gold alone; for this reason, they have called it the Leech <note>original: "Irudinem"</note>, because it is strained in the golden sulfurous liquid just as a leech is in water. Therefore, rust is the reddening in the second work; for in the first work, to "make rust" is actually to whiten the work, in which the Philosophers commanded that the flower of gold and gold itself be placed in equal measure.

**MUNDUS** said: Enough has been discussed regarding rust; I shall therefore speak of the "poison" <note>original: "venenum"; in alchemy, this refers to a potent, transformative substance or the "tincture" that penetrates metals</note>. The poison is not a body, because subtle spirits have made it thin like a spirit, and they have tinged the body and turned it into poison. The Philosophers assert that this poison colors every body; for this reason, they believe that whoever turns gold into poison has already reached the goal; but whoever has not, has accomplished nothing. I say that unless you thin the substances with fire until those things ascend like spirits, you have perfected nothing yet. This, then, is the spirit that flees the fire, and the heavy smoke which, when it enters the body, penetrates the whole, and its nature rejoices in it. And for this reason, it is said:

Take the living black spirit <note>original: *spiritum nigrum viventem*; likely referring to the "prima materia" or the initial dark stage of the alchemical process</note>, and with it enrich and torment the bodies until they are altered according to your pleasure.

**PYTHAGORAS** says: You must understand, O Assembly, that sulphur, and lime <note>original: *calx*</note>, and alum—which comes from gums and Kohl <note>original: *Kuhul*; an ancient eye cosmetic, here used as a technical term for a finely powdered mineral</note>—and the "spittle of the Moon" <note>original: *sputum Lunae*; a poetic term for silver or white mercury</note>, and combustible spittle: all of those things are, in fact, nothing other than the water of sulphur and the burning water. And know that if Magnesia <note>a term for a mineral substance, often associated with lead or antimony in this context</note> is mixed with quicksilver <note>original: *argento vivo*; mercury</note>, the sulphurs are joined together, and the sulphurs follow one another. Therefore, you must not leave that Magnesia without quicksilver; for when they are composed, it is a most powerful composition, which is one of the ten that the Philosophers have established as the Queen. And to congeal it is not merely one single method of governance according to the constitution of the Philosophers. For the first coagulation is of tin, and copper <note>original: *aeris*</note>, and lead; but the second is composed of the water of sulphurs. And it must be known that the science of this art is nothing other than vapor and the sublimation of water, and the joining of quicksilver and Magnesia to the body. Similarly, the Philosophers have demonstrated in their books that the clean water of sulphur from the Sun is sulphur, and that no sulphur is made without the lime of quicksilver and the water of sulphur.

**BELUS** says: Many things have been discussed concerning composition; however, composition and contraction are one and the same thing. Therefore, take a part from the second composition, and a part from the ferment of gold, and place upon them the clean water of sulphur; <margin><</margin> you will have a powerful secret <note>original: *arcanum*</note> which tints every body. But meanwhile it must be noted that the clean water which <margin>x</margin> comes from sulphur is not from sulphur alone, but is composed of several things, which have been made into one sulphur from many sulphurs. Therefore, so that many sulphurs may become one sulphur, mix that which fights with fire with that which does not fight. For when joined in a fire suitable to them, they battle, and a constant friendship is made, because the hot poisons of the Physicians are cooked by a gentle, non-burning fire. And the Philosophers discovered this when they said that in the decoction of these things, the sulphur burns many hard bodies. And the liquid that is left behind is named moist pitch, balsam, etc. Truly, this is the secret that I shall open to you.

**MORFOLEUS** said: It is necessary, wise men, that the moisture first be burned away by a slow fire, as is shown to us by the example of the generation of a chick; and when the fire is increased, let the vessel be hardened on all sides, lest the body of the bronze and its fleeing spirit be drawn out. And the Wise hinted at this when they said: Take the quicksilver from the flower of bronze, which flower of bronze our people have called Water, and the fiery poison has been extracted by men. I also tell you that the **Dragon** <note>The "Dragon" often represents crude matter, mercury, or a volatile substance that must be "tamed" or "killed" to be transformed</note> never dies; nevertheless, the Philosophers have put to death that woman who kills her own husbands; for that woman's belly is full of poison. Therefore, let a grave be dug for the Dragon, and let the woman be buried there with him. He, being strongly joined to that woman—the more he binds her and winds himself around her—the more his body, mixed into the woman's limbs, declines toward death and is entirely turned into blood. When the Philosophers see him turned into blood, they place him in the Sun until the softness is consumed and the blood dries up. And then the poison appears, and the hidden is made manifest.

**Moschus** said: Know that the envious <note>A common alchemical term for authors who deliberately obscured their writings to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note> have described the method of forming lead in many ways so that they might deceive posterity by inventing various instruments. EMIGANUS <note>A speaker in the Turba, likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic name</note> said: The books of the Philosophers must be read; for they did not speak in vain when they said: "Look upon the suckling child and do not hinder him, for in him remains the secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> from which the Wise perform good works." It is necessary, therefore, to destroy the body and for the soul to be separated from it. Hence the Philosophers said: "Body does not penetrate body," but the subtle part of nature—which is the soul itself—is what penetrates and stains the body. Furthermore, they said that while the splendor of Saturn <note>alchemical symbol for Lead</note> ascends into the air, it appears only dark, and Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> meets the rays of the Sun <note>Gold</note>; then the quicksilver, by fiery virtue, vivifies and perfects the body.

->PHILOSOPHY<-

**ATTAMANUS** says: Know, brothers, that our work which you seek is born from the sea, which completes all things after God. Take *Alzum* <note>original: "Alzum"; likely a term for a specific mineral salt or starter material</note> and old sea stones, and roast them over coals until they become white, and extinguish them with white vinegar. If there are twenty-four ounces of *Alzon* <note>a variation of Alzum</note>, extinguish their heat with a third part of its weight—that is, eight ounces—and grind it with white vinegar for forty days. But the second work is made from a cleansed and washed body. Do not add vinegar to this second work, but let it be cooked until it has drunk all its vinegar and becomes fixed earth, like Egyptian earth <note>likely referring to fertile, dark silt or a specific mineral precipitate</note>. And know that some works coagulate faster, and others more slowly. This happens because of the diversity of the cooking: for if the place where it is cooked is humid and dewy, it congeals faster; if it is drier, it congeals more slowly. Therefore, a middle ground must be sought.

**FLORUS** says: I shall complete the arrangement of the cooking, and I say that the sign of the first decoction <note>the process of boiling or heating</note> is the extraction of its redness. However, when you see it already entirely black, know that within the belly of that blackness, whiteness is hidden, and then you must extract that whiteness from the blackness itself with the greatest subtlety. In the second decoction, let that whiteness be placed in a vessel with its instruments, and let it be cooked gently until everything becomes white. And when you see that whiteness appearing in the vessel, be certain that redness is hidden within that whiteness: and then you must not draw it out or end the cooking, but cook it until the whole becomes a very deep red. And know that the first blackness was from the nature of *Mortach* <note>likely litharge or lead oxide</note>, and from that blackness arose the redness, which redness corrected the black, and established peace between the fleeing <note>volatile</note> and the non-fleeing <note>fixed</note> substances. The crucified thing <note>a term for a substance undergoing chemical "torture" or transformation</note> is submerged in the body and turns it into an alterable nature. And know that the sulfur which blackens the body cannot be dyed or manipulated, but it is what manipulates and dyes. Likewise, know that the sulfur which blackens is that which opens the door to the non-fleeing, and turns the fleeing into the non-fleeing; which we also call elsewhere **Sulfur Water**, turning copper into unalterable and indelible colors.

**MANDINUS** says: Unless this secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> contains that which may cleanse it, it is of no use at all. For this reason the ancients said: That which is perfected is a single thing; because diverse natures do not cleanse the thing itself, but only one nature, and one that is suitable, which you must guide with restraint. For ignorance of how to guide the process has caused many to wander into error. Therefore, do not concern yourselves with the plurality of these compositions, nor the various things which the Masters have placed in their books. For the nature of truth is one, by which the natural thing is changed, because the secret of that transforming nature is hidden in its own belly; it is neither seen, known, nor felt except by the Wise. He, therefore, who guides the copper <note>original: "aes," often referring to the base metal or the "body" of the work</note> with restraint, and knows its temperament, extracts from it a nature that overcomes all other natures. Then the words of the masters shall be fulfilled, namely: that Nature rejoices in nature, and Nature overcomes nature, and Nature contains nature; and yet these are not diverse natures, nor many; but truly only one, differing in form, having its own properties within itself, with various accidental qualities by which it works that which is suited to its nature. Therefore the Master did well to begin with one and end with one. Then he called those unities "sulfurous water," which conquers the whole of nature.

**ARCHELAUS** says: Very beautifully described is the pure water of sulfur; for unless the thick bodies are demolished by a nature lacking a body, until they become bodiless bodies and like a thin spirit, you cannot extract that most thin tinting soul <note>original: "animam tenuissimam actingentem"</note> which is hidden in the innermost part of the belly. And know this: unless the body is demolished until it dies, and you draw out from it its soul—which is the tinting spirit—you can by no means tint a body with it.

**PHILOTIS** says: In all the things mentioned by any of the Masters, we signify nothing else to you than the *Albaræris* <note>A technical term likely derived from Arabic, referring to the "White Lead" or a specific stage of the alchemical mercury</note>, because it tints every body that has entered into the composition. # THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS
<note>original: "Turbae Philosophorum"</note>

## *Another Version.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring floral or vine motifs.</image-desc>THESE are the Sayings of the Wise, collected in the third Pythagorean Synod: In which it is said that the Philosopher Arisleus gathered together the disciples of Hermes and the elders of the Wise, and ordered each one to bring something forward into the midst concerning the vegetable stone <note>The "vegetable stone" refers to a stage or type of the Philosopher's Stone associated with growth and life, rather than just minerals.</note>, so that the sacred art might become known to posterity: and those who had applied their minds to grasping this might be led to the path of truth. Moreover, Eximindus, an old man of excellent counsel, was ordered to be the first to speak.

### PROPOSITION I.

**EXIMINDVS.** I make known to you, sons of doctrine, that the beginning of all created things is a certain nature—primary, perpetual, and infinite—cooking and ruling all things, whose actions and passions are known and recognized only by those to whom the knowledge of the sacred art has been given. Furthermore, I say that the stars are fiery, and the air tempers them. For if the thickness and humidity of the air did not exist to temper the flame of the Sun, the Sun would burn up all existing things. But God established the aerial things separately, lest that which He created on the earth be consumed. Do you not see, O sons of knowledge, the Sun ascending in the sky into the air, conquering and heating it with its fire? Once heated, the warmth reaches existing things, thickening and condensing the spirits from which creatures are generated. For the air is compressed and contained by the water, and thus the air is overcome, because its heat is joined to the heat of the Sun, and its humidity is joined to the humidity of the water. Do you not see thin water ascending into the air by the eminent heat of the Sun, and the Sun being delighted and aided by it? For if the water did not aid the air with its thin moisture, without a doubt the fire would overcome it. But the fire draws out moisture from the water, by which the air is tempered, and then it overcomes the fire itself. Therefore, fire and water are enemies, between whom there is no kinship: because fire is hot and dry, and water is cold and moist. Air, also, since it is hot and moist, [provides] harmony—

<meta>catchword: ha- (harmony/habet)</meta>

<summary>This page introduces a secondary version of the "Assembly of the Philosophers," featuring a speech by Eximindus on the cosmological balance of the four elements. He explains how air and water prevent the Sun's fire from destroying earthly life, establishing the fundamental alchemical principle of elemental temperament.</summary>

->T U R B A<-

<note>The title refers to the "Turba Philosophorum," or Assembly of the Philosophers, a famous early alchemical text where various sages debate the origins of matter.</note>

but with the humidity of water and the heat of fire, and because of this, a generative friendship is formed. Look upon all fruits, which are created from a thin aerial vapor, because life is revealed from the air by the heat of the Sun: and this is by God’s ordinance.

### S E N T E N C E II.

**YSINDRUS.** <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek name, possibly Anaximander or Hesiod.</note> I magnify the air, because the work itself is improved by air. When it is thickened, it becomes rare; when it is heated, it grows cold. Its thickness occurs when it is separated in the heavens due to the distance of the Sun. Its rarity, however, occurs when the Sun is exalted and the air melts and becomes clear. Similarly, it happens in the complexion of Spring, in the distinction of a season that is neither hot nor cold. For according to the alteration of the established disposition, to change the divisions of the year, winter is altered; therefore the air is thickened then, when the Sun is distant from it. But when the air becomes rare, the Sun is near, and by its proximity, heat reaches mankind.

### S E N T E N C E III.

**ANAXAGORAS.** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who proposed that "mind" (Nous) was the organizing force of the universe.</note> I say that the principle of all things which God created is piety and reason: because in creation piety appeared, and the thickness of the earth was hoped for by reason: but piety is not seen except in a body. Therefore know, assembly of Sages, that the thickness <term>spissitudo</term> <note>original: "spissitudo"; refers to density or the "gross" material state as opposed to the "subtle" or rare state.</note> of all four elements rests in the earth: for the thickness of fire falls into the air; the thickness of air, and that which is gathered from the thickness of fire, falls into the water. The thickness of water, and that which is united from the thickness of fire and air, rests in the earth. Do you not see that the thickness of these four is joined in the earth? Therefore the earth itself is thicker than all. To this the Assembly replied: You have spoken the truth, the earth is certainly thicker than all. But which of these is rarer and more worthy? He answered: Fire is the rarest among these four, and to it reaches the rarity of these four. Air is less rare than fire. For it is hot and moist, while fire is hot and dry. For that which is hot and dry is rarer than that which is hot and moist. For the sages say that fire is of less rarity than air <note>The text here seems to invert the previous logic, a common occurrence in alchemical manuscripts regarding the hierarchy of elements.</note>, and earth is of less rarity than water, because it is cold and dry. And just as the dry-hot is rarer than the moist-hot, so the dry-cold is of less rarity than the cold-moist.

# PHILOSOPHY

### PROPOSITION IV.

**PYTHAGORAS.** You have well-fitted, O sons of doctrine <note>A traditional address to students of alchemy and esoteric wisdom</note>, the descriptions of these four natures from which God created all things. Blessed, therefore, is he who understands what has been described, for no greater things shall be proposed. Nevertheless, complete your discourse. To these things he said:

### PROPOSITION V.

**PANDOPHIS.** I signify to posterity that what is the thinness of water, and that which is not separated from it, remains above the dry earth; this is the air hidden in the water which is beneath the earth, which carries the earth lest it be submerged in the water that is beneath the earth, and prevents the earth from being soaked by the water. A complex of air was made, separating water and earth between diverse things, and between adverse things, water and fire, lest they destroy one another. I shall propose an example of this matter: The Egg, in which four things are joined: its visible shell is earth, and the white is water; the very thin skin joined to the shell is that which separates the earth from the water—as I said, that air separates earth from water—the red part of the egg <note>The yolk</note> is fire, and the skin containing the red is air, separating the water from the fire; and yet both skins are one and the same. However, the air separating the cold earth and water from one another is thicker than the higher air. And the higher air is subtler and thinner in nature than the lower air because it is closer to the fire. In the egg, therefore, are four: earth, water, air, and fire, and the point of the Sun is in the middle, namely the red part, which is the chick. And for that reason, all Philosophers in this most excellent art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note> have described the egg and have set it as the example for their work.

### PROPOSITION VI.

**ARISLEUS.** Know that the earth is a mound <note>original: "collis," implying a curved or spherical shape</note> and is not flat, which is why the Sun does not rise over the regions of the earth at one single hour. For if it were flat, it would certainly rise over the whole earth in a single moment. Furthermore, I say that God is one, and He begat one, yet He was not begotten; and that the head of all things after Him is earth and fire. And because fire is thin and light, it rules all things; but earth, since it is thick and heavy, carries all things which the fire rules.

<summary>The philosophers Pythagoras, Pandophis, and Arisleus discuss the balance of the four elements, using the famous "Philosophical Egg" as a microcosm of the universe and arguing for the earth's curvature based on the movement of the sun.</summary>

# P R O N O U N C E M E N T  VII.

**LUCAS.** You speak of nothing but the four natures <note>original: "quatuor naturis," referring to the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth</note>, and each of you has said something regarding them. I, however, notify you that all things which God created are from these four natures, and those things which are created from them return back into them. From this, generations and corruptions <note>The natural cycle of birth/growth and decay/death</note> occur, just as God has ordained. And this has been, until now, the most perfect opinion of the Indian and Babylonian Philosophers.

# P R O N O U N C E M E N T  VIII.

**LOCUSTOR.** There are only two natures which Lucas describes: one of which is not known nor described except by piety and reason; the other is neither seen nor felt, and it is the heaven. A third nature is indeed joined to these, which is felt, seen, and known, and this is that which contains whatever exists beneath the heaven down to the earth. And yet, reason perceives these things aided by the five senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. Reason discerns white from black by sight; a good word from an evil one by hearing; sweet from bitter by taste; a pleasant scent from an unpleasant one by smell; and the smooth from the rough by touch. As for that nature which is perceived by none of these senses, it is the sublime nature, which is perceived only by reason and piety; and it is the sublime God, who made the light—namely the Sun—which is more subtle than all other creatures, so that it might provide light to the World. This world consists of two dense things <note>earth and water</note> and two rare things <note>air and fire</note>. And there is nothing of the dense things in the sublime creation, because He is Himself more subtle and rare than the Sun and all inferior creatures.

# P R O N O U N C E M E N T  IX.

**PYTHAGORAS.** I say that God existed before all things, and nothing was with Him before He was; and I say this so that I may strengthen your opinion concerning the elements, the secrets, and the sacred science <note>term: "scientia sacra" refers here to Alchemy, viewed as a divinely revealed art</note>, to which reason does not attain except by the will of God. Understand that when God was alone, He created four things: fire, air, water, and earth. From their lineage He granted both superior and inferior things to exist; and according to His predestination, He made all creatures from these as if from a root, so that the Sublime One might be praised by all such creatures, and that man might [attain] reason and ju—

-> PHILOSOPHY <-

...he exercised judgment. Therefore, before all things, he ordained the four elements from which he formed all things, namely, the diverse creatures. From one element, specifically fire, he made the Angels; from fire and air, he made the Sun, Moon, and stars. Because of this, the Angels are more luminous than the Sun, Moon, and stars, because they were created from a single, singular element—which is the fourth <note>The "fourth" element here refers to fire in the traditional ascending order of Earth, Water, Air, Fire</note>—and are of a rarer <note>In alchemy and medieval physics, "rare" means subtle, thin, or less dense</note> substance. The Heaven is composed of two: one of the rare elements, namely air, and one of the dense, namely water. Living creatures, however, were created partly from fire, air, and earth, such as the brute animals; and partly from fire, air, and water, such as the birds. In plants <term>vegetabilibus: the category of living things that grow but do not move or feel</term> there is no fire. For they are made from earth, water, and air. Yet if any of you wish to claim that fire is present in plants, it would not be absurd; for from the hidden heat of the air, the plant will possess fire, as was said previously in this gathering: that a thin fire is inherent to the air. But the fire about which there can be doubt is not present except in those things possessing spirit and soul.

However, man was created from all four elements—fire, air, water, and earth—which is why he is subject to death; for division follows that which is composed, and that division is death. But that which is created from only one element does not die, because no division can exist within it. From two, or three, or even four elements, it is necessary for every composite thing to be separated, which happens through death. And know this: that every composite thing lacking fire does not eat, nor drink, nor sleep. This is because in all things possessing a spirit, it is the fire that "eats" <note>The "digestive fire" was a common medieval metaphor for metabolism</note>. Angels, however, do not eat, because simple fire—which is called "rare"—does not eat; only "thick" or dense fire eats. Since Angels were created from simple and rare fire, they do not eat or sleep. And thus is resolved the doubt which any of you might have held.

To these things Arisleus <note>A recurring figure in the "Turba Philosophorum," often identified with the Greek philosopher Aristeas</note> said: "Since I have gathered you for the benefit of posterity, I think nothing more useful can be explained to those who come after us than if each of you relates the descriptions of the elements. Do so in such a method that it is not recognized by the ignorant <insert>the uninitiated</insert>, yet does not escape the sons of the doctrine <note>A common alchemical term for dedicated students of the Great Work</note>."

### PROPOSITION X.

EXIMENUS. All things were created from the four elements: namely, the heaven, the thrones <note>A high order of angels</note>, the Angels, the Sun, the Moon, the stars, fire, air, the sea, and all waters, the earth, and things diverse and similar.

# THE ASSEMBLY

There is no contradiction in what I have said, except that each of those creatures is of a different nature, and its nature is varied according to different laws. This diversity exists in all creatures because they were created from different elements. If they were made from a single element, they would be in total agreement with one another. However, when the elements are mixed together, the mixture itself is neither dry on its own, nor moist, nor hot, nor cold. But when they come together, creatures emerge from them, which are never perfected unless they first putrefy and decay in appearance. Then, indeed, God grants growth: namely life, food, nourishment, and governance.

Listen, most beloved, I have not described these elements to you in vain. For within them lies a hidden secret <note>original: "arcanum absconditum"</note>: specifically, two of these elements are visible, and their power and work are known; but the other two are neither seen nor touched, nor is their power or work seen, except within the first two elements. Unless those four elements are joined, they accomplish nothing. But when they are joined, they set aside their individual natures and become something else, as if a new art is being born; therefore, meditate upon these things. Furthermore, know all you sons of doctrine <note>A common alchemical term for students or initiates of the craft.</note>, that there is no true tincture <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is a substance capable of transmuting or coloring base metals into gold or silver.</note> except from our copper <note>original: "aes"; in alchemy, this often refers to a specialized "philosophical" copper rather than the common metal.</note>. Therefore, do not consume your souls and money in vain, nor bring sadness to your hearts. For you will accomplish nothing unless you turn the aforementioned copper into white, and make coins <note>original: "numos"; likely referring to the physical result of the transmutation or the "tokens" of the art.</note> through experience; then make that white into red, until the tincture is achieved. Therefore, break that copper, burn it, and deprive it of its blackness by cooking, soaking, and washing it until it becomes white; then bind it together with art.

Afterward, place it over a gentle fire until the plates are broken down and become water, and join it to the **Ethelia** <note>A technical term in the Turba, likely derived from Greek, referring to a vapor, spirit, or volatile substance.</note>, and roast them together with a slow fire until it becomes a thick broth, and into its—

Turn the Ethelia <note>original: "Ethelia"; likely referring to a vaporous or volatile substance in early alchemy</note> until it coagulates and becomes a varied coin, which we call the Flower of the Sun. Cook it thereafter until it is deprived of its blackness and whiteness appears. Afterward, govern it and mix in the soul of gold, and cook it until it becomes a red Ethelia. Grind this with patience, and do not grow weary of moistening it with the water that came out of it—which is the permanent water—until it becomes red. ### PROPOSITION XII.

**PARMENIDES:** Know that the envious have treated waters, broths, bodies, and metals in manifold ways so that they might deceive those seeking knowledge. Therefore, dismiss these things and cause gold and coins to be made from this copper of ours; take copper or lead for the fatness or blackness, and tin for the liquefaction, knowing that unless you direct the natures of truth and the temperaments, and join blood-like things to blood-like things, you work in vain. Indeed, natures meet their own natures, follow them, and rejoice in them, and when they rot, they are born. For nature is governed, and in the manner that it fell, it is raised up; and while it is destroyed, it is turned into dust and reduced to nothing; then it is regenerated and renewed. 

Strive, therefore, to know what it is that makes it rot and renews it, and what its flavor is, and what its distance and proximity are, and how friendship is made after enmity, and how corruption and generation happen, and how those natures embrace one another, and how they become harmonious in a slow fire. Once these things are known and perceived, apply your hands to the work. But if you are ignorant of the stated qualities, do not approach the work, for it is entirely harmful, unfortunate, and sorrowful. Now understand the words of the Wise, and retain this brief saying: namely, that **Nature rejoices in nature, and Nature contains nature, and Nature conquers and overcomes nature.** <note>original: "Natura naturâ lætatur, & Natura naturam continet, & Natura naturam vincit"</note> The whole work is encompassed in this single word. Therefore, dismiss superfluous talk and take quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> and congeal it in the body of Magnesia, or of sulfur that is not burned, and it is turned—

### O P I N I O N   XIII.

I say "according to the custom" because it has already been coagulated before; therefore it is not the beginning of the ruling. However, I command this: that you take the quicksilver which is of the male, and place it upon the bronze—that is, governed iron—and it will be whitened. For in a similar way white Magnesia <note>A mysterious alchemical substance, not necessarily modern magnesium</note> is made, and the male is likewise converted, since there is a proximity of the magnet.

From this stone, when it is broken, various colors appear; but if you cover it, as I have said, until it becomes white and shines like marble, you will find your purpose.

## THE SIXTEENTH DISCOURSE

**FRICTES** says: Know, seekers of wisdom, that the foundation of this art—because of which many have perished—is indeed one thing, stronger and more sublime than all natures according to the Philosophers; yet among beginners, it is the most vile of all things. But we venerate this: and if Kings recognized this, none of us would ever attain this matter. Oh, how wonderfully nature turns these bodies into spirit, and in what a marvelous way it stands out and overcomes all things. Here the Assembly cried: Name it by its name, not in riddles. And he replied: It is the sharpest vinegar <note>original: "acetum acerrimum"; likely referring to a potent solvent or "philosophical" acid rather than common vinegar</note>, which makes gold become pure spirit, without which vinegar neither the whiteness, nor the blackness, nor the redness can exist; and when it is mixed with the body, it is contained, and becomes one with it, and turns it into spirit, and dyes it with a spiritual tincture that can never be erased. Know this, however: if you place the body upon the fire without the vinegar, it will be burned and corrupted. Know also that the first moisture is cold; therefore, beware of the fire, for it is the enemy of moisture. For this reason, the Philosophers and Sages have commanded us to govern gently, until it becomes an incombustible sulfur <note>original: "sulphur incremabile"; a stable substance that fire cannot destroy</note>: and they have hinted at this until now, saying: It is best that a small force of sulfur burns a strong body. Therefore they venerate it, and describe it in their books, saying: This vinegar burns the bodies, turns them to ash, and whitens them: and if it is cooked well, and deprived of its blackness, it will become a stone and a most white coin. Cook it, therefore, until it is destroyed: then dissolve it, and place it in the water of the sea: and know, that the beginning of this work is whitening <note>original: "dealbatio"</note>, which redness succeeds. Afterward, the perfection of the body is achieved through the vinegar. I have sought this vinegar through long labor; at last, by the will of God Most High, I saw one nature, which is more powerful, noble, and stronger than all natures. And this nature is nothing other than clean water, the sharpest vinegar, and the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens"; the "everlasting water" or universal solvent of the alchemists</note>, which...

<summary>Frictes addresses the assembly, identifying "sharp vinegar" (a philosophical solvent) as the essential agent for transforming metallic bodies into spirit and achieving the stages of blackness, whiteness, and redness. He warns that without this "permanent water," the fire will merely destroy the materials rather than perfecting them.</summary>

### PROPOSITION XVII.

**SOCRATES:** Know, sons of doctrine, that without lead <note>original: "plumbo"; in alchemy, lead often refers to the "raw" or "base" state of matter before purification</note> there is no tincture <note>a substance used to change the color or quality of metals</note>, and that the power of the work lies within it. Do you not see, says Hermes, thrice-graced <note>original: "Hermes gratia triplicis," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, that as often as it is immersed into a body, it turns that very body into an unchangeable color? Therefore, the first power is vinegar, and the second is lead, of which the Sages have said that it may be immersed into all bodies, and it changes and tints them all with an immutable color.

Take, therefore, the lead which is made from stone, and cook it until it turns black; afterwards, grind it with saltpeter water <note>original: "aqua nitri"</note> until it becomes like a thick fat. Then cook it again with a stronger fire until it becomes a clean and shining stone. Afterward, grind it with dew, salt, and rainwater for twenty-nine days; then with salt water for twenty days, and with sweet water for ten days, and you will find it similar to a shining stone. Then cook it again in water until it becomes tin through melting; then cook it until it is deprived of moisture and becomes a dry powder, which, when it is dried out, swiftly drinks up the rest of its moisture because it is "burnt lead"—but take care that it is not truly scorched. This, therefore, is the sulfur that does not burn.

Afterward, grind it with the sharpest vinegar until it thickens; cook it, and take care that the vinegar does not turn into smoke and perish. Now, however, I have shown the arrangement of white lead; once this is known, nothing else follows but the "Work of Women" and the "Play of Children" <note>original: "Opus mulierum & Ludus puerorum"; a common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the difficult initial stages are passed, the rest of the process is easy and requires little effort</note>.

Therefore, know that the secret of the work consists of the male and the female: I have shown you the masculine in the lead, and the feminine in orpiment <note>original: "auripigmento," a gold-colored arsenic mineral</note>. Mix the orpiment, therefore, with the lead, because once the masculine power is received, the female rejoices and is helped by it, and the male shall receive the tinting seed from the female. Accordingly, place the mixture in a glass vessel and grind them with *Ethelia* <note>a term often used for a volatile spirit or "hidden" vapor</note> and the sharpest vinegar, and cook them for seven days, taking care that the secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> does not escape; and so leave it through the nights, and when it is dry, moisten it again with vinegar, and you shall have the great secret. Now, therefore, I have made known to you the power of orpiment, which power is the female, which turns bodies into spirit and perfects the entire work.

<summary>Socrates explains the alchemical preparation of lead and orpiment, describing their symbolic roles as male and female principles that must be combined through a series of washings and cookings to achieve the "Great Secret."</summary>
