# T H E  A S S E M B L Y

### P R O N O U N C E M E N T  XVIII.

**Z E N O N**: Now that you have taught how to make the white doctrine <note>original: "doctrinam albam"; refers to the Albedo or whitening stage of the alchemical process</note> even further, what about the red? I say that you cannot make the red unless you first intend to whiten: for the two natures are nothing other than white and red. Therefore, whiten the red, and turn the white into red, knowing that the year is divided into four seasons. The first season is of a cold complexion: and it is Winter. The second is of an airy complexion: and it is Spring. The third season is of a fiery complexion: and it is Summer. The fourth is Autumn, in which the fruits are ripened. According to this pattern, it is necessary for you to govern the natures: namely, to dissolve in Winter, to cook in Spring, to congeal in Summer: and in Autumn to gather the fruits and to dye <note>original: "tingere"; the act of performing the "tincture" or final transformation</note>. If you cannot do this, you ought to blame yourselves. Furthermore, I shall speak of the reddening of lead: Take the copper <note>original: "æs"; can mean copper or bronze, often representing a base metal to be transformed</note> which the Master commanded to be taken at the beginning of the book, and place lead with it until it becomes thick: congeal it, dry it, until it becomes red: this is surely the red lead of which the Sages spoke, saying copper and lead are a precious stone: mix them equally, and roast gold with them: and if you have governed them well, a mighty spirit is produced in the midst of the spirits. For when the male is joined to the female, she herself becomes a female that does not flee <note>original: "non fugiens"; refers to a non-volatile substance that does not evaporate when heated</note>, and the whole composite becomes spiritual, and from that spiritual composite comes the red, which is the beginning of the world. And thus you have the red lead, without which you can do nothing.

### P R O N O U N C E M E N T  XIX.

**M V N D V S**: You investigators of the art ought to know that the Philosophers in their books have called the Gum <note>original: "Gumi" or "Guma"; a metaphor for the thick, adhesive substance or "glue" of the philosophers</note> by many names: and yet it is nothing other than the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens"; a central alchemical concept referring to a solvent that does not wet the hands and survives fire</note>: from which water, indeed, our most precious stone is generated. Oh, how many are the investigators of this gum: and how few are they who recognize it. I tell you that this gum is not improved except with gold alone. And there are certain investigators who, although they find the applications, are nevertheless unwilling to endure the labors, because expenses are incurred at the same time. Nevertheless, listen to me, and I will describe the applications of this gum. I say that our gum is stronger than gold, and those who recognize it hold it to be more precious than gold.

## *PROPOSITION XX.*

**DARDARIS.** It is true what the predecessors have narrated concerning the permanent water: nothing in this entire work is done without this permanent water: and he who does not know it and its proper regimen labors in vain: for its power is spiritual blood. And for this reason the Philosophers called it "permanent": because its blood, cooked in the body which the predecessors named before, by the will of the Most High turns the spirit into body, and the body into spirit. For once mixed together and reduced into one, they are incorporated and embrace themselves in an inseparable union. And note that whatever has spirit also has blood.

# THE ASSEMBLY

### DISCOURSE XXI.

**BELLUS.** We all know that the Philosophers have treated this permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanente"; a symbolic term for the universal solvent or "mercury of the philosophers" that does not evaporate in fire</note> in many ways, and have taught various methods to make the red from the white: yet they were in agreement through a hidden variety; for this reason, they described its compositions and its governance. I say regarding this blessed stone, that it is a stone and yet not a stone, and it is called by many names so that no foolish person may recognize it. Certain Sages gave it a name from the place where it is generated; others truly from its color, and said it is of the most intense spirit: and that by it, a body is made incombustible: and some called it the green lion; others the spittle of the Moon; some have set it down mathematically; others, better still, because it flows from metals, and for that reason named it the heart of the Sun; and some said that it is made from quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and others will have it that it comes from the milk of winged creatures, and thus they have called the stone itself by legions of names.

### DISCOURSE XXII.

**PANDULPHUS:** I say that this stone described is the permanent water: and that the permanent water is clean water and the water of life, of which the Philosophers said: that nature rejoices in nature, Nature contains nature, and nature overcomes nature. <note>This is a famous alchemical axiom attributed to Ostanes, suggesting the internal sympathy and transformation of matter.</note> And this is the discourse in which the Philosophers briefly placed the foundation of the entire work. I say also, that there is no body more worthy and pure than the Sun <note>gold</note>, and that no dyeing poison <note>original: "venenum tingens"; in alchemy, "poison" often refers to a potent, transformative elixir or tincture</note> is generated without the Sun and its shadow, and he who attempts to make the poison without these, errs by the width of the whole sky. But he who has dyed the poison with the Sun and its shadow has reached the greatest secret, which is called the coin, which when it is made red, is called gold: and he who knows the secrets of the Philosophers knows the whole work.

### DISCOURSE XXIII.

**ARDARIUS:** I shall relate to you the governance and the composition of the stone. Take the hidden and honorable secret, which is the white Magnesia <note>a symbolic term for a primary alchemical substance, not necessarily modern magnesium</note>, and which is mixed with wine, but do not take it unless it is pure and clean: and place it in its own vessel, and pray to God, that you may see this greatest...

## DISCOURSE XXVII.

**MENEBDUS:** Much has been said: yet I advise those who come after us that they should make bodies into non-bodies, and the incorporeal into true bodies. For by this method of treatment <note>Latin: "regimine," referring to the controlled process of heating and mixing</note> the composite is acquired, and the hidden part of its nature is extracted; quicksilver <note>Latin: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver," or mercury</note> is joined to the body, and magnesia <note>A term for the crude mineral starting material</note> and the female are joined to the male. When the Ethelia <note>A technical term in alchemy referring to the volatile spirit or "vapor" of a substance</note> arrives, the hidden nature is extracted, through which the bodies are colored. Therefore, if you understand this treatment, bodies become non-bodies and the incorporeal becomes bodies; and if you govern the matter diligently with fire and join it to the Ethelia, the things become pure and do not flee the heat <note>Meaning they become "fixed" or stable under high temperatures</note>. Know that quicksilver is a fire that burns, kills, and breaks down bodies in a single treatment; the more it is mixed with the body and ground, the more the body is destroyed, and the quicksilver is thinned and becomes alive. However, when you grind the bodies diligently and cook them as is required, the Ethelia results from it—not fleeing the fire, fit for every dyeing <note>Latin: "tinctura," the process of transforming or coloring metals</note>—which breaks down and overcomes all bodies, and retains and colors all spirits, because the colored Ethelia colors all things. And know that a body cannot dye itself unless the hidden spirit is extracted from its belly; a body and soul without the spirit (which is the spiritual dye from which the colors appear) does not dye, because a thick thing does not dye a thin thing, but rather the thinness of nature which is changed into the body. When you treat the body of copper <note>Latin: "æs," often referring to copper or bronze</note> and extract the thinnest part from it, that thinnest part is turned into a dye and colors. Therefore the Wise Man said: that copper does not dye unless it is first dyed; and these are the two dyes, the dense and the moist. The dense is joined to the moist; because sulfurs are contained by sulfurs, nature rejoices when its own nature arrives, and it contains and overcomes nature.

To join and cook the fire with the dung <note>original: "stercori"; likely referring to a "horse-dung bath," a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat</note>, and the colors which appear thereafter are of this sort. On the first day, a black-lemon color appears; on the second, a black-red; on the third, a saffron color like iron; on the fourth, the perfect color appears, similar to common gold coin. This is the Elixir <note>original: "Yxir"</note>, a composite of the moist and the dry, dyeing with an unchangeable tint. And know that the "body" is said to be that in which the gold resides. However, you who are composing the Elixir, take care that you do not extract the spirit too hastily, for perhaps it might die. Instead, extract it as our elixir—that is, as a venom—and the soul will remain, which is the tincture extracted from many things and applied to the coins. This tincture, therefore, is life to those things to which it is joined, but it is loss and death to the bodies from which it is extracted. And for this reason, the Wise Men <note>original: "Sapientes"</note> have said that there is a lust between them like that between a male and a female; and he who knows their natures bears the long duration of the cooking and composition with patience, and receives the profit.

### PROPOSITION XXIX.

**CHAMBAR:** It must be noted, venerable Assembly <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous gathering of alchemical authorities</note>, that the envious have called the stone "antimony" <note>original: "antimonium"; here used as a "cover-name" to hide the true identity of the primary material from the uninitiated</note>. They commanded it to be governed until it becomes glittering and shining like marble, and it is mixed with vinegar and governed until it becomes water. Then it is congealed and becomes a glittering stone, having a splendor like marble. When you see this, I command you to govern it until it becomes red, because while it is cooked until it is broken down and becomes earth, it turns into a red color. And when you see this, repeat the process: cook and soak it until it brings forth the aforementioned color and becomes gold. Then repeat it again, and it will become gold of a Tyrian color <note>original: "Tyrij coloris"; a deep, royal purple-red highly prized in antiquity</note>. It is necessary for you, therefore, when you see the stone thus glittering, to break it and turn it into earth until it conceives some redness. Then you shall take a little of the water (which they previously commanded you to divide into two parts) and you shall soak the sand many times until the hidden colors appear to you in it. If you have governed it well, you will see the colors; if not, you will be frustrated. Look, therefore, to how you make the pairs embrace. For the Male, having embraced his spouse, quickly passes into her body, and melts it, congeals it, destroys it, and breaks it; and thereafter...

### DISCOURSE XXX.

**CUSTOS** <note>The Guardian</note> said: I marvel, O Assembly of Sages, at the great power of this water, which when it enters the body, turns it into earth, and then into dust. If you wish to test whether this dust is perfect, take it in your hand; if it feels almost impalpable <note>so fine it cannot be felt</note>, it is of the best quality. If not, repeat the cooking process until it is perfected. And know that if you take anything other than our copper <note>original: "aes nostrum," a technical term for the alchemical starting material, not common copper</note>, and govern it with our water, you will achieve nothing. On the contrary, if you govern our copper with our water, you will find all that has been predicted. Cook it, therefore, with a gentle fire, and it will become the "scaly stone" <note>original: "lapis numosus," likely referring to a flaky or coin-like crystalline structure</note>, of which the Sages said: Nature rejoices in nature <note>original: "Natura naturâ laetatur," a famous alchemical axiom</note> because of the proximity that these two bodies have with each other when combined with the permanent water. Therefore, the nature of these two is one, and a closeness is mixed between them; if this were not so, they would not mix so quickly, nor would they hold one another, nor become one.

### DISCOURSE XXXI.

**DIAMEDES** said: Know, O Wise Men, that from a human nothing is born but a human, and from beasts nothing but their own likeness. And for this reason I say that Nature is not improved except within its own nature; therefore, use the venerable nature. For from it the art breaks forth, and not from any other; unless you take it and govern it, you will have nothing. Join, therefore, the male of the red servant <note>original: "serui rubei," a symbolic name for a specific chemical substance, often associated with sulfur or gold</note> to his fragrant wife, and once joined they will beget the art. Do not introduce anything foreign to them, neither dust nor any other thing. Let the conception suffice for you, and a true son shall be born. Oh, how precious is the nature of that red servant, without whom the regimen cannot be established.

### DISCOURSE XXXII.

**BASSEN** said: Lead the Citrine <note>The yellow-colored substance</note> with his wife into the bath after their marriage, but do not heat the bath too much, lest they be deprived of sense and motion.

### PROPOSITION XXXIV.

This being finished, God restores the spirit and the soul to it, and frees it from all infirmity, strengthens it, and improves it. ### PROPOSITION XXXV.

### PROPOSITION XXXVI.

It is extracted in this way: grind it, and apply it to water seven times until it drinks all the moisture and receives the power to withstand the battle of the fire; then it is called "rust." Therefore, putrefy it diligently until it becomes a spiritual powder in the color of dried blood—a color which the power of the fire introduces, until it is clothed in an invariable color.

### PROPOSITION XXXVII.

**ZEVNON**: The sayings of the Egyptians lead us into error. That which we seek publicly is sold at a very small price, and if it were known, the merchants would not sell even a tiny bit of it. They have said that it is a stone and not a stone, and that it is the "gum of Scotland" <note>original: "guma Scotiae"; a traditional alchemical deck-name for a specific resinous or gummy substance used in the Work.</note>. And for this reason, the Philosophers have concealed the power of this poison, because in it is the spirit you seek, which tints and vivifies...

And this nature the Philosophers have called the Spirit and the soul. Furthermore, they said that the moist spirit is black, lacking in defilement: and just as in man there is moisture and dryness, so in our work there is nothing else than vapor and water. Therefore the ancients said the work is from two things. And these two joined, some have called a "composite," because those two are four.

## DISCOURSE 38.

**ASSOTES** says: I tell you, that unless you sublimate <note>To sublimate is to heat a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, a process of purification.</note> the matters at the beginning of the cooking, without the grinding of hands, until all things become water, you have not yet found the work. And know, that sometimes they call the Copper <note>original: "Aes"</note> Sand, and at other times even a stone, and throughout the entire process the names vary: nevertheless, the nature and the humidity become water, and thereafter a stone, if they are well mixed: because that which is light and spiritual is sublimated upwards; but that which is heavy and thick remains at the bottom of the vessel. This, however, is the "grinding" of the Philosophers, which is done by decoction <note>boiling or heating</note>, not by hand. And know, that unless you turn all things into powder, you have not yet ground them. Therefore, cook until it is ground down and becomes powder.

## DISCOURSE 39.

**AGADMON**: Cook the copper until it becomes a smooth and impalpable body, and place it in its vessel: then sublimate it five or seven times, until the water descends, knowing that when the water is powder, it has been diligently ground. But if you doubt how water becomes powder, know that the intention of the Philosophers is that the body—which was not water before it fell into water—should become water together with the water, and that the water of the water <note>likely referring to the "mercurial" essence</note> be mixed, and they become one. Furthermore, it must be known that unless you turn both into water, you will not arrive at the precious work: for it is necessary for the body to be seized by the flame of fire, so that it may be destroyed and become weak, while water is in water, until the whole becomes water. The ignorant, however, when they hear the name of "water," think it is the water of the clouds; but if they read our books, they would surely know it to be the "permanent water," which could not be permanent without its partner, with whom it has been made one. This, moreover, is the water which the Philosophers have called the Water of Gold, fire, the good poison, and the sand of many names, which Hermes commanded to be washed many times, so that the blackness of the Sun <note>original: "Solis nigredo," referring to the 'nigredo' or black stage of alchemy</note> might be washed away, which it had received during the dissolution of the body. And know, unless you take this body of mine which lacks spirit, you will by no means achieve what you desire, because nothing foreign enters the work, nor anything except that which is pure. Therefore, dismiss all plurality: For—

### PROPOSITION XL.

**BONELLUS** <note>Likely a corruption of the name Balinas or Apollonius of Tyana in alchemical literature.</note>: Sons of doctrine, mixing the Magnesia <term>Magnesia: here referring not to the modern mineral, but to the "raw material" of the philosophers' stone</term>, place it in its vessel, and close the mouth diligently, and cook it with a gentle fire until it liquefies and is turned into water: for by the heat of the water, the whole will easily become water. Seeing, however, the blackness of the water looming, know that the body is now liquefied. Again, place it in its vessel, and cook it for 40 days, until it drinks the moisture of both the vinegar and the honey. Some, however, uncover the vessel every seven days, or ten: but the final perfection is on the fortieth day, for then it will perfectly drink up the moisture of the decoction; wash it therefore, and deprive it of its blackness, until it becomes a stone dry to the touch. Therefore the Philosophers said: Wash the Magnesia with sweet water, and cook it diligently until it becomes earth and the moisture perishes, and then it is called Brass <note>original: "Aes"; in alchemy, this often refers to a specific state of the purified matter rather than the common metal</note>. Place the sharpest vinegar upon it, and allow it to be soaked by that vinegar, and it will be our brass, which the Philosophers commanded to be washed with permanent water. Furthermore, they said: Divide the poison into two parts, with one of which soak the body, and with the other cause it to putrefy, knowing that the whole work and regimen is not done except with water: because what we seek is one. And unless this thing becomes one, which improves it, that which we seek will not happen. It is necessary, therefore, for us to present the necessary things to it, so that at last it becomes a tincture <term>tincture: a substance capable of transforming or "coloring" base metals into gold</term>, which if it does not follow, repeat the process.

### PROPOSITION XLI.

**CRANSES**: Wise ones, take our brass, and with the first part of the water place it in its vessel, and cook it for forty days, and cleanse it from all uncleanness, and cook it until the days are completed and it becomes a stone without moisture. Then cook it until the dregs remain, afterwards wash it with water: when the water is consumed, allow it to putrefy in its vessel until you see what you seek. Moreover, the Philosophers called this compound, when turned into blackness, **SUFFICIENTLY BLACK** <note>original: "SATIS NIGRVM"</note>, and they said: Rule it with vinegar and blackness: but that which remains, if it is whitened, they called **SUFFICIENTLY WHITE** <note>original: "SATIS ALBVM"</note>, and they commanded that it be ruled by permanent water: that which they called **SUFFICIENTLY RED** <note>original: "SATIS RVBEVM"</note>, they commanded that it be ruled by water and—

### APHORISM XLIII.

ADMION says: You cannot, O wise men, reach the usefulness of this art without a prolonged and continuous regimen. Therefore, he who is patient in the regimen shall enter the art; but he who is not, let him not read our sentences, because having read them will only bring him loss. And for this reason the Master said:
> He who labors in reading our books and devotes himself to them, and is not entangled in various wandering thoughts, and prays to God, shall reign in a kingdom until he dies.

For that which is sought is not of little value, but is a gift of God; for this reason, there is need of patience and labor. For we see that he who grafts trees hopes for fruit in due time; he who sows, reaps after many months. Look, therefore, and learn to mix, to cook, to simulate, to parch, to heat, to whiten, to grind, to level the *Ethelia* <note>a term for the "hidden spirit" or volatile vapor of the matter</note>, and to produce the redness <note>original: "rubiginem"; literally rust, but here referring to the "Rubedo" or final red stage of the alchemical work</note>, and finally to tint. These are many names, yet the regimen is one: but the decoction <note>the process of boiling or heating</note> is continuous, for which reason they have often repeated that the composite should be ground and cooked perpetually; let not the labor weary you. The goal is that you fit the temperaments <note>the elemental balances</note> together: then cook them manifoldly, saturate the decoctions, and cook until the spirits become impalpable <note>too fine to be felt by touch</note>. And when you see *Ysir* <note>likely a corruption of "Osiris" or a term for the prime matter</note> clothed in royal garments and turned into the Tyrian color <note>the deep purple-red of royalty</note>, then you will understand the sayings of the Philosophers.

### APHORISM XLIV.

LARGUS says: The copper <note>original: "Aes"</note> of which the first masters spoke is not the copper or the tin of the common people; rather, it is our "body," which must be mixed with the body of *Magnesia* <note>not modern magnesium, but a mysterious alchemical mineral used to draw out the spirit</note>, so that it may be cooked and ground without weariness until it becomes a stone. Then that stone is ground in a vessel with the water of nitre and is liquefied until it is broken down. It is necessary, however, for you to have the water which, the more it is cooked, the more it thickens, until it acquires the redness which is the foundation of the work. Cook this, and grind it with Egyptian vinegar.

## DISCOURSE XLV.

**CADMON**: I signify to those who come after us, that the round thing, which turns copper <note>original: "aes"; often used in alchemy to refer to the base metal or the "body" to be transformed</note> into four, is from each and every thing. Now, the method of extraction is this: take one part from the air and three parts from the permanent water: then let them be mixed and cooked until they thicken, and become one stone, of which the Philosophers have said:
> Take one part of the pure body, and three of the air of Magnesia <note>a symbolic term for the "prime matter" or the universal spirit, not necessarily the modern mineral</note>: then mix them with true masculine vinegar mixed with earth, cover the vessel, and observe what is within, and cook it continually until they become earth.

## DISCOURSE XLVI.

**ASCANIUS**: When we read in the books of the Philosophers that nature is only one, which overcomes all things, it is necessary to know that the one and the one are composed together. Do you not see that the composition of a human being is from soul and body? Thus it is necessary for us to join two things together: a mixture which the Philosophers have compared to spouses: from whose embrace results the golden water. But this concerns the Second Work: of the first I shall say a few things: Stir up a war between the copper and the quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, until they come to destruction and are corrupted: then the copper, conceiving the quicksilver, coagulates it. Truly the quicksilver, conceiving the copper, is congealed into earth. Therefore, stir up the fight, and destroy the body of the copper until it becomes dust. Join the male to the female (which is made from vapor) and the quicksilver, until the male and female become *Etheel* <note>a term derived from Arabic "al-ithel," referring to the "hidden" or "spiritual" essence of the matter</note>. For he who turns them into spirit through *Etheel*, and then makes them red, tints every body; because when the body is diligently ground, a clean, spiritual, and sublime soul is extracted from it, which tints every body, and is the sulfur of nature, which is called by various names.

### PROPOSITION XLVIII.

It is necessary, therefore, for you to mix that thick substance with the fiery poison, and to putrefy it, and diligently grind it until it becomes a spirit in the other hidden spirit; and then the tincture is made, which tints everything you desire.

## SENTENCE XLIX.

Plato says: When these bodies are dissolved, one must take care that they are not burned, and they must be washed with sea water until all the salt is turned into sweetness, and it becomes clear and provides a tint <note>original: "tingat" - referring to the alchemical power to change the color and nature of a substance</note>. And it is necessary for one to become a tinting spirit, and for the other to remain tinted without fleeing <note>original: "non fugiens" - a technical term for "fixed" or non-volatile substances that do not evaporate when heated</note>. For the spirit, when separated from the body and hidden in another spirit, makes both of them flee. Concerning this, the Wise Men have said: "Unlock the door for the fugitive, lest he take flight." For by turning the sulfurous spirit into itself, it will make it like itself, and both will become fleeing, because they have become airy spirits. Regarding these, the Philosophers also said: They did not flee with the fugitives, and yet they became fugitives; therefore they repeated the process upon them, and they became non-fleeing, but rather one single body, similar to the body from which they were first drawn. Concerning this one body, the Wise Men said: That the tinting and the tinted have become one, and this spirit hidden in the other spirit is moist. Therefore, you must not be ignorant of the fact that of the moist things, one is hot and the other is cold; and although the cold moisture is incompatible with the hot moisture, they nevertheless produce a single thing. And for this reason, we have preferred those two bodies: because through them we perform the entire work, and we rule the bodily things by the bodiless <note>original: "corporea incorporeis" - the solid by the volatile/spiritual</note>, until the bodiless things become bodies that do not flee from the fire. And then those bodies are better and more precious than all other bodies. Take them, therefore, which do not flee, and join them, and wash their bodies with the bodiless, until the body receives the bodiless and does not flee. And turn the earth into water, into fire, and the fire into air; and hide the fire in the depths of the water, and the earth in the belly of the air, and mix the hot with the moist, and the dry with the cold, and you shall have the mastery <note>term: "magisterium" - the completed alchemical work or the Philosopher's Stone</note>; knowing that Nature surpasses nature, and Nature conquers nature, and Nature contains nature.

### DISCOURSE LIII.

BELLUS: Much has been discussed regarding composition; however, composition and contact are one and the same thing. Therefore, take one part from the second composition and one part from the ferment of gold, and place upon them the clean water of sulfur; you will then possess the revealed secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note> which tints every body. But meanwhile, it must be noted that the clean water which comes from sulfur is not from sulfur alone, but is composed of several things which together form one sulfur. Such a composition is made in this manner: Mix that which fights in the fire with that which does not fight; for when joined in the fire, they battle appropriately, and a constant friendship is formed. And the Philosophers hinted at this when they said: In the cooking <note>original: "decoctione"</note>, a little sulfur burns many hard bodies, and the moisture that is left behind is called liquid pitch, balsam, gum, etc. Truly, this is the secret that I shall open to you. This secret proceeds from two compositions: namely, of sulfur and of Magnesia. And the Philosophers, when this composite was reduced into one, named it "Water," and "the spit of mushrooms," and "the thickness of gold." But when reduced into quicksilver, they called it "Water of Sulfur." Moreover, when sulfur contains sulfur, they say the fire is a poison, which is the revealed secret proceeding from those whom you know.

### THE FIFTY-SIXTH OPINION

**YSIMIDRVS:** Regarding the governance of copper and the moist spirit, enough and more has been discussed; I shall now complete what was omitted. It must be known, therefore: that the Philosophers have assigned many names, and that it is sometimes called the **Water of Ethelia** <note>likely a reference to a volatile spirit or "cloud" substance</note>, of which mention was made above; when this water is whitened, it whitens and tints. It is also called by them the **flower of gold**, and before it tints and reaches this end, it is called copper. But when it is joined with four things, which the Wise have called **fermented urines**, they call it the Heart, and the necks of gold. These names are invented: yet they are true, and signify only one thing, namely the **quicksilver extracted by men**, from which and with which all things are made; and it is said to be the **worldly water** which deletes every shadow. 

And it must be known that when this quicksilver extracted by men is whitened, it becomes **sulfur**, which is contained by sulfur, and it is a poison that is likened to shining marble. This the Philosophers have called Ethelia, and **Orpiment** <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>, and **Sandarac** <note>red arsenic or a resin</note>, from which the tincture and the pure spirit ascend by a slow fire, and from which the flower is sublimated. And this entire secret is nothing other than the quicksilver extracted by men—that is, through the agency of men. 

Furthermore, it must be known that the secret copper cannot be whitened until it has been whitened in the prior work. It must also be noted that this sulfur is accustomed to flee; and when it fixes bodies with its thickness and is sublimated like a vapor, it must be retained in another way by quicksilver of its own kind, and its flight must be restrained: and this is what the Philosophers said, namely: **that sulfurs are contained by sulfurs**. ## PROPOSITION LVII.

**OBSEMEGANUS:** I say that the envious ones <note>A common alchemical trope referring to authors who hid secrets from the uninitiated</note> have laid waste to this entire art with a multitude of names: yet there is an art according to which the Philosophers commanded us to make "monetary gold" <note>gold in the form of coin or bullion</note>, and to calcine, sublime, fix, grind, whiten, coagulate, cook, and turn it into red. They called the fire *Ethelia* <note>A term for the volatile spirit or vapor</note>, the vessel a "sieve," the sulfur-water a "bond": and all of this is nothing other than grinding and whitening. Furthermore, I say that quicksilver appears white to the sight. However, when smoke reaches it, it is turned into red and becomes *Combar* <note>likely a corruption of Cinnabar</note>, that is, poison. The Philosophers hinted at this, saying: the nature of lead is easily converted. For this reason, they frequently repeated this word "to grind," so that they might show in many ways how to draw out the spirits hidden in the vessel, and how—once applied—to prevent <note>original: "prohibere"</note> them from being burned up; otherwise, the fire easily consumes them. But when water is applied, the more the flame attacks them, the more the water penetrates into the "innards" and prevents them from being burned by the flame. And for this reason, the ancients treated much of sublimation, because unless the matter is strongly ground by fire, the *Ethelia* will not ascend; this is what Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> wished to hint at when he said: "Sift the things you know, and melt them more deeply."

## PROPOSITION LVIII.

**ARZOCH** says: Unless the things are ground by fire, the *Ethelia* will not ascend, and if it does not ascend, you accomplish nothing. For you see that when the great south wind exhales, it causes the clouds to be sublimated and raises the vapors of the sea; this is the vessel, and the shell, in which the incombustible sulfur resides. I advise you, however, to congeal the quicksilver—which is composed of many things—so that two become three, and four become one, and two become one.

### DISCOURSE 59.

**ANAXAGORAS**: Take that which is burnt and fleeting <note>original: "combustum fugiens," likely referring to a volatile substance that escapes heat</note>, lacking a body, and give it a body. Then take that which is heavy, possessing smoke, and fit for drinking. To explain this matter more clearly: this burnt, fleeting thing, which is capable of being drunk, is Ethelia <note>A term used in alchemy for a volatile spirit or "vaporous" substance</note>. When this is joined with sulfur, place it in a glass vessel over the fire and cook it until it becomes Cambar <note>A technical term for a specific chemical state, often associated with a lead-like or darkened stage</note>, and completes the secret mystery you seek. Therefore, cook it, and do not be weary of repeating the process: for the entire perfection of the sulfur consists in the boiling of the tablet. Let it be cooked, then, until it becomes rust <note>original: "rubigo," often referring to the red stage of the alchemical work</note>. Indeed, all the Philosophers have said: he who can convert this rust into the golden poison <note>original: "venenum aureum," a term for the transformative elixir</note> completes the work; otherwise, he labors in vain.

### DISCOURSE 60.

**PITHEM**: I say that when the Master first treated this water, he wished at the end of his book to speak of the ferment of gold. Therefore, it is a wonder why the envious <note>A common alchemical term for authors who intentionally obscured their writings to hide secrets from the unworthy</note> placed the end before the beginning in their treatises, by instructing that in the ferment of gold, the clean water of sulfur should be mixed with a little gum. Furthermore, they omitted the putrefaction <note>The stage of breaking down or "rotting" the substance to allow for new life</note>, about which I shall say a few words. Putrefaction does not happen without the moist and the dry, and from both of these the beginning of the work is born, even though the envious have divided this work into three parts.

### DISCOURSE 61.

**CONSTANS**: What have we to do with the envious and their treatises? For it is certain that this work has four natures, which are fire, water, air, and earth. Unless these are possessed, nothing is ever generated, nor is anything completed in the art. Join therefore the dry with the moist—that is, the earth and the water—and cook them with fire and air, until the spirit in the soul is dried up. Know that the thin tinting agent <note>The "tincture" or substance that changes the color/nature of the metal</note> takes its power from the thinnest part of the earth, air, and water, and is dried out. For this is the method of our work: that all things are turned into earth. Do not, therefore, multiply the ingredients. The envious have indeed multiplied them and described various regimes in order to deceive seekers, and they have likened this...

## *PROPOSITION LXII.*

**ASTRATUS:** He who wishes to attain the truth, let him take the moisture of the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the spirit of the Moon <note>Silver</note>; I speak the truth, and I bring no contradictions. O how precious is that ash! Wise men, understand this: cook its waters again until it melts; afterwards cook it and soak it with permanent water <note>A stable, non-evaporating solvent</note> until the composition appears sweet, pleasant, and red. Then soak it until it becomes moist; finally cook it with a stronger fire, and, as was said, close the mouth of the vessel. This is the regimen by which fleeing <note>volatile</note> bodies will become non-fleeing, and spirits will be turned into bodies, and bodies into spirits, and they shall be bound to one another, and finally the bodies will become spirits, possessing a soul and tinting and germinating. Therefore, with diligent labor, whiten the bronze with permanent water until redness <note>original: "rubigo"; literally rust or blight</note> happens to it, and it is congealed, and becomes the body of Magnesia <note>A key alchemical substance, not necessarily modern magnesium</note>; then cook it until the whole body is shattered, and thus the fleeing thing will be turned into ash, and the bronze will be made lacking a shadow, and become the tincture of the Philosophers.

## PROPOSITION 73

**ATTAMANUS:** Know, brothers, that our work which you seek is made from the generation of the sea, which after God perfects all things. And know that one work is dried more quickly than another, and another more slowly, and this happens because of the diversity of the cooking.

### SENTENCE 74.

FLORUS: I shall complete the instructions for the cooking <note>original: "coquendi dispositionem"; refers to the controlled heating of the alchemical matter</note>, and I say that the sign of the first decoction is the extraction of its redness. However, understand the redness in this way: When you see the matter already entirely black, know that within the belly of that blackness a whiteness is hidden; it is then necessary for that whiteness to be drawn out from its blackness. In the second decoction, let that whiteness be placed in a vessel with its instruments, and cook it gently until everything becomes white. And when you see that whiteness appearing in the vessel, be certain that redness is hidden within that whiteness; and then you must draw it out and cook it for so long until the whole becomes red.

And know that the first blackness was from the nature of Litharge <note>original: "Martęch"; likely a Latinization of the Arabic 'martak' (litharge or lead oxide)</note>, and from that blackness the redness arose, which redness corrected the black, and established peace between the "fleeing" <note>volatile substances</note> and the "non-fleeing" <note>fixed substances</note>. This happens in this way: The crucified thing <note>the matter undergoing chemical "torture" or transformation</note> is submerged in the body, and turns it into an alterable nature. And know that that blackening sulfur-body cannot be touched or handled; but here it crucifies and tints.

Likewise, know that the blackening sulfur is that which opens the door to the non-fleeing, and even converts the non-fleeing into the fleeing. Do you not see that the crucifier does not crucify with harm or corruption, but for utility and union? Know also for certain, if its crucifixion were harmful or improper, it would not be completed by him until he extracted the invariable colors; and this we have certainly named the Water of Sulfur, which water we prepare for red tinctures, and which thereafter is not blackened. And although it does not blacken afterward, the tincture is not made from that blackness, but I have informed you that it is the key.

### SENTENCE 75.

For this reason the ancients said: That which is perfected is one, and diverse natures do not correct it; which is true. Indeed, only one single thing is suitable for it, which you must govern sparingly. For ignorance of the governance <note>the "regimen" or management of the heat and process</note> often causes one to err. Therefore, do not care for a plurality of arrangements, nor—

It is necessary, therefore, that the lead be converted into blackness, and then the ten aforesaid names will appear in the ferment of gold with Sericon <note>A red lead or cinnabar-like compound used in the work</note>, which is the composition called by ten names. But leaving these aside, we signify nothing else by the variety of names than the White of Copper, because it tints every body that has entered into the composition. Moreover, the composition is twofold: one in the moist and the other in the dry; and when they are wisely cooked, they become one, and it is called "The Good of Many Names." But when it becomes red, it is called the flower of gold, the ferment of gold, the glue of gold, red sulphur, and orpiment. While it remains raw, however, it is called the lead of copper, the rod of metal, and the plate.

### PROPOSITION 78.

**AGMON:** <note>Agmon is one of the speakers in the Turba Philosophorum, a famous early Latin alchemical text.</note> As a corollary, I say that he who does not liquefy and coagulate errs in many ways. Therefore, blacken the earth, and separate its soul and its water, and afterwards whiten it, and you will find what you seek. I also tell you, that he who blackens the earth, and dissolves the white with fire until it becomes like a naked sword, and who introduces the soul to it after its whitening is complete, and fixes the whole with a wasting fire <note>original: "tabido igne," referring to a slow, consuming heat</note> after it has been liquefied, will deserve to be called happy and be exalted above the circles of the world.

Regarding the revelation of our stone, we do not doubt that this is sufficient for the sons of the doctrine; its powers cannot be destroyed. If it is placed in the fire, its strength is increased; if you wish to dissolve it, it is dissolved; if you wish to coagulate it, it will be coagulated. No one can be without it, and everyone has need of it. And although it has many names, it is nevertheless called by one name, and wherever it pleases, there it is hidden. It is also a stone and not a stone, spirit and soul and body; it is white, volatile, hollow, lacking hairs, which no one can touch with their tongue when cooled without injury. If you make it fly, it flies; and if you call it water, you speak the truth; and if you say it is not water, you speak falsely. Do not, however, be deceived by the plurality of names, but hold it certain that it is one thing, to which nothing foreign is introduced. Therefore, investigate its place, and introduce nothing foreign; but let men multiply names, for unless they were multiplied, many would mock our wisdom.

# ALLEGORIES

The principle of nature’s generation exists so that creation may arise and the intended purpose be fulfilled. Take a **bull** <note>original: "taurum"; in alchemy, the bull often represents robust, earthy matter or the element of Earth</note> with its flesh and blood, its horns and the hooves of its feet, and turn it into water, and mix it with the blood, and draw it all out; afterwards, roast it until it grows red. Then, turn the copper into tinctures of the ways. Take a **Cock** <note>original: "Gallum"; the rooster often symbolizes the volatile principle or the "sulfur" of the philosophers</note>, crowned with a red crest, and strip it of its feathers while alive; then place its head in a glass vessel and keep it for an hour. Afterward, preserve the cock again and draw it out until it is softened and purified, and spread it upon marble. Then, with the feathers that were removed from it, draw and shear it most strongly. Next, leave it in horse dung <note>a common alchemical method for providing gentle, steady heat for fermentation</note> until it grows new feathers. And when you hear that cock crowing like a rooster, know that you have walked the right path.

Take a **Viper**, which is called *de rexa* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek or Arabic term for a specific serpent used in medicinal preparations</note>, and deprive it of its head and tail; in these two places its poison liquefies, from which the spirit proceeds. Therefore, divide the head and the tail, and store each by itself in a glass vessel. Take the remaining body and cook it with a slow fire until the flesh is separated from the bones. Afterward, place it upon a metal plate and preserve it for so long until the body is turned into spirit, and its flexibility is taken away from it. For that which is tough cannot be thinned. Then join it to its head, and grind it with it, until the body—as long as flexibility remains in it—[is transformed]. Dry a body of this kind in the Sun, or by fire, so that you may see what you seek. When this is completed, know that you possess a **body piercing through bodies**, and a nature containing nature, and a nature rejoicing in nature, which is called the **Philosophers' Theriac** <note>original: "Tyriaca Philosophorum"; a theriac was a universal wonder-drug or antidote; here it refers to the perfected alchemical medicine</note>.

There is in the sea a round fish, lacking bones and shells, and it has within itself a fatness of marvelous virtue. If this is cooked with a slow fire until its fatness and moisture completely depart, and it is afterward ground most strongly until it shines, let it be soaked in seawater. Then let it be buried for a week, and afterward whitened by roasting. And when it has been well whitened, and its water restored to it, it is afterward soaked in its own moisture. Then, after the soaking of the moisture, having been roasted until it appears lemon-yellow, it becomes the **Philosophers' Eye-salve** <note>original: "collyrium Philosophorum"</note>; the eyes of one anointed with this can easily behold the secrets of the Philosophers. In the sea of the Moon there is a flat sponge...

Men have olives from which they extract oil, and that is combustible. However, the <term>Oil of the Philosophers</term> is not extracted in this way. The method of making it is thus: We take the olives which we have, clean and whole, and we grind them with their own water: afterward we cook them. Then, placing them in a damp place, we leave them there until they are almost dissolved, and until the oil is separated from its thick body. We also make the dregs descend to the bottom, the water remain in the middle, and the oil flow out on top. 

Afterward, we separate the water; placing [the substance] upon a glowing plate, we soak it with its own water until we see most clearly the flexibility that is in it, and then we bury it in moist horse dung <note>A common alchemical method for providing gentle, consistent heat for fermentation or digestion</note>. Then we dry it and roast it in the Sun, and we repeat this seven times, or until it appears clean and whitest from every defilement. Then we return its water to it, and afterward we roast it until, by constant fanning, it is perfected: this is the <term>Ointment of the Philosophers</term>, which burns without fuel and is not consumed. 

Take my ash of woods, soak it with sea water, placing it in a bath <note>likely a "balneum Mariae" or water bath</note> until its blackness is dissolved, which is called <term>Ethel</term> <note>An Arabic-derived alchemical term for the black substance or "spirit" to be sublimated</note>. **Coral** is a certain vegetable growth, born in the sea, having roots and branches, and it is generated moist. However, when the North Wind blows, it hardens and becomes a red body. When a sailor sees this, he cuts it beneath the waters; but when it emerges, it turns into stone, the color of which is red, and they are also fashioned into the stones of the Indians; the common people use it greatly. In a similar way, the Philosophers use our coral in our art: for they take it and grind it strongly, and soak it in sea water for 21 days, and leave it in a bath with much moisture until its tincturing spirit stands out. Taking this spirit, they place it in a glass vessel and set aside the dregs as if dead—being neither white nor red. Afterward, they place it in that sphere which we call a sieve. Then they soak it with warm sea water, and this is repeated seven times, washing and sublimating, until it receives the form of a most white salt. When this is done, they return the tincturing spirit to it. And then they place it in a moist place until it grows red and is made from its own seed. And the Philosophers place some of this upon glass, and it makes it unbreakable. And when it is placed upon silver, it turns it into **pure gold** <note>original: "aurum obrizon"; highly refined or tested gold</note>.

# ON THE CROWD <note>original: "Super Turbam," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>

They allow it to remain for many days in a damp place, until the sulfur which lies hidden within it <insert>appears</insert>, and here they collect it and store it in a glass vessel. But the body, which remains behind looking somewhat dark, they wash in the water of distilled salt; afterwards, they leave it in the heat of the summer sun, and this process is repeated until it gleams like white marble. Dyers have a certain herb which they use for dyeing wool, taking only the dye and leaving the wood behind. We have a similar process in our Art: we place the substance down, grinding and sifting it, and frequently soaking it in the **urine of boys** <note>A common nitrogenous source used in early chemistry for its ammonia content</note> until it becomes soft. And such will be its dye; afterward, we place it in **horse dung** <note>original: "fimo equino"; used as a natural, steady heat source for digestion or fermentation</note> until its dye is purified and appears upon the body. Receiving this dye, we place it in a glass vessel. We do not cease grinding the body itself with its own moisture and placing it in a damp place to wash it, until it is clothed in snowy whiteness. Afterward, we join it to its own purified dye which we had drawn away from it, and we soak the body with that dye in the hot sun, and thus it receives a miraculous power. ### *ENIGMA I.*

<note>The "Vision of Arisleus" is a foundational alchemical myth describing the symbolic death and rebirth of the king's son, representing the chemical process of transformation.</note>

When certain of the more studious disciples of the Philosophers had gathered together again—Pythagoras, the foremost of whom was Arisleus son of Abladus, then Paris son of Belchiotus, Armenius son of Archia, Meditantalus, Phali-fæus, Echamisius and Parmenides, and Eximesias son of Admirus—Auerca asked of Arisleus whether he might be able, by speaking, to bring it about that the seekers of the art might be permitted, by example or parable, to gather fruit from that immortal tree which the aforementioned disciples of the Philosophers and the others in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous gathering of ancient sages in alchemical lore</note> had described? And he said: I will indeed speak gladly, as I am able, though perhaps not to the full satisfaction of your desire. And Pythagoras said again: Speak, therefore, as aptly as you can.

And he said: I saw myself and certain others from the *Assembly* riding toward the shores of the sea, and behold, the inhabitants of the sea were lying together with one another, yet nothing was being born to them; and they were planting trees, yet they were not bearing fruit; and they were sowing, yet nothing grew. And I said: What is the matter with you? Though you are many, is there no Philosopher among you who might teach you? And they said: What is a Philosopher? He said: One who knows the nature of things. And they: What use is his knowledge? And I: If a Philosopher were among you, your children would be multiplied, and trees would be born for you and would not die, and the fruits would not be extinguished, and you would be kings, overcoming all your enemies.

Going forth, they reported these things to their lord, the King of the Sea. And when we had been summoned by him, and he demanded gifts, we replied: We carry hidden gifts—namely, the art of generating, and of planting trees, and of sowing, and whoever eats from these trees and fruits shall never hunger. And he said: A most great gift, if indeed your master has sent this. Tell me then, what do you have? And I: Lord, although you are a king, yet you command and rule poorly; for...

<summary>Arisleus recounts a vision to the gathered philosophers about a barren undersea kingdom that lacks the alchemical knowledge of generation and growth. He promises the King of the Sea that the "hidden gifts" of the philosophers can bring fertility and immortality to his realm.</summary>

For you have joined males with males, knowing that males do not give birth. For generation is the union of male and female, and true generation occurs if nature is mixed with nature, male with female, like with like, and the fitting with the fitting. And he <note>The King</note> replied: "I indeed have a son and a daughter, and for that reason, I am king of my subjects, since they have none of these; yet I have carried both son and daughter within my own brain." And I said: "Lead your son Thabritius <note>original: "Thabritium"; represents the solar/sulfuric principle</note> to us." Having heard this, I also demanded that his sister Beya <note>original: "Beyam"; represents the lunar/mercurial principle</note> be brought to us. The King said: "Why do you want Beya?" And I: "Because generation does not happen without her, and although she is the sister of her brother, and a female, yet she improves him, because she is of his own essence." When Beya was brought forward, behold, she was a girl white, tender, and sweet. When we joined Thabritius and Beya together, the King said: "Has the man now taken his wife?" And I: "So our father Adam commanded his children, and if you acquiesce in this, O King, you will be blessed, and they will bear for you kings and queens, many grandsons and granddaughters; and your son Thabritius and his sister Beya will gain wealth for you, and if they should die, they will live again."

But when the King consented, and the brother lay with the sister, behold, Thabritius died immediately. Therefore the King, blaming me and you, imprisoned us in a glass house <note>term: "domo vitrea"; the alchemical flask or retort</note>, above which house he built another, and above that yet another, and we were held captive in three houses. Then I said to the King: "For what reason, in your haste, have you brought punishment upon us? At least hand over your daughter to us again; perhaps she is destined to return life to your son Thabritius." And he: "Do you wish to kill my daughter as well?" And I: "Do not be hasty, O King, to inflict tortures upon us; wait a little while, and give us your daughter, and a little later you shall have both son and daughter living again."

When she was handed over, she remained with us in the prison for 80 days, and we remained in the darkness of the waves, and the intense heat of summer, and a disturbance of the sea such as never happened to us before. We, therefore exhausted, saw you, the Master, in our dreams, and we begged that you might know how to help us; and you sent your disciple Harforetus <note>A legendary figure in alchemical literature, often associated with nourishment or the "food" of the stone</note>, who is the author of nourishment. When this was granted, we rejoiced, saying to the King: "Behold, your son lives, who had been given up for dead."

# RIDDLES

## RIDDLE II.
### Concerning the Stone.

There is in our sea a small, round fish, lacking bones and skin, which possesses within itself a fatness and a marvelous virtue. When this is cooked over a silent fire <note>A "silent fire" refers to a slow, steady heat, often a sand bath or lamp</note> until its moisture and fatness are utterly consumed and worn away, it must afterwards be ground most powerfully and soaked in sea water until it becomes soft. Then, it is to be buried for a week; then roasted until it glows white-hot. When it glows and has become sufficiently white, and its water has been returned to it, and it is afterwards soaked in its own proper moisture—and finally, after the soaking of the moisture, it is roasted until it appears lemon-yellow—it becomes the "Eye-salve of the Philosophers" <note>original: "collyrium Philosophorum"; a metaphorical medicine to grant spiritual or intellectual sight</note>. When the eyes are anointed with this liquid, the secrets of the Philosophers can easily be seen and understood.

## RIDDLE III.

There is a Root which should be ground while its stalk is green or juicy, using its own proper humidity, in the Sun. Afterwards, let these be sent to the bath <note>The "balneum" or Mary's Bath (bain-marie), a gentle water-heating method</note> and washed until its spirit—or the salt of the root—and the pure, liquid wash appears as if it were a dye. This must be collected in its entirety, and the body (or the black dregs and remaining scales) must be thoroughly washed away in the bath. For a certain flowing and defiled thing resides within them, which cannot be plucked out except by laborious and subtle ingenuity. Therefore, let the body be taken and washed, and ground at the lukewarm heat of a fire, and bedewed little by little with sea water until it is most fully whitened. Once whitened, its spirit or wash shall be returned to it, and in the fullness of time, it becomes a firm and perfect Elixir <note>The "Elixir" is the perfected medicinal or transformative substance of alchemy</note>. This root is also sublimated through a cold retort, and it turns into mercury <note>original: "mercuriascit"; the process of becoming fluid or metallic like quicksilver</note>.

## RIDDLE IV.

Take a Viper, and deprive it of its head and tail; for in these two places rests the venom from which it proceeds. Divide the head and the tail, and place each by itself in a glass vessel. Take the remainder of the body and cook it over a slow fire until the flesh is separated from the bones. Afterwards, place it upon a plate and cook it for so long until the body is turned into spirit, and there is taken away from it—

### RIDDLE V.
->*Mercury speaks of himself.*<-

My mother bore me, and through me she herself is born: they once ruled over me; but henceforth I shall rule over her: because I have become the persecutor of my mother. Yet she now cherishes me as a pious mother, and nourishes her son whom she bore, until he shall come to a perfect state. Therefore, place me in a moist fire, and grind me until the end of the work is brought about. Then, when the work is perfected, drive me to redness with a strong fire. For the moisture of heat increases me, and the consumption of dryness kills me.

### RIDDLE VI.

Lay a red servant equally over a pregnant mother: mortify the mother, cutting off her hands and feet: bathe the servant himself, and betroth these two in a glass cloth <note>likely referring to a glass vessel or lining</note>, which is called a *Sera* <note>a bolt or lock</note>, and place a *Thonar* <note>an Athanor, or alchemical furnace</note> above it: and seal it well with the **clay of Wisdom** <note>original: "luto Sapientiæ"; a specialized sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>. And then take the glass with the bridegroom and bride, and cast them into the furnace, and cause them to roast for three days, and then the two shall be in one flesh. Finally, take that white man from the vessel, and grind him through a mill, and add to him the **key of the art** with the eagle <note>the "eagle" often symbolizes sublimation or volatile spirits</note>, and grind again with olive oil until it is dried. Do this three times, and it possesses the limit of perfection.

# EXERCISES ON THE ASSEMBLY OF THE PHILOSOPHERS <note>original: "In Turbam Philosophorum." The Turba Philosophorum is one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate between ancient sages.</note>

## DEFINITION OF THE STONE, AND of which beginnings it consists.

### EXERCISE I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring swirling vines and foliage.</image-desc>As we are about to treat the Stone of the Philosophers <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note>, we must first see from what beginnings or from what elements the Stone of the Philosophers consists. By the consideration of all Philosophers, therefore, Mercury is the father of all metals. Moreover, the Philosophical Stone is a metallic matter, converting the substances and forms of imperfect metals. Furthermore, it has long since been proclaimed by all Philosophers that this conversion does not happen except through its own kind. It is necessary, therefore, for the Stone of the Philosophers to be birthed from metallic matter. From which metallic species it may be generated, however, is what all the Philosophers declare, especially saying in this little book: In Mercury is all that which is sought by the Wise. For by the same reasoning that its substance or form is joined to those bodies, it takes on such substance and form: and just as it is tinted by the bodies, so also it tints: and just as flesh is generated...

Just as flesh is formed from coagulated blood, so too is **Gold** <note>original: "Sol" (the Sun), the alchemical name for Gold</note> generated from coagulated **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>: and just as blood is the origin of flesh, so is Mercury the origin of Gold: and just as blood is within the flesh, so also is Mercury within the stone of Gold: because Mercury itself is congealed into the stone of Gold, and thus Mercury is Gold, and its Gold is Mercury. And all metallic bodies are Mercury, both the pure and the impure, because they are generated from it. And as Mercury is the beginning of all metals, so Gold is the end and the ultimate of metals; and all metals, clean and unclean, are inwardly Gold, Silver <note>original: "Luna" (the Moon)</note>, and Mercury: but there is one true Gold, which is extracted from them: concerning which much is said in this book.

## *ON NATURAL HEAT.*
### *EXERCISE II.*
### *EXIMIDIVS.* <note>Likely a corruption of a Greek name, possibly Archimedes or a similar authority cited in the Turba Philosophorum</note>

Natural heat is described as that which is present in all created things, especially in minerals: for the Philosophers <note>The Alchemists</note> have need of it: because this heat of nature, by the power of the heat of fire, digests their matter into the proper form and species. For this reason, some have said that the **Philosophers' Stone** is a pure matter, which is of the nature of gold, containing within itself a heat that gives growth, and by its own force and power has the ability to grow and multiply in its own kind, just like all other things.

And indeed these natures agree in their root, which is the "ore of metals," but they are distinguished by accident <note>a philosophical term meaning non-essential or external qualities</note>. A seventh nature is added, namely, the **Mercurial**, which belongs to the other natures—that is, the common matter. This Mercurial nature is composed of the two first simple natures, namely the elemental ones: specifically the nature of water and the nature of earth. For in that mixture, earth is converted into water by the mediation of fire.

Not that earth becomes water, but in such a way that the earth, by means of its dryness through the operation of the heat of fire, causes the moisture of the water to consist with its coldness, so that the nature of water is still observed—which is fluidity in one part—but it loses the other part, which is wetting. Therefore, it is rendered a **dry water**, which flows and does not moisten. Moreover, it is evident that it is composed of earth through the operation of fire: for by an excess of heat, the entire substance of Mercury is converted into red earth. For everything is resolved into that from which it is made, and is properly terminated in itself: because it is gathered into a ball with that which flows. Furthermore, it is evident that it is from water: because it flows, and is not contained by its own boundary, but by the resistance of another's <note>a classic Aristotelian definition of a liquid</note>; for fluidity is from the nature of water. Now, the mercurial nature is the *hyle* <note>original: "ὕλη" - Greek for "prime matter" or "substance"</note>, the common matter for all metals.

But because generation is a movement, and in every movement there is an agent and a patient <note>In medieval philosophy, the "agent" is the active force and the "patient" is the passive matter being acted upon.</note>, two things therefore concur in the generation of a human: namely, the agent <term>which</term> <note>original: "qđ" (quod)</note> is the male, and the patient which is the female. These two sperms are mixed during the union of intercourse and are cast into the field of nature—that is, into the womb of the woman.

Thus, from the intrinsic power of the two sperms (which is called the formative power) and the heat of the container (namely, the womb), the human body is formed, which is nourished by the menstrual blood. These two mercuries are joined together according to the proper proportion, and also with the menstrual Mercury, according to...

# ON THE FIRST ELEMENT
## *Of the Stone, which is Earth.*
### EXERCISE IV.
#### P Y T H A G O R A S.

IN this all Philosophers agree with one voice: that the purest and most subtle earthy substance should be chosen, whether red or white, with which the red or white Mercury <term>Mercury: here referring to the "spirit" or volatile principle of the work</term> is joined in the smallest parts, and fixed until they become one and inseparable. This earthy substance, moreover, is either of the Moon <note>Silver</note>, or of the Sun <note>Gold</note>, or of some imperfect body, or of Mercury alone. Regarding the Moon and Sun, I hold my view; regarding Venus <note>Copper</note>, Arnold of Villanova <note>A famous 13th-century alchemist and physician</note> holds his; regarding Mercury, Geber the Arab <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy</note> holds his. And again, if we must consider whether it comes from the Moon or the Sun, it may perhaps be in doubt whether their "earth" is raw, or whether they are the dregs left over from sulfur; but it must be judged that the earth is from the raw state of either the Moon or the Sun—indeed, from the Sun alone. 

However, the mind of Arnold is not to be disparaged, for he relies on this reason: that every tincture <term>Tincture: the potent medicine or elixir capable of transforming metals</term> must contain the stone that enters into it, and must consist of that which it intends to color. If, therefore, you wish to color Venus with your stone, it will be necessary to have received the earth from Venus as well. This earth is made through calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</note>, and is turned into ash; and the ash, through sublimation <note>The process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note>, is turned into the quintessence <term>Quintessence: the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual core of a substance</term>; and the quintessence, through solution, is turned into water; and the water, through coagulation, is turned into the stone, in which is the beginning of the mastery. For from it, the water and the mineral earth are extracted again; when this earth has been calcined and whitened, it admits its vapor once more, and fixes and unites it in an inseparable union. This is accomplished entirely by purification or sublimation, which is followed by fermentation and nourishment.

It outlines the alchemical cycle of purification—calcination, sublimation, and solution—required to reach the "mastery" of the stone.</summary>

# ON THE RELEASE OF WATER
## or the Dewing upon the earth.

### EXERCISE V.

#### ARISTENES.

This must be noted here above all else: that neither the simple water of the sea alone, nor the copper <note>original: "æs"; in alchemy, this often refers to the "bronze" or "copper" of the sages, a base metallic principle</note> itself alone, can do anything toward the Philosopher’s Stone, or constitute the Stone itself. Neither the Stone, nor the Elixir, can consist of simple water alone or copper alone; rather, it is necessary for both—that is, the simple water and the copper—to be joined together. But before you join or mix these two, namely the copper and the water, see to it that neither is raw or unrectified. Instead, let the water itself be distilled several times and finally restored to its proper state and descent; and let the copper itself be burnt <note>calcined</note> until it is made white and entirely pure. For once these are thus prepared, one may proceed to the Elixir. For if the copper itself were not pure, it is certain that the earth elicited from it would be raw and impure—indeed, perhaps none would be produced at all. Likewise, if the water were not clean and distilled, it would be unable to wash and cleanse the earth itself. For that which is filthy and black is not whitened by the filthy or the black, but by the pure, the clear, and the clean. Therefore, once both are purified, let the copper—beaten into very thin plates and torn into pieces—be mixed with the water.

# EXERCISE

Turn the obscure into the bright, return the moist into the dry, and fix the volatile into its own body. To dissolve is to divide and to corrupt, and to create the *first matter* <note>Latin: *materia prima*, the primitive, formless base of all substance</note>. To wash away is to bury, to distill, and to calcine <note>to reduce a substance to powder through heat</note>. To reduce is to enrich, to wax, and to refine. To fix is to betroth, to resolve, and to coagulate. Through the first, nature works internally; through the second, externally; through the third, above; and through the fourth, below. But the moderns disturb the end of the work: because when they cease to labor, they should instead have only just begun. But one, in dissolving, is [merely] dissolving and coagulating; another is dissolving and fixing; another disturbs the middle, and another the end: thus they hesitate in the art like fools. In short, I say to you, they do not make a tincture <note>an alchemical essence capable of transmuting metals</note> worth a single coin unless all things have been properly digested by conversion into nature, so that in the beginning the thick is converted into the slender—that is, the body into water—then the water into a body or earth. Then you must add, or rather instill, the soul: which happens if you add the soul with the water—that is, the spirit—to the body. Finally, you must nourish such an animated body with its own milk—that is, with its own water—from which the work was created or begun from the start. Regarding the mixing, it is taught that the proportion should relate to one another such that there are three parts of water to one of lead, or better, two of copper to seven of poison <note>Latin: *veneni*; likely referring to mercury or a potent chemical catalyst</note>, as Zeno says later. # ON THE MARRIAGE of the Sun & Moon.

## EXERCISE VII.

### ZIMON.

This Philosopher <note>Zimon is one of the speakers in the "Turba Philosophorum," an influential early Latin alchemical text</note> seems to suggest that both perfect bodies <note>The "perfect bodies" refer to Gold and Silver</note> should be taken for the composition of the Elixir, whether it is intended to be white or yellow <note>White refers to the silver-making stage; yellow/citrine refers to the gold-making stage</note>. The reason is that neither flows easily without the other. Now, the goal of the entire Alchemical secret is that the Elixir should flow immediately—that is, before the flight of the Mercury <note>Mercury is "volatile" and tends to evaporate or "fly" when heated; the goal is to "fix" it so it stays liquid and stable</note>. However, I read no authors, or very few, who recommend this, or who say when these two bodies—namely the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "Solis scilicet & Lunae"; the Sun represents Gold and the Moon represents Silver</note>—should be applied: whether at the beginning of the work, such as in the solution, or at the end, namely in the fermentation. Therefore, let whoever wishes to do so see what should be done and chosen.

This method does not please me very much. Because if it were done this way, the Elixir would necessarily be neither white nor yellow, but of a mixed color. Yet it is possible that this opinion should be interpreted thus: when the Elixir is intended for the red stage <note>The "rubedo," or final perfection of the Alchemical work</note>, let the filings of the Moon be taken first and dissolved with Mercury, and from those joined together let the earth or substance of the Elixir be gathered. Then, let the process continue through all stages using these two—namely Mercury and the Moon—until the fermentation is reached, where only the ferment of the Sun should be received, without adding anything further of the Moon.

Although the Elder Philosopher <note>original: "Senior Philosophus," likely referring to the author Senior Zadith</note> thinks it necessary for three lights to be wedded in the mixing of the work (or of the waters)—namely the Sun, the Moon, and the Serpent <note>The "Serpent" usually represents Mercury or the raw, transformative chemical agent</note>—and says that one of these is the brother and the other the sister of the serpent, through whom he says the serpent can be hardened and restrained. But in my judgment, he errs. For it is enough to bring the serpent to his own sister. The cause of the error is this: because the Sun is not terrified <note>In alchemical terms, "terrified" or "frightened" often refers to a substance being broken down or reacting violently</note> on account of its perfection, as I believe. But if it were purified in a similar way, then nothing would stand in the way: because

->it would be joined to both the Moon and the Serpent.<-

# THAT THE FOUNDATION OF THE ART *is one certain thing, and the Stone is one.*

## EXERCISE VIII.

MANY contend through long disputes that the Stone consists either of diverse things, or of two, or of only one thing, using various names. But this Philosopher—and Bonellus <note>A common authority cited in the 'Turba Philosophorum'.</note> below—say that the entire work and the substance of the entire work is nothing other than water: and its governance consists in nothing other than in water. For the former is simple and pure, while the latter is composed of two things, namely from our brass <note>original: "ære"; likely referring to 'aes' or 'latten', a base metal to be transformed.</note> and simple water. Moreover, these two waters joined together make the Mercury of the Philosophers. Therefore, it must be believed that the substance or the primary matter itself is from composite water. ## ON THE SOLUTION AND DIVI-
## sion of the Elements.
# EXERCISE IX.
->ZENON<- <note>Zenon is one of the speakers/philosophers featured in the Turba Philosophorum.</note>

In the Alchemical work, it is necessary first of all to plainly mortify <note>To "mortify" means to kill or strip away the outward form of a substance, often through heat or acid, to release its inner essence.</note> and exhaust the stone—that is, the body, soul, and spirit—since nothing produces fruit in this art unless it has first been mortified. But the separation of the elements of the mortified [matter] occurs, and the effect of each element is shown: Therefore, if you wish to make the Elixir, it will be necessary first that you entirely dissolve the stone itself into its elements, which is signified to us by the parts of the year <note>A reference to the "Philosophical Year," the time required for the various stages of the work to complete.</note>: Then you must join those same Elements through fire, with Mercury mediating, which is the greatest secret <term>arcanum: a hidden or secret mystery of nature</term>, and thus the mastery is completed, and the entire artifice is situated in dissolving and joining. These solutions or separations, however, are made with Mercury mediating: for it first dissolves the body and makes the separations, which are joined together again through the ferment.

But here it must be carefully noted that Mercury is called "Water" at the beginning of the work; then, when the blackness appears, it is called "Earth"; then, when it has been sublimated <note>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material</note>, it is called "Air"; then, when it has been turned red (for the Air must be cooked by itself until it reddens), it is called "Fire."
