And thus Earth with Water, Air, and Fire is the Body; the Ferment is the Soul; and the final watering is the Spirit of Mercury alone. Thus it is clear, therefore, that the Stone consists of the four elements, namely: water, air, fire, and earth. For in the Stone there are soul, body, and spirit, and yet it is one Stone, as was said above, which must be dissolved and again coagulated. Under "dissolution," all operations are included up to the whitening of the stone; after the whitening, it is cooked again, and becomes a stone once more while it is coagulated; then it is dissolved again, once the ferment is obtained; and that dissolution is repeated until the stone flows like wax.

# ON THE DISSOLUTION OF BODIES into water, concerning the Gum and the division of water.

->THE WORLD.<-

Our most precious stone is generated from water; it is therefore necessary in the beginning to dissolve every thing into water. As for his making a composition of four of them here, they are but two; he gives the gum itself three names, but in truth he calls the copper <note>original: "aes"</note> itself the "gum of the body," and rightly so. Then he adds that the King <note>a symbol for the developing Stone or Gold</note> ought to be nourished seven times, which methods he reviews and teaches in order.

If the previous teaching does not please you, this Philosopher brings forward another, which we shall explain aptly in this form.
Let there be taken of the water extracted from the stone its own weight—that is, equal to the stone—and let the stone itself and the water be well mixed together, and placed under the governance of its own fire, and let care be taken that it does not flow out. But let it be noted that the stone must be dissolved four times; and one must proceed with it through all steps, as the Philosopher suggests. And as many times as the stone is dissolved, so many times must that solution be guarded with the Seal of Hermes <note>original: "sigillo Hermetis"; an airtight or hermetic seal</note> until the Elixir itself is seen to be coagulated: then calcined and once more reduced to powder. And in the fourth dissolution (the Philosophers say) the greatest care must be taken lest the Elixir flow and become glass; for should that happen, it would be of no use. For the Elixir must be calcined—that is, reduced to powder—not vitrified <note>turned into glass</note>. However, the flowing of the Elixir may be avoided if the fire is governed with good reason—that is, very gently. And even if the Philosopher says here that the fire should be made more intense, let it nevertheless be kept perpetually in memory that the fire from the beginning of the work until the end should be one, in the likeness of an infant in the mother's womb. 

Next, let it be noted that the Philosopher here calls the clean white substance the "already fermented stone"; then, when he says the body ought to be soaked seven times, he means those two-thirds are to be divided into seven parts and soaked seven times. ### EXERCISE XII.

#### THEOPHILUS.

Theophilus teaches here that the poison <note>original: "venenum"; a common alchemical term for the transformative solvent or "mercury of the philosophers"</note> must be divided into two equal parts. With one of these, the copper is to be liquefied; with the other, it is to be ground and saturated. Let the parts of the Elixir be two to seven, or three to one, and let there be a fire of proper putrefaction. It must be thought that the Philosophers order the water to be divided into two parts for this reason: to signify that the Elixir, after fermentation, requires as much water for saturation and to be moistened or "nourished" seven times, as the amount by which the dissolved copper itself was carried. And when the said portion has been applied to the Elixir through seven cycles after nourishment, then the Elixir is mature for dyeing <note>original: "tingendum"; the final stage where the Elixir transforms base metals into gold or silver</note>. However, some teach that before the said sevenfold imbibition or nourishment, the Elixir itself must be completely dissolved by the water which they call Vinegar <note>original: "Acetum"; not household vinegar, but a specialized alchemical acid</note>; this is difficult both to believe and to do, and it is to be feared lest the Elixir, already brought to life, be strangled by that dissolution. However the matter stands, this must be perpetually observed: that you pour only as much water onto the Elixir in one soaking as you judge necessary, little by little, and more frequently. In this way, it will be possible to pour over it seven times, or even fourteen times. If you do this, the Elixir grows little by little, and it will seek an increase roughly every eight days, as if gaping and thirsty, and it will acquire its rightful strength. On the contrary, if you use immoderate water beyond what is sufficient, it will drink voraciously, and it will weaken all its strength. And I would think a twentieth portion of water in the increase—

How much water you ought to use in the fermentation, you have gathered from the previous sections. However, how much the vessel should be opened, you must gather from natural reason. <meta>This page continues the discourse on the "Turba Philosophorum" (Assembly of the Philosophers), specifically focusing on the regulation of heat and the composition of the Alchemical Elixir.</meta>

# ON THE ASSEMBLY. 115

At that time, it is not expedient to use a stronger fire than that used for dissolving, putrefying, washing, fermenting, or nourishing. For this reason, countless artisans have been deceived, who immediately after the dissolution and washing, proceed to coagulate and calcine <note>Calcinate: to reduce a substance to powder through high heat.</note> with an increased heat of the Sun: by which error they burn the matter. Because when it is necessary for the matter to be dissolved, it can then only be dissolved with far greater difficulty. It is necessary, however, for the matter to be, as it were, "killed," not converted into glass. Wherefore the Philosophers say: "By a gentle fire you shall perform every decoction <note>Decoction: the process of boiling or heating a substance to extract its essence.</note>, and you shall find all knowledge; if you do otherwise, you will not rejoice in your work." Therefore, great power lies in the *governance of the fire* <note>original: "regimine ignis"</note>. For a strong fire vitrifies <note>Turns into glass.</note> and scorches, while a gentle fire dissolves and cooks the matter, and renders it mature. For we see in conception, right up to the birth, that the heat (unless it happens accidentally, that is, not naturally) does not change in the mother's womb, but is always the same. Therefore, the same gentle heat must be used continuously in the work, right up to the nourishment. Many write that the fire must be strengthened after coagulation, so that the coagulated substance itself may be worn down by the fire. If this way proves useful, I do not object to anyone trying it who wishes. For my part, I believe it must be perpetually observed that when you have moistened the dry substance, you should be sparing with the fire of the coals, until the dry substance has sweetly drunk in that which was offered to it. This you will be able to see if you recognize that the water offered has been devoured. When that is done, then perhaps there is need for a more liberal furnace, due to the great drying of the cooked body, followed immediately by another moistening, which must be proceeded with by adhering to and serving it in a similar manner.

one must use. The meaning of the Spirit is unknown to no one. The Soul, however, is that which vivifies <note>gives life to</note> and gives being to the body and the spirit, and the soul is made from the vivified body itself. For in this place we believe the soul to be nothing other than the vivified body: it is vivified in such a way that it is returned into quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, just as it was before it was coagulated. And if this soul is added to the mortified body and spirit, so that at last the whole Elixir becomes alive: then finally it is to be believed that the alchemical goal has been reached. 

The **Body**, moreover, is called earth, bronze, lead, ash, magnesia, lime, mother, key, holy virgin, king's crown, Talc, Path, glass, golden wood, spirit of brightness, sea, salt, urine, alum, gum of Scotland, sulfur water, spit of the Moon <note>silver</note>, white gum, etc.

The **Soul** is called *Rebis* <note>original: "Rebis," a term for the alchemical hermaphrodite or "double-thing"</note>, fetid water, cleanliness of the dead, blood, water of blood, animal stone, blessed stone, etc. 

Furthermore, there are mutual duties between these three, because the spirit guards the body so that it is not consumed by the fire. And the clear body guards the spirit so that it does not fly away from the fire: because the body is fixed, it preserves the spirit from fleeing, and the spirit is incombustible: therefore it does not allow the body to be burned, because the spirit and body are one through the mediation of the soul, which is present with the spirit and the body. But if the soul were not there, then the spirit and the body would be separated from one another by the fire; but with the soul joined to the spirit and the body, this whole does not care for the fire, nor any thing of the world.

But it is also necessary to observe this in the augmentation: that when the increase is applied to the stone, the increase itself should thereafter be continued through all types of decoction <note>The process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or achieve a chemical change</note> in a tempered fire.

<meta>This page serves as a printer's preface to the reader, explaining the omission of certain allegorical sections found in earlier versions of the manuscript. It establishes a transition from the introductory material to the core alchemical text.</meta>

# THE PRINTER
->To the Reader.<-

FRIENDLY Reader: *You should know that here, at the beginning of this book—truly titled the Golden Hour—we have deliberately omitted an entire treatise of Parables, or allegories. In these allegories, following the ancient custom of those who dwell in darkness (as the times and ages then allowed), the author dragged almost the whole of Holy Scripture—especially the writings of Solomon and the Psalmist <note>The "Psalmist" refers to King David, traditionally credited with the Psalms.</note> himself, and most particularly the Song of Songs—into an allegorical interpretation of Alchemy, even against the text's will. He did this to such an extent that it might seem (if we believe him) that all those works were written for no other reason than for the honor and praise of Alchemy. Indeed—and this is an impious thing—he profanely twisted the most sacred mystery of the Incarnation and death of Christ our Lord into the mystery of the Stone <note>The "Stone" refers to the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting immortality.</note>, along with many other principal monuments of our faith. I do not believe this was done with evil intent (for the author otherwise appears pious), but rather as that age of darkness permitted. Since they were ignorant of the true interpretation of the Holy Scriptures, they forced the texts to serve their own ridiculous inventions, and thought they were touching the truth with their very finger. Therefore, judging it unworthy and a sin for Holy Scripture to be so ineptly forced to serve arts of this kind, I have desired, as much as was in my power, to claim it back and restore it to its proper liberty and honor. This is especially so since those allegories can bring no understanding or utility to this business, but can only greatly offend pious and learned ears. However, he who wishes to be more curious may either transcribe them for himself or read them as printed by others (if indeed anyone wishes to spend their money so poorly). For us, we wish to be satisfied with the small treatise on Allegories drawn from the inventions of the Philosophers and the very inner secrets of the art itself, which we printed above, following the Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: "Turba," referring to the 'Turba Philosophorum,' one of the oldest European alchemical texts.</note>.*

*Farewell.*

<meta>catchword: AURORA</meta>

<summary>The printer explains his decision to censor certain sections of the original manuscript that interpreted the Bible as an alchemical allegory, arguing that such "dark" medieval interpretations disrespect the Christian faith. He directs interested readers to other editions if they wish to find the omitted mystical parables.</summary>

# THE RISING DAWN:
## WHICH IS CALLED THE GOLDEN HOUR, and in its second Treatise,

### PROLOGUE.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring ornate floral and scrollwork patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

IN the aforementioned things, it has been shown to the intelligent person, through the authorities of the Holy Scriptures, that this science <note>The "science" referred to here is Alchemy, often called the "Art" or "Divine Science" by medieval authors.</note> is nothing other than a gift of God and a Sacrament <note>original: "Sacramentum"</note> enveloped in various symbolic speeches, parabolic sayings, and even problems and mystical revolutions. This was done so that the dull-witted and foolish—who are ignorant of nature even if they know how to read their A.B.C.D.—might not draw it to themselves and usurp it. Therefore, for those desiring this science, it is necessary to sharpen the intellect very subtly and ingeniously, and often—indeed, very often—to turn and return the sayings of the wise inside and out, before and behind. For it is not the way of the wise to speak foolishly, even when the meaning of their words is greatly opposed to the sound of the letters themselves. For he who accepts the sound of the words but does not possess the interior understanding finds nothing of use to him; for to him is said that which is written:
> To read and not to understand is to neglect.
What, then, does it seem to you who strive for this divine wisdom, you who take the matter according to the sound of the letters, and least of all consider whether that which is hoped for is in it or not? Do you imitate nature, or do you deprive it? Or what fruit do you have, in the end of which you are ashamed?
> Not so the impious, not so; but they are like the dust which the wind casts away from the face of the earth. <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 1:4, applied here to failed alchemists.</note>
Such will be the operations of those who work without nature and understanding. For Alexander <note>Likely referring to Alexander the Great, to whom many medieval alchemical works were apocryphally attributed.</note> says: If you wish to dissolve snow with cold, you coagulate it more; and if you wish to cool water with fire, you heat it more; and if you turn any nature to its opposite, you corrupt your work further. Have you not read many times that the secret of secrets <note>original: "arcanum arcanorum"</note> and the treasure of treasures is not placed in the path of those passing by? For if it were placed so publicly, the secret—

Is the Son of God truly a vine? Neither is Christ a vine, for they are vastly different things; nor is his Heavenly Father a farmer, nor is the farmer the Father. If you solve one of the smallest points, the greatest will not remain hidden from you. Because of the "little ones" <note>The humble or beginning students of the art.</note>, a five-fold doctrine is placed in this little book, offering something of use to those who search ingeniously: first, by which foreign sciences this science is surrounded; second, which styles of speaking it enjoys; third, to which things it is naturally likened; fourth, by which modes of operation it is carried out and concerning the power of its perfection; and fifth, how anyone may use it as a medicine for the human body.

It is therefore clearer than light from the aforesaid that every species of vegetable has its own disposition, by which it is tempered and changed by the power of one Planet, and is assimilated and attributed to it by the power of two or more Planets, according to what it is able to receive. 

That which is attributed to it assists each property: namely, the <term>first natural power</term> <note>The primary formative force in a living thing</note>, which must be present, establishes its species, such as in taste, color, smell, and shape. And the <term>natural soul</term> <note>The 'anima vegetabilis' or life-force that directs growth and survival</note> collects all properties and natural powers from it, and imitates through them, and makes them endure for as great a space of time as they define and designate for it by their power: because there is no act without motion, and there is no operation without a limit.

# TREATISE ON ASTRO-
## nomy. CHAPTER I.

It must first be understood that this divine science of Astronomy uses terms according to the course of the Planets and their influences, as well as the number and power of the twelve signs of the Zodiac circle. This is as Aristotle <note>The author refers to the "Secretum Secretorum," a text popularly attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages, which links astrology to alchemy.</note> testifies to Alexander, saying: That Saturn holds the earth, Mercury the water, Jupiter the air, and the Sun the fire. This is because everything lacking light among the number of growing things <note>original: "vegetabilium"</note> is ruled by Saturn and attributed to him. And whatever growing thing is flowering but not bearing fruit is attributed to Mars and ruled by him. And every flowering and fruitful growing thing is attributed to the Sun and ruled by him. 

And again he adds: Then compose and join these divisions and days; every growing thing bearing fruit but not flowering, such as the apple <note>likely referring to the pomegranate or "earth apple"</note> and the palm, is attributed to Saturn and the Sun. And every flowering thing not bearing fruit is ruled by Mercury and Mars. Behold how Astronomy weaves this gift of God together with the powers of the Planets. 

For Aristotle says that every growing thing lacking light is ruled by Saturn. He intends this to mean the black and dreg-filled earth <note>The "nigredo" or black stage of the alchemical process</note>. And every flowering and luminous thing is ruled by Mercury; he means the first whitening <note>original: "dealbationem"</note> of that same earth. And every flowering thing not bearing fruit is ruled by Mars; he means the termination, or the reduction to ashes <term>incineration: the process of reducing a substance to ashes through heat</term> after the whiteness, which is called incineration. And every flowering, fruitful thing is ruled by the Sun; he means the tincture <note>the final color-changing agent</note> is now complete. 

For the author of the *Three Words* <note>A reference to the alchemical text "Liber de XXX verbis"</note> says that in the fetus during the first month, when the seed is conceived by the womb, Saturn works by congealing and constricting the womb itself and the matter into a single mass by his coldness and dryness. In the second month, Jupiter works by his heat and moisture, digesting the matter into a certain fleshy mass which is called an embryo. In the third month, Mars works by his heat and dryness, digesting and separating that matter into limbs. In the fourth month, the Sun works by sending in the spirit of life. ### *Natural sayings according to the process*
### *of nature. CHAPTER III.*

Consequently, natural science—just as it is the concern of physicians and natural philosophers—has surrounded this comforting, treasury-like science <note>The "treasury-like science" refers to Alchemy</note> with its own processes, as the Philosophers have established this in many places of their writings. For they say: things are not made except according to their own natures, such as a human from a human, or a lion from a lion. And Aristotle says: The most natural of works is to generate such a thing as itself is, as a plant produces a plant, or a cow a cow. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> says: Nothing suits a thing except that which is closest to it in its own nature, and a similar offspring is generated in that thing. This means: if you seek a medicine that cures metals <note>The "medicine" is the Elixir or Stone intended to "heal" base metals into gold</note>, its origin shall be from metals, since a species is tinted by its own genus. And Senior <note>Senior Zadith, an influential Arabic alchemist known in Latin as Senior</note> says: The seed of the man, cast into the womb of the woman, adheres to it for seven days through its thinness and subtlety, until it is curdled in all the members of the woman; it reaches the flesh and becomes flesh; it reaches the bones and becomes bone; it reaches the nerves and hair and becomes like them. It is curdled, however, in 10 days, and becomes like cheese; it turns red in 17 days, and its color becomes like the color of flesh. On the twenty-fourth day, it is discerned to have members very similar to hairs; then in 40 days, it is formed into the shape of a human, and the soul appears in it. From the 40th day, it begins to be nourished by the menstrual blood through its passage to the navel. The soul begins from the blood and hardens, and the infant grows and hardens gradually and is shaped. When nine months are completed, that by which it was nourished is cut off, and it ascends to the woman's breast and becomes there like a crown, and it becomes its nourishment after its departure from the womb. And this was said for the sake of the designation and preparation of the Stone, and according to this they prepared it. Understand, therefore, this natural process, and others such as how a chick is formed in an egg—in which there was no chick—through the putrefaction <note>In alchemy, "putrefaction" refers to the breakdown of matter to allow for new life/form</note> caused by the heat of the hen. And thus the various processes of nature—

## On the parabolic style of Mother Alchemy.
### CHAPTER IV.

Above all things, however, it must be noted that this secret of secrets <note>original: "arcanum arcanorum"</note> chiefly employs a parabolic, problematic, and even a symbolic style through circumlocution <note>The author explains that alchemists use "riddles" and "roundabout speech" to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note>. For the Philosophers have used various deceptions in their analogies, but the understanding in all of them is the same: therefore, the parabolic style is placed here first, and after this, others in order. For King Artus <note>Likely referring to "Artus" or "Arthephius," a legendary alchemical authority often cited in medieval texts.</note> relates in his fourth book that the noble treasurer, Mother Alchemy, proposes to seek a medicinal medicine among the powers of herbs, with which she might be able to cure and refresh her sick body, so that it might be released from its infirmity and healed. Then, having already received a double-colored hue of splendor and brightness from the Moon and the Sun, she is so colored that from the top of her head down to her breast, her body is golden; and from the part of the breast down to the thigh, the body appears silver; and from the thigh down to the knees, the body appears dropsical <note>term: dropsical (hydropicum) — an old medical term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid; here it likely represents a stage of the alchemical process involving excess moisture.</note>; and from the knees down to the sole of the foot, the body indicates a paralytic state. Therefore, Mother Alchemy is said to have a sick body, because she cannot raise herself up, nor rise; therefore she is weakened. And she sent messengers to the most skilled Physician and master of all herbs, Macer <note>A reference to "Aemilius Macer," the traditional name associated with a famous medieval herbal; here he represents the expert in natural substances.</note>, who cures and heals languid bodies with the powers of herbs, asking that he should come to her and gather the most natural, better, and stronger herbs, and bring them with him, so that he might release her from the dropsical and paralytic infirmity. On account of which, if she should then be healed and find a remedy, she would wish to enrich him and reward him most bountifully. Master Macer, consenting to her petitions, went to Mount Mambracus, in which he gathered many and most noble herbs, the best, strongest, and most noble: and as he thus ascended the mountain, he saw a beautiful herb colored with various hues, which he pulled out by the roots, and he conjectured that he had never seen a more fragrant and courtly herb; and he descended to the most noble Mother Alchemy, and came in haste...

There they will remain, although the amount is small, and even though blackness dominates it; nevertheless, the earth has been given its temperament, and you will perceive many colors within it. The wise man names this **Earth of Wisdom**, **Bronze**, or **Lead**. You shall therefore address it with a strong fire for a "lesser number" of four days; for a "middle number" of seven; and for a "greater number" of ten <note>These numbers likely refer to specific astrological or symbolic timing cycles in the laboratory</note>. The second part of it, which flows, is called the **Water of Wisdom**. The third part is the **White Earth**; you must cause this to distill four times for the lesser and middle numbers, and for the greatest number of seven days, and then it is called **Apparent Gold**. 

The fourth part is a great white substance, and it is called the **Air of Wisdom**, **Golden Gum**, or **Red Sulfur**. Now, take one part of this "air" and mix it with three parts of the "apparent gold." Place it in a bath <note>A water bath or 'balneum Mariae' used for gentle heating</note> for a lesser number of 20 days, a middle of 30, and a maximum of 40. Afterward, distill it, and there will remain the bronze which the wise call the **Desired Body** and **Apparent Gold**; it is also called **Singular Gold**. 

Divide this singular gold into two parts and place those parts in a wide vessel until a third part recedes toward the Sun <note>Evaporates or reaches a state of solar perfection</note>; then it is called by the wise the **Water of Life** or **Alum**. 

Take, therefore, the golden gum and govern it with the singular gold. Place it in the bath for the lesser number of 20 days, the middle of 30, and the maximum of 40. You will then find the singular gold running over the black sulfur; it will become **Red Singular Gold**. Remove and reserve it; it is called the **Tincture of Wisdom**. It is the "fire of the dyers" and the recipient of many masculine names; it is the spirit and the soul which makes pilgrims return to their homeland <note>A metaphor for the elements returning to their perfected, original state</note>. It is called the **Fire of Purple Gold**, and the black sulfur is called the **Exhausted Old Woman**. 

Take this "exhausted old woman" and mix her with the earth of alum, and cover it with the singular gold. Roast it for the lesser number of 3, and the middle and maximum of 7. There will remain your **White Gum**, bright and clear, similar to the body that is glorified on the Day of Judgment; it is called by the wise the **Virgin's Milk**. 

The water which you extracted from this milk, reserve it; you shall whiten and congeal it, and you will possess the "division of all bodies," which nothing can resist. We now have two waters—namely, the **Singular Gold** and the **Division**—and likewise two ointments: the **Purple Golden Gum** and the **Virgin's Milk**. The third of these is the vehicle, namely, the body...

## Symbolic Discourse. CHAPTER VI.

From here indeed follows the symbolic discourse, just as the vision of Arisleus <note>Arisleus is a legendary figure in alchemical literature, often associated with the "Turba Philosophorum"</note> attests, in this manner: Give the good girl—white, sweet, mild, and tender—to his son Cabricus <note>Cabricus and Beya are symbolic figures representing the male and female principles (sulfur and mercury) in alchemy</note> for his dead wife. Because of this, the Philosophers were imprisoned by the king; and they said, "Give us your daughter in her natural state and the color of her senses, as well as the agitation of the sea, for things like this have never happened to her." And the king's son lived again and offspring were multiplied exceedingly, and they rejoiced with a very great joy. Behold how this noble woman, Alchemy, the consoler of the poor, is veiled by various roundabout expressions of meanings and colors, so that she might be hidden from the unskilled and encourage the experts, whom she would enrich with infinite riches: because glory and riches are in her house.

Now, however, it must be considered for the third time to which natural things this science may be compared: for it is likened to the virile human seed for this reason: when it is drawn from all the members of a man, and possesses the virtue <note>power or essential property</note> of all the members, and [is placed] into the natural vessel, which is the womb <note>original: "matrix"</note>,

The womb is poured out: where it dies, and is nourished by its connatural moisture, until a man is formed in the number of his days, and no longer. In the same way, the seed of this science is drawn out from the metallic body, having all the power of metals in potential. It is placed in a natural vessel which is the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens," a term for the transformative solvent or "mercury" of the philosophers</note> and the vinegar of the Philosophers, in which it dies, rots, and is quickened; and that copper <note>original: "æs," often referring to the base material or "body" to be transformed</note> grows, along with other things receiving nourishment. This vessel, however, is one throughout the entire work, completing both the white and the red tinctures <note>The two main stages of the alchemical process: the "albedo" (whiteness) and "rubedo" (redness)</note>. For concerning this vessel, the wise have made diverse descriptions: because it is one in which there are three, namely water, air, and fire: which are three glass alembics <note>distilling apparatuses</note>, in which the offspring of the Philosophers is generated. Because of this, they have named the Tincture "blood" and "the egg." For in these the soul or water is carried, just as the dye of the dyers is carried upon cloths in water.

It is also the vessel of sublimation in which the smoke of quicksilver <note>mercury</note> is sublimated and ascends within it. For when it is estimated that the smoke of the quicksilver is finished, it is called a long and high Aludel <note>a pear-shaped subliming pot</note>, and the lower vessel is called the Dish <note>original: "Scutella"</note>, or the furnace of the Philosophers, in which is the fire of the Philosophers. When this fire goes forth, it blackens the vessel itself and burns every metal: because the oil of every hot thing is fatness, and the oil of every cold thing is humidity.

And it is also the vessel of resolution <note>dissolution</note>, in which bodies are dissolved. For in it, one thing is dissolved after another, little by little in its proper order; the resolution of all parts does not happen at once, but it is dissolved and extracted according to the manner of the Elixir. As Senior <note>Refers to Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist often cited in medieval texts</note> bears witness, saying: "Since their soul does not go out from this stone at one time, but in many." And because of this, this soul is called the flower of the soul and the flowers, blood and bloods, fatness and fatnesses; and yet it is the soul and the living spirit leading it out. And the bodies are two, namely male and female, which are earth and water. And the three sisters entering upon these principles are the nourishment and the increase of that which is nourished and increased: just as much as in an egg, which is nourished and increased by the yolk and the white, and is governed by the shell. For it has everything within itself which the operator needs in the operation.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Like Hair, moreover, in the quality of the fire burning and coming out from the earth, etc.

### *Concerning the four internal parts in the human body.*
#### CHAPTER IX.

It is also compared to the four principal things within man, namely: the brain, in the coldness of water; the heart, in the heat of fire; the liver, in the moisture of air; and the testicles, in the dryness of earth. For the seat of phlegm is in the brain; the seat of red choler <note>yellow bile</note> is in the heart; the seat of blood is in the liver; and the seat of melancholy <note>black bile</note> is placed in the genitals. Nature has notably established these aforementioned things in one body, but their locations and operations are diversified. For in choler, the "appetitive virtue" <note>the power of attraction or desire</note> is understood, because it gives color; in melancholy, the "retentive virtue," because it retains colors; in the sanguine, the "digestive virtue," because it removes superfluities; and in phlegm, the "expulsive" or "cleansing virtue," because it gives true and perfect colors. There is, however, a fifth virtue <note>the Quintessence</note> which is neither heavy nor light, neither hard nor soft; it is properly called Life, which joins these four into one, and bestows upon them a robust and perfect life.

### *Concerning the comparison of the science to an egg.*
#### CHAPTER X.

From this point, indeed, this science <note>Alchemy</note> is compared to an egg, because in it four things are joined together: the visible shell is earth; the white is water; the thin membrane joined to the thick shell, separating the water from the earth, is air; the yolk of the egg is fire; the membrane containing the yolk is also air, separating the water from the fire, and both are one and the same. The air separating the earth from the water is thicker than the higher air; the higher air is hotter and more subtle. For the fire is closer to it than to the lower air. In the egg, therefore, there are four elements: namely earth, water, air, and fire. Beyond these four, in the middle of the yolk, is a fifth thing, which is the chick. This is not to be understood as the egg of a bird, but that of which the Philosophers speak; and therefore all Philosophers in this most excellent art have described the egg itself, and have placed many other examples in their work, so that the sons of doctrine <note>students of alchemy</note> might gain understanding therefrom and investigate nature.

# ON THE BASILISK AND
## poisonous worms.

### *On the comparison of knowledge with the Basilisk, and other poisonous worms, on account of the similarity of their nourishment. CHAPTER XI.*

After these things, it is said to be similar to the Basilisk <note>A mythical serpent-king said to kill with its glance or breath; here used as a symbol for the potent Alchemical Stone.</note> and other poisonous worms, by reason of its nourishment, feeding, or infection. For just as the Basilisk is said to be nourished and fed through diverse food and drink until it becomes large and mature—after which it dies and is killed, and from its powder miracles are then performed—so the little body of our wisdom <note>original: "corpusculum nostrae sapientiae"</note> is nourished and increased by the permanent water <note>A term for the universal solvent or mercurial starting material.</note>, until it appears large and fluid; then death shall reveal it. And just as the Basilisk infects animals and men by its breath and scent, so the odor of our body of magnesia <note>In alchemy, "magnesia" refers not to the modern element, but to the crude mineral ore or the "maternal" matter of the Stone.</note> perfects the quicksilver, suddenly changing it from its own nature into a foreign nature. Whence Morienes <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit.</note> says: know that the stinking earth quickly receives the white sparks. It is also compared to a theriac <note>term: theriac (an ancient herbal jam or medical concoction used as an antidote to poison)</note>, by reason of its curing of all metals. It is also compared to poison, by reason of the manifold white and red tincture, as well as the sudden transmutation of one color into another, from imperfection into perfection: because just as a small amount of poison suddenly infects a large body, so one part of the white and red Elixir transmutes many parts of all metals into a true and perfect lunar <note>Silver</note> and solar <note>Gold</note> body.

Indeed, the property of salts is to dissolve, to corrode, to moisten, and to liquefy an acidic substance; for it is said that bodies are calcined with salt because salt corrodes their corrupting humidity. Now, salts cause bodies to flow easily in the fire. It should be noted that some salts are fixed <note>stable in heat</note> and some are volatile. Just as Alkali Salt is extracted from quicklime, or potash <note>original: "cinere clavellato," literally "clubbed ashes," a source of potassium carbonate</note>, or salt of tartar from calcined tartar itself by means of a suitable liquid until no sharpness remains: so our salt, which is the tincture <note>the transformative essence</note>, is extracted from the lime of metals through putrefaction <note>the process of breaking down or "rotting" the substance to release its essence</note>, until the whole compound strips off its own nature and puts on another. Of such a salt, Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist</note> says: "First it becomes ash, then salt, and from that salt, through various operations, the Mercury of the Philosophers is made."

However, non-fixed salts are used for Spirits, or for sharp, vinegary, and corrosive waters: such as aromatic salt, which is more noble because it is entirely spiritual. After this comes common salt and salt of urine. For aromatic salt is the second element necessary in this work, as Aristotle testifies in the *Book of the Seventy Precepts*, where he says: "Let the Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Almizadic," a Latinized Arabic term for Sal Ammoniac or ammonium chloride</note> alone serve you." As it is written in the book *The Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: for some called it by its place, such as Gum or Moon-Spit <note>original: "Sputum Lunae"</note>; some by its color, such as blood or Bull's Urine; some by its nature, such as quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum," mercury</note>. # DAWN

When the unclean meets with coarse sulfur, a corrupt metal is generated: and such a thing must be removed in the first operation: because in its first origin, it is produced as coarse, fetid, and unclean by nature, as <term>Avicenna</term> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical writings were foundational in the Middle Ages.</note> says. We have seen, therefore, in the beginning of the matter, that its dryness and the destruction of its wateriness would be harmful; and so that it may be heated, let it be pulverized or broken, as the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among Greek sages.</note> says: Behold the **Red Lead**, which is the beginning of our work: for without it the governance <note>The "regimen" or controlled heating process.</note> cannot stand. However, the aromatic salt of the common people is not understood here, for our work is not carried out with it. Moreover, **vitriol** <note>Sulfate minerals, often green or blue.</note> and **atrament** <note>A black vitriol or ink-like substance.</note> are introduced for this reason: because every vitriol and atrament of the Philosophers, when heated and roasted by a weak fire, will be clothed in a rusty-red color, as it is written in the book of the *Assembly*: that on the first day there appears a black-lemon color; on the second, a black-red; on the third, a color like saffron. From this, indeed, certain of the Philosophers have compared this wisdom to mineral spirits, such as sulfur, quicksilver, arsenic, orpiment, magnesia, and marcasite: although none of these is the **Philosophical** substance. It is said to be similar to sulfur because of three actions it exerts upon the quicksilver. First, it binds it from its humidity; second, it blackens it by its scorching; third, it reddens it by its scorching tincture. For the **Elder** <note>Likely referring to Senior Zadith (Ibn Umail), a 10th-century alchemist.</note> says: Our sulfur is not the sulfur of the common people which burns and is consumed by a scorching of blackness and destruction: for our sulfur burns with a scorching of whiteness and improvement. And Avicenna says: Except that that which is scorched belongs to the common people; and the other, which belongs to the wise, is not scorched. And the *Assembly of the Philosophers* says: Take quicksilver, and congeal it in the body of magnesia, or in the sulfur which is not burned. This sulfur which is not burned, however, we call **bronze**. Grind it, therefore, with the sharpest vinegar, and cook it, and take care that the vinegar does not turn into smoke, because the work would perish.

The Philosophers did not set down its arrangement in their books, lest just anyone should recognize it; for if the foolish knew it, they would not fail to despise it. Oh, how many gums <note>In alchemy, "gums" often refer to sticky, resinous substances or thick secretions produced during chemical reactions.</note> there are, yet they recognize ours least of all. Therefore, the Philosophers hid the nature of this poison, because through it the entire regimen <note>The "regimen" is the specific sequence of operations or "rules" followed to achieve the Great Work.</note> is fulfilled: and all mortification <note>The process of "killing" or breaking down a substance to its base components.</note> and slaying consists within it.

The fourth "living silver" <note>original: "argentum viuum" (mercury)</note> results from the former ones, and it is white in color before the fire reaches it. But when the fire reaches it, it becomes red, and this proceeds from the divine stone. Whence *Elbo the Slayer* <note>original: "Elbo Interfector," a legendary alchemical authority</note> says: *Whiten the brass <note>original: "latonem," a base metal alloy often representing the starting material</note> and tear up your books, lest your hearts be torn.* And the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: *Place it upon the coins, and the Elixir is made, and through it comes birth and life, and clean water extracted from many tinctures and things: and its tincture is the life of those things into which it is immersed, and a perfect coloration.* As the *Assembly of Philosophers* testifies, the most precious color is Tyrian <note>A deep crimson or purple dye highly prized in antiquity.</note>, which color it shall first announce: then the purple color will draw near. For this living silver is the fruit-bearer of sweet odors, and is a true and infallible tincture, providing completion to every body.

# THE RISING DAWN.

## *Concerning Marcasite, Magnesia, and Tutty.*
### *CHAPTER XV.*

It is also compared to Marcasite, Magnesia, and Tutty <note>Tutty refers to zinc oxide, often found as a crust in smelting furnaces</note>: to Marcasite in color, because just as Marcasite has silver and gold sparks mixed within the earth, so in the Philosophical Work similar signs appear. As Morienes <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> testifies, saying: "Know that the foul earth quickly receives the golden sparks," as mentioned above.

It is also said to be similar to Magnesia by reason of its weightiness and its ability to break down all metals.

It is also said to be similar to Tutty by reason of its "extinction" <note>The process of quenching a heated substance in liquid</note>. For just as it is commanded that Tutty be extinguished seven, nine, ten, or twelve times so that its earthiness may be refined and its sulfurous nature destroyed, so the Philosophers command their work to be repeated, so that every superfluity in the manifest <note>The outward, visible form</note> may be cast away, and what is absent in the depths or in the hidden <note>The internal, spiritual essence</note> may be added.

It must be noted, however, that the spirit is twofold: one is in the body, and this must be removed—that is, extracted—and it is of a fiery nature. As the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> testifies, saying: "Know that the body cannot dye itself unless the spirit is extracted which is hidden in its belly; it shall become water, and a body without spirit." This spirit is of a spiritual nature, from which the colors appear, because the thick, earthy substance does not dye; rather, it is the thin nature which passes out of the body and provides color. The second spirit is outside the body and is of a watery nature, and it is this which dyes the body into the Elixir. As the *Turba* says: "The male, this is the body; and the female, this is the spirit."

It is compared to gold and silver by reason of the perfection of their colors which persist in the fire, their weight, and also their ductility <note>The ability of a metal to be hammered thin or drawn into wire</note>; yet it is compared especially to gold, since gold is more noble and perfect than all the other three bodies. ## *Concerning the four imperfect metallic bodies.*
### CHAPTER XVII.

In truth, it is compared to the other four bodies—namely iron, copper, tin, and lead—by reason of their hard and soft fusion in their manifest and hidden aspects. For those which are hard in the manifest <note>The "manifest" refers to the outward, physical properties of a substance.</note>, such as iron and copper, are soft in the hidden <note>The "hidden" or "occult" refers to the internal, spiritual, or potential qualities of a substance.</note>: and the same is to be understood of the other two: therefore they are likened to iron and copper because of the lack of these fluxible and liquefiable qualities in the fire. And such things are the binders of tin and lead, which abound in moisture, especially iron, since it possesses less moisture and greater heat, as the Senior says:

> I am iron, dry and hard and strong, crushing and having crushed every good thing. And there is nothing in the world performing my action: for through me is generated the Secret of Secrets: when I grow strong from my weaknesses, then I have the life of a roaring lion.

And this is the alchemical iron <note>original: "ferrum alchimicum" - a symbolic or purified form of iron, not the common metal.</note>. For it is not attracted by the magnet. And if anyone should study to find another performing its operations, he would not be able: therefore it is magnified, and exalted, and made the bronze of all things. Therefore it seems most greatly to be befriended by the Philosophical Quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, since it is its coagulant, but only by a perpetual and firm coagulation. Likewise, tin and copper and lead can be made firm by the same operation, as the Assembly of Philosophers <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says:

> Bronze, like lead, becomes a precious stone: therefore place lead with lead: because Nature rejoices in nature, and Nature makes nature fly: and Nature has contained nature: and Nature has overcome nature: Therefore by the will of God those multiplying natures are made.

### *On the comparison of the science to trees, herbs, flowers, roots, and other vegetables.*
### *CHAPTER XVIII.*

Certain of the Philosophers have compared this divine science <note>The "divine science" refers to Alchemy, viewed here as a sacred art of transformation.</note> through similitude to herbs, roots, trees, flowers, and various other vegetables, as well as to their juices and fruits. Galen <note>A famous Roman physician, though here cited as an authority on alchemical secrets.</note> says: Concerning the Philosophical Tree which has seven branches, as I found in a certain writing, a treatise on the "Moon-plant" proceeding thus: This is a certain herb or plant, named *Lunatica* <note>original: "Lunatica, sive berissa"</note>, or the Moon-wort: whose root is metallic earth, its stem reddish tinged with a certain blackness: its leaves are similar to the leaves of marjoram, and there are thirty of them, according to the age of the moon in its waxing and waning; its flower is citron-yellow: after three days its scent is like the scent of musk at the full moon, or in its complete waning: if taken from it and Mercury is placed within it, it is turned into perfect Moon <note>In alchemical code, "Moon" (Luna) signifies Silver.</note>. If after this it shall have been boiled five times, it is turned into Sun <note>In alchemical code, "Sun" (Sol) signifies Gold.</note>: one part of which turns a hundred parts into the purest Gold. Note that the names of all the aforesaid things are placed as similitudes in this most excellent science, for which every faithful person ought to labor faithfully and constantly during the time of their life.

### On the manifold operations of the Philosophers.
### CHAPTER XX.

Therefore, calcination <term>calcinatio: the process of reducing a solid to a powder through heat</term> is placed at the beginning of our work, just as a father is in the act of generation. Whence we must first see what the calcination of the Philosophers is. And it should be known that the calcination of the Philosophers is threefold: two types for the body, and a third for the spirit. The first is the beginning of our work, of which it is said: calcination is the deprivation of cold moisture by a removing combustion, or the reduction of dry earth to ashes. And the Philosophers have illustrated this using wood, in which there are three moistures: the first is watery and cold, and this prevents the wood from burning; the second is greasy or oily, and this makes the wood burn. These two are vaporizable in fire and can be consumed. But the third is left behind in the ash, and it is very slight and subtle, fixed and perpetual, and not at all flammable. It is this which turns to glass and promises a glassy transparency. And in such a manner is the calcination of the Philosophers commanded to be done, as it is in the wood...

...transforming that resolution by digesting it. For in the first calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances.</note>, two types of humidity are removed: namely, the cold and watery kind, and the combustible kind. But in this, which is the second stage, the earthiness and fieriness are removed through the resolution of our water. For it dissolves, liquefies, and softens all things, then agitates them; and from this, through decoctions <note>Boiling or heating in liquid</note>, aerial resolutions result by evaporation.

Hence, this is the "solution of the Philosophers," when the dry, earthy parts become soft: so that their dryness, which is hardness, is turned into softness, which is called "moistening water," like rainwater or another form of moisture. For it is said: the more dry a thing is, the more it is softened <note>original: "quanto magis siccum, tanto magis molle"</note>, since only the dryness of Alchemy—that is, the rarity of the elements—performs the tinting <note>The alchemical coloring or transformation of metal</note>, and nothing else.

It is also called <term>inceration</term> <note>The process of "waxing" or softening a dry substance until it has the consistency of wax</note> for this reason: since the earth is deprived of its moisture, it is necessary to "wax" it; that is, to drench it with moisture so that it may flow and have the power of penetration, and represent the metallic form, just as the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> speaks figuratively:

> Just as a man lies in the tomb until he becomes dust, when the days are completed, God restores to him his soul and his spirit; once the infirmity is taken away, that thing is purged, and after the flash of lightning, it is improved: just as after the general resurrection, a man becomes stronger and younger than he had been before in this world.

Therefore, inceration is the softening of a dry thing deprived of its humors by means of a "waxing" substance over a fire. And this is the liquefaction of bodies. The Philosopher, however, performs this through water, while the common folk do it through fire: hence it is said, "liquefy the bodies with a non-vulgar liquefaction," but with ours, which is done with water. Therefore, incineration <note>Here used in the sense of "bringing to ash" or "imbibing ash"</note> is the soaking, or making into a paste, or the liquefaction of a dry, hot thing until it is inebriated. For everything that thirsts desires to drink, as <term>Aristotle</term> says: "thirst is the appetite for the cold and the moist." For that reason, it is also called "the thirsting earth."

This second part is also called <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of turning a solid into vapor and back to solid to purify it</note> for this reason: because that which is in the lower part of the vessel is elevated and exalted to the upper vessel, which <gloss>which</gloss> is named an <term>alembic</term> <note>A distilling apparatus</note>, or a long <term>aludel</term> <note>A pear-shaped pot used in sublimations</note>: or rather, so that the density of the elements may pass into their rarity through elevation, such as the dryness of the earth into the moisture of water, and the coldness of water into the heat of air.

And by God, that substance is tinging <note>staining or transforming</note> unto infinity: and in such a manner is the **sublimation** <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again, used here to mean purification</term> of the Philosophers commanded to be done. Whence it is said that to sublimate is to extract from the elementary dregs—which is the earth—the **quintessence** <term>quintessence: the "fifth essence," the purest and most concentrated part of a substance</term>, or the oily nature, or the ascending nature. Or otherwise: Sublimation is to elevate a thing from its dregs, or to segregate the pure substance from the earthly parts. For in every sublimation, the sign of perfection is liquefaction and metallic fusion.

And it must be noted that sublimation is twofold: one is corporal, the other spiritual; corporal in regard to earthiness, spiritual in regard to fieriness. Of the first it is said: *Make the body spiritual, and the fixed volatile.* <note>original: "Facite corpus spirituale, & fixum volatile." This refers to breaking down solid matter into a gaseous or refined state.</note> Of the second it is written: *The thing in which there is combustion, the first thing that is resolved in it is the fiery virtue,* as above. And **Senior** <note>Senior Zadith, a 10th-century Arabian alchemist</note> says: *Let the spirit go forth from the body, which is fire.*

It is also called **Fixation**, on account of the addition of that which is absent: For that which is absent is of a volatile nature, without which the study of the mastery would be in vain. For it is the **Elixir** of whiteness and of redness of the tincture, as well as the tinging spirit, and the metallic water, pouring itself into the body by vivifying it <note>bringing it to life</note>: and the body is the recipient of the tincture from the spirit itself, and from no other. Whence it is said, that the tincture is made from the nature of flying things: And that which firms and fixes the spirit itself is fixed and perpetual and unburnable, and is named the **sulphur of the Philosophers**, or the ash extracted from ash. As **Senior** says: *That which is fixed, fixes the fugitive things.* And **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, a famous Persian polymath and physician</note> says: *Let them therefore seek the tincture which fire does not corrupt, and does not expel, and the substance which is mixed while melting, and the consolidating substance, and the coagulating, fixing, and firm substance over the fire, and the ingenuity of mixing these with one another: so that it may be tinged with that which is in it of the tincture: and be mixed with that which is in it of the mixable substance: and be consolidated with that which is in it of the consolidating substance: and be fixed forever with that which is in it of the fixed substance.* And again he adds, saying: *We have sought the fixed substance, and we have found it to be everything that does not flee from*

Therefore it is said: The Earth fixes, the Water whitens, the Air penetrates, and the Fire colors. This fixation, however, is repeated many times, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> teaches: Until it remains in the fire with its whole substance; then the trunk <note>the core or base material</note> recedes with its whole substance.

This second part is also called washing, or purification, by reason of its blackness and foul odor, as the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says. And do not cease to wash it until it is deprived of blackness and becomes white. And Morienes says: The more something is washed, the clearer it will be; and if it has not been washed, it will not be cleared. And Geber, in the *Book of Perfection*, says: that it is not fixed unless it be enlightened, and the most shining substance be drawn out from it by the method of its own nature. And in the *Book of Disjunctions* it is written: Cleanse the bodies from their blackness or redness, in which their corruption lies, until the white becomes white, and the red, red. For washing is called the deletion of a defiled thing. Likewise, it is said: go to the woman washing clothes, and do thou likewise. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy</note> says: in the beginning it was red, and in the end white. And if its blackness is taken away from all things, it is then turned into a bright and exceedingly pure red. Because it is said: That fire and Azoth <note>a term for the universal solvent or mercury</note> cleanse and wash the brass <note>original: "latonem," an alchemical term for an impure metal alloy needing purification</note>. And Khalid the Younger <note>original: "Kaled minor," referring to the Umayyad prince and alchemist Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says: He who knows how to take the blackness from its surface purifies and increases it by that washing.

It is also called killing or mortification, by reason of the vegetable and ordered life, and the accident—that is, the impressed heat. For everything that has heat moving and acting from within itself by its own transmutation is said to live. And for this reason, Alchemy is said to live imperfectly, and the Philosophers studied how to kill this life, and to restore a life that is eternal and permanent. As Khalid the Younger says: It behooves us to kill it wisely, that is, to burn it: because death will reveal it. And Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the famous Persian physician and philosopher</note> says: Let us grind it after its first mortification with that by which it is mortified—namely, with burning things, or things that make it porous and drying, such as Salt, alum, vitriol <note>original: "atramentum," often used for ferrous sulfate</note>, lime, and other things which have a nature similar to fire. Let us do this many times, until it dies and is softened.

It is also called **vivification** <note>the act of bringing to life</note>, by reason of nourishment, or of quickening, or by reason of the metallic moisture. For everything that is nourished is fed by means of something diminished. And that which is quickened is brought to life for two reasons. The **Philosophers** <note>the traditional term for alchemists</note>, however, wish to nourish their grain with its connatural moisture until it grows and brings forth such fruit as it possesses within itself; and they wish to bring to life that which is dead to the metallic form, until it offers a perfect metallic fusion. And such vivification, or nourishment, some of the Philosophers call **Ingress** <note>the ability of a substance to penetrate or enter another</note>. And this is what **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> means when he says: "Either we give entry to those things which, by their own thickness, are not permitted to enter, through the multiple repetition of the solution of non-inflammable spirits." By these ingenious methods, it is necessary for any thing to have entry; since upon its benefit depends the power to alter through the discovered mixture.

This second part is also called **putrefaction**, or **corruption**, by reason of what is manifest <note>visible to the eye</note>. For everything that putrefies and is corrupted in the sight of the eye casts off its manifest matter and represents the matter of the hidden. The Philosophers, however, intend to corrupt or destroy the manifest, which is earthy, and to lead forth the hidden, which is silver and gold, as **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician and philosopher</note> testifies, saying: "When copper is thinned and cooked in vinegar with medicines until it dies, its whiteness penetrates to the outside, so that its internal becomes external, similar to silver in whiteness. When we have done this, we find its dyeing power remaining, and of greater tint and penetration; so much so that it does not differ from the heat of pure silver in any way; indeed, it is filled with tincture, and is of a more complete whiteness." For such putrefaction is generative, because it generates something like itself. Whence **Senior** <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, a 10th-century alchemist</note> says: "Know that no generation occurs without corruption; therefore, strive in putrefaction." And the **Assembly of the Philosophers** <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: "This putrefaction is the greatest, and it attracts the greatest secret."

It is also called the **separation of the elements**, as was mentioned before in the first calcination; for in this process the elements—namely earth, water, air, and fire—are separated. Earth in that same place...

It remains, therefore, that the other three elements must be rooted within it <note>The "it" refers to the Earth or the "base" element discussed on the previous page</note>; if this were not so, the elements would have no foundation upon which to build the new House of the Treasury. For, strictly speaking, the **separation of the elements** is the segregating of heterogeneous things <note>original: "heterogenea" — things of a different kind or nature</note>, which are merely accidental qualities; and the **conjunction of the elements** is the gathering together of homogeneous things <note>original: "homogenea" — things of the same kind</note>, that is, those which belong to the nature of the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist within all matter</note>. As it is written in the book of the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: To convert the elements is to make the moist dry, and the fleeting fixed.

It is also called **pulverization** <note>original: "contritio" — grinding or wearing down</note>, by reason of density or hardness. For everything that is dense and hard is neither tinting nor penetrating; therefore, it must be ground down so that it becomes most subtle and pervasive. Whence in the *Assembly*, when all things have been diligently made into powder, it is said to be "ground." And it must be noted that there are two types of pulverization: one of the common people, performed by the hands of craftsmen. Of this it is said: "grind by day and roast by night." The second is that of the Philosophers, and it is performed by the fire of digestion <note>original: "decoctionis" — a slow boiling or heating process</note>. Whence the *Assembly* says: "But this grinding is not done by hands, but by the strongest digestion." And Kaled the Younger <note>An Arabic alchemical authority</note> says: "Fire grinds all things." And Elbo the Slayer says: "I did nothing else but grind and whiten." And the Elder <note>Likely referring to Senior Zadith, an influential alchemist</note> says: "Congealing is of no value unless it becomes a powder." The *Assembly* adds: "Therefore, the sons of doctrine must burn that thing without fear until it becomes ash. And know that you have mixed it perfectly because it receives its spirit of life." And this grinding is many times called by the Philosophers "the stone with the runner" or "the mortar with the pestle."

It is also called **digestion** <note>original: "decoctio"</note> by reason of the hard and tenacious earth. For everything hard and tenacious is called to be "digested," so that it may become better, lighter, or more noble. Wherefore Alfidius says: "Know, my son, that you do not need many names, but only one name, which is Water, and one action, which is to Cook, and digestion occurs naturally; thus it happens that the plurality of the thing is removed, and purity remains in its own digestion," as Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician and philosopher Ibn Sina</note> testifies, saying: "The more intense the burial <note>original: "inhumatio" — placing the matter in a warm, moist environment like dung</note>, the further removed the corruption will be from it." Further considering digestion: after boiling in water and removing the corruption, we preserve it by removing the water as many times as it has been tinted, until no tint remains. **Roasting** <note>original: "Assatio"; a slow heating process intended to remove moisture</note> is so named and was invented so that the accidental moisture of a substance might be dried out and destroyed by a light fire. And it must be noted that in roasting, there is a drying out of both the body and the spirit itself. Great care must be taken lest the spirit—which dries the body and is in turn dried by the body—becomes volatile; for if it flies away from the body, the body cannot be made perfect. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician and philosopher whose works were foundational to medieval alchemy</note> teaches such drying, saying: *But since this possesses goodness, it is not burned over the fire entirely, but is warmed, etc.*

### *On other modes of operations. CHAPTER XXI.*

We are therefore excused from laboring in the burning of **calcination** <note>the reduction of a metal to a powder through heat</note>. We have and we know that the preparation is made with it and not with another. We have seen, therefore, in the first stage, that the drying of the substance and the destruction of its sharpness <note>acidity or corrosive quality</note> are necessary, so that it may be heated until it can be pulverized or broken.

It is also called **renewal**. The cause of the drying having been reversed is the dung and the "clay of wisdom" <note>lute or sealant used to protect vessels</note>. Note: the renewal of the Philosophers is done so that the dry earth may always be bedewed with "permanent water" <note>a specialized alchemical solvent that does not evaporate</note> so that it may flow. The Philosophers hint at this through such words: "Dung"—that is, the earth or the body—must always be renewed from the fourth day to the fourth day.

It is also called the **rectification** of bodies and spirits by reason of their imperfection, their diminution, and their impurity or superfluity. For bodies that abound in excessive moisture are therefore too soft in their ductility and melt very easily in the fire, such as lead, tin, and Magnesia <note>here referring to a mineral substance or a specific metallic alloy rather than modern magnesium</note>. These are often used in place of the spirit, which is (metallic water, the cause of softness) the "Water of the Philosophers"; spirits are soft like water. Whence Morienes <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: *Its touch is soft, its taste sweet, its weight heavy.* Therefore it is said: put lead with lead, tin with tin. For nature rejoices and delights in nature, because it has a kinship with it.
Others, however, are deficient in moisture, such as silver, gold, iron, and copper; and these are understood as the "calcined body." Of these Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early Islamic and Western alchemy</note> speaks: *If you seek to soften bodies of hard fusion, in the beginning of their creation a slow*

Let fire be applied. And if you seek to harden soft bodies, see to it that their [excess] moisture is consumed, and the fusion will be perfected. For we find that unless every superfluity is removed from imperfect bodies—whether by medicine or by the method of preparation—they are not perfected: namely, so that the superfluous cause and the unclean earthiness may be filtered from them. This is done so that, after the projection of the medicine <note>The "projection" is the final stage where the Elixir is cast upon a base metal to transform it</note>, nothing is separated from the mixture during melting.

And it is to be noted, that all bodies have one single meaning throughout, by reason of their imperfection, as has been said. For the <term>Assembly of the Philosophers</term> <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate between ancient sages</note> says: That <term>Corsufla</term> <note>A technical term often used in alchemy to refer to the "body" or the base metallic mass before it is purified</note> is the composition of all bodies; and the envious <note>The "envious" refers to ancient alchemists who hid their secrets in riddles to prevent the unworthy from learning them</note> have called it by all names: of Coins, or of copper, tin, iron, or lead, until the colors are removed from it and the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The perfected substance capable of transmuting metals and healing the body</note> is made.

And it must be known, that there is no way of rectifying the aforesaid bodies in nature wholly and completely without our tincture: which is a pure seed, possessing much blessing. And the Assembly testifies to this: for the Senior says, "Know, that no perfect tincture is made without the red hematite stone <note>original: "lapide hematite rubeo," likely referring to a specific red state of the alchemical stone rather than the common mineral hematite</note>, which stone lays down all redness and purges itself." And when you see at the beginning of the work something like red grains, and in the congealing something like fish eyes, and like thick, black peppercorns, know that you have walked the righteous path. But if otherwise, every operation shall be frustrated and brought to nothing, as witnessed by Albert <note>referring to Albertus Magnus, a famous 13th-century scholar and saint associated with alchemical writings</note>, who says: "Those who whiten with white things, and turn yellow with yellow things, while the species of the metal remains the same, are judged to be deceivers."

Furthermore, this must be understood concerning the spirits: for there are some who say they know how to congeal Mercury, or to extract it from a body; others claim to whiten arsenic, orpiment, sulfur, and other mineral spirits; and they assert that they rectify imperfect bodies and spirits by means of purified salts, or <term>sharp waters</term> <note>original: "aquis acutis," referring to corrosive acids like nitric acid</note>, or artificially perfected <term>waxing oils</term> <note>original: "oleis inceratiuis," oils used to soften a substance to a wax-like consistency during the process of "inceration"</note>. The operation of all these is nothing other than harmful and a misfortune: because they prepare that which has no tincture, from every thing which tends toward nothingness. In part, it is conceded that colors, alterations, and weak transmutations may occur, yet no fruit follows from them. This is because nature works nothing toward the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "philosopher's stone" or universal medicine</note> or the perfect <term>tincture</term> <note>The substance capable of changing the quality or color of metals</note> from these aforementioned things; the prudent and discreet worker can subtly investigate these matters above. For the Philosophers have established five differences through which their white and red tincture, or Elixir, is integrally composed and completed; without these, no tincture can exist. 

The first is to evacuate the superfluous; the second is to alter the medicine into a white and lemon-yellow color; the third is to provide metallic fusion; the fourth is to make such fusion endure in the fire; the fifth is to administer the proper weight to every infused metal. And these five can be contained within a triple number—namely, measure, number, and weight—which are the perfection of all necessary things.

Then follows the third part of this work, which is described by Hermes, King of the Greeks and Father of the Philosophers, in this way: 
-> The wind carried it in its belly <- <note>original: "Portauit illud ventus in ventre suo" — a famous line from the Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus</note>
The Philosophers call this part distillation, or clarification. Therefore, after the matter has been <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, deprived of its liquefiable and denominative moisture, and then loosened from its fiery earthiness, it is necessary to distill it: that is, to clarify it and to bring forth the transparency and clarity of the air. For distillation is said to be the clarification of a thing with transparency; and this distillation is the completion of the entire serenity of the work with clarity. And it is done three, four, five, six, seven, eight, or nine times, or twelve times, which is the ultimate. After the final round of distillation, the fourth part follows, which Hermes names thus:
-> Its nurse is the earth, or its power is whole if it be turned into immobile earth <- <note>original: "Nutrix eius est terra, vel vis eius integra est, si versa fuerit in terram immobilem"</note>
And the wise entitle this "Coagulation," the end of the matter, or perfect fusion. And this is what Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose alchemical writings were highly influential in Europe</note> means when he says: 
> When we place it for the final time in a <term>Kinnam</term> <note>likely a specialized vessel or crucible</note> sealed with the <term>lute of wisdom</term> <note>original: "luto sapientiæ" — a specialized airtight sealing clay used by alchemists</note>, we cautiously bind its head. After we have roasted its dew, as we shall say later, we then <term>sublime</term> <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> the medicine until it ascends. It is placed in a tile, sometimes appearing like tin, sometimes like salt or stone, and sometimes like crystal, after we have sublimated it from itself; and these things emerge with dews and experiments.

->THE FINAL CHAPTER.<-

Fifth and finally, we must proceed to the virtue, nobility, and effect of this praiseworthy Philosophical Tincture, which is a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. And it must be known that the ancient sages found four principal effects or virtues in this glorious, treasury-like, consoling, and helpful science. First, it is said to heal the human body from many infirmities; second, to restore imperfect metallic bodies; third, to transmute ignoble stones into certain precious gems; fourth, to make all glass ductile, or malleable <note>The "malleable glass" was a legendary alchemical achievement where glass could be hammered like metal without breaking.</note>.
Regarding the first, all Philosophers have agreed that if the hematite stone <note>original: "lapis hematites"; here referring to the "blood-red" stage of the Philosopher's Stone.</note> has been perfectly reddened, it not only performs miracles in solid bodies <insert>metals</insert> but also in the human body; of this there is no doubt. For it cures every infirmity when taken internally and heals when applied externally as an ointment. For the Philosophers say that if some of it is given in warm water or wine to those with paralysis, frenzy, dropsy, or leprosy, it cures them. Other wise men say that it often eliminates "rose-drop" <note>original: "guttam rosaceam"; likely referring to rosacea or similar skin inflammations.</note> by anointing; hence also cardiac passion, wasting disease <note>original: "ethica" or hectic fever.</note>, intestinal obstruction, colic, jaundice <term>icteritia: a yellowing of the skin and eyes</term>, and the disease of St. Giles <note>original: "morbus Aegidij"; usually referring to epilepsy or lameness.</note> with falling sickness, and all types of fevers are cured by taking it. Often gout <term>arthetica: joint pain or arthritis</term> is cured by it through anointing; and whatever is in a sick stomach, this removes; and it binds and consumes every flow of sinful humors <note>In medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids; "sinful" implies they are out of balance or corrupt.</note> by drinking or anointing; and it plucks away all melancholy or sadness of mind when taken on an empty stomach; and it is also the best [remedy] for infirm eyes...
