# AURORA

->The Healer<- <note>original: "sanatrix"</note>: For it binds every flow of tears: it thins the secretions of bleary eyes and drives away redness. By destroying the film or membrane <note>likely referring to a cataract or pterygium</note>, it softens it. Grains, webs, white spots, and growths, horns, hoof-like callouses, cataracts, inversion of the eyelids, burning heat, darkness, and swellings of the eyes—all these are most easily cured through this **Philosophical Medicine**. It strengthens the heart and the spiritual organs when drunk; it mitigates headache when rubbed on the temples; it even grants hearing to the deaf and aids every pain and swelling of the ears. It rectifies contracted nerves by anointing; it restores corroded teeth by washing; it sweetens the foulness of the breath. 

Through it, all types of abscesses are also healed by anointing, or by applying a plaster, or by introducing a dry powder. Ulcers, wounds, cancers, fistulas, <term>Noli me tangere</term> <note>Latin for "touch me not"; a historical term for corrosive skin ulcers or lupus</note>, carbuncles, ringworm, skin eruptions, discolorations, scabies, itching, and scurf are healed by it. Scars are smoothed by it so that new flesh is regenerated. Corrupted and sour wine is restored if it is mixed in. The stone <note>kidney or bladder stones</note> is dissolved if it is drunk. It expels poison when taken. Worms are also killed if they are powdered with it. Shaggy hairs are removed by anointing with it; it deletes wrinkles and all blemishes on the face by anointing, and promises a youthful face to women. Taken during childbirth, it assists; it brings forth a dead fetus by means of a plaster. It provokes urine; it excites and increases sexual intercourse; it prevents drunkenness; it induces memory; it increases the radical moisture <note>the vital fluid believed to sustain life</note>; it invigorates nature, and provides many other good things to the human body. For this medicine is above all the medicines of Hippocrates, Galen, Constantine, Alexander, Avicenna, and other doctors of the medical art: more excellent in odor, taste, virtue, and effect. And it should be noted that this medicine is always to be mixed with the apothecary's medicine assigned to the specific disease.

Regarding the second <note>property</note>, it is written that it transmutes all imperfect metals. Indeed, this transmutation is manifest enough: for everything that is silver, it makes into gold in color, substance, endurance, weight, ductility, liquefaction, hardness, and softness.

Regarding the third, it is written that it transmutes stones into precious gems, as was alleged above in the book *Sextarius*.

# ROSINUS TO
## EUTHICIA.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring a landscape with a building and leafy flourishes.</image-desc>

I ENTERED one day into the house of the elder Habielfam <note>Likely a corruption of an Arabic name, possibly Zosimos or an associate</note> for the sake of visiting him, and I sat at his right hand. There were two men there, one of whom I recognized, but the other I did not. And when they spoke in my presence concerning the Art <note>Alchemy</note>, I perceived through what I asked that the Art had been introduced to them, but the word was obscured; they did not know that which they were considering in the sayings of the wise, and they were in a state of amazement. My companion turned his face toward me, confident in our friendship, and said to me: "What is the understanding of the wise here? 'Take lead, and that which is likened to lead; and take Azoch <note>term: Azoch; a term for Mercury or the universal solvent</note> and that which is likened to Azoch.' This is the order of the science which the Egyptians knew, and its Enigma, and its reason, and its power, and its abundance. Here are four things, of which two are manifest: for he named lead, and that which is likened to it. What then are these four?" he asked, "and do these words of the Wise have obscurity, and are they from the sophisms of the Wise?" he asked. "How is this?" I said. By this he wished...

# TO EUTHICIA

The Sage mentioned only two things, which are the male—their hidden secret—and the female; yet he added words signifying four, though he intended only two. He asked, "How is it so?" and he himself said, "Four," seeking out the words of the Sages. A second time he spoke, intending by this statement only two; and that Sage said: "There are four, yet you say two." I said to him that in these words, as previously stated, there is the obscurity of the wise and a <term>sophism</term> <note>A clever but misleading argument used here to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note> in this place. If they had intended four by those things from which the male and female are composed, they would have said: "Take water and fire, and mix them, and let each be constituted from two." Then, "make the four one." Nevertheless, the Sage said (make the four one): "Take <term>lead</term> <note>original: plumbum; in alchemy, lead often represents the raw, chaotic state of matter or the 'male' metallic principle</note>, and that which is likened to lead." Then he repeated and said: "Take <term>azoch</term> <note>original: azoch; a term for Mercury or the universal solvent/spirit</note>, and that which is likened to azoch." From these and similar sayings of theirs, they hide the science from men. Understand: and I trust in my God that you may understand this saying of the Sage.

He gave this example: "Take lead." Now, "lead" among them is one of the names for the male; for he named the male, but kept silent regarding the name of the female. And he said, "that which is likened to lead," and the female is likened to lead: because she is from him, and he is from her. Then he said a second time: "Take azoch, and that which is likened to azoch." Now, azoch is the female; here he named the female, and kept silent regarding the name of the male. And he said, "and that which is likened to azoch," and here he named the male: because he had named him at the beginning of the speech, clearly so that doubt might be removed from the discourse. 

Yet this phrasing is as valid as if you were to say: "Take <term>Adam</term>, and that which is likened to Adam." Here you have named Adam, and kept silent regarding the name of the female, or <term>Eve</term>; you do not name her because you know that men who are like you in the world know that that which is likened to you is Eve. Then you repeat it a second time, so that it might be less obscured to the wise and intelligent—though many many think you intend four in this place when you speak—you said: "Take Eve and that which is likened to Eve." Here you named the female, who is Eve, and kept silent regarding the name of Adam: because you named him once and began with him, and there can be no doubt for one who would quibble. And they began to look at one another, and amazement seized us over this, because I had explained it to them. And similarly, from here—

# ROSINUS

As they have said: mix the hot with the cold, and it shall become tempered, being neither hot nor cold; and mix the moist with the dry, and it shall become tempered, being neither moist nor dry. This saying is clearly directed toward the four <note>The four classical elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth</note>, and from these two are generated, namely the male and the female. The male is hot and dry, while the female is cold and moist. When these have been joined together, the hot is then mixed with the cold, and the moist with the dry; and this is not a matter of doubt to one who understands. 

And this understanding supports the name of the Sage, because it possesses this other method which I have demonstrated to you, concerning fire and water, air and earth. There is also another method arising from the preparations, which is as Joseph <note>Likely referring to an alchemical authority or "Joseph the Jew," a common figure in medieval hermetic texts</note> said: "Mix fire and water, and they shall be two. Mix air with earth, and they shall be four; then make the four one, and you have arrived at that which you desire." And then let the body become a non-body <note>original: "corpus non corpus" — a common alchemical paradox referring to the spiritualization of matter</note>, and let that which is weak against fire become not weak, and you have grasped wisdom. 

Act, therefore, according to what Joseph said regarding this, and the preparation of these things is carried out from the beginning until the end. It is the hot and fixed honored water, and it is that which manifests the tincture <term>Tincture: A potent alchemical liquid or spirit capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold or silver</term> in the projection <term>Projection: The final stage of the Great Work, where the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon base metal to transmute it</term>. Unless that water existed, the intention of any sage in any root of wisdom would be nothing. And she herself is the mediatrix between opposites. She is the same: the first, the middle, and the last. 

Understand this which I have demonstrated to you, and know the manner of the word, for she herself manifests the tincture. For such is the usual persistence and sophistry <note>original: "sophisma" — here meaning the intentional use of riddles or "blind" metaphors to hide secrets from the uninitiated</note> of the sages; perhaps they introduced a name in one sense, while beneath it lies another. And I hope that these things will become apparent through the words, because he hints to you many things concerning their secrets and sophistries, and God will grant you prosperity. 

If, however, the method of any sage should be opened one day from their writings, it will not be opened to a man unless he reads the book in our songs <note>original: "carmina" — can refer to poems, songs, or incantations</note>. For I have explained to you and to all my brothers whatever the Philosophers obscured to the best of their ability, and what they cried out for fathers and sons. I have included in a few pages what they spend many pages on, buried in tropes and involved in even darker obscurities, so that the intellect is nowhere able to grasp the meaning. I, however, so that my memory might endure, sat solitary among the ancients, considering the books of the elders and...

# TO EUTHICIA

...and seeking from any of those sitting with you who inquire after this knowledge—whom, when I addressed them, they did not understand me. For they held in their hands books which describe to them *Alkabric Alkakir* <note>original: "Alkabric Alkakir"; likely a Latinization of Arabic al-kibrit al-akbar, meaning "The Red Sulfur," a technical term in alchemy for the Philosopher's Stone or the transformative agent.</note>, that is, the appearances or vain things which they recognize and by which they are occupied. And these are the things which deter those preoccupied by them; they devote themselves to their own questions and deviate from the truth, blinded by ignorance. 

But when I saw you and your face there among them, through that which it signaled, and I explained from a second perception of your intellect, I turned my face toward you. I explained to you from that which my knowledge had enclosed within my breast, so that you might know the soul of science <term>scientia: systematic knowledge or deep understanding</term> and the place of the secret, and that you might distinguish between me and the men devoted to errors and vanities. This is because you have read in the books of others what they have spoken and what they have brought forth from the words of the ancient Sages, the moderns, and those who are sought after. 

None of these men dared to explain a single letter from the sayings of the ancient Philosophers; instead, they placed things in their books according to what the Sages provided, yet they did not reveal any true sense from them. However, it is necessary that since I have become wise, certain things are opened to me, and I should know hidden things. I shall explain the words of the sages and arrive through that exposition at the truth and the manifestation of those things after they have been revealed, so that it might be made manifest to those studying it, and be opened to those who are weary, those who are patient, and those fleeing from the things they have at hand out of ignorance. 

But if I do not explain any of these things, my books will be just like the books of the Sages, and my words like their words—as if I merely took their names and attributed them to myself, which is improper and a disgrace to one who acts so. What utility is there to the one reading my book, unless that which others have hidden is brought near to the intellect of my successors? According to the meanings hidden from the intellect of all those in the open, and that which is veiled, let it be open and revealed in this work. It is, however, open to the studious, the wise, and the intelligent; unless I do this, we shall not manifest our diligence. You may inquire, but my sayings would be like propositions without application or utility, etc. Know, furthermore, that many...

# ROSINUS

They are occupied in the preparation of their **sulfurs** <note>original: "sulphurum"; here referring to the active, combustible principle in alchemy rather than common brimstone</note>, and in the sublimation of their **arsenics** <note>original: "Arsenicorum"; likely referring to volatile mineral spirits</note> which are combustible and corruptible, according to the manifest things they hear and the bare words they read—knowing and recognizing those things while remaining ignorant of the truth. For **Sulfur** and **sulfurs**, and **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> or **orpiments**, and **zandarich** <note>original: "zandarich"; likely a corruption of sandarac, often referring to realgar or red arsenic</note>, all these are names for the **divine water**, the foliated and moist: whose **whitening** <note>original: "dealbatio"</note> is its preparation through **sublimation** <note>term: sublimation; in alchemy, this often refers to the purification of a solid into a vapor and back to a solid, or more broadly, the "lifting" of a substance's spiritual essence</note>, which is distillation, until it becomes white and clear, in which there are no impurities. This is the sublimation of sulfur and zandarich.

Also, the washing of the **body** <note>the solid material or "base" of the work</note> and the returning of the water upon it, continues until there remains nothing of the **soul** <note>the "tincture" or vital force</note> within it—which is the **tincture** <note>term: tincture; the concentrated essence or color-giving power capable of transforming metals</note>—that does not ascend with the **spirit** itself. And when you have received the soul and everything in that water, and nothing of it remains in the body, then you have washed the body from its impurities. He hints by this at the total extraction of the whole from it, so that the clean **ash** may be freed from the ash, in which there is no fatness <note>unctuous or oily impurities</note> to hinder it from the work; it returns a second time to its place.

Similarly, it is said, just as I told you before regarding the **body** and **bodies** according to the examples I gave you of the **spirits** and **spirit**, so in the **soul** there is one body of parts; and then it is called "bodies" according to its parts, but first it is one from one. Whoever says otherwise is ignorant of the science: because he knows neither body, nor bodies, nor spirit, nor spirits, nor soul, nor souls, nor does he know the **stone**, nor from what it is made, nor does he perceive the order of the work in any way. And the reason is: because from any of those false things, one body is incorporated. For this reason, they similarly spoke of "one body" and "bodies," and because of this, that this one is from those: by a manifold operation of spirit and soul, it is the **stone and not a stone**.

This is the stone which the wise men of the art liken to the **Eagle-stone** <note>original: "lapis Aquilae" or Aetites; a hollow geode believed to contain another stone inside, used here as a metaphor for the hidden essence within matter</note>: for the Eagle-stone is a well-known stone: and there is a stone in its belly, a stone that moves, by which he signified the ascending part and the ash extracted from the ash. Similarly, it is the stone in whose belly is a stone that moves; just as when they dissolve it, its water comes forth from it, which was congealed within it, and it moves by ascending and exalting toward the air. They signify by this the **spirit** and the **soul** which is in its belly: and this is the stone in whose belly is a stone; the dregs remain from which that ascending part went out.

He uses the metaphor of the Eagle-stone (Aetites) to illustrate how the volatile essence is hidden within the solid shell of the stone.</summary>

remains immobile: then afterwards, the soul appears from it, and it is the ash of ash, which Maria <note>original: "Marian"; likely referring to Maria the Prophetess, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> named the "congealed coagulant," their water in their earth: she magnified this ash. And this is the leaven <term>fermentum: a substance that transforms or "leavens" the base metal into a higher state</term>, and the leaven of the leaven of the common gold, and of their leaves. The Wise Man said: Take the things of their souls, and exalt them to higher places, and reap them from the peaks of their mountains, and lead them back to their roots: and these are his manifest words, in which there is neither envy nor obscurity; nevertheless, he did not name what the things are. However, by "mountains" he signified cucurbits <term>cucurbita: a gourd-shaped chemical vessel used in distillation</term>, and by the "peaks of the mountains" he meant alembics <term>alembicum: the cap of a still used to direct vapors into a receiver</term>. To "reap," according to the metaphor, is to receive their water through the alembic into the receiver. To "lead back to the roots" is to return it upon that from which it came. And he named the cucurbits "mountains" because the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemy, Sun (Sol) and Moon (Luna) represent Gold and Silver</note> are found in mountains: so also in these mountains, which are cucurbits, their Sun and Moon are generated, and it happens within them; and those are the lesser of their leaves and their gold, and in them he manifests its preparation.

And all of this is by way of metaphor, and it is a wonderful and beautiful metaphor; he does not mean actual men by "mountains," nor does he intend the heads of men by "higher places," nor is that which is reaped from them "hair," as some of the commentators have said. They labored over hair, and consumed their money and their days in the pursuit of vanity; but wisdom is even worthier, nobler, and higher than what they supposed, and men arrive at vanities through such [literalism]. And there are those who said that this art is from eggs, and the hair of a virgin, and urine and blood, gall and sperm, and other such things, and from diminished minerals, combustions, and corruptions—

# ROSINUS

...perishable things, and things coming to nothing. They speak falsely when some, out of the weakness of their own reasoning, have made [the Stone] from a virgin and urine—far be such a thing from the wisdom of the glorious and sublime God!—whereby these ignorant men have woven themselves into tangled cords. The ignorant man ignorantly strikes the colocynth <note>A bitter cucumber-like fruit used as a purgative; here used as a metaphor for a foolish or dangerous endeavor</note> and hopes to eat honey from it; but when he does not see what he had expected, he returns to his own thoughts, expands upon them, and says, "This is due to misfortune." And if it were said to him, "A sheep gave birth to men," or "grains of wheat bear galbanum <note>A bitter aromatic gum resin</note>," or "a palm tree carried pomegranates," or "birds give birth to fish," he would answer, "You speak falsely; things do not generate anything except their own likeness, nor do things bear fruit except their own fruits." For all those aforementioned things designate their **water**; and their water is the **leaven of the bodies**; and the bodies are their **earth**, even after these things are blackened through the preparation of fire. They call it by the name of **black fire**, just as in the second blackening [they call it] **Mountain Coal** and **pitch**, **antimony**, **Alkali**, and **salt of Alkali**, and **Marcasite**, **Magnesia**; and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> extracted from **Cambar** <note>An alchemical term often referring to a specific mineral or processed lead</note>, and its **ash** and **lime**, and **glass**, and **clean water** which has been cleansed from darkness and from the matter of blackness. The art of Astronomy and of Physics is open to those who read. But our Art cannot be known except by the wise. He, therefore, who does not liquefy and coagulate, errs in many ways. Therefore, **blacken the earth**, and separate from it its **soul** and its **water**. Afterward, **whiten it**, and you will find what you seek. It is said universally, that he who blackens the earth and dissolves the white fire until it becomes like a naked sword—and he who has brought the soul into the whitened thing—[possesses] the whole, because he fixes it in the rapid fire. And after it has been liquefied, he will deserve to be called happy, and he shall be exalted above the circles of the world. Here ends [the book]; and let him who knows, know what I have said, etc.

## THE SECOND TO
## EUTHICIA.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring a serpent-like form entwined with foliage.</image-desc>

OBSERVE the figures at the beginning of the book of names, and meditate on why I have placed them here. For I have placed none of them except for those things which the comparison requires. This is the second letter of the exposition of foreign names by Rosinus <note>Rosinus is a Latinized name for Zosimos of Panopolis, a 3rd-century alchemist</note> to Euthicia, and it is conducted through questions and answers. For she says: What is incombustible sulfur? He responds: It is that which fights against the fire and has withstood it, and has received the *Cambar* of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui Cambar"; Cambar is an Arabic-derived term often referring to a specific state of mercury or a "magnesia"</note>, that is, its moisture. For this reason, the Philosopher named it incombustible sulfur. What is *Cambar*? It is water mixed by the permanent; for before it was mixed and joined against [the fire]. Tell me therefore, why did Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> in his book call it the Key of All Goods, or the Book of Philosophers? He responds: Because he who looks into the book of Hermes—where he described the climates, lands, regions, mountains, metals, spirits, waters, powders and their flavors—brought into these the composition of the art, along with the powers of the waters. He interspersed other useless things so that those knowing how to distinguish them from the art would recognize this greatest science. Men have remained ignorant of the true natures of the waters, their virtues, and those things in them which are desirable. And therefore, he says it is the Key of All Goods. And indeed, it is true. She said: Why do they call the vapor both spirit and soul? He responds: Know that Bilonius <note>Likely Apollonius of Tyana</note> said before others: The spirit of the moist is of the black, immaculate of the belly, and he compared it to man. For he said that man is moisture, just as the spirit is; similarly this work, which the Philosophers have hidden, is the secret of vapor and water, that is, the spirit. Sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> is the extraction of ash from ash, for the vapor is not turned; and he did not call it vapor until the tinting and strong spirit enters into it. Here is the warrior against the fire, who has been extracted from the strongest. And she indeed signifies [this]. For Hermes said: Place the spirits <note>original: "ss." abbreviation for "spiritus"</note> in a thick cloth, and set them to cook in the fire. He responds: It should be noted that the Philosopher named the matter of the humors "f." <note>likely an abbreviation for "form" or "fons/source"</note>, that is, the Spirit extra—

...and the vessel, and the nature of the species, because that which is born germinates and flourishes, and from that vein it emerges. Therefore, the first <note>original: "f." likely for "forma" or "figura"</note> signifies the species, and the second signifies the spirit. Wherefore Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher often cited in alchemical texts as an authority on the transformation of matter</note> says: Wash in humidity, and wash away the humidity until its blackness enters. To what end do the Philosophers call that blackness the "blackness of money," yet none of you call it the "face of a bird"? She said: The diversity of names makes me wander in error. He responds: Do not let what you see force you to err; mix the dry with the moist until the soul desiccates the spirit—that is, the concept—and drives it into its belly: because the soul came forth from the spirit and the soul lives by the spirit. 

If therefore, Euthicia, you wish to verify those things which I have told you, take "salt of the seas" <note>original: "alumen marium," likely referring to a bitter sea salt or alum used as a reagent</note>, that is, the Moist Spirit: dry it, that is, sublime it into powder; putrefy it, so that it may be freed from the dregs; and once the humidity is washed away—namely the watery fullness—it is thin, that is, subtle. From there you extract the earth, that is, fix it <term>Fixation: the process of turning a volatile, evaporating substance into a solid that can resist fire</term>, and beware of the fire in the governance of the water. For fire is an enemy until they become agreeable to one another, namely through fixation. 

And know that if you make the fire and water to be in concord—that is, if you have made the volatile spirit fixed, namely the "moist sea"—your work, by God's favor, is improved. And know that it is not burned all at once with the soap <note>original: "sapulo," possibly a reference to a cleansing agent or alkaline salt</note>, but rather little by little; that is, the whole is not fixed at once by a single regimen. And what of the saying "it is burned"? It means: let it be fixed, let it be hidden in the humor. For when it is fixed, the humor is hidden—that is, the spirit—until it smokes entirely and falls together, that is, it has been fixed. And the more it is cooked, the more it is thickened—namely the container and the content—until they become one thing from it, which is our bronze <note>original: "aes nostrum," a symbolic term for the alchemical alloy or "philosopher's copper"</note>. 

Furthermore, it is necessary for the fire of the first decoction to be light: this is in the beginning, when the whole is still volatile, until it utilizes the fire and becomes unyielding. Then, increase the fire little by little: because the more it is cooked, the more it is fixed, etc. And she said: Reveal, therefore, what the philosopher Syrnas says: that the thing is one in which the whole of what is to be worked is made; and unless it is present, you shall find nothing. He responds: I have already demonstrated to you that he who enters into this art seeks nothing other than to turn things into gold; but you [cannot make] gold unless you place gold into gold, that is, the leaven... <note>The text cuts off at "fermentum" (leaven/ferment), the catchword for the next page.</note>

I have left nothing obscure, and I have revealed what is signified by the names themselves, so that this secret <note>Latin: *arcanum*</note> might be opened to those who are not foolish. And she said: Explain to me then, why did the Philosopher, after he had named the golden coin, then call it bronze? He responds: So that you may know that bronze <note>Latin: *aes*, often referring to copper or its alloys in alchemy</note> is in itself red, as are the coin and the gold. And she said: How studiously they have hidden this stone! He responds: It is the key to the work <note>Latin: *clavis operis*</note>. They have also hidden the Earth by a multiplication of names, just as they did the stone, saying it is sand because it is that from which colors are extracted from their elements. The best bronze among us is the "bronze of the thing" <note>Latin: *aes rei*</note>, and he who does not know the bronze of the thing dies in his own distress. Hide it therefore in a similar way, if you can, and know that perhaps it is better that it be required in its own veins. And inspect the Gall <note>Latin: *Fella*, likely referring to bile or a bitter metallic salt used as a flux</note> mixed with gold and less than it, for the perfection of your composition demonstrates the matter to you. And know that unless there is something of this nature in every Gall with which they use this kind of bronze in the earth, it will not have a robust brightness.

## ROSINUS TO SAR-
## RATANTAM
### THE BISHOP.

<note>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring ornate floral patterns.</note>Venerable Father, incline your ears and attend to my words: namely, that the matter of all metals is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; literally "living silver," known today as mercury</note>, cooked and imperfect in the belly of the earth, with sulfurous heat boiling it down. According to the sulfurous truth, diverse metals are procreated in the earth, even though their primordial matter is naturally one and the same. They differ only by the action—namely, more or less heat—occurring or not occurring with temperance; and in this, all Philosophers agree. And I shall demonstrate this to you: because every thing is, and is made from, that into which it is dissolved. For example, when ice is changed by means of heat, it is changed into water; therefore, it was previously water. But all metals are turned into the water of quicksilver; therefore, they were previously quicksilver. However, I shall demonstrate below the method of seeking to turn them into quicksilver. This being established, the opinion of those who said that the species of metals cannot be transmuted is removed. It is true as they say, unless they are first reduced to their first matter <note>original: "primam materiam"; the formless base substance from which all things arise</note>. Truly, their reduction into the first matter is easy; therefore, transmutation is also possible. This is evident. For every created or growing thing is multiplied, as is clear in men, animals, and trees: because just as a thousand grains are procreated from one grain, and infinite branches proceed from one tree—thus diverse trees are made—so also minerals are multiplied when they are born in the earth.

From the aforesaid, it is clear to a subtle intuition that the Philosopher spoke the truth in his obscure words; although he said that our stone <note>original: "lapis noster"; the Philosopher's Stone</note> is from the four elements, and they compare it to the element itself, as will be shown later. Because truly there are four elements there, they said that our stone is from body, soul, and spirit, and they spoke the truth.

For they compare the imperfect body to the perfect body: because it is inferior, and they called the water "spirit," but the leaven <note>Latin: fermentum; in alchemy, a substance that triggers transformation</note> they called the "soul." Truly it is the spirit, as was said above: because it grants life to the imperfect body which it did not have before; although it seemed imperfect, it nevertheless grants it life and brings it forth into a better form. And unless bodies are turned into non-bodies, or non-bodies into bodies, you have not yet found the way of operating. In this they spoke the truth: for in the first stage it becomes water, that is, quicksilver <note>Latin: argentum vivum; mercury</note>: and thus it becomes incorporeal: then it becomes a body. And some say to "convert the natures," and this is true. For in our mastery <term>magisterium: the technical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> we first make the thick thin, and the body a spirit, and afterwards the moist dry, and the water earth, and thus we convert the natures; and we act so that the lower is brought to the higher, so that the spirit becomes a body and the body becomes a spirit. Thus in the beginning of our work we labor in "solution" <note>The process of dissolving a solid into liquid</note>, and that which is lower is joined to that which is higher, and the whole is turned into earth. It is clear, therefore, that our stone is made of the four elements. Moreover, our stone is body, soul, spirit, and water, as the Philosophers say, and it is made in a single vessel, and they spoke the truth. For our entire mastery is made with our water, and from it. For it dissolves the bodies themselves, as has been said—not by a solution such as people believe, where it would turn into rainwater, but by a true Philosophical solution, so that it turns into the water from which metals are made. Then, once calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and reduced to earth, those same bodies are transferred into the substance of that water, and it softens them, sustains them, whitens them, and cleanses the Laton <note>Laton: an impure metal alloy, often associated with base copper or brass</note> according to the word of Morienus <note>Morienus: a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> who says:

> Since Azoth <note>Azoth: the universal solvent or mercury of the philosophers</note> and fire wash and cleanse the Laton.

Laton, however, is an unclean body, and Azoth is distilled arsenic; and diverse bodies are joined together, prepared in the manner aforesaid, by such a union that the power of fire cannot separate them, whether in potential or in act, from the combustion of the fire. And their change within themselves sublimates the bodies—not by the common sublimation intended by the idiots who believe that to sublimate is to ascend upwards. Therefore, they take calcined bodies and mix them with "superior" sublimates, namely Mercury and arsenic, and cause the bodies to be sublimated by a strong fire, and to ascend...

# TO SARRATANT

The mother is indeed the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; representing Silver</note> for the imperfect body: but the Sun <note>original: "Solem"; representing Gold</note> for the perfect body. And nourishment follows, so that it may be increased more, the more it is nourished in its own milk and seed, from which they are abundantly made; indeed, arsenic is imbibed <note>term: imbibition (the process of soaking a solid in a liquid until it is saturated)</note> again and again, so that it drinks two parts, and let this suffice.

Let us descend therefore to the practice. I have told you, therefore, that first of all, bodies must be reduced to the first matter, which is the first work. Take therefore one pound, so that it be clean filings, and mix ten pounds with arsenic, by grinding, and softening with a little salt, until the whole is an amalgam. Afterwards, in other vessels with its own blessed water <note>term: aqua benedicta (a specialized alchemical solvent, often mercurial or acidic, rather than religious holy water)</note>, it resolves the earth into water by continuous distillations, until the whole has been resolved into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; Mercury</note>. This they call the first work.

The second work follows, and is done thus. Place this water in an earthen vessel over a slow fire, until you see a blackness appear on top, which you should remove as subtly and as well as you can; thus cook it and take away the blackness, until no blackness appears, but the water appears clear. Thus you have the earth and the water.

The third work follows and is done thus. Take this earth, place it in a glass vessel, and pour over it the blessed water, that is, until nothing sticks out, so that it floats over it by four fingers' depth; cook it with a gentle fire for one day, and again put in water, and cook it thus successively until the earth becomes white and clear, and this is what the Philosophers have said. This earth with its water putrefies and is cleansed; when these things become putrid, by the help of God, the whole mastery <note>term: magisterium (the successful completion of the alchemical process)</note> is directed: because it is cleansed and whitened, as has been said. When it has been thickened with the aforesaid earth by means of heat, you should cook it with a strong fire in a gourd-shaped vessel <note>term: cucurbita (the lower part of a still)</note> with a strong still-head <note>term: alembicum (the cap of the distilling apparatus)</note> placed on top, and let the earth remain calcined <note>term: calcination (reducing a substance to powder through heat)</note> at the bottom.

Now, however, concerning the ferment: add a fourth part of whatever you wish, that is, if there was 1 pound of the imperfect body, let there be a quarter pound of the ferment. The ferment is indeed the Sun and the Moon, and there are no other ferments. And the ferment thus dissolved, and the earth made just like the imperfect body, joined together prepared in the same way and order, and soak it with the aforesaid water for nine days or more, and grind it with...

Now I shall return, Reverend Father, to applying the aforementioned points specifically to the sayings of the ancient Philosophers and their obscure words hidden in parables, so that you may judge the words of those Philosophers and understand that they have brought forth the truth. For the first word of our discourse or work is the reduction into the "First Matter" <note>original: *primam materiam*; the formless base of all things</note>. And that is what the Philosophers called "solution" <note>dissolving a solid into liquid</note>, which is the foundation of the art, as Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> says: *Unless you dissolve the bodies, you labor in vain.* Of this solution, the Philosopher Parmenides speaks in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba [Philosophorum]*; a famous early alchemical text</note>: "certain ones hearing of the solution of dry oil." Therefore, the Philosophical solution is not merely the soaking of water, but the conversion of bodies into the water from which they were first created, just as frost is turned into liquid water, from which it first came. Behold, by the grace of God, you now have the first element, which is the water of the body itself reduced into its primary nature.

The second word is that it becomes earth. And this is what the Philosophers say: because from the thickness of the water, earth is created together with it. Thus you have the other element, which is earth.

The third word is that which preceded the cleansing of the earth, of which Morienus says: *This earth rots with its water and is cleansed, and then it becomes pure by the help of God.* Regarding this, the Philosopher says in the *Assembly*: "Join the dry to the moist; the dry is the earth, the moist is the water." Behold, now you have both water and earth—that is, the earth whitened with water.

The fourth truth is the water, which can be sublimated <note>turned into vapor and condensed</note> once the evaporation has occurred; in the sublimation of the water, the earth itself is refined, whereas previously it was thickened with water, and coagulated, and held...

# TO SARRATANT

<margin>m 4</margin>

...you will have earth, water, and air; and this is what the Philosopher says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]," a famous early Latin alchemical text</note>. Sublimate that which has been whitened with a sudden fire, until the spirit that flourishes within it is extracted. This spirit is called the *Goose of Hermes* <note>a symbolic name for the volatile spirit or vapor released during heating</note> and the *chick of Hermogenes*. Then the calcined <term>calcined: reduced to a powder by heat</term> earth remains at the bottom, which is of a fiery nature. And thus, in the aforementioned preparations, you will have the four elements—that is, earth and fire <insert>along with the water and air previously mentioned</insert>. Concerning that calcined earth which is a powder, *Morienus* <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> treats it, saying: "Do not despise the ash which is at the bottom; it is indeed in a lowly place, but it is the earth of your body, which is the end of permanent things."

Afterward, place the ferment <term>ferment: a substance, often gold or silver, added to "leaven" the alchemical base into a noble metal</term> with the aforementioned water. The Philosophers call this ferment the "soul." This is because the human body is nothing without a soul; rather, it is like unclean earth without the ferment—that is, its soul. For the ferment prepares the imperfect body itself, as we have said, and converts it to its own nature; and this ferment is nothing other than *Gold and Silver* <note>original: "Sol & Luna," literally Sun and Moon, the alchemical symbols for gold and silver</note>.

Once these are properly assigned, just as this Alus <note>likely a reference to "Aloe" or a specific bitter salt/base</note> dominates the bodies and converts them to its own nature, they are called "ferment" according to the operation in that same body: let that which is its soul be introduced. And this is what *Morienus* says: "Unless you cleanse the unclean body and place the soul within it, you have directed nothing of the mastery." Therefore, the conjunction of the ferment with the cleansed body takes place, and then the spirit is fixed with it and rejoices with them, because the coarse nature has been made subtle. And this is what *Constantius* says in the *Assembly*: "The spirit is not joined to bodies unless they have been putrefied and stripped bare." Through these conjunctions, the greatest wonders appear, as well as all the colors that can be imagined in the world, by which the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment. This ferment is the soul and spirit; by means of it, the soul and body are joined and bound together with it in the color of the ferment: and thus it is one with them—that is, the arsenic <note>here likely referring to the "philosopher's arsenic" or a specific mineral catalyst rather than the modern poison</note> in the earth.

# HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'S' featuring a floral and scrollwork design within a square border.</image-desc>
It follows now how the terms <note>technical vocabulary of the art</note> are to be understood through metaphor. And you should first know that grinding and whitening are necessary; therefore, in whatever ways things are whitened and ground, or refined, or divided, or separated—or by whatever operations these are done—the names of the processes are taken from those methods and operations. And because certain things are purified through distillation, as waters are through an alembic <note>a chemical still</note>; some through sublimation <note>turning a solid into vapor</note>, as spirits are; some through solution, as salts are; some through washing, as cloths are; some through burning, as lime is; some through division, as metals are separated from one another by the cupel <note>original: "cineritium," a vessel used to refine gold or silver from lead</note>; some through straining, as through a cloth or filter; therefore, when it is said "sublime," or any of these other terms, you should understand then that you must whiten by that method. It is said of the substance: it dissolves itself, it washes itself, it congeals itself, it whitens itself, and so on. It performs these things itself. And this is the thickening of these substances, or their nature joined together, and their moisture, so that they are not extracted or scattered, or dissolved from them by smoke, but rather are curdled <note>coagulated</note>; and how this is done through their own dissolution, yet they are strongly curdled, is hidden by the Philosophers <note>the ancient alchemical authorities</note>.

Whatever actions they name, however, understand that these are always done by the action of the heat of a certain fire, which does not cause sublimation because it is so gentle; nor should you naturally raise any smoke because of its weakness. Therefore, if the fire is such that it almost raises [the vapor] but does not actually raise it, that is good. And whatever things they name through which these actions occur—namely whitening and grinding—you must always understand that "natures" perform these things, or are the agents that do them. These are also the hidden method of the Philosophers, through which moistures are preserved and are not dissolved away from each other, but are curdled. For they preserve themselves from the fire, and they join themselves, whiten, and curdle. Know this, for this is the general doctrine: namely, concerning the method, the action, and the things of this art.

And the solution of the end follows the operation: because all things are completed through this, and it is the last of all the works. Whoever is ignorant of this secret should stay his hands from the work until he knows it: because he will not reach the end of his purpose before it is very well known.

# HERE ENDS THE SECOND PART.

## ROSINUS ON DIVINE
## Interpretations.

FIRST, it must be known that there are four principal ways of converting the elements into one another: to dissolve, to wash, to reduce, and to fix. To dissolve is to make the coarse into the simple; to wash is to render the dark into the bright. To reduce is to pour the moist over the dry <note>a process often called imbibition</note>, and to fix is to dominate the volatile substance over its own body.

To dissolve, therefore, is to divide, to corrupt, and to create the primary nature. To wash is to distill into humidity and to calcine <note>to reduce to bone-white ash through heat</note>. To reduce is to wax <note>soften</note>, to impregnate, and to re-sublimate. To fix is to marry, to dissolve, and to regulate. Therefore, the first kind of work of the Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note> is to dissolve; the second is to distill; the third is to calcine the earth and whiten it by sublimating; the fourth is to re-dissolve, distill, calcine, and re-coagulate. Hence, knowing how to sublimate with Mercury is nothing other than the ash which gives what it does not have. Or otherwise, when it extracts the radical moisture from gold, it is nothing other than the ash which does not give what it does not have: because sublimation covers the art just as the chaff covers the grain. And note that sulfur and sulfurs, orpiment <term>auripigmentum: a yellow arsenic mineral</term> and orpiments, and zandaric <note>likely a corruption of sandarac, a red arsenic mineral</term>, all these are names for the divine water—that is, the Mercurial water of the perfected bodies, foliated and clean. Its whitening is its preparation through sublimation (which is distillation) until it becomes white and bright, in which there are no impurities; and this is the sublimation of Mercury and zandaric. But the washing of the body is the reduction of water over it for so long that nothing remains in it of the soul—which is the tincture <note>the coloring principle</note>—that does not ascend with the spirit. When, therefore, you have taken the soul, and the soul is in that water and nothing remains of it in...

And the spirit: that is, of the sulfur of our body: that is, of the Philosophical brass <note>original: "æris Philosophici"</note> with the father: that is, the Sun <note>Sol</note>, who is the Ruler of the planets and the traveler of heaven: with the son: that is, the quintessence <term>Quinta Essentia: the "fifth element" or purest essence of a substance</term>, namely the Philosophical water: into heaven: that is, it shall have ascended to the upper part of the alembic <note>A distillation vessel</note> and descended: that is, it shall have been clarified through sublimation and distillation. Our souls: that is, the tinctures, are remembered: that is, they become the water of life well-prepared from the body, vivifying the dead: from which proceed Pearls, precious Stones, and Corals. And thus you have the first part of the whole work.

The second part follows, which is made thus: The Earth of Pearls: that is, the earth of precious and luminous water, the light of which destroys the eyes, because every light and color adorns it: as the persistent Senior <note>Refers to the alchemist Senior Zadith</note> says while he touches the other earth. If the earth of leaves: that is, of garments: for leaves are the coverings of trees, and our water is the garment of the earth of our water; whence a certain wise man says: 
> If he ascends naked into heaven, 

and my Lunar body, lovely and white: that is, of the whitest sort like flashing marble and the whitest salt, it will shine back, it will tint the first completed work, namely of whiteness: because when one has arrived at this limit, he makes Moon <note>Silver</note> out of all bodies. Then he touches upon the third earth: that is, the earth of gold, when he says: But the body of my beloved, namely the Sun <note>Sol</note>, shall shine back delightful, ruddy, and rosy. Whence Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; the Persian physician and alchemist</note> says in the Book of Moons: 
> That which has been said strengthens the beginning of all roots, and when it has been perfected, it converts Jupiter <note>Tin</note> and Saturn <note>Lead</note> into the best Moon <note>Silver</note> upon the surface. 

Whence Morienus <note>A legendary hermit-alchemist</note> says to Khalid <note>The Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> at the end: After this, dissipate that, looking into its interior, and if white remains in it, well-strengthened and fixed...

Note what I said before, that the spirit of our body is perfected with the father and the son: as Rasis <note>Rhazes, a famous Persian alchemist and physician</note> says in the Book of the Moon. Our Stone <note>original: "Lapis noster"</note> has a name from the creation of the world, which is three and one. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: The confidence of the Philosophers consists in two things, to which they join a third. Therefore the Philosophers called it "the odd one." In no other bodies is Mercury found cleaner and more perfect than in these three: the Sun, the Moon, and common Mercury. Whence Senior <note>Zadith ben Hamuel, an 10th-century alchemist</note> says: nothing generates a thing from itself, except from that which is of itself and its own species, which is homogeneous to it. Similarly Adam and all the human race, and everything agrees with its neighbor and what is similar to it according to its species. Begin therefore in the name of the Lord to know its nature. For it is of its own matter, which is in the same and from the same, nor does anything else enter upon it which is not of it.

It is the medicine of bodies, and it makes bodies receptive to colors; it kills and gives life, God willing. It dries and moistens, heats and cools, and performs contrary works according to its container. When it is alive, and when it is dead, you have certain special works such as gilding; but when it is dead and dissolved, you have the greatest work of all.

It is the serpent that lusts after itself, impregnating itself, and bringing forth birth in a single day. With its poison, it kills all animals and bodies, and if it becomes fire, it kills all in a short or long time. It is a fugitive from fire, yet it awaits the fire through the skills of the wise when it is fed with fire; let it not wait, and wonderful works are made from them. Therefore, when it is tinted, it tints; when it is curdled, it curdles; when it is dissolved, it dissolves. Another part whitens itself like urine, and turns red in the fire. It sharpens its own sharpness, and it is the middle point between the bitter and the sour. It is a water that does not flow in the fire, a softening; it is a congealing made by a gentle fire, bringing forth a crystalline substance, either white or red. As hard as **Mars** <note>original: "Mars" - the alchemical name for Iron</note>: and so on. Therefore **Dantius** says, prepare the bodies and dissolve them, and from that water drink in the washed spirits: then the spirits themselves are submerged into the bodies, and the bodies into the spirits, and thus the bodies are joined with the spirits in a firm fixation. **<term>RASIS</term>** <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a celebrated Persian physician and alchemist</note>: Convert the bodies into water, and from that earth the whole is then made. **<term>Alpharinus</term>**: When the body is first purged and <term>calcined</term> <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, it is then joined with the washed spirits; then those sublimated and fixed spirits make it firm. **<term>Galen</term>** <note>referring to the famous ancient Greek physician</note>: Prepare the bodies and purge them of the blackness in which there is corruption, until the white becomes white and the red [becomes red]: then dissolve both into water, namely the spirit and the body: and congeal them, and thus it is projected upon the washed body.

**Solution** is the resolution of a dry thing into water, through the moist and cold, or through the hot and moist. Moreover, bodies are dissolved so that from them water may be made, through which the spirits are <term>incerated</term> <note>softened to a wax-like consistency</note> and fixed. Whence this entire <term>mastery</term> <note>original: "magisterium" - the completion of the alchemical work</note> is done in four ways: either so that you dissolve the bodies and make the spirits firm; for the spirits ought to be made firm with the waters of the bodies. Bodies and spirits are dissolved for another reason: so that when the water of the spirit is joined to the water of the bodies, they are thus coagulated into one, assisted and made firm, so that they cannot be further separated. And this **universal solution** makes the four Elements return into one substance, firm and fixed. But when both are dissolved, namely bodies and spirits, then a close and particular mixture occurs, which fire can still separate. Therefore, spirits are dissolved in two ways: with the oil of the congelation of <term>tartar</term> <note>potassium bitartrate</note> upon a stone; or in another way by the water of <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note>. There is also another solution by the heat of fire. And note, that the solution of fire is worth more than the others: because that which is dissolved by fire is turned into air. The solutions of bodies are made similarly to those of spirits, such as the <term>flower of copper</term> <note>original: "flos aeris" - verdigris or copper oxide</note>, vitriol, white lead, red lead, etc.

**Distillation**: that is, by the <term>alembic</term> <note>a chemical still consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</note>, and it is the best; it is done so that water and oils, in their ascension through vapors, may be more purified and strengthened against depravity and all corruption, lest they putrefy further. In another way, oil is distilled so that it loses its scorching humidity, as I have experienced in oil of Laurel. It is called restoration. the more they have been distilled, the better their tincture <note>The "tincture" refers to the transformative essence or color-changing property of an alchemical substance.</note> will be. We distill through a filter so that raw waters or dissolved things cannot rot, nor can the dregs be separated from them except through a filter; by this means the thick matter remains behind and all that is pure descends, as is done with orpiment <note>original: "auripigm." - a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> or arsenic on account of their oiliness. And note that a body is not distilled unless it is first dissolved, because its water is not separated from it until it perfectly whitens it or reddens it; for I tested this for many years before I came to the truth. And note, that you should never place cold glass into a boiler or hot water, and conversely, do not put hot glass into cold water, otherwise it would break immediately. And when you wish to remove the glass, allow it to cool beforehand. In fermentation, one must be especially careful with the vessels, lest they be broken. And note that unless a body rots <note>original: "putrescat" - refers to the stage of *putrefaction*, where matter breaks down to be reborn.</note>, it produces no fruit. For first, putrefaction or solution must occur, afterwards it is distilled; do not believe any body can be made unless it is first resolved through decay.

Bodies and spirits are "waxed" <note>original: "incerantur" - the process of *inceration*, softening a substance to a waxy consistency to prepare it for fusion.</note> when, lacking liquefaction upon entry, they are softened so that they flow and have the power of penetration. In no other things is this near-created humidity found more easily than in Venus <note>The alchemical name for Copper.</note> and arsenic. The method is this: their sublimation should be repeated over the part to be waxed so many times until, remaining in that humidity, they provide a good fusion; this does not happen before their perfect purification from every corrupting thing. Therefore, it would be good if their oils were first fixed, as I said above regarding the coagulation of waters. Coagulation indeed occurs—namely of those waters or oils—by the slow fire of candles, increasing it little by little until they are congealed. The space of time for coagulation is three days, and the fire must be continued day and night. In these things, therefore, consists the entire operation of the mastery <note>original: "magisterii" - the *Grand Magisterium* or the completion of the Great Work.</note>. Note, when the soul is joined to the body, the body is quickly consumed and changed into another substance: because in its first operation it is black, in the second more lucid, in the third still clearer, and so on up to fifteen times by dissolving and congealing; and in every congelation, take care that it senses nothing of salt, but wash it again and again. If you place a small particle of these substances, about the size of a grain of barley, upon a glowing hot plate, and it flows and stains the surface of the plate with its color, it is good. If it does not, know that some harm has occurred during the dissolution: for a body that is not well dissolved <note>original: "solutum corpus"; in alchemy, "dissolving" refers to breaking a solid down into its primary liquid essence</note> does not have the fitness to enter another. These failures are caused either by the shortness of time or by the weakness of the heat from the manure <note>Manure was frequently used in laboratories as a source of steady, gentle "digesting" heat</note>. If it penetrates, but not deeply, this happens from a lack of "Air" <note>The element of Air was associated with the volatile, moving spirit of the substance</note>. For the soul entering the body runs swiftly through all its veins, like an ointment. If, however, a part of it flies away, this happens from a multitude of spirits that are not yet "fixed" <note>To "fix" a substance means to make a volatile spirit stable so it no longer evaporates when heated</note>. But if it is laid down flowing, staining, and penetrating deeply through the whole plate, not flying away, yet leaving behind a misty smoke, this is from a slight lack of clarity in the separated elements. Therefore, arrange the airy substance through discernment—namely, within the body of the common Earth—and the earthy substance according to the moisture of the Air, and the heat and dryness of the Sun <note>The "Sun" here refers to gold or the highest degree of heat</note> or a gentle fire, until they agree and are joined. And then join to them the two operative virtues: namely, Water for the White <term>Albedo: the second major stage of the alchemical work, resulting in silver</term>, and Fire for the Red <term>Rubedo: the final stage of the work, resulting in gold</term>. And so, my son, you must have a twofold "imbibed" earth: one soaked with Water and Air for the whiteness, and another soaked with Air, Water, and elemental Fire by weight, for the red. Then you shall have your desires, God granting.

# ROSINUS

One part is in the mountains, another in the sea, a third part is in the ditches, and a fourth in the caverns. One does not know the language of the other, but the father of these parts has joined them into one; when they saw each other, they spoke with one voice, saying: "Let us go seek the natures of the four elements, which women bring forth from the belly of the earth."

Likewise, Massarai <note>Likely a reference to a Persian or Arabic alchemical authority</note> says: There is an impurity in this stone because of which men despise it, and they believe that they cannot separate it. Also, from this stone is born quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, which they call by many names. Likewise, the place of this stone is the four elements, and the spirits are four, the gates are four, and the keys are four, one of which is the sign—namely, the showing of the water through the alembic <term>alembic: a distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>. 

Likewise, this stone—which is not a stone—is cast into common things, and is exalted in the mountains, and lives in the air, and feeds in the river. It is the quicksilver which they call by many names, and it rests on the peak of the mountain; its mother is a virgin, and its father did not lie with her. This same stone is trodden underfoot in dung heaps, and often fools dig to extract it, but they cannot find it. And that stone is likened to the stones of minerals and plants, and is convertible into any color, namely white, red, and lemon-yellow; and it contains within itself the four artificial elements, namely clear water, yellow, red, green, and lemon-yellow. 

And it is called the "lesser world," not because it is a microcosm <note>original: "microcosmus"</note>, but because the world is ruled through it; wherefore Geber the Saracen <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> crushed it and whitened it for 33 days in distilled vinegar. And you should know that the Philosophers called alkali salt <note>original: "sal alkali"</note> and distilled urine "vinegar"; when this has been evacuated, divide the elements—divide them equally and proportionally with careful crushing. Do this so that there is no division or repugnance in it, and you shall have your purpose, the Lord granting.

Mitigo the Philosopher: Although our stone is crushed under the feet of men and animals, yet because of the diligence of the man Geber, it is loved by the wise; and he says "diligence" because it is made by the industriousness of the man Geber. 

Likewise, Malus the Philosopher: This stone is beneath you in terms of obedience; above you in terms of dominion; therefore it is from you in terms of knowledge, and around you in terms of equals. 

Aristotle: Therefore I shall name our stone; it is the limit of the soul <note>original: "terminus ani," likely a corruption of "terminus animae"</note>: for it is the Egg of the Philosophers which exists in putrefaction and purity.

# ROSINUS

It is enclosed within you and you hold it secretly; it is extracted from you when it is reduced and dissolved by you. For without you it cannot be completed, and you cannot live without it; thus the end looks back to the beginning and vice versa. It is born on two mountains: that is, from Venus <note>original: "Venere"; here referring to Copper or the feminine principle</note> and Mercury through the constant decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid</note> of nature, from which all volatile things—namely body and spirit—take their nourishment. Those things which are not fixed receive their coloration and fixation from it. Do not take it unless it is fresh and prepared with its own blood: that is, with Venus not yet melted, or well prepared, whose [nature] is from blood: that is, its life or operation is from living Venus. Let it die in the air, namely through the elevation of fire, or rather sublimation and purification. And if this stone were not of an aerial nature—that is, of the same preparation—it would not be joined to Mercury, and their operation would not be perfect and firm. But because they are similar, once both are prepared, they are mixed and united so that fire cannot separate them.

You shall therefore separate the Philosophy, through this teaching, the saffron-colored from the white, the precious thing from the vile, until the four elements proceed from one thing: and again, the four concur into one. Their roots are water and fire; their opposites are earth and air. Indeed, all things are made from one, and again the four become one. Therefore, the four are made from one thing in this way: first water, second oil, third fire, fourth earth. From these four—so composed and purified that they flow without smoke or combustion, so that they remain, enter, and are mixed with the bodies of metals—the *Iccir* <note>likely a corruption of the Arabic 'al-iksir' or Elixir</note> composite is made.

And note, that one must take four parts of the prepared earth and one part of fire; mix with these two parts of the aforementioned oil, and grind them into a paste. Some have said seven parts of earth, others twelve; and both are true, though the first is better. Others have said that one part of earth tints twenty parts. Others say that one part of double earth tints twice its sevenfold; and thus he shows you the weights, the composition, what is better, and what comes first. Do what you will, yet the regimen is one and the operation is one.

Finally, it must be noted that five things are necessary for this work: that is, the calcination <note>reduction to powder by heat</note> of bodies and spirits, or the sublimation—namely, the reduction of the calcined thing into water is done by the power...

Likewise note, spirits cannot enter bodies unless they are purified, and they do not enter unless they are led by water. Therefore Dantius <note>Likely a reference to an alchemical authority, possibly a corruption of a name like Arnaldus</note> says: "Prepare the bodies and dissolve them, and from that water soak the washed spirits: then the spirits themselves are submerged in the bodies, and the bodies in the spirits: and thus the spirits will be fixed with the most permanent fixation." Wherefore Rasis <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925 AD), a celebrated Persian physician and alchemist</note> says: "Convert the bodies into water, and join that water to the air; that is, to the spirit, namely Mercury, and from those two make water again, and then earth, and the whole is done." Galen <note>A famous Greek physician, though here cited for alchemical wisdom</note> says: "Prepare the bodies and purge them of blackness, in which there is corruption, until it becomes white and red, then dissolve both into water, namely the spirit and the body, and coagulate them, and thus cast it upon the washed body."

When bodies and spirits are dissolved, then a universal solution occurs, which also creates the four elements, and returns them into one firm and fixed substance: but when both are not dissolved, then a nearby and particular mixture occurs, which fire can still separate. Note that when the soul is joined to the body, the body is quickly consumed, and is changed into another substance, and after its first operation it becomes black. In the second, however, it becomes more lucid. In the third, it becomes even clearer, until it is perfected through fifteen solutions and coagulations, and in any coagulation, take care that it senses nothing of salt, but...

There are therefore these four principal spirits in our art: arsenic, Sal Ammoniac—because without it the spirits would neither be dissolved nor enter <note>The "entry" refers to the chemical penetration of a metal by a reagent</note>; for it dissolves and fixes all spirits, penetrates all metals, and softens them. Use it therefore in all your works: but know this, that by itself bodies are neither whitened nor reddened, nor are they transubstantiated as they are by other spirits, but it only provides an entry for the other spirits: but once mixed and joined in unions and perseverances, it departs. The third spirit is **Mercury**, whose definition and nature you have copiously in the works of **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century alchemist</note>. # THE BOOK BEGINS
### *of divine interpretations and definitions.*

TAKE the stone which is black, white, red, and yellow, and the marvelous bird, which flies without wings in the darkness of night and the clarity of day: for from the bitterness existing in its throat, the coloring is obtained, but from its blood the pure water is taken, just as Alexander <note>Likely referring to Alexander the Great, to whom many medieval alchemical works were pseudographically attributed.</note> said. Take the stone of four colors, my son. Take the flying volatile thing that is submerged, and from its redness which kills it, they shall extract it: from that redness, repel it so that it becomes one, and it may remain with you not by flying through the regions, but you shall raise it up by flight, and from the root extract its shadow: and the filth, because the mist looming over it defiles it, and keeps it from the light as if it were being squeezed, and it is burned by its own redness. Take, therefore, this superior water, corrupted just like fire. Laton <note>A term for an impure copper alloy or the "base" metal state in alchemy.</note> is one with the ash, since it separates itself from it until the red of the copper is vitrified <note>turned into glass</note>; then a certain partnership is made for you, it grows warm and rests for you. My son, keep it known that the water was first in the air, then it dwelt in the earth; return it to the higher places and through its own boundaries all things are joined together not unsuitably: then join it to its red spirit, the first element, except for a part. Likewise Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: Take the black stone, the stone from the mountains of India; that which is inside, put outside, and that which is outside, put inside. Wherefore Rasis <note>The Latinized name of Al-Razi, a famous Persian physician and alchemist.</note> says: my son, contemplate the highest mountains, which are on the right and on the left, and ascend there: there our stone is found, and in another mountain, which bears every kind of pigment and spirit or species, it is likewise there. Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says: Climb the high mountains planted with trees: because there our stone is found, and it is hidden. Likewise Hermes: From the Head, take the mixed stone, saffron-yellow and white, and crush it and separate the white from the saffron. The same says: Take the blessed stone, crush and wash the red stone, from which it is extracted, which is found in the mountains, and especially sometimes in old sewers. And note, that nature in the beginning of its origin intends to make the Sun or Mo— <note>original: "Solem vel Lu-", likely referring to Sol (Gold) or Luna (Silver).</note>

# ROSINUS TO SARRATANT

For it is so, but it cannot be on account of <unclear>v</unclear>enereal <note>original: "venerem"; here referring to copper or lustful corruption</note> corruption, the joined quicksilver <note>term: Quicksilver (Argentum vivum) — Mercury, the fluid principle of all metals</note>, or on account of foul earth. For just as a child in its mother's womb contracts infirmity and corruption from the corruption of the womb by the accident of its location—even if the seed were pure—the child nevertheless becomes leprous and unclean because of the corrupted womb. And so it is with all the perfect metals which are corrupted by Venus <note>original: "Venere"; copper</note> and foul earth. The proof of this matter, that metals are generated from Mercury and Venus, is this: because even from these two things produced naturally, the same can be produced artificially, as Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit</note> testifies.

It must be known, therefore, that in truth the science of Alchemy is spread through many books and chapters, and through many species and mineral headings, etc., and named with infinite names; yet nevertheless it is but one thing, whose beginning looks toward its end, and its end toward its beginning. And wherever it may be, and by whatever names it is called, it is nothing but one thing. Whence the verse: *And this art demands one thing, which everyone knows well: many people prepare this thing, yet it is but one thing.* Similarly, this art does not require great expense, nor great labor. Whence Morienus says: *Every thing which is bought at a great price is found to be false and useless in this work.* 

Why then do they say so many species are necessary in the art, if there is only one thing? Morienus answered: Its root is one, which gives and renews its color. Sulphur is the fourth spirit, whose nature you should seek in the works of Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century polymath and "Father of Chemistry"</note>: by its vapor, quicksilver is led forth.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring a central rose-like flower surrounded by scrolling foliage within a square border.</image-desc>Aros the Philosopher <note>Aros is a recurring figure in alchemical literature, often identified as a student or interlocutor of Mary</note> met with Mary the Prophetess, the sister of Moses, and approaching her, he showed her honor and said to her: "O Prophetess, I have indeed heard many speak of you, saying that you whiten the stone in a single day." ...it will happen in less than three hours of the day, and the smoke will penetrate the body, and the spirit will be bound, and they will become a wax-like substance <note>original: "incerans," referring to a stage where a solid becomes soft like wax</note> that melts and penetrates: and that is the secret. To which Aros said: "O Lady, you have been obedient in the society of the *Scoyari*; O Prophetess, have you found in the secrets of the Philosophers that they placed in their books that anyone could perform the art from a single body?"

And Mary said: "Certainly, which Hermes did not teach, because the root of the school is a body that cannot be carved, incurable, and it is a poison <note>original: "toxicum"</note> mortifying all bodies, and it pulverizes them, and congeals Mercury <term>Quicksilver</term> by its odor. And she said: I swear to you by the Eternal God, that when that poison is dissolved until it becomes a subtle water—I do not care by what solution it is made—it congeals Mercury into Moon <term>Silver</term> with the strength of truth, and it enters into the leaf of Jupiter <term>Tin</term>, and 'moon-ifies' <note>transforms into silver</note> it into Moon. And in all bodies there is knowledge, but the Stoics, because of the shortness of their lives and the length of the work, have hidden this; and they found these tinting elements, and they increased them, and all the Philosophers teach those things except for the **Vessel of Hermes**, because that is divine, and hidden from the Nations by the wisdom of the Lord; and those who are ignorant of it do not know the regimen of truth, because of their ignorance of the Vessel of Hermes."

<summary>Mary the Prophetess explains to Aros that the alchemical "medicine" is derived from a "poisonous" root that can transform base metals into silver, emphasizing that the secret Vessel of Hermes is the essential tool for regulating the fire.</summary>
