# THE BOOK OF KHALID, SON OF YAZID

Those who attained that goal concealed certain things about it and revealed others. For thus I found the wise predecessors, agreeing on this in their honored books. From this you should know that my own disciple, Musa <note>Likely referring to a student of Khalid ibn Yazid, the Umayyad prince credited with early alchemical translations</note>—who is more honorable to me than all others—studied their books extensively and labored in the work of the mastery <note>The "mastery" or *magisterium* refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process</note>. Consequently, the composition of the work weighed heavily upon him; he doubted it in many ways and was similarly ignorant of the natures of the composition of things. 

Humble and suppliant for the sake of this art, he sought from me an explanation and direction regarding it. I, however, gave him no answer, nor did I wish to discern it for him; instead, I commanded him to read the books of the Philosophers and to investigate within them what he had sought from me. He then went away and read more than a hundred books, as many as he could find—namely the true and secret books of the noble Philosophers—and yet he could not find what he sought. He remained thereafter stupefied, as if out of his mind, even while searching through them continually for a year. 

Therefore, since my disciple Musa—who deserved to be counted among the Philosophers in his degree and manner of wisdom—doubted the composition in this way, and this happened to him, what shall the ignorant or foolish man do, who does not understand the natures of things, nor knows the complexions of substances? 

When I saw this regarding my chosen and most dear disciple, moved by piety and love for him—and indeed by the divine will and nod—I produced this book of mine at the time of my death. In it, I have omitted certain things that the predecessor Philosophers reported in their books, and I have said certain things which they concealed and in no way wished to say or reveal in their writings. I have explained and exposed things which they covered with their obscure and figurative sayings. And I have called this my *Book of the Secrets of Alchemy*. 

In this book, I have named whatever is necessary for the seeker of this science or mastery, using a language suited to the understanding and sense of the inquirer. And I have named in this book four masteries, higher and better than those the wise men performed. Of these, there is the <term>Elixir</term> <note>The "Elixir" (from the Arabic *al-iksir*) refers to the medicinal or transformative substance capable of transmuting base metals or healing the body</note>: one is mineral and another is animal; the remaining two are mineral but are not a single elixir, of which one is the artifice of washing, which you...

This same failure is contingent upon the quantity of weights; when these are mismatched in the compound, with the parts of that same nature transcending their limits through increase or decrease, the property of the compound is destroyed, and the effect of the compound becomes a failure and a void.

And I show you one example: Do you not see that in soap, with which clothes are washed and cleansed and made white, this property is generated in its correct composition? This is due to the equality and the right and due proportions of the compound, which share in length and breadth. From this participation they come together, and then that which was in it of the truth of the deed appeared; thus the power which previously lay hidden became known, which they call a "property," and it is the power of washing generated in the compound. ### *On the four masteries of the art, namely: solution, congelation, whitening, and reddening. CHAPTER I.*

And I begin to describe the greater artifice, which they call Alchemy <note>original: "Alchemiam"</note>, and I will certify my discourse, concealing nothing; nor will I remain silent here concerning it, except for that which is not fitting to speak, nor proper to name. We say, therefore, that the greater artifice consists of four masteries <note>term: magisteria; the primary stages or operations of the alchemical process</note>, just as the wise men have said: namely, to Dissolve, to Congeal, to Whiten, and to Redden. And these four quantities are participants, of which two are similarly participants with each other, and likewise the other two. And each of these double quantities has another participating quantity, which is the greater participating quantity after these two. 

And I wish to say, regarding these quantities, the quantity of the natures and the weight of the medicines, which are dissolved and congealed in order, where neither diminution nor addition enters. But both of these—namely, solution and congelation—shall be in one operation, and they merit a single act, and this occurs before the composition. But after their composition, the work will be different; yet this solution and congelation which I have named are the solution of the body and the congelation of the spirit <note>In alchemy, the "body" usually refers to solid matter or metals, while "spirit" refers to volatile substances like mercury or sulfur</note>, and they are two, yet they have one operation. For the spirits are not congealed except by the solution of the body, and similarly, the body is not dissolved except by the congelation of the spirit. 

And when the body and the soul <note>original: "anima"</note> are joined together, each of them acts upon its companion, making it like unto itself. An example of this is water and earth: for when water is joined to earth, it strives to dissolve it with its moisture and its virtue and the property that is within it, and it makes the earth finer than it was before, and renders it similar to itself; for water was finer than earth. And the soul acts in the same way upon the body; and in the same manner, the water is thickened with the earth and becomes similar to the earth in density, because the earth thickens—

# THE BOOK OF SECRETS

...is water. And you should know that between the **dissolving of the body** <note>Latin: *solutionem corporis*; the process of turning a solid substance into a liquid state</note> and the **congealing of the spirit** <note>Latin: *congelationem spiritus*; the process of fixing a volatile substance into a solid state</note>, there is no difference in time, nor is there a separate task, such that one could exist without the other. Just as there is no distinct interval of time between water and earth in their joining—where one might be recognized or expected apart from the other in their workings—so too they have one limit and one deed. One and the same operation revolves over both of them simultaneously, before the composition.

I have said "before the composition" so that whoever reads this book and hears of "dissolving" and "congealing" (as I have described) does not mistake this for the "composition" named by the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient alchemical authorities like Hermes Trismegistus or Geber</note>. To think so would be an error in both practice and knowledge. For **composition** in this craft or mastery <term>magisterium: the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work"</term> is the joining or **marriage** of the congealed spirit with the dissolved body. Their union and their suffering <note>Latin: *passio*; here meaning the chemical reaction or "undergoing" of change</note> occurs over the fire.

For heat is its nourishment, and the soul does not leave the body, nor is it joined to it in a total union, except through the transformation of both from their original power and property, and after the conversion of their natures. This is the "dissolving and congealing" that the Philosophers spoke of previously. Know that the wise men have hidden this dissolving and congealing, speaking of it with subtle reasoning and through obscure and covered words, so that the mind of the seeker might be distanced from their true understanding. Here is an example of the covered and obscure speech of the Philosophers:

->**Anoint the leaf with poison, and the beginning of the office (or the mastery itself) will be proven true for you.**<-

And:

->**Work the strong bodies with dissolved broth, until both are converted to their subtlety.**<-

Similarly, the saying of the Wise Man regarding these things is:

->**Unless you convert the bodies into subtlety, so that they are fine and impalpable to the touch, you will not achieve what you seek. And if they have not been ground down, return to the work until they are ground and become subtle; if you do this, your desire will be guided to success.**<-

They set down many such words in this manner. Nor could any of those testing these things reach this hidden fact in any way, until a clear opening of the demonstrated teaching appeared to them, removing previous doubt. And they named the composition in a similar fashion...

### *On the things and instruments necessary and suitable for this work. CHAPTER II.*

And you must know the vessels used in this mastery, namely the *Aludels* <note>original: "Aludela"; pear-shaped earthenware pots used for sublimation</note>, which the wise call "cemeteries" or "sieves": because in them the parts are divided and cleansed, and in them the matter of the mastery is perfected, completed, and purified. And similarly, the things necessary for them are four. They are the bodies, the souls, the spirits, and the waters: and from these four come the mastery and the mineral work. These are explained in the books of the wise, and I have removed them from this book of mine, and I have named herein what the Philosophers did not name. And whoever possesses even a little intellect will know what those things are. For I have not made this book for the ignorant and the unknowing, but I have composed it for the prudent, and for those possessing and knowing sense and wisdom.

### *On decoction and its effect.*
### CHAPTER IV.

The successful completion of an alchemical process or the "Great Work" itself.</note> is like this. Whence our seed, which is regarded thus by the wise, has as its perfection and its process the fire; fire is the cause of life and death, which does not grant life except through an intermediary and its own spirituality, which are not mixed except with fire. Now I have verified for you the truth, which I have seen and also performed.

The subtle mixed itself with the dense, and those things were made into one substance: namely, its warm and moist soul, and its cold and dry body. Afterward, it <note>the substance</note> attempted to dissolve and refine itself with its heat and its moisture, which is its soul. And it attempted to enclose and retain itself with its body, which is cold and dry. And thus, upon this principle, the work of this art revolves and is transformed. I have already asserted to you the truth, which I have seen and performed; and I have commanded you to transform the natures from their subtlety and their substances with heat and moisture, until they are converted to another substance and other colors. And do not transgress what is said in this book, and you shall proceed rightly in the mastery <term>Magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> as you desire.

### *On the fixation of the spirit. CHAPTER VI.*

And you should know that when the body mixes itself with moisture, and the heat of the fire finds it, the moisture is turned upon the body and dissolves it; then the spirit cannot depart from it, because it has soaked itself in with the fire. For spirits are fleeting <note>volatile</note> until the bodies are mixed with them, and they attempt to fight against the fire and its flame. Yet these parts agree but little, except through good operation and continuous, long labor; for the nature of the soul is to tend upward, where the center of the soul is located. And who among the experimenters is able to join two or diverse things whose centers are different, except after the conversion of their natures, and the mutation of the substance and the thing from its own nature? This is a difficult thing to seek. Therefore, he who is able to convert the soul into the body, and the body into the soul, and to mix the subtle spirits with it, shall tinge <note>transform or dye</note> every body.

### *On the decoction, grinding, and washing of the stone. CHAPTER VII.*

And know that what is very necessary in this secret and mastery is decoction <note>boiling or heating</note>, grinding, sifting, and purification, as well as washing with sweet waters. Therefore, whoever shall work upon any part of this, let him purify it well, and wash and cleanse from it the blackness and the darkness which appear upon it during its operation.

### *On the quantity of fire, and its benefit and harm. CHAPTER VIII.*

And let him likewise understand the quantities of fires, and the benefit of this matter; for the harm of the same arises from the [improper] use of fire. Whence Plato said in his discourses, in his book: Fire adds benefit or progress to the perfect, and harm or corruption to the corrupted. <note>Plato is frequently cited in medieval alchemy as a philosophical authority, though the works attributed to him were often later "pseudo-Platonic" texts.</note> Whence, when its quantity is good and suitable, it will be profitable; but when it is increased in things beyond measure, it will corrupt both—namely, the perfect and the corrupted alike. And for this reason, it was necessary for the wise to apply their medicines upon the Elixir <term>Elixir: the "philosopher's stone" or medicinal substance capable of transmuting metals</term>, to prohibit and remove from them the combustion of fires and their heat. 

And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> said to his father: "Father, I fear the enemy in my dwelling." And he said: "Son, take a male Corascene dog <note>original: "canem masculum Corascenem." Likely referring to Khorasan, a region in Persia known for its dogs; here used as an alchemical metaphor for a specific chemical substance.</note> and an Armenian bitch, and join them together, and they will give birth to a dog the color of heaven <note>The "color of heaven" usually refers to a celestial blue or a specific stage of the alchemical process.</note>, and let him drink a single thirst's worth of sea water: for he will guard your friend, and guard you from your enemy, and he will help you wherever you are, always being with you in this world and in the next." 

And Hermes wished to mean, by the dog and the bitch, those things which preserve bodies from the combustion of fire and its heat. And those things are the waters made from limes and salts, the preparations of which are found in the books of the wise concerning this mastery <term>magisterio: the "Great Work" or the technical process of alchemy</term>. And some of the wise have named them "sea waters," and "milk of the birds," and similar things.

## *On the nature of the stone and its origin.*
### CHAPTER X.

Take it, therefore, and work it as the Philosopher said in his book when he named it thus: "Take the stone that is not a stone," or "that which is not a stone, nor of the nature of a stone." It is a stone whose mineral is generated in the peaks of mountains; and the Philosopher meant "mountains" to stand for a living creature <note>The text suggests an "animal" or organic origin for the alchemical prime matter, rather than a literal mineral one.</note>. Go, son, with them: for they quickly vanish away.

# *On the mixing of the separated elements.*
### CHAPTER XI.

And begin the composition <note>The process of combining substances</note>, which is the completion of the entire work: for composition will not occur, except through marriage and putrefaction <note>In alchemy, "marriage" refers to the union of opposites, and "putrefaction" to the breaking down of substances through heat and moisture</note>. And marriage is the mixing of the subtle <note>the gaseous or volatile</note> with the thick <note>the solid or dense</note>. And putrefaction is to roast, to grind, and to moisten, until they are mixed together and become one: so that there is no diversity in them, nor any separation, like water mixed with water. And then the thick will strive to retain the subtle, and the soul <note>original: "anima"; the mediating life-force of the substance</note> will strive to fight with the fire, and to endure it. And the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; the volatile essence</note> will strive to be submerged in the bodies, and to be melted into them. 

And it was necessary for this to be: because the dissolved body, when it mixed itself with the soul, mixed itself with it and with all its parts, and some entered into others according to their likeness, and were converted into one and the same thing. And therefore it was necessary that there should happen to the soul that same benefit, durability, and permanence which happens to the body in the place of mixing. And likewise for the spirit in this state—or the permanence of the soul and body—it was fitting for this to have happened. Because when the spirit is mixed with them through the labor of the operation, and its parts have been mixed with all the parts of the other two (which are, namely, the soul and the body), then they were converted—the spirit and both the others—into a single and indivisible thing, according to a whole substance whose natures remained safe, and its parts came together. 

Whence, when this composite meets a dissolved body, and heat follows it, and there appears upon its surface that moisture which was within it, and it has been liquefied in the dissolved body and passed into it, and mixed itself with that which is of the nature of moisture, it ignites itself, and the fire defends itself with it. Whence, when the fire then wishes to be suspended with it, it will prevent the fire from seizing it: that is, from adhering to the spirit mixed with its own water. And the fire will not adhere to it until it is pure. And similarly water, by its own nature, flees from the fire; and when the fire follows it and wishes to make it fly away <note>evaporate</note>, the body was thus the decisive cause for retaining the water, and the water the cause for retaining the oil, so that it would not be burned or consumed. And the oil was the cause for retaining the dye—

It details the mechanical and spiritual union required to ensure that volatile elements (spirit/water) are fixed by solid elements (body) so they do not evaporate when heated.</summary>

## *On the dissolution of the composite stone.*
### CHAPTER XII.

But afterwards, the Philosophers applied their subtlety to dissolving these things, so that they might mix well together—the body and the soul. For all things that are joined together in grinding, roasting, and watering <note>original: "contritione & assatione, & rigatione"</note> possess a proximity and a binding to one another; therefore, the fire can take the nature from the weaker part until it fails and vanishes. Similarly, the fire returns upon the stronger parts until the body remains without the soul. 

When they are dissolved and congealed in this way, they receive their parts into one another—namely, their great and small parts—and from them a complex union was formed, and it is their joining together; thus those two were converted into one and the same thing. And when it was so, the fire takes from the soul as much as it takes from the body, neither adding nor diminishing, and through these things perfection was achieved. 

Because of this, it is necessary to have a specific chapter in the science of the Elixir, namely the discourse on dissolving simple bodies and souls. For bodies do not enter upon souls—and become restraints for them, and excuse them from every work of sublimating, fixing, retaining, and mixing, and the like—except with the first purification <note>original: "mundificatione prima"</note>. 

And know that dissolution does not go beyond these two methods: either it is to draw out the interior of things to their surface, and for this there will be a dissolution. An example of this is that silver is cold and dry in its appearance, but when its interior appears, it is dissolved, because it is hot and moist. Or, the said dissolution is for a body to acquire an accidental moisture which it did not have, adding its own moisture to it; and therefore its parts dissolve themselves, and for that, there will be a dissolution.

## *The method of operating the stone for the white.*
### CHAPTER XV.

When, therefore, you wish to perform this honored mastery <note>original: "magisterium" - the Great Work or the process of transmutation</note>, take the honored stone and place it in a gourd-shaped vessel <note>original: "cucurbita" - a round-bottomed flask used in distillation</note>, and cover it with a still-head <note>original: "alembico"</note>, and seal it well with the clay of wisdom <note>original: "luto sapientiæ" - a specialized sealant used by alchemists to make vessels airtight</note>, and allow it to dry. You shall do this whenever you seal with the clay of wisdom. Afterward, place it in very hot dung <note>stercus - used as a steady, low-heat source for digestion</note>; then you shall distill it, and place a receiver beneath it into which the water may be distilled. Leave it thus until all the water is distilled, the humidity is dried out, and dryness prevails over it. 

Afterward, you shall extract the dry substance and save the water that distilled from it until it is necessary for you. You shall take the dry body which remained in the bottom of the gourd and grind it, and place it in a copper-leaf vessel <note>original: "Chalcofolario"</note>, the size of which should be according to the quantity of the medicine. You shall bury it in moist horse dung, as excellently hot as possible, and let the vessel be well closed with a stopper and the clay of wisdom, and leave it to remain there. And when you perceive that the dung wishes to grow cold, you shall prepare other very hot dung and place the said vessel in it. You shall do this with it for forty days, frequently renewing the hot dung when it is necessary, and the medicine will dissolve into itself and become a thick, white water. And when you see it thus, determine its weight, and add to it half of its weight from the water which you previously saved. Then seal the vessel with the clay of wisdom and return it again to the hot horse dung...

# *The conversion of the aforementioned stone into red.*
## CHAPTER XVI.

And if you wish to convert this mastery <note>Latin: magisterium; the successful completion of an alchemical process</note> into gold: Take of this medicine, which (as I have said) you have brought to this honored state and to this high rank, the weight of one drachm <note>A small unit of weight, roughly 3.5 grams</note>, and this according to the manner of your example mentioned above. And place it in a copper vessel <note>Latin: chalcofolario; a vessel made of copper or bronze</note>, and you shall bury it in horse dung for forty days: because it will be dissolved. Afterward, you shall give it to drink the water of the dissolved body <note>Likely referring to "liquid gold" or a specific chemical solvent</note>, first as much as is half of its own weight; afterward, until it is congealed, you shall bury it in very hot dung, as was said before. Then, in order, you shall do in this chapter of gold just as you did above in the chapter of silver. And it will be gold, and it will work gold, if God wills. Guard, my son, this most secret book, and do not place it in the hands of the ignorant—the secret of the secrets of God: because you will accomplish what you desire.

# THE BOOK OF THREE
## WORDS BY KALLID
### *the most noble.*

## ON THE QUALITY OF THE
### *Philosophical Stone. CHAPTER I.*

This stone from which this work is made contains within itself all colors. For it is white, red, most deeply crimson, yellow, most intensely yellow, sky-blue, green, and heavy. In this stone are the four elements. For it is of water, of air, of fire, and of earth. In this stone, heat and dryness are hidden <note>original: "in occulto"</note>, while coldness and moisture are manifest <note>original: "in manifesto"</note>. It is therefore necessary for us to hide that which is manifest, and to make manifest that which is hidden. That which is hidden—namely, heat and dryness—is the oil, and this oil is dry. That dryness performs the tinting <note>The process of transmutation or changing the color of metals</note> and nothing else, because the alkali <note>original: "alkale," referring here to the basic salt or essence</note> and nothing else tints. That which is manifest, the cold and the moist, is a corrupting watery vapor. It is necessary, therefore, that this moisture and coldness be made equal to the heat and dryness, so that it does not flee from the fire. Because between that coldness and moisture there is one small particle that is hot and dry; it is therefore necessary that the cold and moist receive the heat and dryness that was hidden, so they may become one substance. However, that coldness and moisture is a corrupting and watery vapor, of which it is said that watery and burning moisture corrupts the body and tints it into blackness. These weaknesses must therefore be destroyed in the fire and through the degrees of the fire.

## *On the property of the stone itself.*
### *CHAPTER II.*

This is the book of the Three Words, the book of the precious stone, which is an airy and volatile body, cold and moist, watery and burning; and in it is heat, dryness, coldness, and moisture. One power is hidden, and another is manifest. So that that which is hidden may become

### *On the hidden heat and dryness existing within the humid and cold. CHAPTER III.*

The wonderful work of the Three Words is the work of the precious stone, in which there is coldness and a watery, combustible humidity, and within that same thing is a hidden heat: and thus that which concerns the three words is read and understood differently by some, so that not everyone may clearly and openly understand the cause within the three words. This is sought in the humid and cold, in which there is hidden heat and dryness, and it is necessary for us to know this, so that we may make the manifest hidden, and the hidden manifest; and this hidden thing is of the nature of the Sun and of fire, and it is the most precious oil of all hidden things, and a living tincture, and a permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens" - a fundamental alchemical solvent that does not evaporate when heated</note>, which always lives and remains, and the vinegar of the Philosophers, and a penetrating spirit: and it is a hidden dyeing, aggregating, and reviving force: which rectifies and illuminates all the dead, and makes them rise, after which its heat and dryness do not flee from the fire. But the watery and combustible coldness flees from the fire and destroys itself.

### *On the works of the Planets and their images*
### *existing in Mercury.*
### CHAPTER V.

<margin>X</margin>
I say therefore that in Mercury are the works of the Planets, and their imaginings in their places, just as they work upon the fetus in its parts and seasons. For in the fetus, in the first month when the seed is received by the womb, Saturn works by congealing and binding the matter itself into one mass by his coldness and dryness. In the second month, Jupiter works by his warmth, digesting <note>In this context, "digesting" refers to the alchemical and biological process of maturation through heat.</note> it into a certain fleshy mass, which is called an embryo <note>original: "embrio"</note>. In the third month, Mars works, acting upon the matter, and by his warmth and dryness he divides and separates that mass and arranges the limbs. In the fourth month, the Sun <note>original: "Sol"</note>, as lord, sends in the spirit, and thus it begins to live. In the fifth month, Mercury works, who makes the openings and the breathing-holes. In the sixth month, Venus arranges and orders the eyebrows and eyes, the testicles, and similar parts. In the seventh month, the Moon <note>original: "Luna"</note> labors with her coldness and moisture to expel the fetus; and if it were born then, it would be able to live; but if it is not born then, it is weakened. And again, Saturn in the eighth month begins to work with his coldness and dryness, then binding the fetus's reception in the womb, and if it were born then, it would not be able to live. In the ninth month, Jupiter works again, and by his warmth and moisture, by nourishing it again, he restores strength to the fetus itself; and thus, the ninth month being completed, it is born and lives well. And these are true words: Water preserves the fetus for three months in the womb; fire guards it for just as many. ### *On the Observation of the Planets in the Work of Alchemy. CHAPTER VI.*

From these three months, it is necessary for us to understand—and for you, with sharp wit, to know—how to compose and extract two; for from two, three are not understood, but from these three, two and seven are understood. ## Explanation of the Three Words. CHAPTER VII.

Let us now return to the explanation of the Three Words, in which the entire art consists. For Water is said to preserve the fetus in the womb for three months. Air nourishes it for three months. Fire guards it for just as many. All of this is said concerning Mercury by way of analogy. And this word and this discourse, though an obscure term, is open to the understanding of the truth. For there is one nature in a pregnant woman, and another in Mercury; nevertheless, by the likeness of the heat found in the womb, the fire is estimated to be thirty-two degrees. Whence that third word of which it is said, "fire guards for just as many," is obscure, and many err in it, and enter an unknown land <note>original: "terram regionem nescientem"; a metaphor for intellectual confusion</note>, because from three they take two degrees, and from these two degrees the remaining degrees are extracted. The little book is divided into 32 particles of the Grid <note>original: "Craticulæ"; likely referring to a specific alchemical diagram or furnace structure</note>; and in these degrees the whole third word is fulfilled, of which it is said "just as many." The first degree completes the water and the air. The second degree completes all this which we have said and "just as many." And this is the gift of God.

## Concerning the Degrees of Fire. CHAPTER VIII.

The Philosopher of the King of the Persians and of the Prince of the Romans said: Divide the three words into two parts, and again let those two parts be divided into two parts, and upon those two let the 32 degrees be divided, which are the limits of the fire, and are called the particles of fire. These are found from the portions of the Ark <note>original: "archæ"</note> which is divided into 32 parts, and they are called *almec* <note>a technical term, likely of Arabic origin, referring to alchemical measurements</note>. All these degrees are spread over the first two parts, which are the two limits, and divided into 4 parts the 32 degrees are partitioned; just as the first degree is one particle of fire *albechir* <note>another technical term for a specific heat intensity</note>, and it is alone and simple, and is said to be as if nothing, and that it is a light fire. # THE THREE WORDS
<note>original: "TRIUM VERBORUM"</note>

The masters of the Persians lead the way through the subtlety of their genius, and thus two words <note>likely stages or operations</note> are completed in 6 *maenchen* <note>a specific Persian unit of time or measure used in alchemy</note>. After these, the third word is fulfilled, which is obscure, and in which many err and lose their way. The Philosopher of the King of the Persians said: let us divide this through the middle. The half consists of three *maenchen*, and this half is governed with two degrees, which are two particles of fire; and so these three words are completed in 22 *maenchen*, and this is the first limit and is without error.

The second limit consists of 16 *maenchen*, and is governed with eight degrees of fire. The third limit consists of 20 *maenchen*, and is governed with 16 degrees: that is, particles of fire. The fourth limit consists of 24 *maenchen* and four *diechen* <note>a smaller fractional unit of measure</note>, and is governed with 32 degrees of fire, which are particles of fire. Raxit Aedianus and all the Philosophers of the Persians said: praised be God and His holy name, because this was spoken concerning the tempered fire over the three words regarding the nature of the pregnant woman <note>an alchemical metaphor for the substance maturing within the vessel</note>, as an example of the fire that is necessary for Mercury.

All these two limits are divided, each through the middle, because both are 23 *manahen* and 7 *diethen*. And at the end of the first limit, open the treasure <note>the sealed alchemical vessel</note>; cast out what you find. If it should leap up and emit smoke upon a red-hot plate, it is not yet finished. Therefore, return it to the fire of 16, which has within it eight degrees of fire. Again, open the treasure and place it upon the glowing plate, and see if it leaps and produces smoke, for then it will not yet be finished. Therefore, return it to the fire of 20, which has within it 16 degrees. Again, open the treasure, and if it still produces smoke, it will not yet be cooked. Therefore, return it to the fire of 24 *maenchen* and four *diethen*, which has within it 32 degrees of fire; and now there will be made a fusible, precious green stone, whether golden or hyacinth-colored or ruby-red. In this hour, praised be God and His holy name, which is blessed above every name for this, His holy gift.

# A LITTLE TREATISE OF ARISTO-
## *tle concerning the Practice of the Philoso-*
### *phical Stone, begins.*

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>
SINCE every body, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle is frequently referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note>, is either an element or generated from the elements, generation is supremely necessary for our mastery. This generation, however, cannot consist of anything except the four natures, which are the four elements. Truly, the elements are four: air, water, fire, and earth, without which all generation is deprived of its effect. For of the elements, two are stony and two are aquatic; the stony ones are fire and earth, while the aquatic ones are air and water. Also, of these, two are friends and two are enemies. Earth and water are friends; fire and water are enemies.

Therefore, make peace between the enemies, and you shall possess the whole mastery. But you cannot make peace between the elements except through their conversion into one another. Moreover, to convert them well into one another is quite possible. Because, as the Philosopher says: It is within the aptitude of all elements that they be changed into one another. For fire is changed into air, and air into water. Thus fire is changed into water, and water into earth, and vice versa.

Convert the elements, therefore, and you shall find what you seek. For our composition, as Morienes <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note> says, is a change of natures, and a mixable connection of their heat with cold, and their moisture with dryness. For the coldness of water and the heat of fire, the moisture of air and the dryness of earth, being bound together in harmony, constitute the complete first generated thing. For the elements are, as the Philosopher says, circularly convertible. And for that reason, they are generated and corrupted into one another, but this is not accomplished except by operation and governance.

The modes of operation are truly four: namely, the <term>dissolution</term> <note>The process of breaking a solid down into a liquid state.</note> of the stone into spiritual water, the <term>separation</term> of the stone into spiritual breath, the <term>reduction</term> of the stone into natural earth, and the <term>betrothal</term> <note>A metaphorical term for the chemical union or "marriage" of substances.</note> of the stone into spiritual lime.

The dissolution of the stone is done through attrition <note>Grinding or wearing down by friction.</note>; the sepa-

# LITTLE TREATISE

->The method is through distillation; the reduction of the stone is through waxing <note>original: "incerationem" — the process of softening a solid substance to a wax-like consistency</note>; the marriage is through fixation.<-

The first step of our governance or work is therefore the dissolution of the stone into spiritual water, as the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, often cited as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts</note> says: "Since the first mode of preparation is that the stone becomes Mercury." For Mercury itself is the first body acting upon coarse things, so that it may return them to its own likeness. For if it left coarse things in their coarseness and did not refine the essence, the stone would neither be dissolved nor undergo putrefaction <note>the stage of breaking down or "rotting" necessary for rebirth</note>. And therefore, if we had no other benefit from Mercury except that it makes bodies subtle according to its own nature, it ought to be enough for us. Take, therefore, your most beloved son and join him equally to his white sister: offer them the cup of love, because the consent of goodwill joins things to things. Pour over them honeyed wine until they are intoxicated and divided into the smallest parts. Nevertheless, keep in mind that all clean things suit clean things; otherwise, it generates dissimilar children for itself.

And therefore, as Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical works were foundational in Europe</note> says: "The first thing you must do in the work is that you sublime the Mercury; then place clean bodies into the clean Mercury; from here, grind, cook, repeat, and let it not weary you to do this." When you truly see blackness appearing on the surface of the water, collect it carefully and set it aside, knowing for certain that your stone is now partially dissolved. Distill all the water through a cloth; what you find dissolved in it, set aside, and put the remainder back to be cooked again until the whole turns black in the manner of soot. Let all these things be done with a tempered fire of the first degree, warm and moist. For if too much heat is present, it will turn the blackness into redness, and the heat of a premature redness is a sign of combustion <note>burning the "seeds" of the stone by applying heat too quickly</note>. And so, if you have well-governed the origin of the art, it will be the "crow's head" <note>original: "caput corui" — the alchemical symbol for the Nigredo or black stage of the work</note>; for in that stage the body is dissolved and reduced into its first matter. And this is because bodies are not altered unless they are first reduced to their first matter. And therefore, as Plato says, you need to labor in their solution so that, the heavier parts being cast away, the work may be completed with the lighter ones. This is indeed done through sublimation. Throat-cut your sons, therefore, and receive their blood, but throw the flesh to the dogs, lest they bark at you. And that...

# ARISTOTLE

Therefore, because the blood is the soul, and the soul is life, and life is **our stone** <term>lapis noster: the "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of the alchemical work</term>. For nothing is suitable for our stone which has not been alive and has not sought the heaven of the air. Convert your stone, therefore, into blood, and blood into air, and air into earth, and you shall have the whole **mastery** <term>magisterium: the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work"</term>.

The second step of our governance is the separation of the stone into a spiritual state: which separation is indeed achieved through the division of the elements and their full purification.

Regarding the purification of the separation, as **Rhazes** <term>Rafis: refers to Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a Persian polymath and influential alchemist</term> says: The nature of the stone is to be divided into the four elements, and to cleanse them individually through distillation. For fire extracts that which consists within the inner parts. It consumes the filth of the stone through distillation and refines it through the smoothing action of the air; and therefore **our stone** is divided into the four elements so that it may be more refined, better purified from filth, and more firmly joined together afterward. But because putrefied things, being more digested, are more easily divided, **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio: the process of breaking down a substance through heat and moisture, often associated with the color black</term> must necessarily precede the division of the elements, so that the elemental parts within it may be dissolved, and thus it is rendered more fit afterward for extraction through the four elements. Take, therefore, as has been said, the dissolved substance, place it in a gourd-shaped vessel <note>original: "cucurbitam"</note>, and pour over it the black powder collected above: close it with its still-head <note>original: "alembico"</note> and receiver, so that it cannot evaporate: apply a very slow fire beneath for a **Philosophical month** <term>mensem Philosophicum: traditionally forty days, the time required for a complete stage of transformation</term>, so that it may become more foul and corrupted.

For as the **Philosopher** <note>Usually referring to Aristotle himself in this context</note> says: Corruption is the putrefaction of the substance of a thing, resulting from the retention of vapor and the action of fire. For if it is dispersed through the air, it putrefies very little. Therefore, close your vessel so that it cannot breathe: when the Philosophical month is completed, gently distill the four elements—namely water, earth, air, and fire—placing each one separately. Nevertheless, take the greatest care lest you burn the tincture by too much fire during their separation. For it is a secret, as **Rhazes** says, to prepare the elements subtly, so that they are safe from scorching in every distillation until the tincture is taken from them. If indeed the **tincture** <term>tinctura: the potent essence or "dye" capable of transforming base metals into gold</term> is burned, its effect will be ended. Therefore, continue gently

# ARISTOTLE

makes it stable. The third and fourth elements are fire and earth, which, as Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis"; refers to the 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician Abu Bakr al-Razi</note> says, should be prepared together to save time. This is also done so that their mixture is good, the preparation is not confused, they are not scorched by the intensity of the fire, and so that one may properly tint the other; therefore, preparing them together is safer and more direct. Take then the elements of earth and fire, join and grind them, and calcine <note>term: calcination; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state or purify it</note> them well with a lit fire. Carefully collect the air remaining in them, because as Rhazes says: The air which is separated more slowly from the earth is considered more precious. When it has been well calcined and emptied of all air, it will be pale in color and ready for "impregnation." If, however, the spirit remains in it, it will stay blackish and is less suited for the work. And for this reason, Plato says:

> You must practice the separation of the elements to the best of your ability, until nothing of the spirit remains in the body, except that which cannot be perceived.

And the sign of this will be when nothing evaporates from the body. When you have separated all four elements by the correct separation, it will be assigned to the air, bright and tinting, and a dry body over which the substance of earth prevails. Therefore, follow part with part at all times, and keep each one of them individually; this is the correct separation of elements and complete purification. For in none of our work is water necessary unless it is white, nor air unless it is saffron-yellow, nor earth unless it is pale and whitish. For then the water is fit for dissolving, the air is effective for entering, and the oil <note>likely referring to the "sulfur" or soul of the matter</note> is abundant for tinting. Divide your stone, therefore, into the four elements, rectify them, and join them into one, and you will possess the entire Mastery <note>term: Magisterium; the completion of the alchemical Great Work</note>.

The third step of our work, therefore, is the reduction of the stone into natural earth. This reduction is achieved through the grinding of the earth and the "waxing" <note>term: inceration; the process of adding liquid to a dry substance to soften it to a wax-like consistency</note> of water upon it. The waxing of water is to lead the parts of the earth, which were deprived of moisture through calcination, back into moisture, and to make them like earth. For a dry and clean body is suitable for drinking, since every dry thing hungers for its own moisture. Therefore, tie the hands of the nursing woman behind her back, so that she cannot strike her son: <note>An alchemical allegory: the "nursing woman" often represents the volatile solvent or mercury, and the "son" represents the developing philosopher's stone.</note>

<summary>This page details the alchemical preparation of the elements of fire and earth, emphasizing the need for thorough calcination and the removal of "spirit" to achieve a pale, purified state. It concludes by introducing the third stage of the work: "inceration," or returning moisture to the dry, calcined earth.</summary>

->### A LITTLE TREATISE###<-

Place a toad <note>original: "bufonem"; in alchemy, the toad often symbolizes the fixed, earthy part of the matter or the poisonous raw state of the "First Matter"</note> upon her hands, so that it may suckle from her until it dies; and when the woman has died in the fire, the toad will be swollen with milk. Therefore, place the calcined <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a fine powder or ash</term> earth into its vessel and pour over it rectified water <note>original: "aquam rectificatam"; water that has been purified through repeated distillation</note>, as has been said. Cook it over a slow fire for a week, and afterward gently calcine the cooked material. Then pour over it more water, as before, cook it lightly for a week, and lightly calcine it: again, replace it with new water for cooking. Do this continually until the earth has consumed ten times its own weight in water. For all things crave water, since it provides nourishment both to fire and to other things, and it embraces a secret worthy of admiration. For it is the wine in the vine, the oil in the wild olive, and through it, fruits of diverse kinds are transformed within the tree. So also in our earth, it is generated from water; for the earth itself is cold, and it is called quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note>, which is hidden in the body of magnesia <note>original: "magnesiae"; here referring to a crude mineral ore or the "mother" of the stone, not modern magnesium</note> and is to be congealed within it. 

And so, when it is congealed, it is made like unto ash: because the earth dries and the water moistens. Therefore, the weight must be noted everywhere, lest too much dryness or superfluous moisture corrupt the work during administration; namely, that you cook by roasting as much as the dissolution added, and you dissolve by burying <note>original: "inhumando"; the process of placing the vessel in a warm, moist environment like a dung heap or sand bath</note> as much as the roasting took away. And so, every time after the calcination of the earth, pour over the water temperately, neither too much nor too little: for if there is too much, it will become a sea of disturbance; but if too little, it will be burnt into cinders. 

For that reason, after you have poured in the water, cook it for a week, and gently calcine the earth, and thus weekly you shall prepare it by grinding, watering, and roasting, until the whole is reduced to whiteness. And know that a slow fire in this arrangement of the work promises the hope of salvation: and because the earth does not bear fruit without frequent irrigation, to water, roast, and bury many times constitutes the highest effect of this business. And whatever things emerge unmixed, set them aside separately, otherwise you corrupt everything. It is necessary, however, for the earth to be nourished first with a little milk, and afterward with more, as is seen in an infant. And therefore wash the earth, grind it, and cook it, until it has drunk of its own water as much as it can drink, or until the earth itself is like a clinging paste—

# ARISTOTLE

To cleanse, therefore, is to sublimate, to wash, and to whiten. For that which ascends to the top is effective purity; but that which falls to the bottom is dregs and corruption. > Extract from the ray its shadow and dregs, which kill it, and sow the gold in the white foliated earth;

but this gold is not the gold of the common people <note>original: "aurum vulgi"</note>; rather, it is the **gold of the soul**, by which the gold of the foliated earth is tinged.

Whence Calidius <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince credited with being an early alchemist.</note> says:

> No one has ever been able, nor will be able hereafter, to tinge gold except with gold.

Plato also says:

> When you have named each species from the parts of the work, return the spirits to the body and sublimate it. That which is sublimated from it will be clear and bright. After this, return the "approved of the soul" over them so that they may be mixed. For the soul is the bond of the spirit, just as the body is the bond of the soul. And when it has stood for a time, that which is stronger will prevail in it, so that it converts the whole—namely, the body into soul, and the soul into spirit.

When the spirit has dissolved the body and the soul, so that they exist in their own form, it does not remain fixed <note>Stable or non-volatile</note> unless you occupy it. This "occupation" truly means that you must join it with the body from which you prepared it in the beginning; for in that body, the spirit is kept from fleeing by the endurance of the body. And for this reason, Plato <note>The author attributes this to Plato, though it likely stems from the "Turba Philosophorum," a famous Latin alchemical text</note> says: "When the spirit has dissolved the soul and the body together, it does not stand fixed. Therefore, join it with the body, so that it may generate its own likeness." Nor should you join it with just anything so that it might stand firm, but only with that from which it originated at the start. If you do this, it becomes *Iccir* <note>original: "Iccir"; an Arabic-derived alchemical term, likely referring to the Elixir or the "tincture" that transforms metals</note>. And know that the purpose of all workers fails after the completion of the work if they omit this secret. Note these words, therefore, and mark these mysteries. Because when the spirit has dissolved the white foliated earth <note>A stage in the process where the matter appears as white, flaky layers</note>, none of them remains fixed unless you occupy it with that body from which it was prepared in the beginning. The spirit is Mercury <term>Quicksilver</term>, and its first body is white and red sulfur. Therefore, when the spirit has dissolved the sulfurous body in all things—as was said above—once prepared, it is not fixed unless you occupy it with the new sulfur from which it was prepared in the beginning. For white and red sulfur, as Aristotle <note>Pseudo-Aristotle; many medieval alchemical works were falsely attributed to him</note> says, congeals quicksilver into gold and silver. Join your work, therefore, with the body, so that it may generate its own likeness; if you do this, that which you join will be *Iccir* over other bodies; otherwise, it will not be fixed, because nature is not contained except within its own nature. And this is because, as Plato says: "Nature follows nature, and nature contains nature, and teaches it to fight against the <unclear>fire</unclear>." Therefore, perform the marriage between the husband and the wife, and you shall have the whole mastery <note>The "Magisterium" or the completed alchemical process</note>. But their preparation, as Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, the Persian physician whose works were foundational to Western alchemy</note> says, is this: That you first cleanse the husband on one side and the wife on the other, so that, being cleansed from filth, they may be better joined; for if you do not prepare the bodies, they cannot be loved. Therefore, make peace between the elements, so that they may love one another in a suitable embrace. For the sharp mastery of the Philosophers places the soul into the ashes <note>original: "calces"; literally lime or metallic powder produced by heat</note> of the bodies; then the vigor of the spirits crushes them into the smallest ashes of the leads. Likewise, when you wish to put the ferment into the Elixir, first mix it with the spirits, because unless you do this, its nature would not be impressed upon them. Therefore, mix the ferment well with the elements, and you shall have the mastery.

# AVICENNA ON THE CONGEALING and cementing of stones. CHAPTER I.

Pure earth does not become stone, because it does not create a continuous bond, but rather a lack of continuity. For the dryness prevailing within it does not permit it to be cemented together. Stones, however, are formed in two ways: by cementing and by congealing. In some stones, earth is the dominant element; in others, truly, it is water. For sometimes clay is first dried out, and it becomes something that is midway between clay and stone, and then it becomes stone. The clay most suitable for this transformation is viscous <note>sticky or glue-like</note>; for this is capable of holding together. Also, on the banks of the Gihon <note>original: "Geon"; likely referring to the Oxus River in Central Asia</note>, earth has been seen which appears to be converted into stones in the space of 33 years.

From water, moreover, stones are formed in two ways. One is that water falling drop by drop is congealed. The other is that something descends from running water which settles on the surface of the bottom of that water and becomes stone. For there are certain places upon which poured waters are converted into stones, which are of diverse colors; and there are waters which, if taken up elsewhere, do not congeal, but if they are poured near their own riverbed, they congeal and become stones. We know, therefore, that in the earth there is that mineral power <term>vis mineralis: a hidden natural force believed to organize matter into minerals</term> which congeals waters.

The principles of stones, therefore, are either made from a clayey or viscous substance, or from a substance in which [water] prevails, which is congealed by a certain mineral virtue, or earth prevails in it, causing it to coagulate. In the same way, Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Sal ammoniacum"; ammonium chloride, used in alchemy</note> is congealed, but the earthy power of the transformed substance is not sufficient for the salt; rather, heat assists it. Heat, arriving, coagulates it by a hidden power. And perhaps it is made from cold, dry earth, and from water earth is made when the qualities of earth overcome it, and vice versa.

There is, moreover, a certain thing which some ingenious men use when they wish to coagulate a dry thing, which is composed of two waters and is called "Virgin's Milk" <term>lac virginis: an alchemical term for a white, milky liquid formed by mixing two clear solutions, often lead acetate and alum</term>, which is its most certain effect. Stones are therefore made from clay by the heat of the Sun, or from water coagulated by a dry earthy power, or from hot water that has been dried out. Similarly, also, certain vegetables and certain animals are converted into stones—

# AVICENNA

### On the cause of mountains. CHAPTER II.

Mountains are also formed sometimes from an essential cause, and sometimes from an accidental cause. From an essential cause, as when the earth is elevated by a violent movement of the ground <note>referring to seismic activity or earthquakes</note> and a mountain is made. From an accidental cause, as when a deep excavation happens due to winds or the flow of water, occurring gradually until a vast depth is created: consequently, a great height emerges next to it, and this is the primary cause of mountains. There are also certain lands that are soft and others that are hard. The soft areas are carried away by watercourses and winds, while the hard areas remain, and thus an elevation is formed. Just as there is a generation of mountains, so too is there a generation of stones, because the watercourse continuously brought viscous mud to them, which is dried out over a long period of time and becomes stone; and it is not unlikely that there is a mineralizing power <note>original: "vis mineralis," a theoretical force believed to transform matter into minerals</note> converting waters into stones. And for this reason, in many stones are found certain parts of aquatic animals and others <note>an early and accurate recognition of fossils</note>. Mountains have been made as if through many ages, as we said before, if they are not decreasing. However, the muddy substances found on the heights are not of that stony matter, but are from that which is worn away from the mountains—either terrestrial or another substance which the waters bring with mud and herbs, which are mixed with the mud of the mountain—or perhaps it is the ancient mud of the sea, as it is of one substance: because part of it becomes stone, and part of it does not, but is softened and dissolved by some prevailing quality. The sea has its retreat and its approach; it hollows out certain places and raises others, and at times it covered the whole earth, and from there it scraped away certain soft things, left the hard things, and piled them up in certain places. Also, the soft things piled up by it when it withdrew were dried out and converted into mountains.

And of these, some are of rare substance and weak composition, and some of strong substance, and some are ductile <note>malleable, like metal</note>, and some are not. -># MINERALS<-

<note>The author categorizes minerals based on how they react to moisture and heat, a common approach in medieval alchemy and natural philosophy.</note>

There are certain substances, some of which are salts, such as those that liquefy quickly from moisture—for example, alum <note>original: "alumen"</note>, vitriol <note>original: "calcamentum"; likely copperas or ferrous sulfate</note>, and sal ammoniac <note>original: "sal armoniacum"</note>. And some are oily and do not liquefy easily by moisture alone, such as sulfur and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. But quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> belongs to the second category, although it is the primary element of ductile metals, or similar to certain ductile things. Furthermore, all ductile metals are liquefiable; for the most part, things that are not ductile are not liquefiable, and they cannot be softened except with great force.

The matter of ductile metals is a watery substance mixed with an earthy substance in a strong mixture, and one cannot be separated from the other. The watery substance of it is congealed with cold after the action of heat upon it, which is <term>epthesis</term> <note>A Greek-derived term referring to a specific type of boiling or refining process in alchemy</note>. An example would be wine that has not yet frozen because of its oiliness; and for this reason, it is not ductile.

Stone-like things, however, among mineral substances, are materially watery, but they are not congealed by water alone, but also with dryness, which alters the wateriness into earthiness. There is no excessively oily moisture in them, and therefore they are not ductile; and because their coagulation comes from dryness, they are not easily dissolved for the most part, except through natural dissolving techniques.

Alum and sal ammoniac belong to the genus of salt, because the portion of fire in sal ammoniac is greater than the earth. Hence the whole of it is sublimated <note>turned directly from solid to vapor</note>, and it is water with which is mixed an exceedingly subtle hot smoke of great fieriness, coagulated from dryness. The wateriness of sulfurous things, however, is mixed with earth in a strong combination with the boiling of heat, until they are made oily, and afterwards they are coagulated by cold.

Vitriols <note>original: "atramenta"; literally 'blackings', used for various metallic sulfates</note> are composed of salt, sulfur, and stones; and there is in them the mineral essence of certain liquefiable bodies which are made from them. For instance, <term>calcamentum</term> and <term>alachar</term> <note>likely variants of vitriol or mineral oxides</note> are generated from the larger grains of vitriol, and it is not dissolved except by its leaping <note>reacting or effervescing</note> with that which is in that sulfurous substance, and afterwards it is coagulated, and it then receives a mineral power from certain bodies. Therefore, that which receives the power of iron will be red or saffron-colored, such as <term>alathar</term>. But that which has received the power of copper will be green. Hence it is possible for these two to be made artificially.

Quicksilver is like water which is mixed with an exceedingly subtle sulfurous earth in a strong mixture, until it does not rest on a flat surface; and this is due to the great dryness which is in...

Its unique property is that it is coagulated by the vapor of sulfur; perhaps in this way it is solidified by lead, or easily by the vapor of sulfur. It appears, moreover, that quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> and things similar to it are the element of all liquefiable substances: either because all liquefiable things, when they are melted, are converted back to it, or because they do not melt until they are heated, and when they have been melted, they appear red. 

But lead, without a doubt, when it is melted, is quicksilver, but it does not melt unless it is heated; and when it has been liquefied, it is converted to the color common to all liquefiable things, namely, a fiery redness. Therefore, quicksilver mixes with these bodies because it is of their same substance. However, these bodies differ in their composition from it, in the same way that quicksilver differs from things similar to it, and by the mixtures that are blended with them until they are solidified. 

And if the quicksilver is pure, the power of white, non-burning sulfur will coagulate it; and that is the best thing that those who practice Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimiam"</note> can find, or those who convert it into silver. But if the sulfur is of the best clean quality with a clear redness, and there is in it the power of simple, non-burning fieriness, it will be the best thing that Alchemists can find to make gold <note>original: "aurum"</note> from it. For these things convert it. 

And if the quicksilver is of good substance, but the sulfur is not pure—specifically, if there is a burning power in it—it converts it into copper <note>original: "æs"</note>. However, if the quicksilver is bad, impure, and earthy, and the sulfur is unclean, iron <note>original: "ferrum"</note> is made from it. Tin <note>original: "Stannum"</note>, truly, seems to have good quicksilver but bad sulfur, and these are not well ground but composed as if of small parts, and therefore it does not become [precious]. Of heavy lead <note>original: "Plumbi"</note>, the quicksilver is bad, heavy, and clay-like, and its sulfur is bad, of a foul and weak vapor; hence it does not solidify well. 

And craftsmen perform a solidification almost similar to this artificially, although artificial things are not the same as natural ones, nor do they have such certain similarities; and therefore it is believed that natural composition happens in this way, or in a way close to this. But art is weak...

# MINERALS.

Art is weaker than nature, nor can it follow her, though it may labor much. Let the practitioners of Alchemy <note>original: "Alchimiæ"</note> know, however, that the species of things cannot be truly transmuted: but they can make things similar to them, such as painting red with yellow so that it appears to be gold, and painting white with whatever color they wish, until it is very much like gold or copper. They may also wipe away the impurities of lead, yet it will always remain lead, even though it may look like silver. But then other qualities will be so well-presented in it that men are deceived, just as those who accept common salt and sal ammoniac <note>A salt of ammonia, historically used in alchemy for cleaning metals and as a flux.</note>. Furthermore, I do not believe it possible that a specific difference <note>The essential quality that defines a species in Aristotelian logic.</note> can be removed by human ingenuity, nor is it possible for one complexio <note>The unique balance of the four humors or qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a substance.</note> to be converted into another: because these sensible qualities are not the "difference" by which a species is changed, but are merely accidents and properties. Their true differences are not known; since the difference is unknown, how can it be known whether it is removed or not, or how it might be removed? But the stripping away of accidents, such as vapor and color, weight, or at least their reduction, is not impossible: for reason does not stand against this, but the proportion of these substances will not be the same in all. Therefore, this cannot be changed into that, unless perhaps it is reduced into prime matter <note>original: "primam materiam"; the formless, underlying substance of all physical things.</note>, and thus they are changed into something other than they were before: however, this does not happen through melting alone, but through external things happening to it.

->*The end of Avicenna’s On Minerals.*<-

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE

Just as the world is composed of four diverse virtues <note>original: "virtutibus"; here meaning powers or natural forces</note>, so too is this art composed of the natures of woman. Some of these we shall briefly narrate, demonstrate, and set down, for the greater world <note>the macrocosm or universe</note> was created from four diverse and composite natural virtues. The first of these is the **appetitive** <note>the power of seeking or desire</note>, the second is the **digestive**, the third is the **attractive or retentive**, and the fourth is the **expulsive**, which is the **cleansing** power. 

And there is a **fifth essence** <term>Quintessence: the purest, fifth element that binds the other four together</term> without an external life, which begets and unites the other four I have described to you. I have explained their arrangement; it is in this art like a key to a chest—if you open it without the key, the whole is destroyed. It is like a bond holding its sides together, because it is necessary to cautiously understand the mastery of this entire matter through these virtues in this art. This art is not perfected except by students through vigilance and through its moderation. 

As I narrated before, the beginning of its action comes from the four acting virtues: namely, the **appetitive**, **retentive**, **digestive**, and **expulsive** (which is the cleansing). The fifth is the **soul**, most bright with light. Now, however, let us narrate the dispositions of these species and explain their power. Let us tell, therefore, which of them is hot, which is cold, which is masculine, and which is feminine, so that we do not err or deviate through the diversity of their heat and the difference of their kind. For if there is a difference between hot and cold, and masculine and feminine, the work will by no means be perfected for you unless it is directed on the right path. 

And you should know that nothing is born without male and female, and no sprout is created without heat and moisture, and coldness and dryness. 

*   The **appetitive virtue** is masculine, hot, and dry; and it is the containing fire. 
*   The **retentive virtue** is feminine, cold, and dry; and it is the earth. 
*   The **digestive or transformative virtue** is masculine, hot, and moist; and it is the air. 
*   The **expulsive virtue** is feminine, cold, and moist; and it is the cleansing water. 

The **fifth essence**, however, is life itself, which is unique; it is neither hot nor moist, neither cold nor dry, neither masculine nor feminine. Yet, if it is turned toward dryness through the power of these others, its opposite is corrupted. Therefore, lest you err in your labor by seeking it in some river-like place, I will show you its location. If, therefore, you wish to dissolve the **water of life** <note>original: "aquam vitae"; a potent alchemical solvent or spirit</note> by coldness, you will instead coagulate it. If, however, you wish to make cold water...

And you should know that certain bodies require dissolution, while others require elevation <note>sublimation or rising as vapor</note> so that they may tint, and become bright and illuminated, in which all bodies may be dissolved. I swear, therefore, that I have concealed nothing, nor have I described any other species by a foreign description, nor placed types in foreign places. Therefore, if you read and understand my letters, you will reach your purpose and give thanks to God. But if one whose composition is weak and whose understanding is brief does not reach his purpose, let him not blame me for his ignorance, nor say that I have erred, but rather himself, who did not reach his goal.

# THE ALLEGORY OF MERLIN

...they burned him with fire, blowing upon him until he was completely liquefied, descending through a hole into another crucible placed below. Then the King, thus rising again from death to life, cried out with a loud voice and said: "Where are my enemies? Therefore, all who heard this came before him and said: "Lord, behold, we are ready to obey your commands in all things." And so, from 그 hour as before, all the kings and powerful men of other regions honored and feared him. 

And when they wished to see some of his wonders, they would place one ounce of well-washed <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "Mercurij"; here referring to quicksilver or the "spirit" of the metal</note> into a crucible, and they would cast upon it something like a single grain of millet from his nails, or his hair, or his blood. Of this stone, they would cast a small amount upon purified <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturnum"; the alchemical name for Lead</note>, and immediately its form was changed, as I know. Afterward, they would place one part of this upon ten parts of <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for Copper</note>, and the whole was of one color and quality. 

Likewise, in another way: they took the said stone, crushed it, and mixed it with salt and the <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Sole"; the alchemical name for Gold</note> as before; they liquefied it and cast the said dissolved salts into goat's blood, and then it became the best for all things. 

Guard this treatise well, brother, and keep it safely, because it is a great jest among fools, but no jest among the wise. For this is the "Way of the Three-Day Kings," since those who endure but little labor desire to obtain great profit. Let us return praises to the greatest Creator, who has freely inspired his faithful to transmute accidents into substances according to their will, and so that what lies hidden in the potential of things may be wisely brought into reality.

->*The end of the Allegory of Merlin.*<-

# RACHAIDIBI, VERADIANI,
## *Rhodiani, and Kanidis, the Philosophers of the King*
## *of the Persians: A Fragment of their most*
## *acute dialogue concerning the matter of the*
## *Philosophical Stone.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial D with ornate floral and circular patterns.</image-desc>
Rachaidibi, son of Zetheibida and Philosopher to the King of the Persians and the Prince of the Romans, said: The seed <note>original: "sperma," referring to the foundational substance or "semen" of the work</note> of the stone is cold and moist in its outward appearance, and in its hidden nature it is hot and dry. He says, therefore: make that which is cold and moist hidden, and place that which is hot and dry in the outward appearance. In this way, its coldness and moisture will be so concealed that they shall never be diminished; for if they were diminished, the stone itself would also be diminished. Therefore, when the coldness and moisture are hidden, act by concealing them so that you may compose that heat and dryness which was in the hidden part and the outward part together. Thus, from the spirit, a body is made in two stages, and it shall become a sphere <note>or "mass"</note>, and blood, and flesh. Rhodianus says: The seed is white and liquid. This liquid first forms a sphere in its proper place within five days; it receives flesh and blood, limbs and an image, and the imaginative power from God Most High; it comes to its birth, and it shines and rises in its own time. These are the two stages and the seven <note>likely referring to the seven planetary metals or stages of transformation</note>. And now we speak of the second seed. Veradianus says of the second seed that it is a stone alone, nor is there any other like it in this world, which impregnates itself, conceives within itself, and brings itself forth; and by this is understood a single stone, which is called a white and liquid seed, and afterwards a red one. Rhodianus says, however, that this seed is a certain stone that flees from heat and dryness; it is airy and volatile, and it is cold and moist, as well as hot and dry. And after this living thing dies by the "red death," being dead it is now a companion to heat and dryness, and thus it does not flee from that which is hot, nor does it flee the fire, nor emit smoke, nor make a sound; it is melted like wax, and is like oil, and it is dry. This dryness tints with a red and white tincture <term>tincture: a potent alchemical liquid or powder capable of transforming the properties of base metals</term>, and thus from the spirit, a body is made: then this body truly—

# AVICENNA
