it belongs to it, and therefore it does not stick to what touches it. Its whiteness comes from the clarity of that water and from the whiteness of the subtle earth that is within it. Its specific property is that it is coagulated by the vapor of sulfur, and perhaps in this way it is frozen by lead, or easily by the vapor of sulfur. It appears, moreover, that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"; literally "living silver" or mercury</note>, and things similar to it, are the element of all liquefiable substances: either because all liquefiable things, when they are melted, are converted toward it, yet they do not melt before they are heated, and when they have been melted, they appear red. But lead, without a doubt, when it is melted, is quicksilver, but it does not melt unless it is heated, and when it has been liquefied, it is converted to the color common to all liquefiable things, namely a fiery redness: and for this reason, quicksilver is mixed with these bodies, because it is of their substance. 

But these bodies differ in their composition from it, in the same way that quicksilver differs from things similar to it, and the mixtures that are mixed with them until they are frozen. And if the quicksilver should be pure, the power of **white sulfur** <note>original: "sulphuris albi"</note> that is non-burning will coagulate it, and that is the best thing that those who practice **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimiam"</note> can find, or they convert it into silver. But if the sulfur should be pure and of the best quality, clear with redness, and there should be in it the power of simple non-burning fire, it will be the best thing that Alchemists can find, so that from it they may make **gold**. For these things convert it. 

And if the quicksilver is of good substance, but the sulfur is not pure—namely, that there is a burning power in it—it converts it into **copper** <note>original: "æs"</note>. However, if the quicksilver is bad and impurely earthy, and the sulfur is unclean, **iron** <note>original: "ferrum"</note> is made from it. **Tin** <note>original: "Stannum"</note>, truly, seems to have good quicksilver but bad sulfur, and these are not well ground, but as if composed of small parts, and therefore it does not become such <note>referring to a perfect metal</note>. Truly, the quicksilver of **heavy lead** <note>original: "Plumbi... grossi"</note> is bad, heavy, and yellowish, and its sulfur is bad, of a foul and stinking vapor, and weak; hence it is not well frozen. And craftsmen perform a freezing almost similar to this artificially, although artificial things are not in the same manner as natural ones, nor do they have such certain similarities; and therefore it is believed that natural composition occurs in this way, or something close to it. But art is weak...

<summary>Avicenna explains the "Sulfur-Mercury theory," detailing how different proportions and purities of quicksilver and sulfur combine to create specific metals like gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead.</summary>
<keywords>quicksilver, mercury, sulfur, alchemy, transmutation, gold, silver, metallurgy, Avicenna</keywords>

--- Page 275 ---
<meta>This page concludes the discourse on minerals attributed to Avicenna and begins a new section featuring a pseudo-epigraphical letter from Alexander the Great regarding the Philosopher's Stone.</meta>

# MINERALS.

Art is weaker than nature and cannot follow her, no matter how much it labors. Let the practitioners of **Alchemy** <note>original: "Alchimiæ"</note> know that the species of things cannot truly be transmuted. However, they can make things similar to them, such as tinting a red substance with yellow so that it appears to be gold, or painting a white substance with whatever color they wish until it closely resembles gold or copper. They may also wipe away the impurities of lead, yet it will always remain lead, even if it appears to be silver. In such cases, other qualities are so well-presented that men are deceived, just as those who mistake common salt for sal ammoniac <note>A salt used in alchemy, often ammonium chloride</note>. Furthermore, I do not believe it is possible for a specific difference <note>The essential characteristic that defines a species in Aristotelian logic</note> to be removed by human ingenuity, nor is it possible for one complexio <note>The unique balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, dry—that makes up a substance</note> to be converted into another. This is because these sensory qualities are not the "differences" by which a species is changed; rather, they are accidents and properties. Their true differences are not known to us, and since the difference is unknown, how can it be known whether it has been removed or not, or how it might be removed? However, the stripping away of accidents—such as vapor, color, and weight—or at least their reduction, is not impossible. Reason does not stand against this, but the proportion of these substances will not be the same in all things. Therefore, one cannot be changed into another unless perhaps it is reduced to **prime matter** <note>The formless, fundamental material from which all things are made</note>, and thus they are changed into something other than what they were before. This, however, does not happen through melting alone, but through the influence of external factors.

->*The end of Avicenna’s Minerals.*<-

# EXPOSITION OF THE EPISTLE

Just as the <term>greater world</term><note>Latin: *maior mundus*, referring to the Macrocosm or the universe at large.</note> is composed of four diverse virtues, so too is this Art composed of the natures of woman. We briefly narrate, demonstrate, and set these down because the greater world was created from four diverse and composite natural virtues: the first of which is **appetitive**, the second **digestive**, the third **attractive** or **retentive**, and the fourth indeed is **expulsive**, which is **cleansing**. 

And there is a **Fifth Essence** <note>The *Quinta Essentia* or Quintessence; the purest, highest element that binds the others.</note> without any foreign life, which generates and unites the other four that I have narrated and described to you. I have explained their arrangement, and it is in this Art like a key to a chest; if you open it without this key, the whole thing is destroyed. For it is like a knot holding its sides together, because it is necessary to cautiously understand the entire mastery of this matter from these virtues in this Art. 

This Art is not perfected except by students through vigilance and through its temperance. Since, as I narrated before, the beginning of its action comes from the four acting virtues: namely, the **appetitive**, **retentive**, **digestive**, and **expulsive** (which is cleansing). The fifth is namely the **soul**, most brilliant from the light. 

Now, however, let us narrate these arrangements of the species and explain its power. Let us therefore narrate which of them is **hot**, which is **cold**, which is **masculine**, and which is **feminine**, so that through the diversity of their heat and the difference of their kind we may not err nor deviate. For if there is a difference between hot and cold, and masculine and feminine, the work will by no means be perfected for you unless it is directed on the right path. 

And you should know that nothing is born without male and female, and no sprout is created without heat and moisture, and coldness and dryness. 

*   The **appetitive virtue** is masculine, hot, and dry: and it is containing **fire**. 
*   The **retentive virtue** is feminine, cold, and dry: and it is **earth**. 
*   The **digestive** or **alterative virtue** is masculine, hot, and moist: and it is **air**. 
*   The **expulsive virtue** is feminine, cold, and moist: and it is **cleansing water**. 

The **Fifth Essence** truly is **life**, which is its own; it is neither hot nor moist, neither cold nor dry, neither masculine nor feminine. However, if through the power of these [virtues] it is turned toward the dry, its opposite is corrupted. Therefore, lest you err in your operation by seeking it in some river-like place, I will show you its location. If, therefore, you wish to dissolve the **water of life** by coldness, you coagulate it further. If, however, you wish to make cold water...

# OF KING ALEXANDER.

And you should know that certain bodies require dissolution, while others require elevation <note>In alchemy, "elevation" often refers to sublimation or raising the spiritual quality of a substance</note> so that they may tint, and become bright and illuminated, in which all bodies may be dissolved. Therefore, prepare the bodies which heal themselves when the earth is white, so that they remain fixed, and place them above so that the fire does not consume them with its flame, but rather melt them just as melted wax. And be mindful that this is called the "water entering again" <note>original: "aqua intrans iterum," likely referring to the process of recirculation or reflux</note>. Therefore, in your arts in which you study, believe that there are two hammers, one of which is owed to the Sun <note>Gold</note>, the other to the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Afterward follow two orders, the governing of which our head figures quite appropriately. Behold, I have numbered them, I have revealed the celestial secret, I have illuminated the difficult and hidden science, and I have certified the perfect method of governing the science. I swear, therefore, that I have concealed nothing, nor have I described any other species by a foreign description, nor placed genera in foreign places. Therefore, if you read and understand my letters, you will come to your purpose and give thanks to God. If, however, one whose composition is weak and whose temperament is brief does not come to his purpose, let him not impose the part of his ignorance upon me, nor say that I have erred, but rather himself, who will not reach his goal.

# *THE ALLEGORY OF MERLIN*
## *Perfectly containing the most profound*
## *secret of the Philosophical Stone.*
### <note>The "Philosophical Stone" refers to the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note>

<margin>4</margin>
A certain King, desiring to overcome other powerful rulers, prepared himself for war against them. And when he wished to mount his horse, he commanded one of his soldiers to give him some of the water to drink which he loved above all else. The soldier, answering him, said: "Lord, what water is this that you seek?" And the King said: "That water which I seek is a water greatly desired by me, and it loves me above all others." <note>In alchemy, this "water" often represents the "mercury of the philosophers" or the initial solvent used in the Great Work.</note> And the soldier, considering this, went immediately and brought it to him. The King, receiving it, drank and drank again, until all his limbs were filled and all his veins were swollen, and then he became greatly discolored. When this was done, his soldiers said to him: "Lord, behold the horse; mount it if it pleases you." He, answering, said: "Know that I cannot mount." The soldiers said: "Why can you not?" He replied: "Because I feel myself weighed down, and my head aches; and it seems to me that all my limbs are being separated from one another. I command you, therefore, to place me in a bright chamber, and let it be established in a warm and dry place, continuously tempered by day and night; thus I shall sweat, and the water which I drank shall be dried up within me, and so I shall be delivered." They did, therefore, as the King had commanded them. But when the time was completed, they opened the chamber and found him as if dead. His relatives immediately ran to the Egyptian and Alexandrian physicians <note>Egypt and Alexandria were traditionally regarded as the ancient birthplaces of alchemical wisdom (Hermeticism).</note>, who were to be honored above all others, and brought them to him, telling them what had happened to the King. When they had seen him, they said that he could undoubtedly be delivered. And the relatives asked: "Which of you shall be the master?" The Alexandrians answered: "We, if it pleases you." The Egyptians said: "It does not please us; rather, we wish to be the masters. For we are more ancient than you, even though we may appear younger." <note>This likely refers to the idea that Egyptian wisdom is the "parent" of Greek/Alexandrian science.</note> The Alexandrians then consented. Then the said masters took the King and tore him into the smallest parts,

into very small pieces, grinding them, and they mixed them with their own medicines which were somewhat moistening; and so they placed him, thus prepared, in his chamber in a warm, tempered place, just as before, for a day and a night. When this was done, they drew him out as if half-dead and still possessing a small spark of life. Seeing him, his parents cried out, saying: "Alas, the King is dead!" To whom the Physicians, responding, said: "We have killed him for this reason: so that he may become better and stronger in this world after his resurrection on the day of judgment than he was before." Indeed, when his parents heard this, they believed them to be frauds <note>original: "truffatores" - deceivers or tricksters</note>, and immediately took their medicines away from them and expelled them from the kingdom.

This being done, they spoke among themselves, considering what they ought to do with this poisoned and dead body. And they agreed that they should bury him, lest he should rot and his stench cause harm. But the Alexandrian Physicians <note>The "Alexandrians" often represent the true masters of the Hermetic art in alchemical literature</note>, hearing this, went to them and said: "Do not bury him, for (if it pleases you) we shall restore him healthier, more beautiful, and more powerful than before." Then they began to smile, saying: "Do you wish to deceive us just as the others did? Know that unless you perform what you promise, you shall not be able to escape our hands." The Physicians, however, binding themselves to this, took the dead King just as the others had left him; grinding him, they washed him well until nothing of the medicines of the others remained, and they dried him. Then they took one part of Sal ammoniac <term>Sal armoniacus: ammonium chloride, used as a flux in alchemy</term> and two parts of Alexandrian nitre <term>nitrum: likely soda or saltpeter</term>, and mixed them with the powder of the dead man, and made it into a paste with a little linseed oil. They placed him in a chamber made in the manner of a crucible perforated at the bottom, and beneath the hole they placed another clean vessel made in the manner of a crucible, and left him there for one hour. Then they covered—

# THE ALLEGORY OF MERLIN

...they [the King's servants] surrounded him with fire, blowing upon him until he was completely liquefied, descending into another crucible through a hole in the bottom. Then the King, thus rising again from death to life, cried out with a loud voice and said: "Where are my enemies? Let them know that I shall kill them all, unless they come before me without delay and obey me." Therefore, all who heard this came before him and said: "Lord, behold, we are ready to obey your commands in all things." And so, from that hour as before, all the kings and powerful men of other regions honored and feared him. 

And when they wished to see some of his wonders, they would place one ounce of well-washed Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"; here referring to quicksilver or the philosophical principle of fluidity</note> into a crucible, and they would cast upon it a single grain—like a millet seed—of his nails, or his hair, or his blood. They would blow lightly with the coals and let it cool with them, and they found a stone such as I know. Of this stone, they would cast a small amount upon purified Saturn <note>original: "Saturnum"; the alchemical name for Lead</note>, and immediately its form was changed, as I know. Of this [transformed lead], they would later place one part upon ten parts of Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for Copper</note>, and the whole became of one color and quality. 

Likewise, in another way: they would take the aforementioned stone, crushed, and mix it with salt and the Sun <note>original: "Sole"; the alchemical name for Gold</note> as before; they would liquefy it and cast the dissolved salts into goat's whey, and then it became the best [medicine or reagent] for all things. 

Guard this treatise, brother, and keep it well, because it is a great jest <note>original: "truffa"; can mean a trick, a joke, or a trifle</note> among fools, but no jest among the wise. For this is the "Way of the Three-Day Kings," because those who endure but little labor desire to obtain great profit. Let us return praises to the greatest Creator, who has freely inspired his faithful ones to transmute accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are the outward qualities (color, hardness) as opposed to the "substance" or essence</note> into substances according to their will, and so that what lies hidden in potential within things may be wisely brought into actual reality.

# RACHAIDIBI, VERADIANI,
## *Rhodiani, and Kanidis, the Philosophers of the King*
## *of the Persians: Concerning the matter of the Philosophical*
## *Stone, speaking most acutely*
### *A Fragment.*

<note>This text is a Latin translation of an older Arabic alchemical dialogue. The names Rachaidibi, Veradiani, and Rhodianus are Latinized versions of Eastern names, likely representing a lineage of secret knowledge.</note>

RACHAIDIBI, son of Zetheibida, Philosopher to the King of the Persians and Prince of the Romans, said: The seed <note>original: "Sperma," referring here to the 'starting material' or 'essence'</note> of the stone is cold and moist in its outward appearance, and in its hidden nature it is hot and dry. He says, therefore: make the cold and moist hidden, and place the hot and dry in the outward appearance. In this way, its coldness and moisture will be hidden so that it might never be diminished; for if it were diminished, the stone would also be diminished. Therefore, when the coldness and moisture are hidden, act by hiding them so that you may compose that heat and dryness—which was in the hidden part—into the outward appearance. Thus, from the spirit, a body is made in two stages, and it shall become a globe <note>or 'mass'</note>, and blood, and flesh.

Rhodianus says: The seed is white and liquid. This liquid first forms a globe in the proper place within five days; it receives flesh and blood, limbs and form, and the imaginative power from God Most High. It comes to its birth, and it shines and rises in its own time. These are the two stages and the seven <note>likely referring to the seven planetary metals or the seven stages of the alchemical process</note>. And now we speak of the second seed.

Veradianus says of the second seed: it is the stone alone, and there is no other like it in this World, which impregnates itself, conceives in itself, and gives birth to itself. By this, it is understood to be one stone, and it is called the white and liquid seed, and afterwards the red.

Rhodianus says, however, that this seed is a certain stone that flees from heat and dryness; it is airy and volatile, and it is cold and moist, and hot and dry. And after this living thing dies by the "red death," <note>The 'red death' refers to the stage of rubedo or fermentation where the matter is fixed by high heat.</note> being dead it is now equal to heat and dryness, and thus it does not flee from that which is hot; it does not flee the fire, nor does it emit smoke, nor does it make a sound <note>meaning it does not crackle or decrepitate when heated</note>. It flows like wax, and it is like oil, and it is dry; this dryness tints with a red and white tincture. Thus, from the spirit, a body has been made; then this body turns...

# A LITTLE TREATISE
## BY AVICENNA.
### I SHALL DIVIDE THIS BOOK
->into eight chapters or parts.<-

**IN** *the first chapter I shall speak of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note> and its nature, as well as the sulfur which it contains within itself.*
*In the second I shall speak of the nature of the perfect bodies <note>The "perfect bodies" usually refer to gold and silver</note>, and their sulfur.*
*In the third I shall speak of the joining of the body and the spirit, and the dissolution of the stone into the first matter.*
*In the fourth I shall speak of the extraction of water from the earth.*
*In the fifth I shall speak of the foundation or even the fusion upon its own earth.*
*In the sixth I shall speak of the method of sublimating the earth.*
*In the seventh I shall speak of the multiplication and fixation of the stone.*
*In the eighth and final chapter I shall speak of the method of projecting the medicine, and of tinting any metal into the Sun and Moon <note>original: "Solem & Lunam"; in alchemy, these represent Gold and Silver</note>.*

### C H A P T E R I.

Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum," literally "living silver"</note> is cold and moist, and God created all minerals from it or with it: and it is of the nature of air and a fugitive from fire, but when it has remained in the fire for a little while, it performs strange and wonderful works.

And it alone is the living spirit, and there is nothing like it in the world that can perform such works as are performed through it. And it enters any body, penetrates, lifts, and surpasses it. It is the ferment of the bodies with which it is mixed, and then the whole will be the Elixir for whiteness and redness <note>original: "albedinem & rubedinem," the two main stages of the alchemical Great Work</note>. It is the perennial water, the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitae"</note> and the virgin's milk, the fountain and the light, from which he who drinks does not die. When it is "living," it has certain effects; when it has been "killed" <note>referring to the chemical stabilization or solidification of mercury</note>, it has other effects; and when it has been dissolved, it has the greatest effects of all.

# THE TREATISE OF AVICENNA

It is the lecherous serpent, impregnating itself, giving birth in a single day; it kills all things with its poison, and it flees from the fire. However, the Sages <note>The "Sages" or "Wise Men" refers to the established alchemical authorities and practitioners.</note> make it face the fire, and then it performs works and transformations: for just as it is changed, it changes others; as it is colored, it colors; and as it is curdled, it curdles. Therefore, among all minerals, the generation of quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the common term for Mercury</term> is to be preferred. For it is found in all minerals and shares a common symbol with them all. 

It is composed of a terrestrial and moderate substance, and of subtle water or "living oil" in moderate proportions, and of a very subtle spirit. From its terrestrial water, it derives its heaviness and downward motion, its brightness, its fluidity, and its silvery color. For it comes out of the earth and leaps back into the earth; it defends itself by nodding <note>Likely referring to the "shimmering" or "beading" movement of liquid mercury</note> and joins itself together again by its moisture. Through heat and the extinguishing of its spirit, it is fixed <term>Fixed: rendered solid or non-volatile, a primary goal in alchemy</term>; it mixes with all minerals, and it will firmly adhere to whatever it sits upon, which is why it is called the "Mother of Minerals." 

Indeed, quicksilver is clearly seen to have a dense substance, like the unicorn <note>original: "monoceros." This likely refers to the legendary density or singular strength of the unicorn's horn as a metaphor for mercury's unique physical properties.</note>, because of the greatness of its immense weight: for it outweighs gold while it remains in its own nature. It is of the strongest composition and uniform nature, for it is not separated from itself, nor does it allow itself to be divided into parts in any way. For it either withdraws from the fire with its entire substance, or it remains in the fire with it.

In it, of necessity, is the cause of perfection, since it alone suffices for the mode of perfection in every single degree—namely, with ignition—because of its good adherence and the strength of its mixture. But when its parts are thickened by the fire, it no longer allows itself to be corrupted, nor does it suffer itself to be raised further by the entry of a furious flame: for it does not endure its own rarefaction because of its density and its lack of "combustibility" <term>Sulphureitas: the quality of containing sulfur, which alchemists believed caused metals to char or burn</term>, which it does not possess.

Quicksilver, in its operations, is clearly and most perfectly a preservative against burning, and an agent of fusion when it is fixed. For it is a tincture of redness, of most abundant restoration, and of shining splendor; it does not withdraw from that which it is mixed with as long as it exists. For it is an amicable and placable metal, and a medium for joining tinctures, because it mixes with them down to the smallest parts, and in the bot- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "fundamento" (bottom/foundation), matching the catchword "fun-"</note>

->*Concerning the nature of the perfect bodies: that is, the Sun and the Moon, and their sulfur.*<-

### CHAPTER II.

Gold is the most perfect body, the lord of stones, the King and head of all others, which neither the earth corrupts, nor burning things consume, nor is it diminished in the fire, but is rather improved by it; for in the fire it is moistened by a certain humidity, nor is it altered by water. Its complexion is temperate, and its nature is balanced in heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; nothing superfluous or diminished is found within it. For it is created from the most subtle and clear substance of quicksilver, and from a small amount of the substance of pure and clean sulfur of a fixed redness, which clearly tints the substance of the quicksilver itself.

Gold is held to be the body and the ferment of the Elixir, both white and red. It is neither improved, nor perfected, nor completed except with this and no other; just as dough cannot be leavened except by its own ferment <note>yeast</note>. Gold is a body enduring, remaining through the ages of ages.

# LITTLE TREATISE

And for this reason, the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" usually refers to the ancient alchemists and natural scientists like Aristotle or Geber.</note> preferred it and magnified it: for they said that gold relates to other bodies just as the Sun relates to the stars. For the Sun, in its light and splendor, causes all plants to sprout and brings all fruits to perfection. Therefore, <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts were attributed.</note> says: A true tincture <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is a substance capable of transmuting or coloring base metals into gold.</note> is never made without the red stone.

Gold holds the first rank of nobility among all bodies: because it is the most perfectly tempered due to the mixing and purification of sulfur and Mercury. It possesses much of the power of sulfur but little of its substance; conversely, it has much of the substance of Mercury but little of its power. For this reason, on account of the Mercury, it is heavy, and on account of the power of sulfur, it is very red. And because of the strongest compaction of sulfur and Mercury in its "lime" <note>original: "calce"; refers to the powdered or calcined state of a metal.</note>, it is not as moist to the touch or oily as other bodies: therefore, it does not make black marks like other metals when it is drawn across parchment. But if silver or another metal were mixed with it, then it would make black marks: because the oiliness of the body mixed with it tends toward the surface, making it whiten and become moist. And because its parts are deeply concentrated toward the center, it is heavier than its "living silver" <note>original: "argentum vivum"; the common term for quicksilver or mercury.</note> alone would account for.

Lead, however, is heavy more because of its "living silver" than because of the consolidation of its parts, which adhere to one another weakly; and therefore, among all bodies, it is the least resonant.

Gold, however, because of the strong and tenacious coherence of its parts, has the sharpest sound of all. Gold also is not consumed by a fire proportioned to it. For the most vehement fire consumes all things existing beneath the lunar globe <note>The "sublunary" sphere in medieval cosmology—the Earthly realm where things are subject to decay.</note>. It is also not burned by those things which burn other bodies, such as sulfur and arsenic. And craftsmen are accustomed to purge it to the highest splendor using bricks and salt.

Silver has much of the substance of sulfur but little of its power, and little of the substance of Mercury but much of its power; therefore it is white: because color follows the abundance of the power; and the power is located in the vapor.

# A LITTLE TREATISE

<margin>One kind</margin> is from the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti viui"; mercury</note>, included within them at the beginning of their mixing, which we call "supereminent." The other, however, is a sulfur foreign to its own nature, which we call "corresponding."

And it must be noted most diligently, that the joining of these two bodies is necessary in this art, for the white and for the red <note>The "white" and "red" refer to the two stages of the Alchemical Great Work: the silver-making and gold-making tinctures.</note>. And there are two reasons, the first of which is: Since gold is the noblest among metals, and the most compact, perfect, and fixed, yet if it be dissolved and separated into its smallest parts, it becomes spiritual and fleeting, just like Mercury. And this is by reason of its heat: and then it possesses a tincture <note>A "tincture" in alchemy is the power to transform or color other substances.</note> without number, and this tincture is called the hot masculine seed. If, however, silver is dissolved into lukewarm water, it nevertheless remains fixed as before, and has little or no tincture: yet it is ready to receive that same tincture in a temperament of hot and cold: and it is called the feminine seed, cold and dry: therefore their joining is fitting. There is also another reason, because since gold and silver are each difficult to melt and liquefy on their own, yet if they are joined, they flow and liquefy easily, as the goldsmiths know who make solders for gold. Hence, if in our stone there were only one of these two, the medicine would never flow easily through any mastery, nor would it give a tincture. And if it did give a tincture, it would not tinge except in as much as it was itself, because there would be no receptacle for the tincture. Do not understand all of this as referring to common Moon <note>original: "Luna vulgari"; common silver</note>, but to the philosophical Moon, which is also called Lunaria. Therefore I advise <unclear>that</unclear> you do not work except with Mercury, the Sun <note>Gold</note>, and the Moon <note>Silver</note>. Since the entire benefit of this art consists in those three.

# AVICENNA

<note>original: "AVICENNAE" - This text is attributed to the Persian polymath Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, though it belongs to the "Pseudo-Avicenna" corpus of medieval Latin alchemy.</note>

All metals are truly generated from Mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, and therefore they are resolved back into it.

The first regimen of the Stone <term>Stone: the Philosophers' Stone, the goal of alchemy</term> is therefore to dissolve it just like thick quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, so that it may be reduced back into its first matter. This is entirely accomplished through quicksilver, because it has the power to reduce the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note> back into their nature and first matter. 

But since quicksilver contains within itself dross <note>original: "fœculentiam"</note>, a burning without flame, and a watery substance, it is necessary to remove its excesses and fulfill its deficiencies if you wish to create a complete medicine from it. It is absolutely necessary to remove the drossy earth through sublimation <term>Sublimation: heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again to purify it</term>, and to fulfill what is lacking, lest it create a leaden color during projection <term>Projection: the final stage where the medicine is cast upon base metals to transform them</term>. In the same way, one must destroy its wateriness, lest it cause the entire material to fly away <note>evaporate</note> during projection.

It is the property of this substance to save the essence of the medicine, to remain unburned, but to fix it <term>Fixation: making a volatile substance stable under heat</term> and defend it from burning. Therefore, it happens that Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, Venus <note>Copper</note>, iron, etc., are created from it, which necessarily occurs due to impurity.

It should be noted that there are two types of "first matter." One is "near" and the other is "remote." The near matter is quicksilver; the remote matter is water. This is because quicksilver was first water, and afterwards became quicksilver. The true beginning of our work, therefore, is the dissolution of the Stone, because dissolved bodies are reduced to the nature of spirit, which makes them more fixed. For the dissolution of the body occurs simultaneously with the coagulation of the spirit. 

Therefore, be patient: cook, grind, and soften with wax <note>original: "incera" - a process of adding liquid to a dry substance to give it a waxy consistency</note>, and do not let it weary you to repeat this many times. For those things which are soaked are softened by the water. The more you grind, the more you soften and refine the coarse parts until it is sufficient. These parts are divided when the spirits are made into a paste, and everything that is made into a paste is totally dissolved. This "impastation" is achieved through excessive grinding, waxing, and roasting. For through grinding, roasting, and fire, the bound and viscous parts within the bodies are divided. Truly, bodies that have been dissolved and reduced to the nature of spirit shall never be separated, just as water mixed with water cannot be parted. Indeed, nature rejoices when...

### *On the extraction of water from the earth.*
#### *CHAPTER IV.*

After the matter has been putrefied <note>Putrefaction was the first stage of the Great Work, involving the breaking down of the substance</note>, to create the body and the spirit—which is nevertheless impossible to do except in the air, that is, through sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify materials</term>.

Know therefore that our stone is divided into two principal parts: namely, into the upper part which ascends, and into the lower part which remains fixed at the bottom. And yet these two parts agree in their power.

And for this reason the Philosopher <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus in the Emerald Tablet</note> says: that which is below is like that which is above. And this division is necessary to perform the miracles of the one thing, namely the stone; the lower part is the earth, which is called the nurse and the ferment: and the upper part is the soul, which vivifies the whole stone and makes it live again.

Hence, once the celebrated separation is made, many miracles are performed by the joining of the stone. It should be noted that although among some people our stone is not divided into four parts—namely into the four elements in the first operation, as was said above—there are four principal parts: namely one which ascends above and is not fixed; another which remains below, which is called fixed; and the earth or ferment, which nourishes and ferments the whole stone, as has been said. Truly, of that non-fixed part, it is necessary to have a good quantity and give it to the stone, which is most pure and entirely without filth, until it carries the whole stone upward by the power of the non-fixed spirit through sublimation. And this is what the Philosopher says: "It ascends from the earth to heaven." Afterward, it is necessary to repeat the process with the stone thus exalted upon a marble slab, with the element extracted from the stone itself in the first operation. That element is called the water of the stone. # AVICENNA

The Crowd <note>original: "Turba"; likely referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, an influential early alchemical assembly text</note> says: Let there be a change of temperaments <term>complexionum: the balance of the four bodily humors or qualities</term>, namely from cold and moist into hot and dry, or from phlegmatic into choleric according to the physicians. ### On the method of sublimating the earth.
### CHAPTER VI.

A certain great Philosopher says: In the dregs is what you seek. Therefore, let the dregs be taken when they are extracted from the alembic <term>alembico: a distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term>, and let them be ground strongly, and soaked with their own water, and dried in a slow fire or in the Sun; and let this be done many times. For from such a preparation, that smoke is made fit for sublimation <term>sublimationem: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term>. Whence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in alchemy</note> says: From the multiple repetition of soaking and roasting, the greater part of its wateriness is destroyed. The remainder is truly removed through sublimation.

Therefore, let the aforementioned dregs be taken and prepared for sublimating by first administering to them a slow fire, proportionally increasing it until that clean and white smoke ascends; and if it does not happen at first, let the soaking be repeated over the same dregs until they become so, and finally [sublimated] without the dregs that adhere; then one fixed part is produced from them. Truly, according to its diverse operation, a diversity of medicine is created, sometimes Saturn <note>Lead</note>, or Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, etc.

However, no one ought to sublimate the earth for sophisticated <note>deceptive or imitation</note> works, but only for our Elixir. And do not mix that which remains below with that which ascends above, but set each one aside.

First, the matter is to be sublimated, and it is to be fixed: when the appropriate union has preceded, fixation should follow. However, do not make the fixed matter volatile; rather, incorporate one part of the fixed matter and two parts of the prepared Mercury well together. Afterward, sublime it, collect the sublimate, and always repeat that which remains at the bottom, grinding it with new Mercury in the manner aforesaid until the whole has been sublimated. For according to the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note>, the power of white, non-burning <term>Sulphur</term> congeals the Mercury. And if there shall be excellent sulphur, clear with redness, and if there be in it the power of the silveriness of non-burning sulphur, it will be the thing from which the elixir for gold is made. 

And as the Philosophers teach, let the sulphur first be made for the white (for silver), and afterward for the red (for gold): because gold is not made unless it was first silver. Indeed, no thing can come from the first to the third except through the second, because there is no passage from one extreme to the other except through the middle. Therefore, a perfect yellow <note>original: "citrinum"</note> cannot be made from black unless it was first white, because yellow is composed of a tiny amount of red and the purest white. Nor can white be made from yellow unless it was first black.

Thus gold cannot be made into silver unless it was first corrupted and black. Because the better cannot be made worse except through its own corruption: since the corruption of one is the generation of another. Therefore, he who wishes to convert gold into silver, let him act thus through corruption, and likewise silver into gold: because their non-burning sulphur, through a greater digestion of fire, can become red sulphur, because yellowing <note>original: "citrinatio"</note> is nothing other than complete digestion. Blackness is nothing but washing <note>original: "ablutio"</note>. For heat acting on the moist first produces blackness. And heat in the dry causes whiteness, as well as yellowness in the white, and ni— <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "nigredinem" (blackness) or "nitorem" (brightness) on the following page.</note>

->*Now I wish to tell you what Sublimation is.*<-

Sublimation is the elevation of the most subtle parts from the fixed parts. The non-fixed parts are raised by smoke: that is, by wind: because as we have said, one must take care lest they flee; rather, they are fixed with the fixed parts, and remain, and provide a swifter fusion. Understand true sublimation to be when we make a separation of the parts which are raised above from those which remain below: rather, we desire that they should come together as one in their own proper way, because in our stone—after the first purification which is accomplished through solution—we find nothing diminished or superfluous.

For this reason Geber <note>Referring to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the famous 8th-century alchemist often cited as the father of chemistry.</note> said: Let the stone be sublimated with itself, until it finally arrives at the purity of sublimation. For he said "with itself": that is, without any other addition or any foreign thing. Because of this, all those laborers are deceived who sublimate with dregs and do not know what they are doing, or what the Philosophical Stone is, and they gain nothing: because they are ignorant of Philosophical sublimation.

Geber says: For the Stone of the Philosophers is one medicine, in which the whole mastery <term>magisterium: the complete alchemical process or the "Great Work"</term> consists, to which nothing foreign is added, nor is anything diminished, except that which is superfluous in the operation is removed; and this is the first purification, which is completed through sublimation. ## *On the method of projecting the medicine, and of tinting any metal into Gold and Silver.* <note>original: "Solem & Lunam" (Sun and Moon), the standard alchemical symbols for Gold and Silver.</note>
### CHAPTER VIII.

I have fulfilled my promise up to this point regarding the great mastery <note>The "Magisterium" refers to the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work."</note> for making the most excellent white and red Elixir. Here, finally, I shall speak of the method of projection, which is the completion of the work and the long-desired and expected joy. Truly, the white Elixir whitens unto infinity, and it brings any metal whatever to a perfect whiteness. But it must be known that one metal is brought to the Elixir more easily than another. For those things which are near <note>referring to the "proximity" of a metal's nature to gold or silver</note> are perfected more easily than those which are remote. And when we find a metal that is perfect and very near, the vice of imperfection in that near thing is excused by those things far remote: which metals are far remote or near is made clear enough in many books.

And because the white or red Elixir is highly spiritual, yet works beyond the power of nature, it is no wonder that it is able to mix with the body <note>In alchemy, "body" refers to a solid metal.</note> upon which it is projected, provided that it merely melts it.

It is also a heavy task to project upon a thousand thousand parts and have it penetrate them instantly. Therefore, I shall hand down to you one great secret. One part is to be mixed with a thousand parts of a closely related body, and shut all of this firmly in a suitable vessel: and it must be placed in a smelting furnace for three days, until the whole has been inseparably joined together.

And that is the work of three days. Then, one part of that joined body is to be projected unto infinity upon a thousand parts of any body. However, the nearer things are always more closely related. And that is the work of one day, or an hour, or a minute.

There is also another method of projection. Take one hundred parts of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"</note> washed with salt and vinegar, and place them in a crucible over the fire: when it begins to smoke, project one part upon these hundred parts of Mercury, and the whole becomes a medicine. Then, place one part of this medicine upon another hundred parts of Mercury, over a boiling fire:

## Epilogue of the Whole.

I say, therefore, that the sum of the entire Work is nothing other than this: that the Stone known in the chapters of the books be taken, and when the urgency of the work is applied steadily upon it, the work of sublimation of the first degree is performed, so that it may be cleansed from corrupting impurity. Then, with the substance dissolved, its white or red addition <note>The "ferment" or tincture used to determine the final metal</note> should be refined until, in the final stage of sublimation, it becomes volatile.

Furthermore, let it be fixed by methods of fixation until the whole rests within the harshness of the fire. Then, indeed, you should make the fixed part volatile with the reserved non-fixed part by means of solution and sublimation, making the volatile fixed, and the fixed dissolved: and again the volatile, and the volatile fixed, until it flows and transforms in a certain solar-making <note>gold-making</note> and lunar-making <note>silver-making</note> completion. And in this way is wrought the most precious secret, valuable above every price in the World, and the incomparable treasure of all Philosophers.

# PATHWAYS

The matter is one, and naturally works in diverse ways solely through greater or lesser action—either burning or not burning—and in this, all Philosophers agree. And I shall demonstrate this in such a way: Because it is certain that every thing is made of and from that into which it is resolved, and this is a true and comparable example. If ice is changed into water by means of heat, therefore, it was previously water; but all metals are converted into Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"; here referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the fluid principle of all metals rather than common quicksilver</note>, therefore this Mercury is their first matter <term>materia prima: the primordial, formless base of all physical things</term>. However, I will teach the method of converting them below. Having grasped that, the opinion of those who say the species of metals cannot be converted is dissolved; and this is true, as they say, unless they are reduced back into the first matter. Moreover, their reduction into the first matter is easy, as I shall show; and transmutation is easy and possible. For everything that grows or is born is multiplied within its own species, such as men, trees, grains, and the like. For from one grain, a thousand are generated. Therefore, it is possible for things to be increased even unto infinity. From the aforesaid, it appears to the subtle observer that the Philosophers have spoken obscurely in their books, but truly. For they said that our stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> is composed of body, soul, <unclear>and</unclear> spirit, and they speak the truth. For they compared the imperfect body to the "body" because it is weak; and they called the water "spirit," and truly it is spirit: because it grants life to the imperfect body—which is dead by itself—which it did not have before, and brings it forth into a better form. They called the ferment the "soul," which, as will be said below, similarly grants life to the imperfect body, and raises and converts it into its own nature. The Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: "Convert the natures, and you will find what you seek"; and this is true. For in our mastery <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical work</term> we first make the slender from the thick: that is, spirit from the body; and afterwards dry from the moist: that is, earth from water. And thus we convert the natures, and we make the higher the lower, which happens when the spirit is made body, and conversely the body is made spirit. Likewise, our stone, as the Philosophers say, is made from one thing, and in one vessel, and they speak the truth. For the whole mastery is done with our water, and from it. For it dissolves the bodies themselves, as has been said—not, however, by that kind of solution as the ignorant believe, namely that it is converted into rainwater <note>original: "aquam nubis"; literally "water of the clouds"</note>. And this same [water] calcines <term>calcinatio: the process of reducing a solid to a powder through heat or chemical action</term>, and...

# THE PATH

it leads back into the earth. This same water transforms the bodies into ash; it incinerates, whitens, and cleanses them according to the word of Morienus <note>Morienus was a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit of Jerusalem, said to be the teacher of King Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, who says: That *azoth* <note>original: "azoth"; a term for the universal solvent or Mercury</note> and fire cleanse the *Laton* <note>original: "Latonē"; an impure copper alloy or the "base" state of the metal before purification</note>: that is, they wash it, and entirely snatch away its darkness from it. For *Laton* is an unclean body, and *azoth* is quicksilver. And it joins the diverse bodies prepared in the aforementioned way with such a union that neither fire nor any action can separate them from the combustion of fieriness. And by one rushing into the other, it changes and refines the bodies—not by a common refinement, as the ignorant or inexperienced believe, thinking that to "sublimate" is merely to ascend upward. And therefore they take calcined <note>burned to a powder</note> bodies and mix them with sublimated spirits, namely Mercury, arsenic, and sulfur, etc., and they cause them to sublimate by a strong fire—that is, they make the bodies rise with the spirits—and they say that the bodies are then "sublimated." And they are deluded: because they still find the bodies more unclean with the spirits than they were before. Therefore, our "sublimating" is not to ascend upward; rather, the sublimation of the Philosophers is to make another, more pure thing out of a most vile and corrupt thing (from the earth). Just as when we say, "He has been sublimated to Bishop": that is, exalted or placed in a worthier state. So also we say the bodies are converted or exalted into another—that is, a better—nature. Whence to sublimate is the same as to refine, all of which our "water" accomplishes. And thus Philosophical Sublimation is to be understood, in which many have been deceived. Our water also mortifies <note>kills or breaks down</note>, illuminates, cleanses, and vivifies; and it makes black colors appear first during the mortification of the body while it is converted into earth, and afterwards many and varied colors appear before the whitening, the end of all of which is whiteness <note>original: "albedo"; the second major stage of the Great Work</note>. Truly, in the mixing of the water and the body of the ferment <note>original: "fermenti"; the substance that triggers the transformation of the base metal</note>—that is, in the preparation of the body—infinite colors appear. And thus it appears that our mastery is from one thing, and is done with one thing, and is from four, and from three, one.

Whence you should know, Father, that the Philosophers multiplied the names of the "mixed stone," and this they did so that they might hide it. And they called the mixed stone "corporeal" and "spiritual," and they did not lie, as a wise man can understand. For there is both body and spirit, and the body is as much a spirit...

the ritual is in the dissolution, and the spirit is made; and it is bodily in the joining of the spirit with the body. And some call it the ferment, while others call it the bronze <note>original: "aes"; often referring to the base metal or the "leper" to be transformed</note>.

Morienes <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist, teacher of King Khalid</note> says: Because the knowledge of our ingenuity—that is, of the mastery—is likened to the order in the creation of a human being. I shall make you understand these words: since our sperm, which is quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, is joined with the earth—namely, with the imperfect body which is called the mother earth, because earth is the mother of all elements—then it is called coitus. And this is what the Philosophers meant when they said that our mastery is nothing but male and female, and their joining. Therefore, when the water arrives—that is, the quicksilver—it grows and increases in the earth, because the earth is whitened, and then it is called pregnancy. Then the ferment is coagulated: that is, it is joined with the prepared imperfect body, as has been said, until it becomes one in color and appearance, and then it is called birth: because then our stone is born, which is called the King by the Philosophers, as it is said in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>:

Fifth and finally follows the nourishment, because the more it is nourished, the more it is increased. However, it is nourished by its own milk: that is, by the sperm from which it originated. Moreover, the quicksilver is imbibed, often and repeatedly, until it drinks two parts or what is sufficient.

### *The practice now follows.*

Let us now descend to the practice as I said before. The bodies must be reduced to the first matter <term>First Matter: the "Prima Materia," the formless base of all substance required before transmutation can occur</term> for this purpose, so that the transmutation may take place.

Then take all this earth: that is, the blackness which you collected, and put it in a glass vessel, and pour over it the aforesaid blessed water, until nothing stands out, and it floats upon it, and cook it for so long with a light fire for ten days; grind it, and again put in water, and cook: and so on: that is, cooking the earth thus coagulated and thickened with water without the addition of other water with a strong fire, as above, until the earth becomes white and clear. # THE PATHS

As Morienes <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> says: Unless you cleanse and whiten the unclean body, and place the soul within it, you have directed nothing in the mastery. And then the spirit is joined, and rejoices with them, and is fixed. For the water is altered, and all coarse things are made subtle.

And this is what Astanus says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>, the spirit is not joined to the bodies until they have been perfectly stripped of their impurities. And in this union the greatest miracles appear, because all the colors that can be imagined in the world appear, and the imperfect body is colored with the color of the ferment, by means of the firm ferment, as Barsen says. O pious father, may God increase in you the spirit of understanding, so that you may weigh in your mind what I am about to say. For the elements are not generated except from their own sperm: and the sperm is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum," or Mercury</note>. Just as it is evident in the generation of man, because there is no mixing of any thing except through sperm, and in vegetables except the seed, as far as their generation and augmentation are concerned. Others, looking more subtly, sublime the Mercury, and fix it, and join it with the bodies, and yet they find nothing. The cause of the error is this: For the seed cannot be transformed, neither as it is nor as it was, nor does it profit unless it be cast into the womb of the woman. Thus Mechardus the Philosopher says: Unless the stone is cast into the womb of the woman, so that she may nourish it, it does not profit. O my father, thus you have according to your wish the description of the Philosophers' Stone: Praise be to God.

## A WONDERFUL AND MOST ATTENTIVE TREATISE, excerpted from a certain very ancient writing.

# ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE
->*faithfully and physically explaining it to all Philosophers.*<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'I' featuring a stylized floral design with scrolling vines and leaves within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>In the name of the Lord, Amen. The sound of the trumpet concerning the blessed <term>Philosophical Stone</term><note>The "Stone" is not a literal rock, but the goal of alchemy: a substance capable of perfecting matter and prolonging life.</note>: Which thunders wonderfully in its kind of operation and virtue: Concerning which the Philosophers have set down various opinions and writings. Whence, concerning the <term>first essence</term><note>original: "prima essentia"</note>, the first Philosopher, Thales of Miletus, says: *God is the most ancient of beings, unbegotten and eternal.* Whence also Pythagoras says: *I say that God was before all things, when nothing was with Him when He was.* And understand, that since God was alone in the beginning, He created one substance, which we name <term>First Matter</term><note>original: "primam materiam"; the formless "stuff" from which the universe was shaped.</note>. And from that substance He created four other things: fire, air, water, and earth. From these, once created, He created all things, both of the sublime <note>the heavens and stars</note> and of the inferior <note>the earthly realm</note>. And so, before all other things except the first matter, He created the four elements, from which He afterwards created what He willed, namely, diverse natures. Whence God created by His word, to which He said: *Be*, and they were made, namely the four elements and the rest. For from these four elements all things are created as if from a root: the heavens, thrones, Angels, stars, the Sun, the Moon, the sea, and all things that are in the sea, which are various and not alike, whose natures God made diverse just like their creation, because they were created from diverse elements. For if they had been created from one element, they would have matching natures. But because these diverse elements, when they are mixed together, lose their own natures—because heat mixed with cold becomes neither hot nor cold, and moisture mixed with dryness becomes neither moist nor dry—therefore the creatures coming forth from them have diverse natures. # THE TRUMPET
<note>original: "BVCCINA" - likely referring to the "Trumpet of Hermes" or a similar alchemical/philosophical clarion call</note>

He created certain of the creatures from a single element, and these are the **Angels**, whom He created from fire alone. From two elements, namely from fire and air, those three were created: the **Sun**, the **Moon**, and the **stars**. Therefore, the Angels are more luminous than the Sun, Moon, and stars, because they were created from one singular element, which is the fourth and rarest <note>The author refers to fire as the most subtle or "rare" of the four elements</note>. The Sun, Moon, and stars, however, were created from a composition of fire and air.

But the **souls** (as the Philosophers say) which are infused into bodies today and hereafter, every day, are not created anew within the mother's womb; rather, they were created from fire alone from the primordial principle of all things. They are nourished in the mind and power of the Creator until the appointed time when they must be infused into a new body, as if into a pre-existing matter. This infusion into the body happens through a medium, which is the **spirit** <note>In this context, "spirit" (spiritus) acts as a bridge or vaporous link between the immaterial soul and the physical body</note>. And they do not depart from the body unless the spirit has first departed and vanished; once it has departed and vanished, the soul also departs. This is so even though the theologians say that the soul is infused into the body, and in the infusing, it is created, and that God delights in this—that He creates new souls daily, and this from the first matter.

Furthermore, God created the **heaven** from water and air. The heaven is also composed of two: from one of the rarer elements, namely air, and from one of the denser, namely water.

And from three elements, God created the **birds**, the **brute animals**, and the **vegetables** <note>meaning plants or growing things</note>. Thus, the birds were created from fire, air, and water; and all things having a spirit among the vegetables were created from air, water, and earth. Yet, nothing is more "vegetable" <note>possessing the power of growth</note> than the matter of fire. In plants, the element of fire is present only hidden within the heat of the air. However, "thick" or dense fire is not present except in those possessing spirit and soul.

But from all **four elements**—fire, air, water, and earth together—our father **Adam** and his children were created.

And everything that God created from a single essence does not die, except on the Day of Judgment. For the definition of **death** is the separation of a composite. However, in that which is not composite, there is no separation; hence, there is no death <note>referring to the immortality of the soul and angels</note> except for the separation of the soul from the body. But in everything composed of two, three, or four elements, it is necessary for the composite to be separated, which is the act of death. And know that no composite lacking fire eats, drinks, or sleeps. And since the Angels are made of fire...

Note that there are four primary qualities, namely: **heat, dryness, coldness, and moisture**; and they are called the primary qualities because from them all elements are composed, and all things are formed of elements, and all things receive their temperament <note>complexionem: the specific balance of qualities in a body</note>. And the elements are made of these simple qualities. That is, they have the power to convert and change matter from one quality into another quality, sometimes into dry, sometimes into moist, sometimes into hot, and sometimes into cold, according as the division of nature is strengthened by the temperament of its elements, or even weakened.

And the qualities are like the matter of the elements, in which they place their forms. They are also retained within them, as their nature demonstrates in every generation. Likewise, a single element cannot be destroyed nor generated within itself, because there is not a sufficient nature there; wherefore it is necessary that there be several. Likewise, that nature is one subtle substance into which the qualities of the elements enter. Therefore, the qualities of the elements draw more to themselves from that in which they most abound. 

And so the qualities are like the matter of the elements, into which they place their forms, and in them they are retained, as their nature demonstrates in every generation; and in the subtle substance, the qualities of the elements are condensed in every generation. And if that nature had not been in the subtle essential substance of the elements, then that nature—the essentiality of the elements—could not have existed or been bounded in substance. And also, if any element were a mineral separately according to its own nature, that substance could not penetrate it, nor have entry, nor give it color. Therefore, because of that property, it is fitting that fire should predominate in the aforesaid substance of the elements, according to its nature. Thus says Raymond <note>Refers to Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull), a major figure in medieval logic and alchemy</note>.

# TRUMPETS
<note>original: "BVCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets" of knowledge or a specific series of alchemical revelations.</note>

All hidden things participate in the four elements and the four natural humors, namely: yellow bile, blood, phlegm, and black bile <note>original: "cholera, sanguis, phlegma, & melancholia"</note>. They also share in the four temperaments: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness; the four principal colors: white, black, yellow, and red; the four flavors: tasteless, sour, sweet, and bitter; and the four scents: pleasant, foul, sharp, and faint. They possess two sexes: masculine and feminine, according to their three dimensions, namely: height, length, and depth.

Common height is its manifest <term>manifest: the outward, visible appearance of a substance</term> part; depth is its hidden <term>hidden: the internal, occult properties of a substance</term> part; and breadth participates as the medium between these two. Therefore, all bodies must be considered in every way according to these three aforementioned dimensions. For this reason, if a body is earthy in its height, there is within it something cold, dry, melancholic, bitter, sour, foul-smelling, black, and feminine. Consequently, in its depth, it is airy, hot, moist, sanguine, yellow, sweet, fragrant, and masculine. And if on one side it is watery, it follows that it is cold and moist, white, tasteless, smelling both sweet and foul, and feminine. Consequently, on the other side, it will be fiery, hot, dry, red, bitter, sharp, and masculine. These are the bonds by which all bodies are joined to one another, which is most clearly perceived in liquefied bodies, namely: gold, silver, lead, tin, iron, and <term>sandarac: likely referring here to realgar or a specific arsenic ore used in alchemy</term>. For it is the property of every element to have within itself a contrariety, and to act upon its opposite.

And note that there are four elements, namely fire, air, water, and earth: because each of them is composed of two primary qualities, and no more. For example, fire is from heat and dryness; air from heat and moisture; water from cold and moisture; and earth from cold and dryness. Likewise, heat in fire is its <term>essential quality: the defining characteristic that makes a thing what it is</term>, and dryness is its <term>accidental quality: a secondary characteristic that can change without destroying the substance</term>. In air, moisture is its essential quality, while heat is accidental. In water, moisture is its principal or essential quality, but cold is its accidental quality. In earth, dryness is its principal beginning or essential quality, and coldness [is its accidental quality].

...accidental. Likewise, fire is properly hot and dry by its property. For heat is greater in a thing when it comes from its qualities than from its property. Understand the other qualities of the elements in the same way. Likewise, concerning the principle of the four elements, Mycretis <note>likely a corruption of Democritus or a similar ancient authority</note> says: Know that the earth was previously water; then it was turned into stone and became rocky. Water, indeed, was previously air; then it was liquefied, thickened, and turned into water. The principle of air, however, was fire, because it comes from thickened fire. But fire lacks a beginning, except for its Creator. And note, that earth is the body of water, and from earth, man is made. Fire, moreover, is not absent from the three elements, by which those three also persist. 

And we speak concerning the degrees of those elements. Because fire, as it exists in a mixture, is hot in the fourth degree and dry in the third. Because heat is inherent to it in the first place, it is evident because nothing is hotter than it; and that dryness is inherent to it secondarily is evident because if there were as much dryness in it as there is heat, as soon as it heated something, it would dry it out just as quickly, which does not happen. Water is cold in the fourth degree and moist in the third; for although it tends toward the opposite so that it can be heated, since it cannot be congealed into a dry state while its coldness remains, it is more cold than it is moist. <margin>Note: I have written as I have found it, but the opposite seems true to me.</margin> Air is primarily moist in the fourth degree, and secondarily hot in the middle of the third; because moisture blunts the heat. Earth is primarily dry in the fourth, and secondarily cold in the middle of the third. 

And such is the circulation of all the elements. Fire pours its heat into the air. Air pours its moisture into the water through rarefied heat. Water sends its coldness into the earth by drying it through the heat of the air. And the earth, drying its coldness—having been made cold, moist, and warm—pours it into the air. And so fire recovers its heat, which had been sent out, through the qualities of the other elements. Air likewise recovers its moisture, water its coldness, and earth its dryness. And thus, according to this mixing, the mixture of the elements is made. Therefore, fire is in the water because it is in the air existing in the earth. And water is in the fire because it is in the earth existing in the fire; and earth is in the air because it is in the fire existing in the air. And thus their mixture is limitable to any proportion. Likewise, Raymond <note>referring to Raymond Lull, a major figure in medieval alchemy and logic</note> says, in the beginning...

The theory of the Testament: Because the primordial principle of all things is one nature, which God created out of nothing, in one pure substance, which we call the **quintessence** <note>The "fifth essence," a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>, in which all nature is contained. From this substance, divided into three parts according to its essence, God created the angels and the **empyrean heaven** <note>The highest heaven, believed in medieval cosmology to be the abode of God and the angels, composed of pure light or fire.</note> from the purest part. Through this clarity and through truth, pure souls participate in nature with the angels; through this participation, there is a perfect union between them in glorification.

And from the second part, God created the heaven: that is, the firmament, the planets—namely the Sun and the Moon—and all the stars. And from the third part, which was less pure, God created this World. And you must understand this not exactly as it is traditionally handed down, but as the whole was created simultaneously at the will of the superior Creator, without any succession of a worker <note>Meaning God created it instantly, unlike a human craftsman who works step-by-step.</note>, and without preceding matter that would look toward a succession of kind: because it would be neither a creation nor a divine work—which looks toward the Creator, the Lord of entity—if it were not led **summatively** <note>original: "sumentificaliter" - a technical term implying a creative act that brings the totality of being into existence at once.</note> as a creation out of nothing into a true substantial entity.

For which reason, that which I have said and am about to say, you should wish to understand with a **summative spirit** <note>original: "spiritu sumentifico"</note> and not a coarse or common one: because here we speak with respect to the work of nature, to which you must be assimilated in our **mastery** <note>original: "magisterio" - the Great Work of alchemy.</note>. And therefore we speak to you with the language of example, so that you may understand us well, as has already been said.

Because the supreme Creator divided that less pure part into five parts. From one purer part, God created the **quintessence**, the substance of the elements, which participates with celestial things. And this he divided into four parts:
1. The first and purest is given to **fire**, which God created from the second part of the nature of the elements.
2. The second pure part of this is attributed to **air**, which was created from the third, less pure part of the nature of the elements.
3. The third, less pure part is given to **water**, which is the element created from the fourth, less pure part of the nature of the elements.
4. And the fourth, least pure part is given to the **earthly element**, which was created from the fifth, least pure part of the whole nature of the elements.

And the less perfect a nature is, the more it hungers for its own perfection; and one is perfected with the other because of the harmony of their properties with their fifth instrument,

### *Various Enigmas Concerning the Philosophical Moon.*

Likewise, Ptolemy says in the *Almagest* <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek mathematical and astronomical treatise</note>: Because the Sun does not heat the earth, nor impress its virtue upon the earth except by means of the Moon, which among other stars is more receptive to the Sun's light and heat, acting as a medium between the Sun and the earth. Wherefore, as the Philosophers say, there are two impediments that prevent one thing from impressing its virtue upon another, namely remote distance and an intervening medium. And so it is there between the Sun and the earth, because the Sun is far distant from the earth, and because the Moon mediates there. So also in our Alchemical art, the Sun <note>In alchemy, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold</note> does not perfect the tincture alone except by means of the Moon <note>The Moon (Luna) represents Silver</note>, because it is remotely distant, since it has not yet reached that subtlety so that it may tinge; and also because of the mediums themselves, namely density and coarseness. Wherefore the Moon is necessarily required there, so that she may subtilize the Sun itself, make it rare and volatile, and segregate its impurity. Since she herself stands in greater need of his light and nature than the other planets: that is, the metals. Therefore Hermes and Aristotle say in *On Plants*: The Sun is its father, the Moon is its mother. Therefore the Moon is the mother and the field in which the solar seed ought to be sown, and thus we do not need anything else from...

For then the species are changed into a form other than they were before—not indeed the species themselves, but the individuals of the species: since the individuals themselves are objects of sensible actions, because they are corruptible among themselves. But the species, since they are universal, are not subject to sensible actions, and therefore are not corruptible among themselves. Indeed, the species of silver, which is "silverness," is not changed into the species of gold, which is "goldness," nor vice versa: because true species cannot be changed, but the individuals of the species are indeed reduced into their first matter. Because when the form of that thing has been corrupted and resolved into the first matter, then also a new form is necessarily introduced, because the **corruption of one is the generation of another**. But because matter can in no way be so destroyed that it does not remain under some form, when one form of metals is destroyed, another is immediately introduced—namely, through the **transmutation of Mercury into sulfur**, toward our intended operation. Also, every individual multiplies the form of its own species, and not of another, as Aristotle and Raymond say. And therefore, once the first form of the body is dissolved through "elementation" <note>The process of breaking a substance down into its constituent elements.</note> converted into Mercury, it is in a blackish color, in a foul odor, and in a subtle and discontinuous touch. In such a simple nature, however, there are four elements—composed, separable, and resolvable into the water of Mercury after **putrefaction** <term>the stage of "blackness" or decay in the alchemical process, necessary for rebirth</term>. Thus says Raymond.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical theory that all substances can be reduced to a universal "first matter" (Mercury), arguing that while the abstract essence of a metal cannot change, individual physical objects can be broken down and reformed into new substances like gold.</summary>
<keywords>first matter, Mercury, Raymond Lull, Aristotle, sulfur, silverness, goldness, corruption and generation, transmutation, putrefaction</keywords>
