<meta>This page continues the discussion of alchemical principles, specifically focusing on the nature of the "Mercurial water" and its role in the dissolution and transformation of metals.</meta>

-># THE CLANGOR<-

And when I say **Mercurial water** <note>Latin: *aqua Mercurialis*; a symbolic term for the universal solvent or "First Matter" of the alchemists</note>, I do not mean simple, raw mercury, but the **Mercury of the Philosophers** of a red substance, extracted from minerals that contain within themselves the matter of sulfur and mercury. Therefore, *The Lily* <note>likely referring to the alchemical text *Lilium Intelligentiae*</note> says: It is necessary to gather the sulfur which blackens the body. And we say such sulfur is the water which blackens, whitens, and reddens itself, and fixes itself. Therefore, Mercurial water is the **first matter** <note>the primordial substance from which all things originate</note> of all metals, and with it all metals are dissolved, which cannot be dissolved in any other water. And if metals were not dissolved into their first matter by this Mercurial water, that which is sought would not be achieved, as **Aristotle** says. And this work is not the work of the craftsman, but of nature, with the craftsman serving and assisting her.

**Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar and patron saint of scientists</note> says: because among all arts, **Alchemy** most closely imitates nature, and this is because of its cooking <note>decoction</note> and growth; for it is cooked in metallic, fiery, red waters, having the most of form and the least of matter. For other arts imitate nature by way of resemblance; Alchemy, however, does so by pure truth. Therefore, it is not weaker than nature: because the art or the craftsman only serves it; but nature herself works naturally and is perfected. And so it is said: You need to labor first in the **dissolution of the luminaries** <note>the "luminaries" refer to Gold (the Sun) and Silver (the Moon)</note>, which is the first step of the operation, so that they may become **quicksilver** <note>Latin: *argentum vivum*; liquid mercury</note>. For the Philosophers say: Unless bodies are made incorporeal, and vice versa, we achieve nothing.

And you should not understand this to mean that the body becomes simple, pure elemental water: because no metallic body proceeds from such a thing, since a simple element is not altered, nor does it persist in the court of nature, but rather a well-composed thing: that is, a thick substance. For a single element by itself causes slow corruption and slow generation within itself. And because of this, simple elements are of little use in this art: because in them are not the primary essences of the elements, in which are the virtues that change, generate, and corrupt. Therefore, simple elements are against generation and corruption, and this is because they do not reach the **natural humidity** which causes all things to be born. Even if it were returned to water, it would then be dry, by force and not by nature, in the manner of salts or alums, and thus it would be melted by fire. And

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the elemental composition of matter and the alchemical process of reduction, following the previous discourse on the origins of substances.</meta>

# TRUMPETS
<note>original: "BVCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Philosophers," a common title for alchemical revelations.</note>

According to the truth of the matter, if a body ought to be reduced into its first element—following those who say it must be reduced into water—water was not actually the first element among the elements. Although they say this and cite Genesis 1, where it is said: *The Spirit of the Lord, before the creation of heaven and earth, was carried over the waters* <note>original: "Spiritus Domini... ferebatur super aquas"</note>, it does not follow that in the actual creation of the elements water was the first element, since the elements of air and fire existed before it, as was said above. 

However, in our work <note>The "Great Work" or alchemical practice.</note> among the visible elements which are seen and touched by us, water is indeed the first element. Thus, in the Art <term>The Art: Alchemy</term> there are only two formal elements that are seen and touched, namely water and earth, though virtually there are four: namely, air within the water and fire within the earth. For Rhazes <note>original: "Rafis" - Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian polymath and physician.</note> says: All things which were created below the lunar globe by the Supreme Architect participate in the four elements, not only by sight, but also by effect. For we call the "aqueous element" the humidity of the water itself; we call "air" the nature of the air itself; "Fire" we call that virtue which it possesses, by which it burns, calcines, and dissolves bodies. "Earth" is the thick and coarse body itself; and thus water and earth are seen and touched by us, while the other two are understood to be within these two.

Therefore it follows and is necessary that in the Art of Alchemy, metals are first reduced into Mercury: that is, into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, which is the matter and seed of all metals. Whence Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Islamic alchemy.</note> says: Mercury is cooked and thickened in the belly of the earth by a sulfurous heat cooking it. And according to the variety of the sulfur and its multiplication, diverse metals are procreated in the earth. For their primary matter is one and the same, yet they differ among themselves only by accidental action: that is, by greater or lesser cooking, tempered or untempered, burning or not burning. 

In this, all Philosophers agree. Since each of those—namely, quicksilver and sulfur—is first converted into an earthy substance, then from both of these earthy substances a certain very thin, subtle, and pure smoke is released. Because of the heat in the bowels of the earth, having been cooked and digested, it is converted into the nature of a certain earth, and thus it receives a certain fixation and is converted into metal.

<summary>This page discusses the elemental theory of metals, arguing that while four elements exist, only earth and water are tangible, and that all metals originate from a combination of mercury and sulfur cooked within the earth.</summary>

# THE TRUMPET BLAST

Note, the final limit of nature’s recommendation and the transmutation of the cooked and the raw—namely, that toward which the artist naturally strives—is the substance of **non-burning sulfur**. When this has been converted, it is the immediate material of our real elixir and pure metal; the first and closest nature, yet altered through the heat of its own body. This occurs with that alteration through which it can more appropriately and closely receive its own species and form, in accordance with the harmony of the mineral nature.

And this humidity was nothing other than **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> raised from the body, liquefied inside and out. With this quicksilver, the qualities of sulfur are mixed through digestion. And therefore it is altered just as nature requires through its own internal heat. By the conversion of nature, it is converted and congealed into sulfur. You can perceive through nature that no other humidity is converted more properly and promptly into the substance of sulfur than that into which the qualities of its own sulfur have been sufficiently introduced by natural ingenuity (which is done through the Art). This humidity is quicksilver in the form of clear water, like milk in the breasts; and sulfur is like the seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> in the testicles. That quicksilver has no contrariety <note>internal opposition or conflicting elements</note> that comes from its own temperament; therefore, it is necessary that this quicksilver be exceedingly tempered in respect to the temperament of its body.

Therefore, I notify you that the material of this is not common quicksilver in its entire substance, etc. Now, the reason why it is necessary to reduce metal to the nature of a vapor is because we see all things are generated by the mediation of **living Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio vivo," referring to the philosophical principle of fluidity rather than store-bought mercury</note>, by which it was itself generated. For example: A man, having been generated by a father through the mediation of seed, generates another son through the mediation of seed, and so it is with others. Therefore, the Mercurial nature is that by which we are fed and nourished; for without it, there is no life for animals or plants. Indeed, when it is removed from any thing whatsoever, corruption and death immediately follow, since it is the element of life and the existence of all things, as the **Philosopher** <note>likely referring to Aristotle, often cited as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts</note> says.

Likewise, **Raymond** <note>referring to Raymond Lull, a famous 13th-century polymath and alchemist</note> says: That the body which is the principal converter of the inconvertible must first be converted itself, so that it may first [turn] that convertible thing into sulfur...

<summary>This page describes the alchemical process of creating the "non-burning sulfur" and the "real elixir" by refining quicksilver into a biological-like seed. It emphasizes that Mercury is the vital principle of all life and the essential medium for metallic transmutation.</summary>

# TRUMPETS

...be converted into substance and congealed. For no quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury</note> is more readily converted into the substance of sulfur than that into which the qualities of sulfur have been sufficiently introduced through dissolution. Nor does any sulfur congeal quicksilver more promptly than that in whose substance the quicksilver itself exists, having been converted by the ingenuity of nature and art: that is, gold converted into its first matter <note>The "prima materia" or the original, undifferentiated state of a substance.</note>. For then nature embraces its own nature more amicably and rejoices in it more than in a foreign nature, as all the Philosophers cry out: nature alone delights in its own nature, nature alone conceives its own nature. And Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: nothing suits a thing except that which is closest to it in its own nature, and it generates offspring in that thing similar to itself. This means: If you seek a medicine that generates metals, its origin will be from metals, since a species is tinted by its own genus, as the Philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle.</note> says. Also, in those things having a shared symbol <note>original: "symbolum"; a shared characteristic or affinity.</note>, the transition is easy; and you should not understand this to mean that metals are reduced into simple elemental water, because nothing is made from a simple thing, but rather from a composite.

### *The beginning of the Work follows.*

There are four regimes or stages of this art: The first stage of the regime is by calcining <note>Heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder.</note>: that is, the body must first be calcined. The second is by dissolving, because it must be dissolved. The third is by distilling, because it must be distilled or sublimated. The fourth is by congealing with a light fire. And in these four regimes and stages consists the right and true preparation. Therefore, the body and the spirit of Mercury are necessary to perform the miracles of this thing, as Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, a famous 8th-century alchemist.</note> says. And for this art only two things are required, as Hermes says: Trust consists in two things, to which a third is joined. And he says, three faces: that is, I saw three species in one father: that is, in the lineage. Because Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist.</note> says that three species are sufficient for the whole mastery, namely: white smoke (that is, the fifth essence <note>original: "vis quinta"; the quintessence or purest part of a substance.</note>, namely the heavenly water), the green lion, and the copper of Hermes, from which and with which they prepare the work itself in the beginning, in the middle, and in the end.
Likewise, Eximidius in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note>: Through heat...

# THE CLANGOR

->The Resounding Horn<-

From the tempered matter, a certain oily, subtle moisture mixed with earth and perfectly purified is extracted from the metallic material; this is called the **Elixir**, by which metals are transmuted. Therefore, it is required that the extrinsic heat—that is, the artificial or material fire—be moderately warm, so that it does not exceed the intrinsic <note>internal</note> heat. This ensures that the intrinsic heat retains its own moisture which it naturally carries with it. For if the exterior heat exceeds it, then the oily moisture mixed with subtle earth evaporates due to the strength of the fire and does not remain in the body. It is necessary, therefore, that whatever is superfluous, coarse, and harmful be gradually purged, preserved, and refined through the power of slow decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling to extract essence</note>.

Likewise, every thing in the world—that is, every elemental body—possesses within itself a radical or formal heat, by cause of which it persists; this is its "fixed" part by which it endures, and in which its seed is multiplied. In **Mercury**, this is its "middle substance," and in **Gold**, it is its **Sulphur** <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle, while Mercury represents the passive, fluid, and feminine principle</note>, which direct the matter toward its end, form, and proper species. There is no thing so cold that it is not fostered under heat—namely, heat included within itself as if in a root, as the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle</note> says.

Likewise, the proper tincture of Mercury is a very subtle earth, in which the fire of both the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Menstruum <note>the solvent or "monthly" dissolving agent</note> is retained; it is the subtle middle substance of Mercury, and the burden and foundation of the Mastery <note>the Great Work or Magistery</note>. This is the matter from which our medicine is made, which takes its origin from **Quicksilver** <note>original: "argento viuo"</note>, and from that it must be created immediately. Do not introduce anything foreign into it in any way, except that which had its origin from it in the property of its own nature.

And in this step, the doctrine is truly shown to the "son" <note>the student of alchemy</note> that this matter from which we compose the medicine is not Quicksilver in its raw nature, since it has already been changed into Sulphur; nor is it in its total substance, since the extreme parts of earth and water have been separated from the middle substance. Rather, it is the **Blessed Stone**, and a spirit participating in two extremes. Nevertheless, although the stone—namely the Sulphur—has been made from its middle substance, it is simply called Quicksilver. Because the Sulphur illuminates and preserves it from burning <note>adustion</note>, which is its own property, like a sign of perfection. This is the world.

The paternal seed and the proper substance of Mercury is its mother, because its menstrual fluid <note>In alchemy, "menstruum" refers to a solvent or the "impure" fluid that must be purged to reach the essence.</note> must be erased and cast aside, and only the paternal seed must be preserved and received; this is its middle substance which perfects it and defends it from burning.

You cannot extract this seed of Mercury from Mercury, nor can its menstrual fluid—that is, the superfluous moisture—be cast aside from it, except by means of a coagulant <note>original: "coagulo"</note>, so that such a seed may coagulate in the Mercury and be retained, lest it also recede within the superfluous moisture; just as the rennet of milk coagulates the milk, and draws its better substance—that is, its middle substance—to itself and retains it. And thus the spirit—that is, the water—is not coagulated except by means of a body that has been dissolved within it, since bodies are the "rennet" of this milk—that is, of Mercury. And such a coagulant must be either the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the Moon <note>Silver</note>, dissolved within the Mercury itself. However, only the Moon is for the white work, and the Sun is for both the white and the red work, because the Sun is called the "Copper of Hermes" when the Philosophers speak only of their copper—that is, the Sun—since such things, or such a thing, are the coagulant which coagulates Mercury—that is, our water. # THE CLANGOR

The stone is composed of the spirit of metals, and that spirit, in the consideration of the **Alchemists**, is called **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note>. This is said to be the primary and most immediate nature considered in this art, and the first matter of metals. It must be brought back over the earth again, so that if any of the spirit remains with the earth, the said spirit may be sublimated <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material.</note> by the sublimation of fire of the third degree. It will then be converted into **foliated earth** <note>original: "terra foliata"; a flaky, purified state of the matter often compared to the leaves of a book.</note>, which is called the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the "quintessence" or purest celestial element beyond the four earthly ones.</note> of the earth of metals, and by some Philosophers, **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>, or Mercury, or the **sulfur of nature**.

And the earth then remaining below like a powder is called dregs and slag, a condemned powder which you do not need, because it is a despised powder that vanishes with a slight breath. However, the exuberant quicksilver is the earth of the body, passing through the **alembic** <note>term: alembic; a distilling apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube.</note> together with the **menstruum** <note>term: menstruum; a solvent, named after the monthly cycle because of the timing required for digestion.</note>. And the sulfur of nature is the spirit of metals sublimated and converted into foliated earth, which is the primary and most immediate matter of metals. This primary matter is also called foliated earth.

Furthermore, it is necessary that the exuberant spirit be converted into foliated earth through sublimation, so that the pure may be separated from the impure, the subtle from the thick or coarse terrestrial matter, and so that the vivifying spirit may be drawn out—just as the gaze of the **basilisk** <note>A mythical serpent whose glance was thought to be fatal; here used as a metaphor for a powerful, penetrating force.</note> is drawn in animals, or as sulfur is in the melting of metals. Likewise, it is necessary that you guard the spirit of the fifth essence if you wish to accomplish anything, because it depends on the "first thing," like a **form of forms** <note>A philosophical term for the highest organizing principle or soul of a substance.</note>, which placed itself within the four honorable natures and is called the **soul of the elements**.

And for this reason—because every substantial form descends immediately from a nearby fifth thing—we wish for it to be called the **mother of all other forms**. And you must not understand this form or spirit to be hot or cold, or moist or dry, nor male nor female; but you must well understand that by reason of its great perfection, it participates with each of the other four natures. For without it, there would be no **complexion** <note>term: complexion; the specific balance or "temperament" of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) in a body.</note> in any complexioned thing, as we clearly see and know with certain experience in the binding, joining, and mixing of the four elements. These elements fight through their contrary qualities; because of this repugnance, the said contrary elements cannot agree so that they might be united into one...

of fire and air, gold to the red, and silver to the white. These are the definitions as tincture <note>The "tincture" is the concentrated essence or agent used to transform base metals into gold or silver.</note> is considered in this art, according to which you may note that every alchemical tincture must necessarily exist from the aforementioned metals. Because like produces its like in nature, both naturally and artificially. For gold is thus the principle for all craftsmen. Therefore, he who wishes to signify anything <note>original: "ignificationis" - likely a scribal error for "aurificationis" (gold-making) or "ignificationis" (setting on fire/coloring).</note> should not seek a stone or a plant, but fire, which is the principle of ignition. **To Tincture** is to transform the thing tinted into its own nature by tinting, and to remain with it without any separation, in the nature of the fixer, the tinter, and the tinted.

**The Stone** is a body composed of the fifth essence <term>Quintessence: the purest, most spiritual element beyond the four physical elements</term> of metals. Which is otherwise called quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, brought from their potentiality into actuality through the mastery of all the principles of this art.

**Oil** is the natural sliminess of all metals [floating] upon the menstruum <note>A solvent or liquid medium used to dissolve solids.</note> after their dissolution. Moreover, it is necessary that bodies be converted into oil, because if they are not converted, they remain solid in themselves, and what we seek will not happen, and there would follow a deprivation of all the principles of this art.

**Menstruum** is that by reason of which the bodies of metals are dissolved by natural dissolution, and their spirits are led from potentiality to act; and according to this definition, it is demonstrated that the dissolution of metals ought not to be done except with the aforesaid principle, and if it were done otherwise, nothing would be achieved in effect.

The **Elixir** of the Philosophers, however, is composed of three: namely the lunar, solar, and Mercurial stone. In the lunar exists the white sulfur, in the solar the red sulfur, and the stone of Mercury embraces both natures, the white and the red, and this is the strength of the entire mastery.

Likewise, Rhazes <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and one of the most influential figures in the history of medicine and alchemy.</note> says: the white and the red proceed from one root, with no body of another kind intervening, they sprout forth: that is, from the Sun: for with the Sun itself being absent...

For quicksilver can in no way be united with metals without a medium, just as the soul cannot be united with the body without the spirit, which holds the middle place between the soul and the body; and thus the spirit holds the middle between body and soul. And because of this, the wise men say: Our copper <note>original: "æs"</note>, like a human being, has a spirit, a body, and a soul. For this reason they spoke of three, and these three are one, and in the one are three; spirit, body, and soul are one, and all are from one. And this is the preparation which they call conversion and division, because it is turned from thing to thing, just as the seed of a man is converted in the womb in a natural preparation from thing to thing, until a perfect man is formed from that which was his root and beginning. Nor is it changed from this, nor does it depart from its root and its division from thing to thing without the entry of another thing upon it: except for the menstrual blood from which the seed was made: that is, from a blood similar to it, and in this it creates its growth. And similarly, an egg, without the entry of any other thing upon it, is converted from state to state, and is divided from thing to thing, and finally becomes a flying chick like the other from which it had its root and beginning. And similarly, all things growing from the earth rot and are changed, and corruption enters upon them, then they sprout and are increased like the growths from which they had their root and beginning.

And because of this, minerals are not nourished so that they depart from their root, but each thing returns to that which it was, nor...

He who understands these things apprehends wisdom.

And note that that which is not good in the imperfect body may be perfected by that which is good in the perfect body: because the perfect body, remaining in its thickness, can by no means have the power of separating the sulfurous earth from the imperfect mixture, nor of converting that mixture into perfection according to its own perfect nature. It is necessary, therefore, that the perfect body be thinned <note>subtilized or refined</note> before it possesses such power. Now, it is thinned when it is reduced to **living silveriness** <note>original: "argenteitatem viuam," a term for the metallic essence or Quicksilver</note>. And since this living silveriness of the perfect body is **fixed** <note>stable and resistant to fire</note>, it fixes the non-fixed living silveriness of the imperfect body itself. But the non-fixed living silveriness which is in imperfect bodies, with its flight and velocity, draws out the fixed living silveriness from the perfect bodies, and causes it to penetrate, transform, glorify, and entirely perfect them. For it is certain that every thing is made of that into which it is resolved. But all metals are reduced into living silveriness, therefore they were once living silveriness. And thus is solved the opposition of those who say that the species of metals cannot be transmuted; which is true as they assert, unless they are reduced to their **first matter**. For then they are held...

Indeed, it performs the entire benefit of the art.

And note that <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note> or spirit is twofold: namely, the preparing and the dyeing.

The preparing spirit dissolves the body and cleanses it from corrupting causes, and extracts the second spirit existing and dyeing within the body; it leads the bodies to itself through dissolution, softens their hardness, illuminates the bodies, and raises them up by segregating and removing their dark impurity from the purest parts. It exalts the bodies by leading them back into a sublime nature; it inspires and refines them, and makes the solid spiritual. And these are the benefits and effects of the spirit—or the preparing quicksilver—extracting from the body the dyeing spirit. This spirit, however—that is, the quicksilver—is at first coarse, unclean, and fleeting because of the <term>sulfur</term><note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle, while mercury represents the passive, fluid, and feminine.</note> which it encountered and was mixed with in the depths of the earth: but by means of the art, which is done through distillation and sublimation, it is renewed, cleansed, purified, and decocted...

And this preparing spirit <term>spiritus præparans; the active volatile agent used to break down substances</term> is twofold. The first is a dry, non-viscous vapor of great acidity, exceedingly subtle, fleeing the face of the fire with ease, possessing a great power of penetration, and dissolving mineral bodies. And this spirit, by a name used equivocally <note>meaning the term is used loosely or has multiple meanings</note>, is called Mercury; but Mercury is a spirit, therefore in the final term of reason it is called a "dry spirit." It is necessary that such a spirit be shut away in a well-sealed flask, and this is according to the intention of Albert <note>referring to Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note>. For that spirit is generated from "pontic" things <note>harsh, bitter, or acidic substances</note>, and he himself calls it a "fiery dry-moist."

The other preparing spirit is moist in its vapor, not oily, but viscous, of the greatest acidity, moderately subtle, easily fleeing the harshness of the fire and vanishing in it, possessing the power of dissolving bodies and spirits, being water existing within itself.

Albert also wishes this, as do many others, though under different terms. And such a spirit is also called Mercury by an equivocal name, and this is by way of comparison and metaphorical speech. For Mercury, as the Philosophers say, has the greatest power of altering and penetrating bodies, not resting on a flat surface, and not awaiting the test of the fire; so it is with these two spirits, and by reason of this, both are called Mercuries. From these things, receive understanding of the sayings of the Philosophers, and your comprehension will be easy here and elsewhere, and you will see that the Philosophers do not err among themselves as many have thought. And thus it must be noted that an oily substance is one thing, and a viscous substance is another: for from a viscous moisture a stone is generated, but from an oily moisture, metals are generated.

But the tinting spirit <term>spiritus tingens; the agent that changes the color and quality of a metal</term> is the Philosophical Mercury with its red or white sulfur, naturally mixed with it in the mineral itself and in the bowels of the earth, moderately prepared, and left to the judgment of the craftsman until its perfect consummation. Another "quicksilver" <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note> is the permanent tincture, which is extracted from perfected bodies through dissolution, distillation, sublimation, and refinement. And such quicksilver is called oil...

To dissolve is to convert the body into the nature of the spirit, but to coagulate is, conversely, to make the spirit corporeal; so that the fixed becomes volatile, and the volatile becomes fixed. # THE CLANGOR

<note>The title "Clangor" likely refers to the "Clangor Buccinae" or "The Sound of the Trumpet," a well-known alchemical treatise.</note>

...the active [force] may be suffocated in some way. For the seeds of all things springing from the earth are not multiplied, nor do their generative powers grow, if they are removed by some external heat, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle is frequently referred to simply as "the Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> says. And cleanse it through distillation, first with a gentle fire: then with a slightly stronger fire distill the Mercury. This Mercury carries with it the soul of the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the Moon <note>Silver</note>, according to whether Sun or Moon is present there. And do not distill with such a strong fire that the earth—that is, the element of earth—also passes over in the distillation; rather, it is sufficient that only the superfluous Mercury, which cannot be dried out with the body, [passes over]. And what remains below in the gourd <term>cucurbita: the lower part of a distilling apparatus</term> is our salt, which is to say, our earth, and it is black in color: the dragon devouring its own tail. For the dragon is the matter remaining at the bottom after the distillation of the water from it, and that water is called the dragon's tail; the dragon is its blackness, and the dragon is soaked in its own water and coagulated, and thus it devours its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, a symbol of the cyclical nature of the alchemical work.</note>. And do not despise the ash which is at the bottom of the vessel, for it is the diadem of your heart and the ash of permanent things, as Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> says. And distill with such heat that the body is not reduced into a solid mass, or too greatly dried and burned. And distill with such a fire that when a drop begins to fall, you shall count sixty-eight—as Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova</note> says—or seventy (some say eighty) moments before the fall of the next drop; and if the drop falls faster, withdraw the fire, as the Rosary <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text</note> says.

And if it falls more slowly, increase the fire slightly, and do not follow your own imagination regarding the strengthening of the fire at the end of the distillation, but proceed with a gentle fire. Whence the following verse:

->*Nature rejoices in a favorable [path] balanced by the senses.*<-

And so await the distillation with the patience of the wise.

The sign of completed distillation is that half of the Mercury (or more than you put in) distills from the earth through the still-head <term>alembicum: the cap of the distilling apparatus</term>, and that the earth remains soft and liquid, as Arnold says. Place this earth, thus soft and liquid, into a glass with a good long neck and a firm Seal of Hermes <note>An airtight or "hermetic" seal</note>, and place it in hot ashes.

First for eight days slowly in hot ashes, but afterwards let the ashes be hotter for [the following] days: and let it stand in such a heat...

<meta>This page continues the technical alchemical instructions regarding the preparation of the "Stone" and the manipulation of the four elements, following the tradition of Raymond Lull and Hermes Trismegistus.</meta>

# THE TRUMPETS

<note>original: "BVCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Philosophers," a common title for alchemical proclamations.</note>

...heat for 25 natural days, or up to thirty, until the earth is dried out and remains arid at the bottom of the vessel. Afterward, shake the vessel strongly and suddenly by hand, because the material—that is, the earth—will adhere to the sides of the vessel.

The more the material has been putrefied <note>Putrefaction is the alchemical stage of breaking down a substance through warmth and moisture, often associated with the color black.</note>, the more strongly it will adhere, as the *Rosary* <note>The "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> says. And if the fire were increased several times at sunset, so that the material was too heavily trampled down into the lower parts of the vessel, then it would be necessary to perform the aforementioned grinding in the glass with a glass pestle. And thus you have the earth which was there before. For there are only two formal elements in our stone, namely water and earth, although virtually all four elements are within it. And where it is said "our stone is made of four elements," this is not to be understood literally—that it is common earth, nor water, nor air, nor fire—but rather it is only one nature, which contains within itself the nature and properties of all the elements.

Likewise, the whole mastery <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process</term> consists of this: to divide the elements from the metals, to purify them, and to divide the sulfur of nature from the metals. For the entire labor and the whole exhaustion of the mastery lies in this division of the elements and the sulfur. Thus says Raymond <note>Referring to Raymond Lull, a major figure in medieval alchemy.</note>. But where it is said, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> says: "You must extract the four elements," this truly means nothing else than to awaken the seminal virtues themselves—that is, the active or passive qualities—because many natural exponents have fallen into infinite errors. And we say that our virtue is a spiritual mineral one, which can be intensified and strengthened so that the power of budding and germinating may be implanted. And when wishing to receive the mineral elements to create the stone, do not take from the first nor from the last, but from the middle; for the first are very simple, and the last are very coarse. When you wish to eat, take the bread and leave the flour; and when you wish to make bread, take the flour and leave the wheat. This is our word and Philosophical doctrine. Thus says Raymond.

Likewise, the separation of the elements is to segregate the heterogeneous things, which are accidental. And the conjunction of the elements is to accumulate the homogeneous things: that is, those which are of the nature of the radical moisture <term>humidum radicale: the essential, life-sustaining fluid believed to exist in all matter</term>, as the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts.</note> says. This arrangement of **whitening** <term>dealbatio: the process of purifying and turning the alchemical matter white</term> is continued after the imbibing of its water, and its drying and congealing, until it becomes a white mass of perfect whiteness, enduring in the fire, melting and flowing, and congealing **Mercury**, and perfectly retaining and transforming any imperfect metallic body into a true, unified whole.

And if you wish to volatilize or imbibe your prepared **Elixir** a second, third, or fourth time, this must be done with a fourth part of the Mercury of the elixir. However, if you place a greater weight of that water upon the body itself than a fourth part of it—provided it does not submerge it—it will be better; it will whiten the body, and it will be more subtle, more penetrating, and will convert with a greater weight.

Likewise, when any thing is soaked in corruption, it cannot tolerate the fire, nor can the fire suffer corruption within itself: wherefore it is necessary that the **Stone** be masterfully extracted, cleansed, and separated from all corruptible dregs, before you presume to fix it, until it becomes the pure element of the first matter.

And note that the **medicine** which converts Mercury is more subtle than that which converts bodies. You should know that there is greater labor in whitening on account of the weights and mixtures than in **reddening** <term>rubificatio: the final stage of the Great Work, turning the white stone into the red stone or gold</term>, because after the whitening until the reddening, no error follows. And for making the red, it is said that it must be done in the same way and with a similar regimen in all things as you did in its whitening; and it ought not to go back so that it begins from the start, but only so that it is multiplied: and apply as much Mercury through the solution of the earth and drying as in the whitening, except that the heat is greater. And know that however much more the earth is dissolved with its non-fixed spirit—that is, its water—and coagulated, so much more is it multiplied; and not only in quantity, but also in power and subtlety of the tincture, so that in **projection** <term>proiectio: the final act of casting the elixir onto base metal to transform it</term> it will convert and transmute a great weight.

Regarding the whitening of the earth, **Hali** <note>Hali: likely referring to Khalid ibn Yazid or Al-Razi, famous authorities in medieval alchemy</note> says: Take what has fallen to the bottom of the vessel, and wash it in a hot fire so that its blackness is taken away, and its thickness recedes...

Indeed, whitening is the beginning and foundation of the whole work; for from that point on, you cannot err in the decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling</note>, because after the whitening, both of the fleeing things—namely the soul (which is the Mercury of the body) and the spirit (which is the living Mercury)—turn into non-fleeing earth. They make it spiritual, cleansed of earthiness, airy, and subtle. And thus the spirit and soul are not united with the body in a true way except in the white color; because then, in that very whitening, all colors that can be imagined in the world today appear, and then they are fixed and meet in one color, namely whiteness.

And note, that this diversity of colors does not appear in our stone except in the conjunction of the soul with the body, as Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note> says. In only one turn, the fire renews diverse colors in it. The soul is the tinting spirit, which, finally overcome by the altered body, rejoices in it, the body having been made incorruptible; and thus one passes into the other, and one receives the power of the other by the disposition of nature.

Senior <note>referring to the 10th-century alchemist Ibn Umail</note> says: The first lunar work is to wash, to whiten, and to putrefy for one hundred and fifty days. After this, however, through vinegar <note>often a metaphor for a sharp solvent or "philosophical" acid</note>, by the will of God, the whole perfection occurs, which is to dissolve and to coagulate. And concerning that whitened earth, Morienus says: You can do nothing with it if it has not been fermented. And because without ferment no perfect tincture <note>the power to transform metals</note> is made, as the Philosophers say—just as good bread is not made without unfermented dough—so it is in our stone. For the ferment is like the soul, which grants life to the dead, imperfect body through the mediation of the spirit: that is, Mercury. Because Aristotle says: Nothing is completed except with a thinned ferment, like a spirit. Verse: *For good dough you should use water, and also ferment*; in a similar way in our stone. You will find these three things similar to the sayings of the Philosophers. Likewise, the ferment is made from the pure matter of metals: that is, the sulfur of nature and the vapor of the elements. Likewise, the ferment is nothing other than from the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "Sole & Luna"; alchemical code for Gold and Silver</note>. And the ferment does not exist until the said bodies are converted into their first matter or nature, because it is necessary that the ferment should be composed from the Sun and the most subtle earth. Therefore, if you do not know how to reduce the two perfect bodies into their first nature, you will not be able to have any of the ferments. Thus says Raymond <note>likely referring to Raymond Lull, a famous 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note>.

Note, the white ferment is made thus: Feed one part of the purest Moon <note>Silver</note>, filed into small pieces or beaten into thin leaves, with double its weight of Mercury, which must be very clean and white. Grind them together strongly in a stone mortar until the Mercury drinks up the filings and becomes like butter, so that nothing of the filings can be found. Then wash this ferment strongly with strong vinegar and common salt, well prepared, until the vinegar comes out clear and very pure; then wash away the salt with fresh water, and dry the water by the fire. From here, add to it one part of sulfur, grinding it all together until it returns as if into one body. Then soften it with one part of water, and send it to be sublimated, etc.

In the same way, the red ferment is made with the purest Sun <note>Gold</note> as above, although Pandolphus says in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba" referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> that no staining poison <note>term: poison (venenum) — here used to mean a potent, transformative substance or elixir</note> is generated without the Sun and its shadow, which many others also maintain: Because no other ferment is made for both the white and the red tincture than the Sun. Aristotle says: The white and the red sprout from one root, with no thing of another kind intervening.

Likewise, the *Rosary* <note>referring to the text *Rosarium Philosophorum*</note> and Peter of Zalento say: The ferment, which is the medium that joins them, if it is placed at the beginning or in the middle, the work is completed more quickly and does not need repetition; however, they do not say this by way of denial. Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist</note> says: When you wish to ferment the aforesaid medicine, then dissolve it in the said distilled liquid, as was said above, until it becomes watery.

# ->TRUMPETS<-
<note>original: "BVCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Alchemists," a common title for revelatory texts.</note>

Mercury <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers," not necessarily common quicksilver.</note>, then place it in a vessel over the fire throughout the entire process, until the colors appear as they did in the first stage, until you have the Elixir, which as before is fusible and capable of tinting. And then the effect of that same elixir is doubled in its fermentation, quantity, and projection, etc. Since in every solution and fixation it acquires for itself a tenfold increase in multiplication, therefore the more the medicine is dissolved, fixed, tinted, and melted, the better and more powerfully it operates.

Likewise, note concerning the **ferment**. Nothing is made from that which is already perfect, because it is already complete, just as this material or artifice completes it. We have an example: Bread that is leavened and baked is perfect in its state or being, and has reached its ultimate end; you cannot ferment it any further. So it is with gold: Pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient alchemical authorities.</note> hold it is impossible to ferment it further unless one possesses the **First Matter** <term>Prima Materia: the formless primal substance from which all metals grow</term> of metals, in which it may be resolved back into the first matter and into its miscible elements. Let us therefore take that matter from which gold is to be made, and by means of the artifice, let it be led into the true **Ferment of the Philosophers**; let us change this with ingenuity into the perfect matter, or into the species of perfect bodies, and only then let us begin the operation. This is why many modern workers, even those working philosophically, are deceived: because they abandon the work at the very point where it ought to begin.

Note, the **Water** is the spirit that purges, refines, and whitens the body. And the **Ferment** is the **Soul**, which grants life to the imperfect body by means of the water—life which it did not have before—and leads it back into a better form. Even if only one of these were present in our Stone, the medicine would never flow easily, nor would it give a tint; and if it did give one, it would fly away in smoke like Mercury, because there would be no receptacle for the tint within it.

And in the hour of the greatest **Conjunction** <term>The union of opposites, often symbolized as a marriage of Sun and Moon</term>, miracles appear: for then the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment. This ferment is the soul of the imperfect body, and the spirit, by means of the soul, is joined with the body; it is bound together with it into the color of the ferment, joined and made one with them. And thus, from the imperfect body, there is first extracted that which is seen—

# THE CLANGOR

For if you do not mix the ferment with the <term>Elixir</term><note>The "Elixir" here refers to the medicinal or transformative substance in its developing stage.</note>, the body is not colored as it ought to be, because without the ferment neither <term>Sol</term><note>Gold</note> nor <term>Luna</term><note>Silver</note> will emerge, but rather something else which does not remain in the <term>tincture</term><note>The permanent color or quality imparted to a metal</note> of a metallic nature, unless you have prepared it—namely the imperfect body. But when the sulfur—that is, the imperfect body—has been joined with its own body—that is, the ferment—the body does not cease to act upon the other until it converts the whole into itself, namely the ferment. Therefore, when you wish to ferment, mix it together with the body so that the whole may be ferment, because the ferment brings back or reduces our sulfur to its own nature, weight, and color in every way; and there will be a white ferment for the white, and a red for the red. This is evident: because if you place the ferment of silver with the sulfur of gold, it will reduce it to its nature, but not to its color. Conversely, if you place the ferment of gold with the sulfur of silver, it converts it to its nature, but not to its color, and vice versa. Therefore, do not mix the white water with the red, nor conversely the red water with the white, because with white water you shall whiten, and with red you shall redden. See to it, however, my son, that you do not think this water is red [in appearance], but rather white in appearance, carrying the power of reddening in its effect. Thus says <term>Raymond</term><note>Referring to Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and purported alchemist.</note>.

When the body has been cleansed, and incorporated and sublimated with the spirit, then both are made into one oily thing. And unless the body becomes a vapor, you have accomplished nothing in this work, since this is done by means of the purified water of <term>Mercury</term>. Therefore, whiten and wash the body, because the <term>whitening</term><note>Latin: dealbatio; a key stage in the Great Work (Albedo)</note> is the beginning and the ferment of the whole perfected work. For if the sulfur has not been sublimated, it will not have an entering substance or a penetrating power, and consequently, it will not be effective for the true Elixir. And common Mercury is called the spirit, the Mercury of the body is called the soul; the spirit is not joined to the body except by means of the soul, and conversely, the soul is not joined to the body except...

The second sign is if it is placed upon the fire, it by no means melts nor burns.

From these things it is clear that the gold of nature is not the material of the ferment; rather, the gold of the Philosophers is the tinting ferment itself.

Likewise, Hermes, the head of the Philosophers, says: When you wish to mix the natures, O Alchemists, mix the stone of gold with the humor <note>moisture or liquid</note>, which is the permanent water <note>original: "aqua permanens" - a specialized alchemical solvent that does not wet the hands</note>, and place it upon a light heat until it liquefies; and then leave it until the water dries up and they join together. # THE TRUMPETS
<note>original: "BVCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Sages," a common title for alchemical revelations.</note>

The beginning of the secret, namely: from which to soak and dry perfectly. Indeed, do this many times until the watery parts perish; that is, they fail, so that the water no longer ascends, and its colors appear to you. However, I command you not to pour the water all at once, lest the elixir <note>original: "ykesir," a Latinization of the Arabic 'al-iksir'</note> be submerged, but rather little by little. That is, pour it in seven times, grind it, and dry it; and do this many times until the water is consumed.

Barfen <note>A sage cited in the 'Turba Philosophorum,' an early Latin alchemical assembly text</note> says in the *Assembly*: And the water is placed upon it seven times, until it drinks all the moisture, and receives the power that withstands the fire during the battle of the fire, and it becomes red. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says: Moisten and grind for many days: and he commanded this to be dissolved and coagulated nine times, which are designated by the **nine eagles**. For in every dissolution and coagulation, its effect will be increased. Whence the Philosopher says in the *Assembly*:

> But all you investigators of this art, seeing that
> whiteness appearing in the vessel, be certain that
> the redness is hidden within the whiteness.

At that time, you must not take it out, but rather cook it until the whole becomes red; and thus, through many soakings of **solar water** <note>likely a reference to gold-water or a highly purified acidic solvent</note>, it is required that the earth be made red, even through a greater administration of fire. Likewise Barfen says: I command them to whiten the copper with white water, by which they make the copper red—namely, our copper <term>Aes Nostrum: "Our Copper" refers to the philosophical substance, not common metal</term>. Therefore, it must first become white before it becomes red: because there is no passage from one extreme to another, or from one contrary to another, except through a mediating means. That is, there is no passage from blackness into yellow or red, except with whiteness mediating: because yellowness is caused essentially by a very high or intense white and a small amount of clear red. 

Wherefore nature shows that **yellowing** <note>original: "citrinatio"</note> is a perfect and complete digestion. Nor, conversely, can there be a passage from yellow to white until the compound is turned into black. Neither can gold be made into indivisible silver unless it is first destroyed, and becomes black, and is corrupted; nor can the better be made into the worse except through the corruption of itself: because the generation of one is the corruption of the other. And this is done with the addition of the dyeing thing <note>the tincture</note> which is known to nature, and it is perfected. And then the ferment is applied.

The spirit dries out the body, and in turn, is dried by the body—that is to say, it is perfectly purged of its phlegm <note>original: "flegmate"; refers to the watery, inactive residue or moisture within a substance</note>.

Note that in every roasting <term>assatione: a dry-heat cooking or calcination process</term> and decoction <term>decoctione: boiling a substance to extract its essence</term> where spirits and bodies are separated and joined together, you must know that the soul, though separable from its subject, is not easily separated from the fixed part except during the process of fixation; nor is the living easily joined to the dead, except in a moist state. But in all these things, nature does not allow for sudden changes. Therefore, the greatest care must be taken lest the spirit becomes volatile: for if it flies away from the body, the body will remain imperfect.

**Note:** For this reason, sublimation is performed so that, once the purest and lightest parts are separated from the dregs of the coarse elements, they may possess the power of the **fifth essence** <note>The "Quinta Essentia" or Quintessence; the purest, most medicinal, and celestial form of matter</note>, which forms and disposes the matter toward a durable and perfect species. I call this fifth essence the "tinting soul," which colors and brings forth a pure form; to extract this, sublimation and thinning <note>original: "subtiliatio"</note> were highly necessary. For through this process, the oiliness of arsenic is extracted—that is, the purest oily nature and incombustible greasiness—which is bound and mixed with the dross, slag, and coarser elementary parts.

Sublimation is performed for no other reason than to extract the tinting soul from the body and to turn it into a penetrating spirit. For through sublimation, the body is reduced into a spirit—specifically, when the bodily density passes into a state of thinness. Since bodies are heavy and ponderous, as was also said above: if they are to be sublimated, it is necessary that they be incorporated with **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"; likely referring to "Philosophical Mercury" rather than common quicksilver</note>, thinned, and cooked until one single body is made from them (that is, from the Mercury and the body). Do not grow weary of repeating this many times, because unless the Mercury has been incorporated into the body, it does not ascend. However, it can in no way be incorporated unless it is first dissolved in the Mercury.

Therefore, take the "first water" <note>A reference to the primary solvent or "mercurial water" used in the Great Work</note> separated from all corruption, in which you shall cook the thing (called by its own name) for 40 days in its vessel, and you will find the body converted into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>. And when, through sublimation, it has been deprived of its blackness, it will become a sublime nature lacking shadow—that is, free from the coarse dregs of the earth and from burning <term>adustione: the state of being scorched or "burnt" which alchemists believed hindered perfection</term>. Therefore, thin the body as much as you are able, and cook it with clean Mercury, and—

And when the body has absorbed and enclosed some part of the Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"; here referring to the "spirit" or "quicksilver" of the metals</note> within itself, heat it quickly with a subtle fire, and then with the strongest fire you can, until it ascends in the likeness of a very white powder, in the manner of snow, adhering to the joints of the *aludel* <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pottery vessel used as a condenser in the sublimation process</term>. For that is the subtle middle substance of Mercury, from which our medicine is fashioned, which takes its origin from the matter of quicksilver—the sought-after good, the white foliated earth, arsenic, and white sulfur, the primary matter of metals: thus says Raymond <note>likely referring to Ramon Llull, a famous medieval scholar and alchemist</note>.

### *How the white and red sulfur are perfected into the finished Elixir.*

Take, therefore, the aforesaid white sulfur, and place it upon its own white, fixed, and cleansed body—that is, upon silver. And take the red sulfur upon its own red body—namely, upon gold—as Pythagoras, the master of the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba Philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate among Greek philosophers.</note>, teaches, saying: That the quicksilver extracted from bodies by dissolution, thinning, and sublimation, if not coagulated into white or red sulfur that can withstand the fire—that is, so that it be fixed—has no power for whiteness or redness. Therefore, you must work prudently and discreetly, since without ferment <note>A substance, usually gold or silver, added to the alchemical mixture to "ripen" it and direct it toward the desired metal.</note> neither the Sun <note>Gold</note> nor the Moon <note>Silver</note> can exist. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the chemical composition of metals, specifically focusing on the interaction between Mercury and Sulfur as the primary constituents of all metallic bodies.</meta>

# OF METALS. 353

Their substance is watery, mixed with an earthy substance by a strong combination, so that one cannot be separated from the other. For this reason, that watery substance is congealed with cold more effectively after the action of heat, and they will therefore be ductile or malleable. Water alone is not congealed except by an earthy dryness which alters the wateriness, since the moisture in them is not oily. Because their solidification is caused by earthy dryness, they are not easily dissolved except by the action of intense heat upon them, according to how strongly or powerfully they are mixed.

### *How metals are specifically generated from Mercury. CHAPTER III.*

The nature of all liquefiable things <note>substances that can be melted</note> is from quicksilver <note>original: "argento viuo," referring to Mercury</note> and its own substance, because by that same quicksilver it is coagulated from vapor, without the heat of white or red sulfur that does not burn. Whence Aristotle says in the fourth book of *Meteorology*: "If there be white sulfur that does not burn, it congeals Mercury into good silver. If, however, the sulfur be pure with a bright redness, and in it there be the power of simple fire that does not burn, it congeals into the purest gold, better than what the mine produced." This is because every dry thing naturally drinks its own moisture, so that it becomes continuous in its parts. Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur that coagulates the quicksilver is from an earthy, subtle, airy substance, boiled and digested from the first mixing, united to itself by the action of heat, afterwards elevated, boiled, and digested until it has the sulfurous power of coagulating quicksilver into metallic bodies. But when the sulfur is simple or burning, it causes perfection or imperfection in metals, as the example of these will later make clear: that their primary matter is quicksilver, since when they are melted by heat, they are converted into it. It is certain they were previously quicksilver, because every thing is made of that into which it is resolved. Take the example of ice <note>just as ice melts back into the water it came from, metals melt back into a mercury-like state</note>.

Quicksilver in its primary root is composed of a white, subtle, exceedingly sulfurous earth, with water...

And add as much Mercury through the dissolving of the earth and the drying as you did in the whitening, except that the heat should be greater. And know that however much more the soul is dissolved with its non-fixed spirit—that is, its water—and is coagulated, so much more is it multiplied; and not only in quantity, but also in power and the subtlety of the tincture, and in projection <note>the act of casting the elixir onto base metal to transform it</note> it will convert and transmute a great weight.

# TRUMPETS

And cause the additions of moisture to fly away from it, until it becomes an exceedingly white <term>lime</term><note>calx: a powder produced by heating a substance; the "body" of the metal reduced to its purest state</note> in which there shall be no stain. And note, that this diversity of colors does not appear in our <term>stone</term> except in the conjunction of the soul with the body, as <term>Morienus</term><note>A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit of Jerusalem</note> says. In only one turn, the fire renews diverse colors within it. The soul is the tinting spirit, which, having finally been overcome by the altered body, rejoices in it, the body having been made incorruptible: and thus one passes into the other, and one receives the power of the other as nature disposes.

<term>Senior</term><note>Referring to Senior Zadith, an influential 10th-century Arabic alchemist</note> says: The first lunar work is to wash, to whiten, and to rot <note>putrefacere: the process of breaking down the substance</note> for one hundred and fifty days. And the whitening of the whole is the driving away of darkness from it. And <term>Flidius</term> says: Know that the beginning of the whole work is whitening, which redness succeeds: then comes the perfection of the work. After this, however, through vinegar <note>acetum: often a metaphor for a sharp, dissolving solvent</note>, by the will of God, the whole perfection is achieved, which is to dissolve and to coagulate. And concerning that whitened earth, <term>Morienus</term> says: You can do nothing with it if it has not been fermented. And because without <term>ferment</term> no perfect tinting <note>tinctura: the power of the stone to transform metals</note> is made, as the Philosophers say—just as good bread is not made without unfermented dough—so it is in our <term>stone</term>, since the <term>ferment</term> is like the soul, which grants life to the dead, imperfect body by means of the spirit: that is, <term>Mercury</term>. Because <term>Aristotle</term> says: Nothing is completed except with a refined <term>ferment</term>, like a spirit. Verse:

-> For good dough you should use water, and also ferment: <-

...the gold or silver of the Philosophers, not the gold or silver of nature <note>The author distinguishes between common metals and the "living" metals used in alchemy</note>: Wherefore the ferment of gold is nothing but its own sulfur, which converts the white into silver, because that never fixes <note>term: Fixation (turning a volatile substance into a solid that resists fire)</note> what is not naturally fixed, nor ever was.

Likewise, ferment is made from the pure matter of metals: that is, the sulfur of nature and the vapor of the elements. Likewise, ferment is nothing other than from the Sun and Moon <note>original: "Sole & Luna"; referring to gold and silver</note>. And it is not a ferment until the said bodies are converted into their first matter or nature, because it is necessary that the ferment be composed of the Sun and the finest earth. Therefore, if you do not know how to reduce the two perfect bodies into their first nature, you will not be able to have any of the ferments. Thus says Raymond <note>Likely referring to Raymond Lully, a famous 13th-century polymath and alchemist</note>.

**Note, the white ferment is made thus.** Feed one part of the purest Moon <note>silver</note>, filed into tiny pieces or beaten into thin leaves, with double its weight of Mercury, which must be very clean and white. Rub them together strongly in a stone mortar until the Mercury drinks up the filings and becomes like butter, so that nothing of the filings can be found. Then wash this ferment vigorously with strong vinegar and common salt (well prepared) until the vinegar comes out clear and quite pure; then wash away the salt with fresh water, and dry the water by the fire. From here, add to it one part of white sulfur, rubbing the whole together until it returns as if into one body. Then soften it with one part of water <note>original: "incera," meaning to bring to a waxy consistency</note>, and send it to be sublimated, etc.

In the same way, the red ferment is made with the purest Sun <note>gold</note>, as above, although Pandolphus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> that no staining poison <note>term: Poison (here used to mean a potent, transformative elixir or tincture)</note> is generated without the Sun and its shadow, which many others also maintain: Because there is no other ferment for both the white and the red tincture than the Sun. Aristotle says: The white and the red sprout from one root, with no thing of another kind intervening.

Arnold <note>Arnold of Villanova, a 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> says: When you wish to ferment the aforesaid medicine, then dissolve it in the said distilled liquid, as was said above, until it is as watery as...

# TRUMPETS
<note>original: "BUCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Philosophers," a common title for alchemical treatises signaling the revelation of secrets.</note>

Mercury <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers," not necessarily common quicksilver</note>, then place it in a vessel over the fire throughout the entire process, until the colors appear as they did in the first stage of the work, until you have the Elixir, which must be fusible <note>capable of being melted</note> and tinging <note>capable of dyeing or transforming other metals</note> as before. Then the effect of that same elixir is doubled in its fermentation, quantity, and projection <note>the act of casting the elixir onto base metal to transform it</note>, and so on. Since in every solution and fixation <note>the process of turning a liquid into a solid that resists fire</note> it acquires a tenfold increase in multiplication, the more the medicine is dissolved, fixed, colored, and melted, the better and more powerfully it operates.

Also, note this concerning the ferment. Nothing is made from that which is already perfect, because it is already complete, just as this material or craft reaches its own perfection. We have an example: Bread that has been leavened and baked is perfect in its state or being; it has reached its ultimate end, and you cannot ferment it any further. So it is with gold: Pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and the Philosophers <note>the ancient alchemists</note> hold it impossible to ferment it further unless one possesses the "First Matter" of metals, into which the gold may be resolved back into its primary material and miscible elements. Let us therefore take that matter from which gold is made, and by means of the craft, let it be led into the true ferment of the Philosophers; let us change this with ingenuity into a perfect material, or into the species of perfect bodies, and only then let us begin the operation. This is why many modern workers, even those working according to Philosophy, are deceived: because they leave off the work exactly where it ought to be started.

Note, the water is the spirit that cleanses, thins, and whitens the body. And the ferment is the soul, which grants life to the imperfect body by the mediation of the water—a life which it did not have before—and leads it into a better form. Even if only one of these were present in our Stone, the medicine would never flow easily, nor would it give its tincture; and if it did give it, it would fly away in smoke like Mercury, because there would be no receptacle for the tincture within it.

And in the hour of the greatest conjunction <note>the union of the chemical ingredients</note>, miracles appear: for then the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment. This ferment is the soul of the imperfect body, and the spirit, by means of the soul, is joined with the body; it is bound together with it into the color of the ferment, joined, and made one with them. And so, in the imperfect body, there is first extracted that which is seen—

Wherefore the quintessence <term>quinta essentia: the "fifth essence" or purest element beyond the four earthly ones</term> is a body differing in itself from all elements and things composed of elements, as much in matter as in form, as much in nature as in power, having no contrariety within itself, and therefore no cause of corruption. Thomas <note>likely referring to Thomas Aquinas, to whom several alchemical treatises were falsely attributed</note> says this in his compendium: where he places the difference between an element, a thing composed of elements, and the quintessence.

And know that in this solution of the stone, one part [reaches] many more...

# THE SOUND

<note>original: CLANGOR</note>

...parts of Mercury, or of any body whatsoever, into true Moon <note>Silver</note> or into Sun <note>Gold</note>, according to how the stone has been prepared, it tints. Likewise, the common earth is to be separated from the Philosophical earth in this way: The calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> earth is to be taken, etc., and placed in a glass or glazed vessel, in which there is clean and pure water, very hot. And you must stir it with a glass rod until that which can be dissolved is dissolved. And know that the good earth is dissolved and becomes white water like milk; set this dissolved portion aside, and again grind the earth which remained undissolved, and join to it again very hot water, continuing until you see clearly that nothing more can be dissolved. The sign of this is that the earth which remained at the bottom, when placed upon wood, leaves nothing behind. The second sign is if it is placed over a fire, it by no means melts nor burns. And after you see these things, then take all your earth dissolved in the aforesaid water, and place it in a glass vessel, and you shall congeal it by strong drying; and when it has been congealed, then know that you have the Philosophical earth, clean and prepared. Cast the other away, for it is dregs and dross; it is also called "white earth." And always take care that you do not roast it unless it is dry. Whence Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says:

> Sow your gold in white foliated earth, which through calcination has been made fiery, subtle, and airy—namely, this much: sow the gold (that is, the soul and the tinting virtue) into the white earth, which by due preparation has been made white and clean, in which there are no impurities.

From these things it is clear that the gold of nature is not the material of the ferment; rather, the gold of the Philosophers is the tinting ferment itself.

Likewise Hermes, the head of the Philosophers, says:

Moreover, let the water itself, having been soaked—that is, dried—be a more intense fire than it had been before, until it dries up and becomes earth—that is, a powder.

# ->TRUMPETS<-
<note>original: "BVCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Philosophers," a common title for alchemical revelations.</note>

...the beginning of the secret, namely, from which to soak and dry perfectly. Indeed, do this many times until the "parts of water" appear: that is, until they fail, meaning that the water no longer rises, and its colors appear to you. However, I command you not to pour the water on all at once, lest the *ykesir* <note>an Arabic-derived term for the elixir or "the stone"</note> be submerged, but rather little by little: that is, pour it on seven times, grind it, and dry it, and do this many times until the water is consumed.

Barfen says in the *Assembly*: <note>referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> "And the water is applied to it seven times, until it drinks all the moisture, and receives the power that withstands the fire during the battle of the fire, and it becomes rust." <note>In alchemy, "rust" often refers to the red state or the oxidized metallic spirit.</note> Hermes says: "Moisten and grind for many days." And he commanded this to be dissolved and coagulated nine times, which are designated by the "nine eagles." <note>The "eagle" is a common alchemical symbol for sublimation or the rising of vapors.</note> For in every dissolution and coagulation, its effect will be increased. Whence the Philosopher says in the *Assembly*:

->Seeing, however, all investigators of this art that whiteness appearing in the vessel, be certain that the redness is hidden within the whiteness.<-

At that time, you must not take it out, but rather cook it until the whole becomes red; and thus, through many soakings of "solar water," <note>likely a reference to gold-enriched acid or a specific philosophical solvent</note> it is required that the red earth be made, even through a greater application of fire. Likewise, Barfen says: "I command them to whiten the copper with white water, by which they make the copper red, namely, *our copper*." <note>Alchemists distinguished "our copper" (the philosophical substance) from common metal.</note> Therefore, it must first become white before it becomes red: because there is no passage from one extreme to the other, or from one contrary to another, except through a mediating middle: that is, there is no passage from blackness into yellow or red, except with whiteness mediating. For yellowness is caused essentially by a very high or intense white and a small amount of clear red. Therefore, nature shows that "citrination" <note>the yellowing stage</note> is a perfect and complete digestion. Nor, conversely, can there be a transition from yellow to white until the compound is turned into black. Nor can gold be made into indivisible silver unless it is first destroyed, and becomes black, and is corrupted; nor can the better be made from the worse except through its own corruption: because the generation of one is the corruption of the other. And this is done with the addition of the "dyeing thing" <note>the tincture</note> which is known to nature, and it is perfected. And then the ferment is applied.

-># THE CLANGOR<-

The spirit dries out the body, and in turn, is dried out by the body, specifically when it is perfectly purged of its phlegm <note>original: "flegmate"; refers to the watery, inactive residue or moisture within a substance</note>.

Note that in every roasting <note>original: "assatione"; a dry-heat process</note> and decoction <note>original: "decoctione"; boiling to extract essence</note> where spirits and bodies are separated and joined together, you must know that the soul, though separable from its subject, is not easily separated from the fixed part except through drying; nor is the living easily joined to the dead, except in a moist state. But in all these things, nature does not allow for sudden changes. Therefore, the greatest care must be taken lest the spirit becomes volatile: for if it flies away from the body, the body will remain imperfect.

Note: Sublimation <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the substance</note> is performed so that, once the purest and lightest parts are separated from the dregs of the coarse elements, they may possess the power of the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quintæ essentiæ"; the "quinta essentia" or quintessence was believed to be the purest, most potent celestial element beyond the four earthly ones</note>, which forms and prepares the substance for a durable and perfect appearance. I call this fifth essence the "tinting soul," which provides color and brings forth a pure form; to extract this, sublimation and refinement were highly necessary. For through this process, the oiliness of arsenic is extracted—that is, the purest oily nature and incombustible greasiness which is bound and mixed with the dregs, slag, and coarser elemental parts. Sublimation is done for no other reason than to extract the tinting soul from the body and to turn it into a penetrating spirit: for through sublimation, the body is reduced into a spirit—namely, when the bodily density passes into a state of thinness. And since bodies are heavy and ponderous, as was also said above: if they are to be sublimated, they must be incorporated with **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio"; in alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity and transformation</note>, refined, and cooked until one single body is made from them—that is, from the Mercury and the body. Do not let it weary you to repeat this many times: for unless the Mercury has been incorporated into the body, it does not ascend. However, it can in no way be incorporated unless it is first dissolved in the Mercury. Therefore, take the "first water" <note>A symbolic term for the initial solvent or purified mercurial liquid</note> separated from all corruption, in which you shall cook the thing (called by its own name) for 40 days in its vessel, and you will find the body converted into quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>. And when, through sublimation, it has been deprived of its blackness, it will become a sublime nature lacking shadow: that is, free from the coarse dregs of the earth and from scorching. Therefore, refine the body itself as much as you are able, and cook it with clean Mercury,
