However, if something of the valuable material still remains at the bottom, you shall repeat the sublimation by means of the Mercury incorporated into it, until everything that belongs to the pure essence of those bodies has ascended. For if you do not do this, do not place it into the Great Work <note>Latin: *magisterium*, the mastery or completion of the alchemical process</note>. The alembic <note>A teardrop-shaped glass vessel used for distilling</note> should indeed be made of glass, coated around with good lute <note>A clay-based sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>, which must be joined with the lower vessel so that the Mercury cannot finally exhale. For Mercury is not sublimated except through an airy smokiness, carrying with it the purer parts of the body; and therefore the earth is then converted into air, and the body into spirit, and density into rarity; finally they ascend in the manner of air. Thus, by reason of truth, they receive the power of acting strongly and of penetrating into the depths; and by reason of perfect clarification, they receive perfect tincture and coloration. Therefore, see diligently that the vessels are well joined; for if the Mercury finds an open place, it flies away as smoke, and thus the operation will perish and be annihilated, and your Great Work will be in vain.

## *The rule of fixation follows.*

### *How the white and red sulfur are perfected into the finished Elixir.*

Take, therefore, the aforementioned white sulfur, and fix it upon its own white, fixed, and cleansed body: that is, upon silver. And take the red sulfur upon its own red body, namely upon gold, as Pythagoras, the master of the *Assembly of Philosophers* <note>Latin: *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts</note>, teaches, saying: That the quicksilver extracted from the bodies by dissolution, thinning, and sublimation, if not coagulated into white or red sulfur that can withstand the fire—that is, so that it is fixed—has no way to reach whiteness or redness. You must therefore work prudently and discreetly, since without ferment <note>A substance, like yeast in bread, that "leavens" or transforms the base metal into gold or silver</note> neither the Sun <note>Gold</note> nor the Moon <note>Silver</note> can exist. And there is no other ferment...

Their substance is watery, mixed with an earthy substance through a powerful union, so that one cannot be separated from the other. For this reason, that watery substance is congealed with cold even more after the action of heat, and they are therefore ductile or malleable <note>Latin: *fabrilia*, meaning capable of being worked by a smith</note>. Water alone does not congeal except when combined with terrestrial dryness, which alters the wateriness, since the moisture in these things is not oily. Because their solidification is caused by terrestrial dryness, they are not easily dissolved except by the action of intense heat upon them, according to how strongly or powerfully they are mixed.

### *How metals are generated from Mercury*
### *specifically. CHAPTER III.*

The nature of all liquefiable things <note>Metals that can be melted</note> is from quicksilver <note>Latin: *argentum vivum*, or Mercury</note> and its own substance, because that same quicksilver is coagulated from vapor without the heat of white or red sulfur that does not burn. Whence Aristotle says in the fourth book of the *Meteorology*:
> If there be white sulfur that does not burn, it congeals
> Mercury into good silver. But if the sulfur
> be pure with a bright redness, and in it there be the power of
> fieriness that simply does not burn, it congeals into the purest gold,
> better than that which the mine produced: because every dry
> thing naturally drinks its own moisture, so that it
> becomes continuous in its parts.

Therefore, the vapor of the sulfur that coagulates the quicksilver is from an earthy, subtle, and airy substance, boiled and digested from the first mixing, united to itself by the action of heat, and afterwards elevated, boiled, and digested until it has the sulfurous power of coagulating quicksilver into metallic bodies. But when the sulfur is simple or scorching, it causes perfection or imperfection in metals, as the example of these things will later make clear—that their primary matter is quicksilver: since when they are melted by heat, they are converted into it. It is certain they were previously quicksilver, because every thing is made of that into which it is resolved. Take the example of ice <note>Just as ice melts back into the water from which it formed, metals melt back into a mercury-like liquid state</note>.

# THE CLANGOR

The gold or silver of the Philosophers <note>original: "aurum vel argentum Philosophorum"; this refers to the refined spiritual or chemical essence rather than common metal</note> is not the gold or silver of nature. Therefore, the ferment of gold is nothing other than its own sulfur, which converts the white into silver; for that never fixes <note>term: Fixation; the process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note> which is not naturally fixed, nor ever was.

Likewise, the ferment is made from the pure matter of metals: that is, the sulfur of nature and the vapor of the elements. Furthermore, the ferment is nothing other than that derived from the Sun and the Moon <note>original: "Sole & Luna"; alchemical code for Gold and Silver</note>. And the ferment does not exist until the said bodies are converted into their first matter or nature, because it is necessary that the ferment be composed of the Sun and the most subtle earth. Therefore, if you do not know how to reduce the two perfect bodies into their first nature, you will not be able to have any of the ferments. Thus says Raymond <note>likely referring to Ramon Llull, a famous 13th-century polymath and alchemist</note>.

Note, the **white ferment** is made thus: Feed one part of the purest Moon <note>Silver</note>, filed into small pieces or beaten into thin leaves, with double its weight of Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> that is very purely white. Grind them together strongly in a stone mortar until the Mercury drinks up the filings and becomes like butter, so that nothing of the filings can be found. Then wash this ferment vigorously with strong vinegar and common salt (well prepared) until the vinegar comes out clear and very pure; then wash away the salt with fresh water and dry it over a fire. From here, add to it one part of white sulfur, grinding it all together until it returns as if into one body. Then soften it with one part of water and send it to be sublimated, etc.

In the same way, the **red ferment** is made with the purest Sun <note>Gold</note>, as described above, although Pandolphus says in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: "Turba [Philosophorum]"; one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> that no staining poison <note>term: Venenum; here used in the archaic sense of a potent transformative elixir or "tincture"</note> is generated without the Sun and its shadow, which many others also maintain. For no other ferment is made for both the white and the red tincture than the Sun. Aristotle says: The white and the red sprout from one root, with no thing of another kind intervening.

Likewise, the *Rosary* <note>referring to the "Rosarium Philosophorum"</note> and Peter of Zalento say: If the ferment, which is the joining medium, is placed at the beginning or in the middle, the work is completed more quickly and does not require repetition. However, they do not say this by way of denial <note>meaning they do not exclude other methods</note>. Arnold <note>likely Arnold of Villanova</note> says: When you wish to ferment the aforesaid medicine, then dissolve it in the said distilled liquid, as was said above, until it becomes watery like...

And then the effect of that same elixir is doubled in its fermentation, quantity, and projection <note>The act of casting the medicine onto base metal to transform it</note>, etc. Since in every solution and fixation it acquires for itself a tenfold increase in multiplication, therefore the more the medicine is dissolved, fixed, colored, and melted, the better and more powerfully it operates.

Also, note concerning the ferment. Nothing is made from that which is already perfect, because it is already complete, just as this material or craft achieves perfection. We have an example: Bread that has been leavened and baked is perfect in its state or being, and has reached its ultimate end; you cannot ferment it any further. So it is with gold: Pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient alchemists</note> hold it impossible to ferment it further, unless one possesses the "First Matter" of metals, in which it may be dissolved back into its primary material and into its mixable elements. Let us therefore take that matter from which gold is made, and by means of the craft, let it be led into the true ferment of the Philosophers; let us change this with ingenuity into a perfect matter, or into the likeness of perfect bodies, and only then let us begin the operation. This is why many modern workers, even those working according to philosophy, are deceived: because they abandon the work at the very point where it ought to begin.

Note, the water is the spirit that cleanses, thins, and whitens the body. And the ferment is the soul, which grants life to the imperfect body by means of the water—life which it did not have before—and leads it back into a better form. Even if our Stone contained only one of these two, the medicine would never flow easily, nor would it give a stain <note>tinctura: the power to change the color/nature of a metal</note>; and if it did give one, it would fly away in smoke like Mercury, because there would be no receptacle for the stain within it.

And in the hour of the greatest conjunction <note>The symbolic union of opposites, often depicted as a chemical marriage</note>, miracles appear: for then the imperfect body is colored with a firm coloration by means of the ferment. This ferment is the soul of the imperfect body; and the spirit, by means of the soul, is joined with the body and bound together with it into the color of the ferment, joined and made one with them. And so, in the imperfect body, first there is extracted that which is seen—

# TRUMPETS
<note>original: "BUCCINÆ" - likely referring to the "Trumpets of the Sages," a common title for alchemical revelations.</note>

The beginning of the secret <note>original: "arcani initium"</note>, namely, from which you should soak and dry it perfectly. Indeed, do this many times until the watery parts perish: that is, they fail, so that the water no longer rises, and its colors appear to you. However, I command you not to pour the water on all at once, lest the *ykefir* <note>An Arabic-derived alchemical term, likely referring to the "lead" or the base matter of the work</note> be submerged, but rather little by little: that is, pour it in seven times, grind it, and dry it; and do this many times until the water is consumed.

> But when all investigators of this art see that whiteness <note>The *albedo* stage</note> appearing in the vessel, be certain that the redness <note>The *rubedo* stage</note> is hidden within the whiteness.

At that time, you must not take it out, but rather cook it until the whole becomes red; and thus, through many soakings of **solar water** <note>likely a reference to gold-infused acid or a specific philosophical solvent</note>, it is required that the earth be made red, even through a greater administration of fire. Likewise, Barfen says: "I command them to whiten the copper with white water, by which they make the copper red, namely, **our copper**." <note>Alchemists distinguished "their" copper (the philosophical substance) from common metal.</note> Wherefore it must first become white before it becomes red: because there is no passage from one extreme to another, or from one contrary to another, except through a mediating means: that is, there is no passage from blackness to yellow or red, except with whiteness mediating. For yellowness <note>original: "citrinitas"</note> is essentially caused by a very high or intense white and a small amount of clear red. Therefore, nature shows that yellowing is a perfect and complete digestion. Nor, conversely, can there be a transition from yellow to white until the compound is turned into black. Nor can gold be made into indivisible silver unless it is first destroyed, and becomes black, and is corrupted; nor can the better be made worse except through its own corruption: for the generation of one thing is the corruption of another. And this is done with the addition of the thing that tints it, which is known to nature, and it is perfected. And then the **ferment** is applied.

<meta>This page continues the alchemical discourse on the relationship between spirit and body, specifically focusing on the process of sublimation and the role of Mercury in refining the "soul" of the matter.</meta>

-># THE CLANGOR<-

The spirit dries out the body, and in turn, is dried by the body; that is to say, it is perfectly purged of its phlegm <note>original: "flegmate"; in alchemy, this refers to the watery, inactive residue or moisture</note>.

Note that in every roasting and decoction <note>the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</note> by which spirits and bodies are separated and joined together, you must know that the soul, though separable from its subject, is not easily separated from the fixed part except through drying; nor is the living easily joined to the dead except in a moist state. But in all these things, nature does not suffer sudden changes. Therefore, the greatest care must be taken lest the spirit becomes volatile; for if it flies away from the body, the body will remain imperfect.

Note: Sublimation <note>the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify</note> is performed for this reason: so that once the purest and lightest parts are segregated from the dregs of the coarse elements, they may possess the power of the **quintessence** <note>the "fifth essence" or purest celestial soul of a substance</note>, forming and disposing it toward a durable and perfect species. I call the quintessence the "tinging soul," which colors and induces a pure form; to extract this, sublimation and refinement were highly necessary. For through this process, the "oiliness of arsenic" is extracted—that is, the purest and incombustible nature of oily richness which is bound and mixed with the dregs, dross, and coarser elementary parts.

Sublimation is done for no other reason than to extract the tinging soul from the body and to turn it into a penetrable spirit. Indeed, through sublimation, the body is reduced into spirit—specifically, when the bodily density passes into rarity. And since bodies are heavy and ponderous (as was also said above), if they are to be sublimated, it is necessary that they be incorporated with **Mercury** <term>Mercury: often referring to "Philosophical Mercury," the fluid principle of transformation rather than just common quicksilver</term> and refined, and cooked until one single body is made from them—that is, from the Mercury and the body. Do not let it weary you to repeat this many times; for unless the Mercury has been incorporated into the body, it does not ascend. Moreover, it can in no way be incorporated unless it is first dissolved in the Mercury.

Therefore, take the "first water" <note>likely the primary solvent or "mercurial water" of the alchemists</note> segregated from all corruption, in which you must cook the thing "named by its own name" for forty days in its vessel, and you will find the body converted into **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum viuum"</note>. And when, through sublimation, it has been deprived of its blackness, it will become a sublime nature lacking shadow—that is, lacking the coarse foulness of earth and scorching. Therefore, as much as you are able, refine the body itself, and cook it with clean Mercury.

And when the body <note>the metallic body</note> has absorbed and enclosed some part of the Mercury within itself, heat it quickly with a subtle fire, and then with the strongest fire you can, until it ascends in the likeness of a very white powder, in the manner of snow, adhering to the joints of the *aludel* <term>aludel: a pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process</term>. Then, having cast away the dregs, repeat the sublimation of the very white powder by itself without its dregs, until it is fixed, and until it leaves no further dregs, but ascends most pure in the manner of snow. This is our pure *fifth essence* <term>quinta essentia: the most purified and potent form of a substance</term>, and then you possess the soul that tints, coagulates, and cleanses, and the arsenic sulfur that does not burn: which Alchemists can use, and with it they make silver.

In the solar matter <note>gold-based material</note>, however, although a certain part may ascend most white, there remains at the bottom a fire tinted with redness, in the manner of scarlet. And that sulfur converts quicksilver into the purest and truest gold. This is the most perfect composition of white and red sulfur that does not burn, according to the highest operation of the Philosophers: for you will find nothing superfluous or diminished in these words, but only what the Philosophical truth contains.

Likewise, if you sublimate Mercury with the *calxes* <term>calx: the powdery metallic oxide remaining after heating</term> of the two luminaries—namely, the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>—then you will sublimate usefully and cleanse with ease. For in those materials, their sublimation is of easy operation through generation: and always collect only that which has been sublimated, because this is not yet fixed, but that which consists in the middle of the *aludel* above the dregs; for that is the subtle middle substance of Mercury, from which our medicine is made. It takes its origin from the matter of quicksilver—the sought-after good, the white foliated earth, arsenic, and white sulfur, the primary matter of metals: thus says Raymond <note>likely referring to Raymond Lully, a famous medieval alchemist</note>. Moreover, we perform this sublimation so that we may reduce the bodies into a subtle nature, so that they may be like spirits, penetrating and reducing every body into true *solific* <note>gold-making</note> or *lunific* <note>silver-making</note> form, or so that we may reduce them into the primary matter—namely, Mercury and sulfur—and so that their most firm incorporation may be achieved, and

# OF MINERALS

Their substance is aqueous, mixed with an earthy substance through a powerful combination, so that one cannot be separated from the other. For this reason, that aqueous substance is congealed with cold more effectively after the action of heat; they are therefore ductile or malleable. Water alone is not congealed except by terrestrial dryness, which alters the wateriness, since the moisture in these metals is not oily. Because their solidification is caused by terrestrial dryness, they are not easily dissolved except by the action of intense heat upon them, according to how strongly or powerfully they are mixed.

### How metals are specifically generated from Mercury. CHAPTER III.

The nature and substance of all liquefiable things <note>Things that can be melted, such as metals.</note> come from quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, because due to that same quicksilver, it is coagulated from vapor without the heat of white or red sulfur that does not burn. Whence Aristotle says in the fourth book of *Meteorology*: If there be white sulfur that does not burn, it congeals Mercury into good silver. If, however, the sulfur is pure with a bright redness, and in it there is a power of fire that is simply non-burning, it congeals into the purest gold, better than what the mine itself produced. This is because every dry thing naturally drinks its own moisture, so that it may be made continuous in its parts. Therefore, the vapor of sulfur that coagulates quicksilver is from an earthy, subtle, and airy substance, boiled and digested from the first mixture, united to itself by the action of heat, and afterwards elevated, boiled, and digested until it has the sulfurous power of coagulating quicksilver into metallic bodies. But when the sulfur is simple or burning, it causes perfection or imperfection in metals, as will be shown later by the example of these things: that their primary matter is quicksilver, since when they are melted by heat, they are converted into it. It is certain they were previously quicksilver, because every thing is made of that into which it is resolved. An example of this is ice <note>Just as ice melts back into the water it came from, metals melt back into a mercury-like state.</note>.

### *On the formation of wonders which do not take their origin from Mercury. CHAPTER V.*

There are, moreover, lesser or middle minerals, according to what has been said, which do not take their origin from Mercury. And of these, some are salts which are easily liquefied by moisture, such as alum, simple salt, sal ammoniac <note>original: "sal armoniacū"; ammonium chloride, often used in alchemy for cleaning metals</note>, rock salt, and all kinds of salts. And some are "virtuous" <note>meaning they possess strong active qualities or "virtues"</note>, nor are they easily liquefied by moisture alone, such as orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, arsenic, and sulfur, since the wateriness of sulfurous bodies is mixed with viscous earth by a strong mixing with the boiling of heat, until they are made virtuous, and were first coagulated by cold. Vitriols <note>original: "Atramenta"; literally "inks" or "blackening substances," referring here to metallic sulfates</note>, however, are composed of salt and sulfur and stones, and it is believed that within them is the mineral power of certain liquefiable bodies which are made from them, such as chalcanthum <note>original: "calcantū"; blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note> and *olocar ager* <note>likely a corruption of "olochryson" or a specific mineral earth; the author describes it as a red, earthy substance</note>: which are generated from the larger grains of vitriol, and are not dissolved unless the saltiness within the sulfur itself is dissolved with them, and they are first congealed in the cold. And that substance already receives a mineral power from certain bodies existing naturally in the earth. That which receives the power of iron will be red and earthy, like *olocar*. That which receives the power of copper <note>original: "aeream"; referring to 'aes', meaning bronze or copper</note>, this will be the green chalcanthum. Whence it is possible for these two, namely *olocar* and chalcanthum, to be generated from it, since nevertheless all these aforesaid things participate in the mineral power with metals. But metallic bodies cannot be made from them artificially, since they are of another nature, and they did not take their origin from the same primary material as metals—namely, with Mercury—but rather from quicksilver <note>The author distinguishes between the philosophical "Mercury" and common "quicksilver" here</note>. I do not deny that metals can be purified or dissolved with them, or a sophisticated <note>deceptive or artificial</note> form introduced through them to deceive men, by which the blackness of lead can be wiped away; nevertheless, lead always remains lead. Since it has been said that the sulfur which causes metals is an element of metals along with Mercury, I now set forth the difference in the generation of Mercury and of sulfur, although they both contribute to the creation of metal—namely, by the essential Mercury and the accidental sulfur. It does not rest upon a flat surface, nor does it adhere to what it touches because of the dryness of the earth, which has altered its watery nature <note>original: "aqueitatem"</note> by means of a strong mixture. Therefore, it is an element combined with simple sulfur <term>sulfur: in alchemy, the active, masculine principle of combustion and soul</term> of all ductile things, or is very nearly similar to certain ductile things. Thus, it is characteristic of the one to be the adherence of the other, since one cannot be generated into a metal without the other. And insofar as the sulfur is more simple, to that extent it more greatly rejoices and coheres with simple and pure Mercury, and is more strongly joined with the other; thus, more perfect metals are then generated from them.

### *Question.*

Since the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle, often called "The Philosopher" in medieval texts</note> speaks generally, saying that sulfur coagulates, it must be said that this is not the case. For according to the Philosopher, all common sulfur is foreign and contrary to metals. Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose alchemical writings were highly influential in the West</note> says: "That which did not originate from it does not enter into the mastery <note>original: "magisterium," the alchemical process or the production of the Philosopher's Stone</note>." Because it always infects, blackens, and corrupts, in whatever way it may be prepared by art. For it is itself an infected fire; therefore, it hinders melting. If indeed it is calcined <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to powder</term>, it returns into an earthy substance, like dead dust. In what way, then, can it breathe life into others? For it has a double superfluity: namely, an inflammable substance and an earthy dross. Therefore, by these things consider that this is the sulfur of the common people and not of the Philosophers, since the sulfur of the Philosophers is a simple living fire, quickening other dead bodies and maturing them, so that it supplies the defect of nature, since it is of overflowing maturity, according to which it is perfect in its own nature and more and more purified by art. Whence Avicenna says: "Such sulfur is not found upon the earth, except insofar as it issues forth in those bodies, the Sun and the Moon <note>The Sun (Gold) and the Moon (Silver)</note>, and in another thing, which is that which is told to no one, unless it be revealed to him by God." In the Sun, however, it is more perfect, because it is more digested and cooked.

## How it is possible for lesser minerals to *artificially* become metals. *CHAPTER VII.*

But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that it is impossible for lesser minerals <note>The author refers to "minora metalla" or "minora mineralia," likely meaning non-metallic ores or salts like vitriol, alum, or sulfur, which were often contrasted with the seven "noble" metals.</note> to be artificially made into metals, it remains here to be proven. First, in this way: because lesser minerals are not generated from the first matter of metals, which is Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius." In alchemy, "Mercury" often refers to the philosophical principle of liquidity and metallic essence rather than just the common liquid metal.</note>: because their generation and the generation of Mercury differ primarily in form, in nature, and in composition; therefore, they cannot become metals. For things of one species have one first matter and seed <note>original: "sperma"</note> from which they are generated.

The first part of the preceding statement is clear: that lesser minerals are not generated from Mercury. The reason is that Mercury always remains in the first matter of metals, and not in foreign sulfurs. Whence Aristotle and Avicenna <note>Two of the most cited authorities in medieval science; Avicenna was a Persian polymath whose works on chemistry were foundational to European alchemy.</note> say:
> Therefore, if they were to become metals, it would be necessary that they first pass into the first matter of metals.

But because this cannot be done artificially, it is therefore impossible for metals to be made from them. Thus the first part of the premise is sufficiently declared.

Secondly, to the same point: Because the lesser minerals cannot artificially become the principle of metals, which is Mercury, they also do not reach the middle and the end, which are the metal and the tincture <note>A "tincture" in this context is a substance capable of transforming or coloring a base metal into a noble one, like gold.</note> which it holds. Just as nourishment in a human cannot become a human through generation unless it is first converted into seed, and thus, added to its like, a new human is generated. But because lesser minerals are of a foreign nature to metals—even though they may participate well in some mineral power—they are of weaker virtue and are combustible <note>original: "adustibilia." This refers to the tendency of non-metallic minerals to burn away or sublimate when heated, unlike stable metals.</note>. Therefore, the metallic nature does not delight in them, but rejects them, and preserves those things which are of its own nature. For example: if water is mixed with earth, they are separated from one another, because the earth seeks the bottom since it is heavy and dry, while the water seeks the surface; and they can by no means be so joined artificially that these contrary natures stand together in one nature. Indeed, water can wash and cleanse the earth, but that the dryness of the earth should be artificially changed into an aqueous moisture should not be believed, even though the earth is moistened by the water. Thus, lesser minerals can

Nature does not allow [these substances] to be joined with metals, to purify them, or in any way to introduce a new form, but rather to remain with them and ripen that which is immature <note>The author refers to the alchemical belief that "base" metals like lead were simply "unripe" or immature versions of gold</note>. These men are truly harmed by an apparent loss. They wish to perfect the best thing with the worst things, and to fulfill the defect of nature with such materials, truly imagining no virtue in them nor searching them out; they wish to sow dung and reap wheat, which seems impossible to anyone. Whence it is said: *Whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap.* Therefore, if he sows dung, he reaps filth also.

There are also other Alchemists <note>original: "Alchimistæ"</note> laboring in the "lesser minerals," namely in the four spirits: such as common sulfur, arsenic, orpiment <note>a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, and sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>, wishing to create a tincture <term>Tincture: a potent substance or "elixir" capable of transforming base metals into gold or silver</term> from these. If they are to be converted, then it is not a tincture, as is clear by the definition. If they are to convert the metal, then by dyeing they convert it into their own nature, which is earthy—a nature foreign to the metallic nature. Therefore, they cannot create metal by dyeing.

That a substance converts things into its own nature while dyeing is proven by this: because every generating thing generates its own likeness. But since here the "tincture" of the four spirits is the generating force, and it is earth, it will therefore generate its own likeness, which is earthy just like itself. Thus, you should despise this tincture and every other that is not found in the property of nature, along with other foreign ways; for in them there is nothing but the consumption of resources, and the loss of time and labor. ### *Again concerning the simple, non-burning Philosophical Sulfur. CHAPTER VIII.*

The Philosophers have subtly imagined how they might extract those sulfurs from within these more perfect bodies <note>referring to gold and silver</note>, and how to purify their qualities through art, so that they might possess through art—mediated by nature—that which did not appear in them before, even though they possessed it fully and secretly from the start. And they concede that this can by no means be done without the dissolution of the body and its reduction into the first matter, which is <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argentum viuum"; the liquid metal mercury, considered the "mother" of all metals</note>, from which they were made from the beginning. This must be done without any mixing of foreign things, which, being of an alien nature, do not improve our stone; for nothing suits a thing except that which is most closely related to it, since it is a medicine of a simple and powerful nature, produced from mercurial water in which gold and silver were previously dissolved. For example: If ice is placed in simple water, it is dissolved in it by heat and returns to its first watery substance, and thus the water is tinted by the hidden power that was in the ice. But if the ice is not resolved into water by heat, it does not join with the water in which it lies, nor does it tint that water with its power which was previously congealed within it, in terms of its species. In the same way, if you do not resolve the body into Mercury, you cannot obtain the hidden power from it with the Mercury—namely, the sulfur digested and ripened by the work of nature in the mine. For thus the stone is one, a single medicine, which according to the Philosophers is called <term>Rebis</term> <note>original: "Rebis" from "res bina," meaning "a double thing"</note> from a dual thing: namely, from body and spirit, white or red, in which many fools have erred.

### CHAPTER X.

It may be asked, and not without merit, whether this white and red sulfur <note>In alchemy, "white sulfur" refers to the agent for making silver, and "red sulfur" for making gold.</note> for dyeing Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium"; here meaning the transformation or "tinging" of quicksilver into a precious metal.</note> can be drawn out from other sick bodies <note>The author refers to "imperfect" or base metals like lead or iron as "sick" or "infirm" bodies.</note>. I say that it cannot, because it was said previously that there is no other thing of greater temperance <note>Balance of qualities.</note> than what is found in these two bodies [gold and silver], in which the dyeing rays reside. For it was said before that sick bodies contain within themselves a foul and combustible sulfur, and not one of a virtual nature <note>A nature possessing the "virtue" or power to act.</note> as in these. Since all art is of no value unless nature is first possessed, which art may then follow. You could, however, purge metals with lesser minerals; yet even when purged, they still do not possess a golden or silvery nature in themselves, because the golden digestion and decoction <note>The alchemical process of "cooking" or maturing a substance over time.</note> was not in them as it was in the others, nor was their sulfur so mature. And therefore, these immature things must be aided by mature things so that they may be ripened. Therefore, they do not dye, but are dyed, because the tincture <note>The transformative essence.</note> of gold and silver has a nature proportional to those immature or imperfect things, because they all drew their origin from Mercury. From this it is clearly evident that lesser minerals cannot dye, because imperfect metallic bodies—which do not agree with gold and silver on the part of mature Mercury—cannot dye, nor can they infuse the nature of gold or silver. And therefore, one must not dye except with those things in which the power of dyeing resides. Dye, therefore, with gold and silver, because gold bestows a golden color and nature. For this reason, you should despise all other things which do not virtually or naturally possess the power of dyeing, since in them there is no fruit, but only the loss of things and the gnashing of teeth <note>A biblical allusion to the frustration and ruin of failed alchemists.</note>.

The Philosophers have known the truth. Why do you weary yourselves in such high matters which you cannot reach by laboring in such a way, unless it happens miraculously, as occurred to the Blessed John <note>Likely referring to a hagiographical legend of St. John the Evangelist turning sticks into gold</note>, who made gold from brushwood. I advise you to study, to turn over the sayings of the wise, from which you may elicit the truth; do not approach the work by chance. Pay no attention to "Take, take <note>original: "Recipe, recipe"</note> this and that, I know not what, and do it in such a way, I know not how: Instruct me in this, and I will teach you that." Thus the deceived man deceives another, and so the whole world is defrauded by such people. For if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the ditch. For wherever you see "Take" <note>Recipe</note>, consider that it signifies "Deceive" <note>Decipe</note>, by changing the 'r' to a 'd'.

You must make Mercury by means of Mercury, which dissolves and opens separated natures, so that one thing can simply pass into another, and the perfect can send its power into the imperfect, so that it may be perfected along with it. Wherefore, through the test and the harshness of fire, the imperfect is burned away while the perfect remains: because one nature cannot come to the aid of the other.

## ON THE GENERATIONS of Metals in the Bowels of the Earth.
### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' featuring stylized foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>
Of all those who philosophize rightly, the opinion and sentiment is the same: that all Metals are generated by the vapor of sulfur and by quicksilver. For when the fatness of the earth <note>A traditional term for the combustible or "sulfurous" element of the soil</note> has been heated and encounters the substance of water in a somewhat gathered mass, it consolidates those most beautiful bodies—gold, silver, copper, tin, iron, and lead—within the veins of the earth. # ON ART

It is evident that Nature herself has openly failed in her own operation. For Art sometimes corrects and supplements Nature with the help of Nature herself, and in a certain way—especially in this magnificent discourse <note>original: "diatribe"</note> on mineral things—Art seems to surpass her. This was dedicated to memory long ago by those ancient Philosophers. There are two kinds of Philosophers. Some, investigating Nature only by herself, have handed down in literary monuments the virtue and power which sublunary things possess—derived both from elementary qualities and from the heavens and stars—such as Physicians; and certain others who described the natures of animals, trees, herbs, metals, and precious stones. The other group, far more illustrious indeed, most sagaciously and keenly penetrating not only Nature, but finally the very secret of Nature and her innermost sanctuaries <note>original: "adyta," referring to the most sacred part of a temple</note>, have claimed for themselves the name of Philosopher in a truer sense of the word. But because Nature produces all metals from two things, sulfur and Mercury, and has left to us the superior bodies generated from them along with the inferior, it is certain that diligent men can fashion the same from their three operations, and lead the inferior bodies to the nature and perfection of the superior bodies.

# ON THE ART

...the illuminating power, beyond all falsehood, is able to generate its like. From this, the Philosophers <note>The term "Philosophers" here refers to alchemists and natural scientists of the medieval and Renaissance periods.</note> conceived the idea of introducing the light and splendor of the most perfect body into the inferior bodies, since they had discovered that metallic bodies differ among themselves only by a greater or lesser degree of decoction <note>A process of heating or "cooking" substances to achieve maturity or purity.</note>. They found that Mercury was the primary origin of all metals; by extracting the metallic gold with Mercury, they reduced the gold to its primary nature. Since this reduction is both easy and possible, the Philosophers concluded that the transmutation of metals is likewise easy and possible. And when those original Philosophers had reduced gold to its primary nature, they utilized celestial influence <note>Astrological timing or "heavenly influx" believed to be necessary for successful alchemical work.</note> so that the metal would not return to its previous state. Then, they purified its nature, separating the unclean from the clean. Once this was done, they called that thing the "transmuting Stone of the Philosophers." For its preparation, various operations were invented by different Philosophers, so that what was left unfinished by nature might be completed by artifice, since nature itself is always inclined toward its own perfection.

->*He discusses what the Philosopher's Stone is, and deals first with its first part.*<-

### CHAPTER V.

And because the Philosophers had declared that skill so obscurely—with marvelous entanglements of words and shadows of figures—many people have doubted the Stone of the Philosophers: what it actually is, and from what things it is made? But if you are willing to prick up your ears diligently: we cut the Stone into two parts. The first part we call the "Earthly Sun" <note>original: "Solem terrenum"; a common alchemical metaphor for gold.</note>, a point on which both the ancient Philosophers and the more recent ones clearly support me with their testimonies in the *Assembly* <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>. Without the Earthly Sun, the Philosophical work is not completed. For all assert that no tincture is true without its own copper: because in it is the purest "sulfur of the wise," in which wise nature contains its own seed. And just as the Sun diffuses and strikes its most vivid and penetrating rays into this elementary world, so the Stone of the Philosophers—from the gold of the Sun, the son (so to speak) of the Sun—by a Philosophical operation...

# CHEMISTRY.

Once composed, it sprinkles itself into other metals, and will make them equal to itself in virtue, color, and weight forever. And because all metals are contained within gold, we rightly accept gold before all others. For when we wish to cause gold or silver to wander <note>original: "errare"; likely referring to the process of transmutation or spreading the metallic seed</note>, it is necessary to take those very substances. From man, man is generated; from a tree, a tree; a plant produces a plant, and a lion a lion; since every thing generates and produces its like according to the tempering of its nature, which they call its "complexion." Yet, more truly, the Philosophers do not "create" gold or silver: rather, it is nature, purified by the skill of the operator.

### *Concerning the second part of the stone, where the most glorious spirit is compared to the Virgin Mary. CHAPTER VI.*

The second part of the stone we call "living Mercury" <term>Quicksilver: the volatile, fluid principle in alchemy</term>. Since it is living and raw, it is said to dissolve the bodies themselves: because in its depths, it naturally clings to them. This is the stone without which nature performs nothing. Whence the Philosophers advise us that we should not work except in the Sun <note>Gold</note> and Mercury, which, when joined, constitute the Philosopher's Stone. Who, then, is sufficient to pursue the merits of Mercury with praise, since he alone is the one who makes gold thin: and who prevails with such power that he can reduce the Sun itself to its primary nature? No thing in this world is known to possess such power. Of Mercury itself, it is said: "Whatever the wise seek is in Mercury." Mercury destroys all leaf-gold; it dissolves it, softens it, and takes the soul from the body. If it be sublimated, the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitæ"</note> is then generated. If anyone, therefore, should ask of you: "What are the stones?" You shall answer: "The Sun and Mercury are the Philosophical stones." Truly, these stones are dead upon the earth, and they perform nothing, except what is administered to them by the industry of man. In the profound likeness of gold, the Ethereal Heaven was closed to all men, so that all men descended to the infernal seats, and were detained there perpetually. But Jesus Christ opened the gate of Ethereal Olympus <note>A classical reference to Heaven</note>, and has now laid open the Plutonian realms <note>The underworld or Hell</note>, so that souls might be rescued, when in the virginal womb, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, by an ineffable mystery—

# ON THE ART

And the Virgin Mary conceived through a most profound mystery <note>original: "sacramento"</note> that which was most excellent in the heavens and on earth; and at last she brought forth for us the Savior of the entire world, who by his most exuberant kindness shall save all those given over to sin, if the sinner turns to him often. Moreover, she remained a virgin, unharmed and undiminished. For this reason, Mercury is not undeservedly compared to the most glorious and divine Virgin Mary. For Mercury is a virgin, because it never propagated any metallic body in the womb of the earth, and yet it generates the Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of alchemy</note> for us; by dissolving the "heaven"—that is, gold—it opens and leads forth the soul (by which you should understand its divine nature). It carries this soul in its womb for a little time, and at last, in its own time, transmits it into a purified body. Whence a child—that is, the Stone—is born to us, by whose blood the lower bodies, having been tinted, are restored safely into a golden heaven; and Mercury remains a virgin without stain, just as it ever was before.

### CHAPTER VII.

As for why the Philosophers commended this science to posterity and to the "sons of wisdom" through receding similarities and obscure allegories, Hamul <note>likely a reference to the alchemist Adfar Khalid ibn Yazid or a similar Arabic source</note> in the *Senior* <note>The "Senior Zadith," a famous alchemical text</note> posits the chief cause: So that they might attribute it to the glorious God, who would reveal it to whom He willed, and withhold it from whom He willed. Also, Rasis <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi, a Persian physician and alchemist</note> reports in the *Book of Lights*: "For if I wished to explain all things according to how they truly are, there would be no further place for prudence, since the foolish would be made equal to the wise." It is also read at the end of the *Turba* <note>The "Turba Philosophorum" or Assembly of the Philosophers, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note>: "For unless names were multiplied in the Philosophical art, children would laugh at our wisdom." Therefore, we do not think much of those who mock this divine skill as being adulterated; from this art, the most celebrated philosophers used to receive almost all knowledge of all things—just as in the past, sculptors used to take the "thefts and threads" <note>The proportions and secrets of the craft</note> of their art from the statue of Polyclitus <note>A famous Greek sculptor known for his "Canon" of perfect proportions</note>. Likewise, it would be most absurd to suspect that those ancient Philosophers of venerable authority recorded anything false, especially in this discourse on natural things.

I have commended these matters to history, for those who have always devoted their greatest efforts to seeking the truth, even if they did not ascend to the height of the nature of the soul-saving faith or the highest summit of the divine essence. Who then, unless he be a Zoilus <note>A harsh, cynical critic; named after the ancient Greek grammarian known for his critiques of Homer.</note>, would not praise this science and pursue it with singular favor? From it, nearly all the arts of its detractors have been drawn; from it, so many colors highly suitable for the art of painting took their beginning. I am silent regarding the art of minting coins; I am silent regarding that learned distillation of the physicians, by which the virtue—which they call the **fifth essence** <note>The "quintessence," a pure substance beyond the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note>—is accustomed to be drawn out. What shall I say of those bronze vessels? By which lightning and thunder are accustomed to be summoned among mortals, if only they were used against the sacrilegious enemies of the Christian faith!

There is, furthermore, the science of the **Stone** <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the goal of alchemy.</note>, so sublime and magnificent that in it nearly all of nature and the entire universe of things may be beheld, as if in a clear mirror. For it possesses the likeness of a **Microcosm** <note>original: "Mundi minoris" or "Lesser World," the idea that man or a small system reflects the entire universe.</note>, where there are the four elements and the fifth essence, which they call "heaven," in which another most noble essence has placed its seat. This essence certain Philosophers have been accustomed to compare (I speak with all due respect) to Almighty God and the most holy and indivisible Trinity. It is neither of the nature of heaven, nor of the natures of the elements, and they have called it by the peculiar name of the **mediating soul of nature**.

And just as God, the craftsman of the world, is present everywhere in this **Macrocosm** <note>original: "Mundo maiori" or "Greater World."</note>: so this essence, which is judged by the title of God, is everywhere in the whole world: that is, in the **Philosophical glass** <note>The alchemical flask or vessel.</note>. And just as Almighty God is immense and infinite: so that thing seems almost innumerable in the procreation of its own likeness, even until the extreme end of the Greater World. For then the generative nature shall be taken away from every procreatable thing. From these words, one skilled in nature can gather that the Stone is able to "tinge" <note>To transform or transmute; a technical term for the Stone's power to change base metals into gold.</note> many parts, by which many other difficulties can also be dissolved.

Farewell then, to that Aristarchus <note>A reference to a severe critic, likely a specific contemporary theologian the author opposes.</note> the Theologian, who does not blush to profess himself an interpreter of divine letters, yet does not fear to attack with his most impudent insults this skill of nature established by God—than which God has conferred nothing more magnificent or sublime upon this world, after the Sacred Scriptures. Tell me, by the immortal God, what is more unjust than that men should hate that which they do not understand?

No one, unless they are out of their mind, will deny that these things will be of use to philosophical practice. But at this point, we must trace the cradles of nature from a bit deeper. Therefore, do not be affected by weariness if I make a digression somewhat further than the scope of this particular undertaking might perhaps require.

The most glorious God, the craftsman of all things and their inexpressible author, needing nothing before the beginning of the World but being sufficient unto Himself, and always remaining in the deepest sanctuary of His divinity, wished—out of His most abundant goodness—for things known from eternity to come into being. In the beginning, He created a certain essence of these things, still unformed in crude outlines (if I may put it that way), which that famous Moses—whom I am pleased to call the fountain of the Philosophy of Philosophers and the primary High Priest—called at one time "the earth, empty and void," and at another "the abyss and the water." <note>original: "terram inanem & vacuam, modò abyſſum & aquam"</note> Anaxagoras, however, called it "confused Chaos." Others have rightly called it the "Mother of the World," the "Foundation," and the "Face of Nature." While all things sat within her womb, undistinguished and undigested, and were not yet visible in their own proper forms, the Spirit of God intervened. According to the pattern and likeness of the *intelligible world* <note>The "intelligible world" refers to the Platonic idea of a perfect, conceptual realm that serves as a blueprint for our physical reality.</note>, the Daedalian <note>A reference to Daedalus, the mythical Greek craftsman, used here to describe God as a skillful, artistic creator.</note> Creator graphically and precisely expressed and drew out this visible World. From this, He decorated the sky itself, suspended on high, most skillfully with glowing fires; He composed and arranged its motion and that of the stars so that they might run through the vault of heaven by a wonderful logic to produce the varieties of succeeding seasons, and so that they might warm, cherish, and preserve the lower things in their essence by their motion and light. For this reason, He placed the lower things beneath the higher, as an egg is placed under a hen to be cherished, or as a woman is joined to a man to be made fruitful. Into these things, from the very beginning, He scattered certain "seminal reasons" <note>term: seminal reasons (rationes seminales). A Stoic and Augustinian concept of latent "seeds" or formative principles implanted in nature by God that develop over time.</note> so that, when opportunities were received, they might multiply themselves with a perpetual—so to speak—fecundity and offspring. Moreover, God fashioned this framework of the World with a certain harmony and a musical proportion related to itself, so that those things which are in the Upper World are also in the Lower, but in a terrestrial manner; likewise, those things which are in the lower regions may also be seen in the higher, but in a celestial manner and according to their cause. To this, perhaps, you might apply the opinion of Anaxagoras, who posited that "anything is in everything." Wherefore, congruously...

<meta>This page continues the theological discussion on the nature of God, following the previous page's exploration of divine presence.</meta>

# ON THE ART

It is established that God governs and fills all things that He has created. We do not say that God fills all things in the sense that they contain Him, but rather that they are contained by Him. Nor should it be thought that God is in all things in such a way that each thing receives Him according to the measure of its own portion—as if larger things held more and smaller things held less. Instead, God fills all things so that there is nothing where He is not. Therefore, we understand Him to be within all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not excluded. He is within so that, by His own uncircumscribed magnitude, He may enclose all things. For this reason, Saint Dionysius <note>original: "diuus Dionysius"; likely referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher</note> says: All things can be affirmed of God, since He is the author and governor. Conversely, it is more true that all things can be denied of Him, since He is none of these things which He has established. This latter view seems to me more pleasing and certain, both because of the variable course of this World and because of the unsearchable abyss of the highest divinity. For God has placed a vast interval between Himself and created things.

Moreover, **G O D** is indeed immeasurable, and ineffable, unthinkable, unintelligible, beyond all imagination, beyond all thought, beyond all intellect, beyond all essence <term>essence: the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term>, unnamable, to be preached in the heart by silence alone, most powerful, most wise, most merciful, Father, Word, Holy Spirit, incomprehensible height, indivisible Trinity, immutable essence. Every nature is His image, however attentive the eye may be. He is the unity of all creatures, and the hinge of all, and the One who is stronger than all power, greater than all excellence, better than all praise.

Saint Plato <note>original: "diuus Plato"; the author treats the Greek philosopher with high religious reverence</note> posited that He dwells in a fiery substance: understanding, evidently, the unspeakable splendor of God within Himself, and the love surrounding Himself. Others have asserted He is an intellectual and fiery spirit, having no form, but transforming Himself into whatever He wishes and equaling Himself to all things. In a manifold way, He is in some manner bound to His creatures. Again, exceeding them by His infinite eternity and omnipotence, He may be introduced into the purified minds of men through fervent love, sincere faith, and solid hope—He who is blessed through all thousands of thousands <note>original: "chiliadum chiliades"; a Greek-derived term for an immense, uncountable number of ages</note>.

The one whom Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author known for "The Marriage of Philology and Mercury," an encyclopedia of the seven liberal arts.</note> is said to have greeted by the proper name of Arithmetic, when she, in greeting Jupiter, brought forth seven hundred and seventeen numbers by folding her fingers into them. In this number, we discover all numbers and every proportion, both Musical and Geometrical. Add something even more difficult: the Name of God is found most exactly within these numbers. But, to return to the purpose, hear Dionysius <note>Likely Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> reciting that God is in all things, or all things are in God, just as numbers are in unity, and as all straight lines of the lunar circles are in the center. And just as the powers of the limbs belong to the soul. Because just as unity is the common measure, source, and origin of all numbers—containing every number uniquely joined within itself—it is the principle of all multitude. Yet it remains always the same and immutable within every multitude: so in like manner do created things stand in relation to the Creator. And just as the individual human soul stands as the ruler of its body, present as a whole to the whole body and to each of its parts: so similarly God is everywhere in this World, filling it, governing it, and continually preserving it through the virtue which He <unclear>bestows</unclear> daily upon created things...

Not that the World itself is a literal animal—an idea which we may reject at the very threshold of Christian philosophy, partly in Christian Metaphysics and partly in this consideration of the **Stone** <note>original: "lapis"; referring to the Philosopher's Stone</note>. While the sublimity of nature persuades one to weave that argument with a more polished thread of speech, here it has pleased me to proceed in plain prose.

We place that Soul of the World chiefly in the **Sun**. For there is nothing in the very circle of the firmament, besides the soul, which bears a greater likeness to God than light itself. Since every single thing claims for itself, so to speak, as much of God as it is capable of receiving light. And since nothing is more keen-sighted than the Sun, many of the followers of Plato, imitating **Orpheus** <note>The legendary Greek musician and prophet</note> in this especially, have named the Sun the "Eye of the World." For in it, as if in a most brilliant mirror, all things are seen and show themselves.

Hence **Heraclitus** <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrines on change and fire</note> says that all things become known [only] if you take the Sun away from the World. What is our little body if the soul is missing? No pulsing vein can be felt there; no judgment for sensing remains within. There is no vital breath in it, nor any respiration. For this reason, it has also seemed fit to some to call the Sun the **Heart of Heaven**. Because just as in the heart of an individual there exists the fountain of blood, moistening and watering the other members of the human body and infusing vital motion, so in the Sun there is seen to be the vegetation and conservation of all things, both lower and higher. For it inspires life and heat into the lower things, after a fashion, by its light.

Light, moreover, is a certain simple act, turning all things toward itself with life-giving heat, permeating all beings, leading their qualities and virtues through all things, and dispersing darkness and gloom. Therefore, **Phoebus** <note>A name for Apollo, the sun god</note> sits in the middle with his shining golden hair, like a King and Emperor of the World holding a scepter and a helm. Not only **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on theurgy and Syrian philosophy</note> but many others have confirmed that all the virtues of the heavenly beings reside in him. And **Proclus** <note>A Greek Neoplatonist who significantly influenced Western medieval theology</note> says: At the sight of the Sun, all the powers of all the heavenly beings are gathered and collected into one, which at last [he pours] into this lower world through his fiery breathing-holes...

### *On Nature. CHAPTER IX.*

We assert that Nature is a certain infinite force in things, procreating like from like. For nature generates, increases, and nourishes all things. Therefore, it contains within itself the names of all things. An animal is from nature, as is a stone, wood, a tree; and the bodies which you see are from nature and held by its bond. Nature is the ligament of the elements and the power of mixing, which effects the mixtures of elements in any given thing of this sublunary World <note>The "sublunary world" refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, which in ancient science was the realm of change and decay.</note>, and it has impressed a form suitable to its own species, through which that thing is distinguished and separated from any other thing. Nor is nature of any one color, yet it is a participant in and the producer of all colors; it is of no weight or quality, yet it is the fertile mother of all qualities and things. What then is nature? God is nature, and nature is God. Understand it thus: from God arises something closest to Him. Nature is therefore a certain invisible fire, from which Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet often cited in alchemical texts as a master of natural magic.</note> taught that all things were born; Heraclitus of Ephesus <note>A Greek philosopher famous for the idea that "all things flow" and that fire is the fundamental element.</note> seems to agree with this. Did not the Spirit of the Lord, which is a fiery love, when it was carried over the waters, give to them a certain fiery vigor, since nothing can be generated without heat? When it was said at the birth of the World: "Increase and multiply," God breathed into created things a certain germination—that is, a "greenness" <note>original: "viriditatem." In alchemy, this "greenness" or *viriditas* represents the life-force and the power of growth.</note>—by which all things might multiply themselves. Whence certain people, speculating more deeply, said that all things were "green," since to be green is said to be to grow and to coalesce; and they used to call that greenness Nature. But Aristotle says: if motion is unknown, nature is unknown, since it is now volatile and in a continuous motion of generation, augmentation, and alteration, which finally at the very end of the World will be stable and fixed. For then God will take away that power and potential of generating from things, and will collect it in the most hidden treasury of His omnipotence where it was from eternity...

will place it. Therefore, it has pleased some to call this power of generating and preserving things the **Soul of the World** <note>Latin: *Anima Mundi*; a concept suggesting the universe itself is a living being</note>: not because the World is a living animal, as the Platonic arguments and even the testimonies of the Arabian, Egyptian, and Chaldean astrologers seem to prove. For the Philosophers posited that the World is an animal and that the heavens and stars are living creatures, and that the souls of things are intelligent, participating in the divine mind. Furthermore, Democritus and Orpheus and many of the Pythagoreans were of the opinion that a God or a certain soul presides over every single thing, and that all things are full of gods: for which they established divine honors, and dedicated prayers and sacrifices to them, and worshipped them with diverse cults. Moreover, they reduced all souls of this kind to one single Soul of the World. Similarly, they referred all gods back to one Jupiter. This is what Aristotle and the Aristotelian Theophrastus, what Avicenna and Al-Ghazali <note>original: *Algazeles*</note>, what the Stoics and all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy</note> confess, and have endeavored with great effort to prove.

From this, I have no doubt, emanated all the errors of the heathens: from here the fictions of the Poets, the diabolical sacrifices, and the sacrilegious offerings. From here the land of Egypt worshipped and adored certain animals and other monstrous portents in their *Lararia* <note>term: *Lararia* - private shrines originally intended for Roman household gods, here used to describe Egyptian shrines</note>. Who, therefore, would not say that the philosophy of the Pagans is vain? Which, by this most common error and many others, is most miserably undermined. In this, the Philosophers seem to me like the daughters of Danaus <note>original: *Pelidibus* - likely a reference to the Danaides, though the text uses a variant form</note> and girls who busy themselves drawing water from a great well with perforated jars.

However, we can judge them worthy of pardon, since the true light, Jesus Christ the Savior, had not yet shone upon them. Therefore, it is the concern of the Christian Philosopher—whose authority is weightier and whose judgment is more certain—to lead back whatever things seem to pertain to the mystery of the faith or of nature into the fold of the Catholic Church, as if they were being possessed by unjust heirs. This should be done in the manner of Virgil, who said he collected gold from the dung of Ennius <note>A famous literary anecdote where Virgil claimed to find poetic "gold" in the crude works of the older poet Ennius</note>. Likewise, in the manner of little bees, while they suck the sweeter flowers of Mount Hymettus <note>A mountain in Greece famous for its honey</note> for the sake of producing honey. Who would not moisten with tears the untimely death of Pico della Mirandola <note>original: *Pici Mirandulani*; a famous Renaissance philosopher who died at 31</note>? Whom the Sister Fates <note>The Parcae, or the three Fates of mythology</note> singularly envied in our age. Who, if he had performed the gift of life for a while longer...

Through her, we explore the inner chambers of the World, the tracts of the lands and the sea, and the deep sky, as much as we are able by divine grace and natural light. She herself distinguishes the heavens and the innumerable multitude of the stars: then the journey of the golden-haired Sun and the labors of the moon <note>original: "trivia" - an epithet for Hecate or Diana, referring to the moon's phases or its place where three ways meet</note>. What gathers the rains, what the glassy hail: What are the seeds of gold, and what the seeds of iron. From whence comes the savage thundering. From whence the springs of perennial waters take their beginnings, and other things of that kind. Let tender youths learn this Philosophy thoroughly in their nursing years, and let them everywhere avoid the old wives' fables of those Philosophers who posit that the World is a living animal, and that it consists of innumerable living beings, and those divine. What is more futile? What is more foolish? For what else is it to say that the Sun, or other celestial bodies, are animated souls participating in the divine mind, than to slip into evil heresy and the abominable treachery of idolatry? Nor must it be conceded (as Saint *Augustine* bears witness) that those starry globes live by certain souls of their own, and those intellectual and blessed. I certainly know that only the human soul is a divine light, created in the image of the Word, the first exemplar of the cause of causes, shaped by the substance and seal of God: whose character is the eternal Word, by participation in which the soul itself...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the nature of motion and the soul, specifically addressing the celestial bodies and the limits of human artifice compared to divine creation.</meta>

# ON ART

We believe that a faint likeness of the rational soul, bearing a modest trace of it, exists even in the brute soul drawn from the bosom of nature; just as an Echo is the image and likeness of a living voice. But as for the "vegetative soul," others may laugh at the idea. The Doctors of Theology admit that there are "moving intelligences" of the spheres <note>The medieval belief that angels or spiritual beings guided the rotation of the planets.</note>, not because they give form to the spheres themselves, or render them sensible or intellectual—according to the opinion of Saint Jerome <note>original: "D. Hieronymi"</note>—but so that they may assist them by providing motion. And yet, those spheres could be made to revolve by their own inherent reason if the divine will so commanded. Nevertheless, Almighty God, out of His ineffable goodness, willed that secondary causes should preside over this worldly fabric, so that whatever moves by itself also grants the power of moving to others. For this reason, He even assigned angels to the guardianship of human souls, although He Himself primarily guards them. One must not think, however, that these intelligences are attached to the revolving spheres out of necessity, as if the spheres could not be versatile in their own rotation.

Indeed, certain industrious men fashion a similar celestial machine out of bronze or brass <term>orichalcum: a golden-colored alloy, often used for scientific instruments</term>, stabilizing the earth in the very center. Then, consequently, they attach the other elements, as well as the spheres of the stars and heavens, to certain little wheels, by which they strive to express the motion of the planets and the face of the heavens with great precision. There are other meticulous men who strive to build clockwork machines and certain mill-wheels that are perpetually turning. If man can thus emulate divine reason, who would not think that those starry globes could be rotated by their own power?

But what shall I say of the various forms of Astrology, which our Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher who wrote a massive critique of astrology.</note>—renowned in every branch of learning—weakened with powerful arguments in recent days? Tell me, Astrologer, why do you refer everything to the heavens? Why do you devise theories about the natures of the stars and signs, and the motions of the planets? You, who are in no way able to predict the powers and properties of even the smallest earthly thing? Why do you fear the stars and constellations, or rather, why do you lie about them? You, who cannot even grasp the measurement of a tiny earthly body. What is more ridiculous? What is more absurd than to imagine in the ninth or tenth heaven such configurations, and images of lines, or figures of the eighth heaven made from the wandering stars...

For water is the spirit; likewise air; the middle fire, so to speak, is the spirit; we call the earth not spirit, but body, because it is the tether, the matter, and the seat of the other elements.

# CHEMISTRY

Through purification, the hindrance to the tincture <note>The "tincture" is the transformative essence or Elixir capable of changing metals.</note> is destroyed, so that it can propagate its own likeness infinitely. If this propagation of its likeness is to be achieved through the spirit—since every spirit is the author of generation and is otherwise restrained by thick matter—we say that a dissolution is necessary. Through this, gold is made "living" and (so to speak) spiritual, and is reduced into its primary nature—that is, into the spirit of water and the vapor of earth. Thus, we finally obtain the sulfur and mercury <note>original: "☿"</note> from which metals are generated in the belly of the earth. Moreover, the dissolution is perfect when you have separated the spirit and the soul of the gold.

But since gold is considered by the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to the ancient and medieval alchemical authorities.</note> to be the most tempered body, having equal parts of the hot, cold, moist, and dry, it is therefore more difficult to corrupt and dissolve because of the equal harmony and proportion of its elements. It is necessary, therefore, for a discord to be created among the elements by means of contrary elements; this discord brings about the dissolution and mortification <note>The "death" or breakdown of the metal's outward form.</note> of the body. Once this is done, the purification of nature occurs, which nevertheless cannot happen without the Philosophical separation of the elements.

Truly, the elements of the body must be separated in such a way that the generative nature remains in the flower and the bud. For if anyone should burn the flower while separating the elements from one another, the generative seed <note>original: "sperma generativum"</note> would be lost, and no creature would be able to join them together again so that they might produce. This is the truest consideration of the Philosophers; if anyone should consider otherwise out of their own fantasy, they are indeed a natural fool, because they reason falsely against nature.

Now let us descend into the practice, which we shall divide into two works. In the first, mention will be made of the first solution, and of separation and distillation. In the second, we shall treat of conjunction and fixation, where consideration will be given to the most secret augmentation, which you will find in no other book in the world. But here, I wish to interpose the stages of the work in a general sense. For first we compose, we putrefy the composition, we dissolve the putrefied matter, we divide the dissolved, we cleanse the divided, we unite the cleansed, and thus the work is completed. Our discourse shall labor over these things in detail.

The Philosophers, however, judge that in the practice of the stones, less than a 12th part of <term>Mercury</term> <note>original: "☿" — the symbol for Mercury or Quicksilver.</note> ought to be taken. Also, among them, there is a danger to the dissolved body if compression were made through its skin <note>likely referring to the practice of straining mercury through chamois leather</note>. Likewise, some of the more recent practitioners thought that the solution could be made in a shorter time if a long-lasting pounding or grinding of gold leaf were first done by a certain mill or mortar.

Therefore, let the Mercury first be purified with prepared common salt, or any other suitable thing, so that its most subtle substance may be obtained. Let several parts of this purified water be very well mixed with one part of purest <term>Sun</term> <note>original: "Solis" — the alchemical term for Gold.</note> beaten into leaves or thin plates, and let them be placed in a longer glass flask, stopped up with cloths and the sign of the cross <note>a common ritualistic or protective sealing method for vessels</note>. Let the glass be covered with ashes up to the surface of the water, and let a very light fire be applied, lest the water should seem to rise; rather, let it remain "living" with the gold, and let it be kept as if for a long duration. This heat should be balanced until a certain vaporous and subtle earth sweats out upon the water of Mercury, which is usually recognized by a marvelous color when it is to be extracted. It is like the rainbow itself, appearing through the waters, yet not according to all the colors as the rainbow does in this greater World <note>The "greater World" refers to the Macrocosm or the universe at large, as opposed to the "lesser world" of the alchemist's flask.</note>. The arch of the rainbow itself stands in the middle of pure, liquid, and flowing water, and in the middle above the earth. From this, the entire property of sulfur and its natural likeness is expressed through the rainbow; nor is the rainbow seen in the sky unless the Sun is shining, which rain is also accustomed to follow. However, when mists or dark clouds arrive, the Sun itself, and likewise the arch of the rainbow, is hidden. It has pleased the Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicis"</note> to explain the rainbow thus: when the image of the Sun colors a moist, hollow, and dense cloud like a mirror, and intersects the middle of its orb—this explanation comes closer to our divine and wonderful skill. Yet it must not be thought that the sulfur itself turns black when you have extracted it, as some have believed. Finally, once Venus <note>The metal copper, or a specific stage of the process associated with the planet Venus.</note> has been extracted, you shall distill the water in which the soul of the Sun <note>Gold</note> or the metallic Mercury of gold resides, using a slow heat, so that sixty moments <note>roughly equivalent to seconds</note> can be counted between drop and drop. And that distilled water is called our "living water" <note>original: "aqua viua"</note>, which brings life to all bodies and is composed of two natures: understand these to be the spirit and the soul, the ferment, since the spirit is the seat of the soul and its tether. This water is called by many names: the sharpest vinegar, the moon, the female, the seed or the feminine menses, heaven, Mercury, the red hair of a man—that is, the spirit of the Sun, which is to say, of gold. Sulfur, however, is called the body, the male Sun, the male seed, earth, and Mercury.
