## CHAPTER XIV.

There remains now the second part of Philosophical practice <note>original: "Philosophicæ praxeos"; refers to the actual laboratory work guided by theory</note>, which is by far more difficult and more sublime. In this stage, we read that all the nerves of talent and all the mental paths of many Philosophers have grown weary. For it is more difficult to make a man return to life than to seek death. Here, the work of God is sought: it is indeed the greatest mystery for souls to wander and to fashion an inanimate body into a living statue. Do you not think it requires a lively wit to lead the soul back to the spirit, then the spirit to the soul, and finally those two back to the body? In this body of ours, it is fitting to know how much is of the spirit, how much of the soul, and how much of the body. Furthermore, one must know how much of the soul's middle nature is in the spirit, and how much in the body, so that you may join these two natures—kindred and related to one another—in their due proportion. Therefore, we must join two waters: the sulfur of gold and its Mercury, the soul and the body, the Sun and the Moon, male and female, two seeds, heaven and earth, and two, so to speak, quicksilvers <note>original: "argenta viua"</note>; and from these quicksilvers is made the living Mercury, from which alone the Philosophers say their Stone is established. Wretched men have hallucinated this to be about raw Mercury <note>common quicksilver</note>; but that Mercury is all metals, male and female, and a Hermaphroditic monster in the very marriage of soul and body. This I call the "solution" and the "putrefaction" of the Philosophers. The earth of gold is dissolved by its own spirit, which you will grasp in these proportions. The body must be dissolved in the midst of the most subtle air; likewise, the body is dissolved by its own heat and humidity, where the soul—the middle nature—holds dominion everywhere in the whole glass vessel within the heat of the blackness. This blackness of nature, the Philosophers called the "head of the crow" <note>original: "caput corvi"; the *nigredo* stage signifying the death of the old forms</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the "Second Practice" of alchemy, focusing on the difficult task of reuniting the soul, spirit, and body to create "Living Mercury." It emphasizes that the true Stone comes from a philosophical union of opposites rather than common quicksilver.</summary>
<keywords>Philosophical practice, Spirit, Soul, Body, Living Mercury, Sulfur of Gold, Sun and Moon, Hermaphrodite, Putrefaction, Nigredo (Blackness)</keywords>

# ON THE ART

The ancient Philosophers used to call this the raven, or the **Black Sun** <note>original: "Solem nigrum"; a famous alchemical paradox representing the first stage of the work, where matter is decomposed</note>. From this, a certain man brought forth this proposition: "I saw three circles in a circuit, I saw three Suns in the firmament having three faces: namely, a black Sun, a white Sun, and a red Sun." This blackness was also called by the names of all black things, after which all the colors of the world that can be conceived by the mind are accustomed to appear; these are finally referred back to the true whiteness as if to a center and a hinge. In white are all colors, and from it the others, so to speak, seem to be colored. White and black are colors by their very nature, and indeed they are the extremes: from whose manifold mixing with one another and the proportion of the middle, we believe those which they call "intermediate colors" arise. We also opine that from a certain confusion of white and black, a redness is fused together.

Indeed, we call that whiteness the **white stone**, the **white Sun**, the **full Moon**, the **calcined moon** <note>silver that has been reduced to powder by heat</note>, **white silver**, **fruitful white earth** (purified and calcined), **white lime**, and the **salt of metals**, and the **calcined body**; we name it by many other names besides. Furthermore, it is called **living earth** and **living white sulfur** when the soul has been introduced into the body and the impediment has been removed.

Here we solve this question: whether the earth ought to be airy or fiery. We say it is both at once. For if it existed only as fiery, it would be burned into the ash of the dead. If, however, it were only airy, having been made volatile, it would vanish when dyeing the metals. But what shall I mention concerning the fire by which the dissolution of the earth is made? Behold the heat in the bowels of the earth, which nature alone provides; where you might seem to perceive almost none, yet, instigated by the heat of the Sun in the metal-bearing mountains, by ascending and descending many cubits everywhere, it coagulates the thicker water and associates it into one body together with the fatness of the earth.

But since nature scarcely completes her operations in five hundred years, and so great a loan of life has not been granted to us—nor is it given to us to live longer than an elephant, or until the so-called "Year of Plato" <note>The Great Year, a cycle of roughly 25,000 years when the celestial bodies return to their original positions</note>—the Philosopher attributes a greater degree to the fire, by which he may emulate nature as his guide in a shorter time. Therefore, you might rightly say that he who can show you a fire agreeable to nature is blessed with a singular happiness of intellect.

# CHEMISTRY

The Philosophers call their natural fire a "bath," or their "Sun," or "horse dung" <note>original: "fumum equinum"; a common alchemical term for the gentle, moist heat produced by fermenting manure</note>: which others produce with wood or any other material, but we truly create with charcoal in a furnace especially adapted for this purpose. Furthermore, the Stone is usually placed in a triple earthenware vessel so that a slower little fire may be maintained, which is—I say—as similar as possible to the heat of a hen while she hatches her eggs. And by that heat the dragon—that is, the earth of gold—mortifies itself when it gives forth the elements and spirits from within itself. Conversely, it vivifies itself when it receives the spirits back into itself. For this reason, it is compared to Jesus Christ, who voluntarily offered himself to death for us, and afterwards, through the glory of the resurrection, restored himself to life by his own power, never to perish again. We also say in this place that the dragon spits out from itself all darkness and poison, and afterwards drinks it back and becomes white. 

And since we said above that heaven must be joined with earth, this question arises: Whether heaven ought to descend to the earth, or the earth ought to ascend to heaven. It is certain that the earth cannot ascend unless heaven has first descended; however, the earth is said to be sublimated into heaven when, having been dissolved by its own spirit, it is finally made one single thing with it. I shall satisfy you with this likeness: The Son of God, having descended into the Virgin and there being formed as flesh, is born as a man; when he had shown us the way of truth for the sake of our salvation, having suffered and died for us, he returns to the heavens after the resurrection. There the earth—that is, humanity—is exalted above all the circles of the World, and is placed in the intellectual heaven of the most holy Trinity. In like manner, when I die, the soul (aided by the grace and merits of Christ) returns to the vital fountain from whence it descended. The body returns to the earth, which, having finally been purified at the final judgment of the World, the soul gliding down from heaven leads with itself unto glory. 

But because it is fitting for the soul to ascend to heaven, another certain doubt presents itself: Namely, whether the spirit <note>In alchemy, the "spirit" often refers to the volatile medium that connects the "soul" (the essence) to the "body" (the solid matter)</note> ought to pass to heaven with the soul, or whether both ought to remain below heaven? We have said that the spirit is the tether of the soul in this World, but when the Stone shall have arrived at the fixed whiteness, there will be another World far more excellent than the former, where the spirit remains—

will be in the middle, the Soul in heaven, and the Body at the bottom: understand that the earth is the heaven of the soul. Conversely, the soul is the heaven of the body. And because the spirit weakened the soul during the process of dissolution <note>original: "solutione"; the chemical breaking down of a substance</note>, both perform penance, and the soul is purified through the spirit, as is the body likewise. Only the purified soul ascends into heaven, while the spirit departs with its offenses. For if that spirit were to remain with the soul and the body, there would be perpetual corruption in that place, and a proper harmony and equality of the elements would never be achieved. You may appropriately compare this spirit in certain respects to an angel, which is accustomed to descend with the human soul (when it is infused into the central point of the heart and from there through all parts of the small body). We also imagine the body, spirit, and soul speaking by way of a dialogue: the spirit saying to the soul: "I shall lead you to eternal death, to the underworld, and to the house of darkness." To which the soul replies: "My dear spirit. Why do you not lead me back to that bosom from which you received me with your flattering? I believed you were bound to me by necessity. I am indeed your friend, and I shall lead you to eternal glory. But you think of the body, which you make glorious by giving it life." To which the spirit says: "I shall certainly do so, but wretched am I, forced to depart once I have established you above all precious stones and made you blessed. Therefore I beseech you, when you arrive at the throne of the kingdom, be mindful of me at some time." To which the body finally gave countless thanks, because it had given it a most excellent essence, through which it beheld God as if in a mirror; it promised to remember, and congratulated it on having the first place on the throne of the kingdom.

which becomes Phoebe herself. Cynthia <note>original: "Cinthia"; another name for the Moon</note>—that is, the Moon—opens the way for Phoebus the Sun. Phoebus, in turn, encloses and congeals his sister, the Moon. In this very marriage of the Sun and the Moon, understand this proposition: In the shadow of the Sun is the heat of the Moon, and in the heat of the Moon is the coldness of the Sun. For indeed, when the moisture of the Moon receives heat and light from the Sun, the Sun is said to enter into the Moon; upon his entry, the Moon receives her increase and begins to grow warm. The Sun, however, begins to grow cold and moist, because he has taken the water unto himself and lost his heat and dryness, whereby, deprived of light, he grows dark. But when the Moon goes into the Sun, the Sun himself begins to revive and to shine, because light is restored to him, and the Moon, widowed of her splendor, grows thin and is overshadowed. Whence I assert that the shadow of the Sun is the coldness and moisture of the Moon, but the shadow of the Moon is the day. Take away, therefore, the shadow from the Sun, and his entire light is dispersed everywhere. Yet do not imagine that the Moon can take light from the Sun in a single moment of an hour; rather, the body is dissolved little by little. In the beginning, when Phoebe is joined to the Sun, she is set on fire by him; once ignited, she is seen to shine gradually before midnight. But when she stands full in her entire orb, she is accustomed to bathe the whole night in her brilliance. As she decreases again and grows dull in her light, the heat of Phoebus begins to flourish. Here you will clearly recognize in the Moon when the Sun ought to shine, if, following the intent of my writings, you penetrate inward with your mind—though it may also be understood by another talent. When the Moon—that is, the white stone <term>lapis albus: the intermediate stage of the alchemical Great Work</term>—begins to turn lemon-yellow or to redden, it is a sign of the shining Sun. The beginning of the redness is the dawn; who would not call the dawn lemon-yellow? Tithonia <note>original: "Tithonia"; referring to Eos/Aurora, the goddess of dawn</note>—that is, the dawn—seems to be bound to this common number, so that she may bedew the air and demonstrate the rapid path of Phaethon <note>original: "Phaëthontis"; here used as a name for the Sun</note>—that is, the Sun—at the first light. Where at last the tawny Morning Star <note>original: "Eous"</note> pours out its visible light from the Nabataean <note>Eastern</note> axis, which appears to be the soul. Because, as was disputed above, it is necessary for the Sun to go into the Moon and then the Moon into the Sun, we detect two impediments in the heavens between them: Venus and Mercury. Once these are removed, their union will be miraculous; when this is done, the Moon will no longer lose her light, but will shine with her own light. And the Sun likewise.

### CHAPTER XVI.

It is pleasing now, son of wisdom, to bring the philosophical skiff to the happy harbor; come then, ply the oars: expand the sails, give a swift and fertile wind, for the harbor of salvation must be sought. After our stone has been made white, we say our son is born: although the boy is now a perfect human, consisting of body and soul, he is not yet able to generate another offspring until he is first nourished by the food of his own nature, until he reaches an age mature for generation. We have received from those ancient Philosophers, who worked by nature alone, that their living water <note>original: "aquam suam viuam"; likely referring to mercurial water or the solvent used in the work.</note> was divided into two parts. When they had arrived at the fixed whiteness <term>albedo: the second major stage of the alchemical process, signifying purification</term> with one part of the water, they made the same thing red <term>rubedo: the final stage of the work, representing solar perfection</term> with the other reserved part, or perhaps even by fire alone. Others, working with the red stone—because it had ascended to the highest degree and could not be increased by itself—began again the labors they had previously completed. Dissolving that redness with the other part of the reserved water, they reduced it once more to its first essence, so to speak; and they labored in almost all things just as from the beginning, but indeed with a greater industry of both fire and labor: and they believed this repetition to be the truer or greater augmentation. For which reason the first Philosophers also used a more prolonged time in completing the stone. Those younger and later in birth were accustomed to finish it within the course of a year. For that reason, so that they might tinge the white stone into Moon <note>Silver</note> by means of the lunar seed throughout, or to it—

By adding other spirits—namely white ones, drawn out from Jupiter <note>original: "Ioue"; refers to the metal Tin</note> and Saturn <note>refers to the metal Lead</note> through sublimation—they have increased its power. Furthermore, they may have turned the white stone red by augmenting it with solar seed <note>gold</note> or other reddish spirits from Mars <note>Iron</note> and Venus <note>Copper</note>. And you should not think this is done without reason, since these lower bodies <note>the base metals</note> contain much tincture <note>the coloring or transforming principle</note> within themselves. For if you extract the more perfect part from these bodies and add it to a more perfect body, why should anyone doubt that the whole is made perfect? And these lower bodies are called "spirits" when we say: "dissolve the body"—that is, the stone already made—"and join the spirits to it." They are likewise called "boys" <note>original: "pueri"</note> when we say: "The boys play with the stone," meaning when they have made it greater in weight and virtue. 

Hence also in other works, we know that the "urine of four-year-old boys" is actually the water of the four lower bodies <note>Tin, Lead, Iron, and Copper</note>; since this is called the *Aqua Fortis* <note>Strong Water/Nitric Acid</note> of the Philosophers, it is said to dissolve Gold, from which we do not deny that a certain stone is created. We distinguish the mineral stone in three ways: 

1.  **The Stone of the Philosophers** is made from gold alone and nature alone; this is the most sublime, which is said by the Philosophers to cure all ailments. 
2.  **The Simple Stone** is when only the root and the sulfur of gold or silver is augmented at the end by the spirits of the lower bodies. Here, the weights—one to three, or two to seven—as set down in the *Minor Turba* <note>referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text</note> are discussed, requiring only sulfur, either of gold or silver. For golden sulfur, three reddish spirits are brought back; for silver, three whitening spirits. Now there are two sulfurs and seven spirits, from which that number of nine <note>the ennead</note> grows and is gathered. Concerning this, many have commented stupidly even unto this day. 
3.  **The Third Stone** we say is constituted by the sulfurs of all metals with their spirits. 

That the stone could tinge <note>transform</note> innumerable parts is decreed among those most learned in philosophy thus: that every spirit is capable of multiplication, but no body is. And since our stone is made exceedingly volatile and, so to speak, spiritual, and entirely fiery—having been nourished in the fire by long-lasting decoction, and repeated often through manifold solutions and coagulations—why would you not believe that this stone could tinge innumerable parts? If, with a clear mind <note>literally "wiped nostrils," a Latin idiom for being sharp-witted</note>...

...as he wrote to Dionysius regarding the nature of the first being. He says one must write through circuitous paths and riddles, so that if by chance the book happens to be tossed about by sea or land, whoever reads it may not understand it. I believe this also gave poets the occasion for storytelling, so that sublime matters would not descend to the ignoble common folk; they hid the sweetest nourishment of Philosophy within the strange outer bark of fables. We read that the Egyptians, in order to keep their dogmas in sanctuaries, hid them with unrecognizable letters—that is, with certain figures of animals—as if they were the seal of nature. If I remember correctly, a vulture was depicted. A dragon drawn into a circle and biting its own tail <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of infinity and the cyclical nature of the universe.</note> represented the image of the passing year. Do not certain more curious men strive to assign a proper character <note>A unique symbol or sigil.</note> to any given thing, so that the notation of that thing might be more hidden? Thus it happened that those ancient Philosophers decided to hand down this divine art under more obscure words. You will find the reason in the seventh chapter. Therefore, I thought it would be useful and worth the effort if I explained to you, as a son of Philosophy, certain obscure propositions from which you might very easily shake off other difficulties cast your way.

The Philosophers say that their stone is found everywhere, in mountains and caverns. From that misunderstood proposition, I am persuaded that all errors have flowed down to posterity—those who have worked with sheep's blood, hair, and other vain and foreign things. Understand it this way: Just as the celestial Sun itself is everywhere in this Greater World <term>Macrocosm: the universe at large</term> through its rays, so this earthly Sun—that is, gold—is everywhere in the whole glass <note>The alchemical flask or vessel.</note>, which is the Lesser World <term>Microcosm: a miniature representation of the universe, here the alchemical experiment</term>. "In the mountains" means in the head of the glass and the "heavens," and "in the caverns" means in the bottom of the glass and the "earth." They say the stone is born on two mountains. By the mountain of heaven and earth, understand the glass vessel. Furthermore, they assert that their stone is in all things: that is, in all metals, which are their "things." Likewise, the stone is in every thing: that is, Nature is in every thing; and because Nature has all names within itself, and Nature is the whole World, therefore the stone has many names and is said to be in every thing. However, it is closer in one thing than in another, since the Philosophers demand only the generative nature of metals. Whence they say the "rich"—that is, the perfect bodies, such as gold and silver...

They possess a nature like the poor: that is, they are imperfect metals. However, the nature of gold and silver is more perfect and more permanent in the fire than in the other metals. Furthermore, the Philosophers <note>The "Philosophers" refers to alchemists, who viewed their work as a branch of natural philosophy.</note> seek a fixed and permanent thing which might rule the whole World, such as the Sun or the Moon. Whence, in ancient times, they used to call the Sun the Lord of the World; in him is the life for healing all things, he who creates the day and the night by his motion, and illuminates the whole World with his brightness. Therefore the Sun says: *I am the stone.* Or: *Within me is the stone.* The Philosophers also say: *The work of the stone is women's work; and children's play.* <note>A famous alchemical paradox: "women's work" refers to the patience required (like washing or cooking), and "children's play" refers to the ease of the process once the secret is known.</note> The "woman" is sometimes the earth, sometimes Mercury; who seems to complete the entire work. The "children" play with the stone; that is, the three elements play with the earth; or the inferior bodies play with the golden stone when they have increased it at the end. Similarly, children play with a stone and throw it away; that is, the ignorant and unskilled throw the earth itself to the bottom when they have performed the sublimation. Some Philosophers have compared the work of the stone to the creation of the World. Similarly, to the generation of man and his natural state.

But later Philosophers have hidden this skill not only with modern words, but also with painted images. I myself saw, depicted with the most beautiful thread <note>Likely referring to a tapestry or fine embroidery.</note>, a naked virgin, youthful in age, with ivory hair, dark eyes, and cheeks of white and red, whose breasts were milky and remarkably smooth and well-turned. And this virgin was so distinguished by the whiteness of her whole body, and so gracefully adorned and composed with all the gifts of nature, that she could be judged most worthy of a royal bedchamber—one whom all Philosophers, both ancient and modern, might long for. She was such as the Poets are accustomed to describe Venus, or Juno, or any other lovely girl or maiden. Moreover, this Nymph held two burning torches in her hanging hands, and under her right foot was a golden stone, from whose bosom a certain golden fountain flowed out into many small veins. Under her left foot was a silver stone, vomiting forth a silver flame from itself. On the right was depicted Titan <note>The Sun (Sol).</note> himself, sparkling on all sides with his rays. ### Chapter 18.

Indeed, that the stone is able to cure all ailments is a subject with which the books of all Philosophers are filled. Nevertheless, I shall strive to the best of my ability to demonstrate this by natural reason. All nature is in the Sun, and the Sun is in nature: therefore we can catch its spirit in all things, and especially in gold. And when nature is sick, that stone heals nature. In the propagation of gold, the Heavens have labored most greatly, as have the Sun itself and Jupiter. The Sun indeed has bestowed all its gifts upon it, on account of its fiery virtue and splendor. Jupiter, however, whom [we call] the patron of life...

# ON THE ART

what Physicians call <term>temperamentum</term> <note>a balanced mixture of qualities</note>, and he infused into it an equality of the elements. From these endowments, gold was made so incorruptible that no fire can act upon its substance or power to destroy it. Added to this is the dissolution of gold, the purification of its nature, and its long nourishment in the fire, from which it has obtained a wonderful and nearly divine operation. If you were to consume that stone in food or drink, in the weight of a mustard seed, it would preserve the oil of life and the little spark of life with its heavenly vigor in balance, and it would bind and temper the elements of your body in peace and alliance. When these are tempered, the soul would be joined to the elements, and man would always exist unharmed, even until that end which almighty God established for man on account of the disobedience of the first parent <note>referring to Adam and the Fall of Man</note>. In the body of Christ, there was such an affinity of elements and such a binding—because he was liable to no sin, as well as on account of the wonderful union of the divine essence—that he would never have died naturally, unless for the sake of redeeming man (for whom he was also born) he had voluntarily sought death. Give perpetual thanks to Him who created you, who redeemed you from the infernal regions with his precious blood, and who gifted you with this great reward, by which you might pass through health and a long life in happiness: for which reason especially our stone is to be sought. I am silent regarding the abundance of riches which overflow most densely and copiously for man through this art, having <term>potable gold</term> <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a liquid form of gold believed to be a universal medicine</note>, or the golden liquor. If you dissolve that stone in the <term>water of life</term> <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; concentrated alcohol or brandy</note> pressed from Malmsey wine, or some other Falernian—that is, a noble wine.

### CHAPTER XIX.

Combine the masculine price <note>a coded term for gold</note> in leaves or filings with Mercury, in a proportion of twelve parts to the price. Place it over a slow fire, and continue it until, in the Mercury dissolving the bodies, <term>Venus</term> <note>alchemical shorthand for copper, or here, a specific metallic tint</note> appears swimming on top; extract this, until nothing of the body [remains] at the bottom

# CHEMISTRY

Let it remain at the bottom: and you have the first part of the **philosophical work** <note>The "Great Work" or Magnum Opus of alchemy</note>. The second part of the work is the **sulfur** <note>In alchemy, sulfur represents the active, combustible, and masculine principle of matter</note>; place it in a glass vessel without water, and [add] the water of the body, in which the soul of the **Moon** <note>Silver</note> is found by distilling. Join this water to the sulfur, and allow it, through many forces, to sometimes rise and sometimes be pressed down <note>A process of circulation or refluxing within a sealed vessel</note>, until **Venus** <note>Copper, though here likely referring to the intermediate state of the matter</note> has conceived its water, which occurs in a most brilliant white color; and you have the **elixir for the white** <note>The medicine capable of transmuting metals into silver</note>. The third part of the work is this: you shall turn the obtained brilliant white earth yellow with a strong fire; then, by the force of the fire, you shall make it red; and this is the **elixir for the red** <note>The highest goal: the Philosopher's Stone capable of making gold</note>.

### Concerning another method of operating

Furthermore, it is pleasing to comprehend this divine skill in brief and with marvelous ingenuity. Dissolve the body, take the sulfur, purify it, sublime the spirit, join the spirit with the sulfur, and you will have the **philosophical art**. In every perfect alchemical work, however small it may be, it is necessary to have the spirit and the sulfur of **gold**. The spirit tints with a golden color. The sulfur gives the golden weight and also coagulates. If it lacked one or the other, the work would achieve nothing. They say that the whole secret of nature lies hidden in the **Venus of the Philosophical Gold** <note>original: "Venere auri Philosophici"</note>, and they speak most truly. For this reason, it is customary to call it the **coagulum** <note>A rennet or curdling agent; the principle that solidifies the liquid mercury</note>, as it is said: "Take the coagulum from the body, and you have the mastery, than which there is nothing greater in nature." Similarly, purify the coagulum, and remove the impediments, and you shall tint. But because an unclean cloth, not compared to sulfur, cannot be purified without water: so the sulfur of nature is not washed without water. To wash is to dissolve, to dissolve is to purify; the water is **Mercury**, he is the key: he alone opens the body and whitens the sulfur; once it is whitened, he departs with the impurity. I would say you flourish with singular erudition if you are able to remove that [impurity]. It is the impediment and eternal death. Therefore it shall not go into heaven, as I have remarkably demonstrated above in the 14th chapter. And I say to you by God the creator of heaven, that this is one of the greatest secrets. Furthermore, the science of the **Stone** itself is nothing other than the purification of the earth or of nature. Nor is alchemy anything other than the purification of nature. The earth cannot be strained and purged of its filth unless it receives water into itself as a medium. And this embraces the whole art in brief, if you have understood nature. You may [discover] more things similar to these by yourself through divine grace...

<summary>This page outlines the three stages of the alchemical Great Work—the preparation of the base, the White Elixir, and the Red Elixir—while emphasizing that alchemy is essentially the "purification of nature" through the union of Sulfur and Mercury.</summary>

### *He presents the questions asked by the Necromancer Illardus*
### *to the Devil, concerning the Stone of the Philoso-*
### *phers. CHAPTER XX.*

A certain Necromancer <note>A practitioner of magic who communicates with the dead or spirits</note>, named Illardus, in the province of Catalonia <note>original: "Catilania"</note> put these questions to the Devil. *Question I. Whether the Stone of the Philosophers can be made to convert imperfect metals into the Sun and Moon <note>In alchemy, the Sun (Sol) represents Gold and the Moon (Luna) represents Silver</note> by the judgment of fire? Answer.* In gold, all metals exist essentially along with their earths in manifold color. From its earth, together with its essence, the Stone is fashioned, which by its own nature removes all impurity, and when cast upon imperfect things, fixes them forever. *Question. What and of what sort is that essence? Answer.* It is the soul of a middle nature <note>original: "anima media natura," a mediating spirit or force that bridges the physical and spiritual</note>, which allows one form to be converted into another. *Question. In what way does the soul of a middle nature act? Answer.* All Angels or men, even through their sharpest intellects, cannot in any way see or comprehend it inwardly. For this is God’s own property, which He has reserved for His own majesty. *Question. Can a man fashion that Stone? Answer.* Whatever God created that possesses a specific property, it is possible for man to act upon it: but it is exceedingly difficult to fashion the Stone; nevertheless, it can be fashioned. *Question. Does the soul of a middle nature have a body? Answer.* The color of gold is the body of the soul of a middle nature. *Question. In what way can the color be separated from the gold? Answer.* The soul of a middle nature, with its heat and humidity, divides and joins both together. *Question. Is the color of gold white, or black, or of what kind? Answer.* It is white to human sight, but in spirit it is dark blue <note>original: "cyaneus"</note>. *Question. In what way, and from what things is the color made? Answer.* Nature makes it from pure earth and pure water. *Question. Is color in all metals? Answer.* Not only in metals, but color is hidden in all the elements. *Question. Of what power is the Stone? Answer.* The Stone...

# CHEMISTRY

It can purify all imperfect metallic bodies from every leprosy <note>In alchemy, "leprosy" refers to the impurities or oxidation found in base metals like lead or copper.</note>, so that they may be everlasting, even until the final judgment. It heals human bodies of every sickness, even until natural death. **Question:** What kind of thing, and what thing, is the soul of the human body? **Answer:** It is a living fire of celestial life, and it possesses within itself a soul of a middle nature. By this soul of a middle nature, it is called God, the creator of all things that are in the world. **Question:** Did Virgil <note>The Roman poet Virgil was often reimagined in the Middle Ages and Renaissance as a powerful magician or alchemist.</note> possess the Stone? **Answer:** Not only did he possess the Stone, but many Philosophers possessed it, and they wrote about it in manifold ways with obscure names and through many operations. **Question:** How and why is it called a "stone"? **Answer:** I tell you, "stone" is its name, and I have not been granted the freedom to reveal anything further to you. **Question:** In how much time can the Stone be brought to completion? **Answer:** Twelve months are necessary from the first day of its beginning. In thirty days, the earth is generated from Saturn <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for lead.</note>, or the nature of the earth causes Saturn to grow. In one hundred days, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum viuum"; mercury.</note> grows in the water. In sixty completed days, the air grew from Jupiter <note>Jupiter is the alchemical name for tin.</note>. In the other days of the year, fire grows from the Sun <note>The Sun (Sol) represents gold or the perfected masculine principle.</note>. At the precise point of the year, the soul of a middle nature descends from heaven into this earth, and mortifies the higher and lower powers. It is an image of manifold victory for consuming the war in the heart of their belly, even until the perpetual judgment of fire.

->I shall say no more<-
->to you.<-

# PREFACE

...a triple collection of virtues, evidently attributed to him by the Lord God. For he was at once **King**, **Philosopher**, and **Prophet**. This was indeed Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure often credited with the invention of writing and magic</note>, who after the Great Flood was the first inventor and publisher of all arts and disciplines, both the liberal <note>The "liberal arts" such as grammar, logic, and rhetoric</note> and the mechanical. For all those who came after him strove to walk in his path and to follow in his footsteps. Why say more? It would be long for us, and even difficult, to bring to mind at present the virtuous ornaments and deeds of such a great man. Furthermore, we have not undertaken this style of teaching in the translation of this divine book; nor could the thinness of our talent, our study, or the labor of writing be sufficient to explain these things to you.

But we have introduced his name into the Prologue of this book for this reason: because he was the first to find and publish it. For this is a **divine book**, and most full of divinity. In it is contained the true and perfect proof of the two testaments (namely, the Old and the New). For if anyone studies much in this book and understands it fully, the truth and power of the testament, as well as the way of both lives <note>Likely referring to the active and contemplative lives, or the earthly and eternal lives</note>, cannot remain hidden from him. This, moreover, is the book which is named—

# PREFACE

<note>original: "PRAEFATIO"</note>

*...the book concerning the composition of Alchemy was born. And since your Latin world* <note>The author refers to the Latin-speaking scholarly community of Medieval Europe.</note> *has not yet truly recognized what Alchemy is, nor what its composition entails, I shall clarify it in the present discourse. I have set down this word, though it be unknown and strange, so that it might become clear through a definition. Indeed, Hermes the Philosopher* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure regarded as the founder of alchemy.</note> *and others who came after him define this term as follows, as in the book "On the Mutation of Substances": Alchemy is a bodily substance composed from one and through one, joining together precious things through kinship and effect, and by that same natural mixing, naturally converting them by means of superior skills.* <note>original: "ingenijs melioribus"</note> *In the following sections, what we have said will be explained, and its composition will be fully treated. But we, although our intellect is young and our Latinity quite modest, have nevertheless undertaken to translate this so great and significant a work from Arabic into Latin.* <note>This marks a pivotal moment in history: the transmission of secret sciences from the Islamic world to the West.</note> *Wherefore, for the singular grace bestowed upon us by God among the moderns, we return thanks to that highest living God, who exists as Three and One. Furthermore, I decided not to keep my name silent at the beginning of the Prologue, lest someone else should claim this labor of ours as their own, and also claim its praise and merit for themselves as if it were their property. What more? I humbly ask and beseech everyone, that...*

# THE DISCOURSE OF MORIENUS THE ROMAN
## HERMIT OF JERUSALEM.

The divine mind of Hermes fully grasped all parts of Philosophy <note>In this context, Philosophy refers to Alchemy or the "Great Work" of transforming matter.</note>. When he had studied for many years in the discovery and publication of the superior mastery <note>original: "magisterij," referring to the Magisterium or the Philosopher's Stone</note>, he was the first to finally find and publish the mastery. He composed a book about it, which he claimed as his own, and after his death, he left it as an inheritance to his disciples. Indeed, after his death, his disciples studied this book and its precepts for a long time, specifically so that they might be able to achieve its effect. Therefore, after they attained their goal, they gave various and even innumerable instructions concerning it. They did this for the purpose of ensuring that those who acquired this knowledge after them would not reveal it to the foolish as if it were something common or vulgar. 

A long time after the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, there arose a certain divine man, endowed with spiritual gifts, who, having studied divinity for a very long time, found this book among the divine books. This man was a native of Alexandria; hence he was called by his name, Adfar of Alexandria. After he found the aforementioned book, he did not cease to study it with a watchful mind and great industry. After he had studied it for a long time, he fully attained its effect and knowledge. From this knowledge, therefore, this divine man gave many various and innumerable instructions. When these had been spread under his name through all parts of our region, the fame of this man’s name and of that science reached me—almost as if flying—while I was staying at that time in the city of Rome. For at that time I was established in Rome (where I had also been born). I was then a young man,

<note>original: "MORIENI ROM." - referring to Morienus the Roman, a legendary figure in alchemical literature</note>

Whose chin the first down of youth had not yet covered, being a student and made a Christian in doctrine from his earliest years by both parents; to whom also the whole of Latin literature <note>original: "latinitas"</note> had already revealed itself. Therefore, having heard the name and fame of this man <insert>Adfar</insert>, I hastily abandoned both my parents and my homeland, nor did I allow my limbs too much rest until I had arrived at Alexandria. Indeed, I entered the city and walked through the streets and lanes as a new guest for a long time, until I had found this man's house. At last, I found his home and entered it; and when I had entered, I found this man sitting in his oratory <note>a private room for prayer or study</note> and studying his books. But after he fixed his eyes upon me, looking at me, he said: "Friend, come here." I approached him and sat down next to him on a straw mat that had been placed there. He was a man already much weakened by age, but still vigorous in countenance, and handsome in face and stature. For his face indicated everything that lay hidden in his mind to those who looked at him diligently. 

After we had conversed, he asked by what name I was called, where I was from, and what the reason for my journey had been. And I responded and said to him: "I am called Morienus, a Roman by nation, whom the fame of your name and knowledge forced to depart from parents and homeland." And he added: "What is your faith, or which of the gods do you worship?" And I responded: "I profess the Christian faith, for I am a worshiper of Christ, and I adore Him as God, Three and One." 

Afterward Adfar said: "It is good that you sought me out and found me while I am still hedged in as a worldly man <note>meaning: while he is still alive in this world</note>. You, however, be present for me with all the strength of your mind intent; for I shall make you the son of my entire discipline." 

Therefore, after these things were said between us, I rejoiced with exceeding joy. Why say more? It would be a long task for us to enumerate and tell every single thing we discussed with one another in the foundations of this work. At last, I remained with him and showed myself so lovable to him that he told me the secrets of the whole divinity. Afterward, Adfar died; and a few days after his death, I [departed] from...

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

I departed from Alexandria and arrived in Jerusalem, and within its borders I chose for myself a hermitage <note>original: "eremum," a secluded place for religious retreat</note> where I could lead a life suited to my faith and profession. Not many years later, however, there arose a certain King in Egypt named Macoya <note>likely Muawiya I, the first Umayyad Caliph</note>. He fathered a son named Gezid <note>Yazid I</note>, who reigned in Egypt after his father's death and held his kingdom. Gezid then fathered a son named Calid <note>Khalid ibn Yazid, famously associated with the beginnings of Arabic alchemy</note>, who reigned in Egypt for a long time after his father's death. This King was a wise and prudent man, clear-sighted in every branch of knowledge; for he greatly loved wise men and Philosophers on account of the knowledge contained in this book. He did not cease to search through the provinces, among both the known and the unknown, to see if he could find anyone who could reveal to him the teachings of this book. Compelled by this passion, he kept many wise men and Philosophers with him who claimed to know the mastery <term>magisterium: the successful completion of the alchemical process or the "Great Work"</term> of this book, though they were utterly ignorant of it. He enriched these men with many great gifts, having trusted in their words for a long time.

One day, while I was in my hermitage, the fame of this king was brought to me by a certain traveler. When I had heard of it, I left the wilderness and crossed over to the borders of his region as quickly as I could; not, indeed, to seek riches or gifts from him, but rather to diligently instruct him in spiritual gifts. After I entered his borders, I traversed many places as I traveled, and at last I found the king. When I had found him and conferred with him on certain matters, I found him to be a man of great wisdom, adorned with every virtue, and most prudent. I said therefore to him: "O good King, may God turn you toward better things. I wish for you to command that a house be prepared for me, suitable for my mastery." The King therefore ordered a house to be prepared for me and furnished according to my wish. I entered this house and did not leave it until I had completed the entire mastery; and having finished it, I left it in the house. But around the vessel in which it had been placed, I painted these words:

-> **ALL WHO HAVE ALL THINGS WITHIN THEMSELVES,** <-
-> **HAVE NO NEED WHATSOEVER FOR THE HELP OF OTHERS.** <-

After I wrote these words, I secretly departed from the city and that entire region, and returned to my hermitage. Afterward, the King entered the house which I had left,

# MORIENUS THE ROMAN

...and he found the completed mastery <note>The "mastery" refers to the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work, or the Philosopher's Stone</note> which I had left behind. When he examined it more and more diligently, he saw the words which I had left written around the vessel. Once these were completed and well understood, he immediately wept for my absence, and he ordered the heads to be cut off of all those whom he had kept with him for many years for the sake of this mastery. <note>The King executed the false alchemists who had failed where Morienus succeeded.</note> Afterward, the King said: "Call Galip, my faithful servant." Now Galip was his captive, whom his father Gezid had given to him before his death on account of his faithfulness. For the King trusted him greatly, and said to him: "O Galip my servant, I do not know what I must do hereafter." Galip said to the king: "My leader, God will provide what we are to do next." The king was greatly saddened, and he grieved day and night beyond what can be believed.

It happened then, after some years, while the king went out one day to the place called Dirmaroni <note>likely a Latinization of Deir Maroni, a monastery or location in the Levant</note> for the sake of hunting, that the captive Galip found a certain man praying in the wilderness. He questioned him and said to him: "Friend, who are you, or where do you come from, or where are you going?" And that man replied: "I am a Jerusalemite; for I was born in Jerusalem, and for many years I lived in the mountains of Jerusalem with a certain hermit. While I was staying there, I heard how King Khalid <note>original: "Rex Calid"</note> was incessantly searching for someone who could demonstrate the mastery of Hermes <note>The "Mastery of Hermes" is a traditional term for Alchemy, named after the legendary founder Hermes Trismegistus</note> to him. After I heard this about the king, I soon departed from my homeland so that I might announce this to King Khalid. For I know a man most learned in this mastery whom I greatly desire to show to the King."

Then Galip said: "Be silent, brother, be silent; let it suffice that you have said this much to me. I prefer that you live rather than die; for many have come to the King who professed to know this mastery, and when they could not reach the result of their profession, they were killed by the King. I fear, therefore, that if you stand in the sight of the King with speech of this kind, you may be killed." Then that man said: "Do not fear this, but do not delay in bringing me into the sight of the King." Galip then said: "This pleases me now, but take care that you do not die." # THE ROMAN MORIENUS

->May you fare well, my King: The good which I now possess, and that which I expect in the future, is from God, and placed in His hand. Let Him do as He wills. Nor do I doubt that I find greater rest among gatherings and assemblies, and labor in the solitudes and mountains; but no one reaps unless he sows, and what he has sown, that he shall also reap. <note>A reference to Galatians 6:7, emphasizing the law of cause and effect in both spiritual and alchemical work.</note> I hope, therefore, that the goodness of the Divinity will not abandon me in the life of this world; for the entrance to rest is exceedingly narrow, nor can anyone enter it except through the affliction of the soul.<-

The King then said: "Everything you say is undoubtedly true; but because these words proceed from a faithful soul, they seem false." The King said this because he was still a worshiper of idols. <note>The text highlights the religious tension between the monotheistic hermit and the King, who is portrayed here as a pagan prior to his conversion to the "divine art."</note>

Morienus responded: "If you concede that the things I bring forth are true, it is necessary for you to concede that the soul from which they proceed is true and truth-telling. For from true things, truths proceed; and from false things, falsehoods; from eternal things, the eternal; from transitory things, the transitory; from good things, good; and from evil things, evil."

The King then said: "O Morienus, many things have been reported to me concerning you, your constancy, and your faith; wherefore I wonder greatly, since I now see and hear those things to be true. This was the reason why I long desired to see you and hear you at the same time. For I wish that, among certain matters which we shall discuss, you might instruct and teach me with certain other proofs, as it were."

Then Morienus said to him: "O King, may Almighty God turn you toward the better; for I am not one at whom you should wonder much. I am one of the sons of Adam. <note>original: "ex filijs Adae"</note> We all indeed proceeded from one; and again to one, though by a different path, we shall return. The long change of times confounds and changes man, who is established under time. Nor have I yet been changed so much that many others who were before me are not changed more. Dread death follows the final change, than which no punishment is judged worse. For before the joining of the body and soul, and after their dissolution, a punishment more cruel than any death awaits the soul. But may the Almighty Creator, who creates and forms all things from Himself, be always in our aid."

For this is the science which draws its master away from the misery of this world, and leads him back to the knowledge of future goods. In times past, they always inherited this wisdom from one another in turn; but afterward, that science was almost held in contempt. Yet many books of the ancient masters remained, in which that science is contained entirely true and without falsehood: nevertheless, no one was found who could evidently bring it to its effect then: because of the many and diverse names which had long ago been imposed upon the things pertaining to it by the older wise men. I departed from Alexandria and arrived at Jerusalem, and within its borders I chose for myself a hermitage where I could lead a life suited to my faith and profession. Not many years later, however, there arose a certain King in Egypt named Macoya <note>likely a Latinization of Muawiyah I</note>. He fathered a son named Gezid <note>Yazid I</note>, who reigned in Egypt after his father's death and obtained his kingdom. Gezid then fathered a son named Calid <note>Prince Khalid ibn Yazid, a historical figure often associated with the beginnings of Arabic alchemy</note>, who reigned in Egypt for a long time after his father's death. This King was a wise and prudent man, clear-sighted in every science; for he greatly loved wise men and Philosophers on account of the knowledge contained in this book.

He did not cease to search throughout the provinces, among both the known and the unknown, to see if he could find anyone who could reveal to him the teachings of this book. Driven by this passion, he kept many wise men and Philosophers with him who claimed to know the <term>mastery</term> <note>Latin: magisterium; the successful completion of the alchemical Great Work or the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note> of this book, though they were utterly ignorant of it. He enriched these men with many great gifts, having trusted in their words for a long time.

One day, while I was in my hermitage, the fame of this king was brought to me by a certain traveler. When I had heard of it, I left the desert and traveled as quickly as I could to the borders of his region—not, indeed, to seek riches or gifts from him, but to diligently instruct him in spiritual gifts. After I entered his borders, I traversed many places as I went, and at last I found the king. When I had found him and conferred with him on certain matters, I found him to be a man of great wisdom, adorned with every virtue, and most prudent.

I said to him: "O good King, may God turn you toward better things. I wish for you to command that a house be prepared for me, suitable for my mastery." The King therefore ordered a house to be prepared for me and furnished according to my wish. ->Bb 2<-

If you examine this, you will clearly recognize that we all agree and that everything we say is true. Therefore, concerning what you asked, understand it thus: the first and principal substance and matter of this thing is one, and from it comes one thing, and it exists with it, and nothing is added to it or taken away. Behold, you now have what you asked for. Now, however, I will bring you the testimonies of the ancients, so that we may all be judged to harmonize as one.

Indeed, a certain **Hercules** <note>original: "Hercules"; likely referring to a legendary figure or a specific alchemical author rather than the Greek hero</note>, a wise King and Philosopher, when he was questioned by some of his followers, said: "This mastery <term>mastery: the alchemical process or the production of the Philosopher's Stone</term> proceeds first from one root, which afterwards expands into many things, and again returns to one; and it is necessary to know how to receive the air."

**Arficanus** <note>original: "Arficanus"; an Arabic-Latinized name for an alchemical authority, possibly Africanus</note> the Philosopher also says: "The four elements—that is, heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—proceed from one source, and some of them are made from others of the same. Of these four, some are like roots, and some are as if composed from these roots. Those which are roots are water and fire; those which are composed from these are earth and air."

Likewise, **Arficanus** to **Maria** <note>referring to Mary the Prophetess, a foundational figure in alchemy</note>: "Our water," he says, "has mastery over our earth, which is great, bright, and pure. For from the thickness of the water, the earth is created."

**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> also says: "Earth is the mother of the elements; from the earth they proceed, and to the earth they return." **Hermes** says again: "Just as all things proceed from one, so my mastery is made from one substance and matter. And as the four elements are contained in the human body, so God created them situated, distinct, and joined, collected together and diffused through the whole body; because one body merges them and retains them in one, and yet each of them performs a work dissimilar from the work of another. And although they are in one body, yet they have a different color and a different dominion." In the same way, therefore, this mastery must be understood.

The Philosophers have spoken many such testimonies about this mastery, some of which we shall mention in what follows.

**King Calid** <note>original: "Rex Calid"; Khalid ibn Yazid, an Umayyad prince credited with being the first Arab alchemist</note>: "How, and by what reason, can it be that there is one root, one substance, and one matter for this mastery, when many and manifold names for that root are found among the Philosophers?"

**Morienus** <note>Morienus Romanus, the legendary hermit and teacher of King Calid</note>: "The names of that root are indeed manifold..."

...names, but if you look upon those things which were mentioned above in the correct order, you will find its single root, substance, and <term>matter<note>original: "mariam" - likely a variant of "materiam" or a reference to the "Materia Prima," the formless starting material of alchemy.</note></term>. Morienus: A certain Hercules said to some of his disciples: The little stone of the date is nourished by the palm tree, and the palm tree grows from its own little stone, and from its root many branches grow together, which multiply and increase their number because of it. Hermes, however, says: Look upon the perfect Red, and the Red diminished from its redness, and all redness; consider also the perfect yellow, and the yellow diminished from its yellowness, and all yellowness; and the perfect black also, and the black diminished from its blackness, and all blackness. Also, a certain wise man, who for the sake of God had left the whole world, brings to us a similar example. Again, the same wise man says: Consider the tailor, who is accustomed to sewing clothes, for from a cloth he composes a tunic or any other garment, the parts of which receive diverse names; yet if they are considered naturally, they will be found to be formed from that same cloth. There is, however, one cloth and principal matter from which the garment is made. For the <term>coverlet<note>original: "torale"</note></term>, and the sleeves, and the <term>gussets<note>original: "girones" - pieces of fabric used to taper or strengthen a garment.</note></term>, although they have different names as far as the parts of the garment are concerned, nevertheless their principal matter is the cloth. For even the threads by which the parts of the garment are joined into one are drawn from the cloth itself, not because the cloth requires anything else different from itself for this purpose. In a similar way, this mastery is one thing existing by itself, nor does it need anything else. Since among the Philosophers this mastery is covered and hidden, and wherever it may be, it is called by a thousand names. It is also sealed, nor...

And these names are those which the wise have named in their books, of which one is "sperm," which when it is turned, is changed into blood; and finally it is curdled, and becomes like a fruit of mixed flesh; and it happens in such a way until one creature takes on another form, namely, that of a succeeding human, and then it must necessarily become a human. Among these names, there is another name such as "the palm tree," just as from the color of its fruits, and from the color of its natures, before they arrive at their perfection. There is also another name such as "the pomegranate tree"; and like "wheat" and "milk," and many other names, of all of which there is one root. But according to the diverse effects, diverse colors, and diverse natures, they impose many and diverse names upon the thing itself, as the Philosopher Herizartem says: "I tell the truth, that nothing else has thrust the artisans of this mastery into errors, except the variety and the multitude of its names." But if anyone rightly understands that these names are nothing but the colors appearing during the joining <note>the chemical or symbolic union of substances</note>, he will not stray from the path of this mastery.

*King Calid*: I desire greatly to understand whether these colors, of which you spoke a little while ago—namely, that they are changed from one into another—are so changed by one arrangement or preparation <note>original: "confectione," a mixture or medicinal preparation</note>, or by two or more.

*Morienus*: By one single preparation or species the matter is thus changed; but the more the fire renews its color, the more numerous are the names imposed upon it. Whence *Darin the Philosopher* says to *Euticus*: "I shall show you that the wise have not multiplied the arrangements or preparations of this mastery for any other reason than to instruct the wise in this mastery, and to utterly blind the foolish." Since this mastery has one name, and this is assigned as its own; so also it has one arrangement and also one linear path. And in this way, although the Wise have changed its names and their sayings, nevertheless they intended to understand only one thing, and...

Because although the four elements were previously in the sperm, God the Creator nevertheless set a defined time for it in which it should be completed; and when that time is finished, the creature itself is strengthened. This fire must burn there for two days and as many nights, remaining equal without any increase or decrease. When all this is done, the vessel is removed from the furnace with everything inside it, for by the help of God, the repetition of the art is now complete.

**The King:** We shall act in this manner that you describe, and likewise, blessed be the name of the Lord.

**Morienus:** O King, you must also know that the entire perfection of this mastery consists in the capturing of joined and concordant bodies. For these bodies are joined to one another by a natural and substantial affinity; they agree, they melt, and they even receive one another. For they improve and direct one another so that, through the strength of the fire, they appear more beautiful. 

Whenever the seeker of wisdom perfectly understands the capturing of these bodies, their decanting, their necessary solution and composition, as well as their mixing and decoction <term>Decoction: the process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence</term>, he should then learn their quantity, the construction of his furnace, and the lighting of the fire—specifically in which part of the furnace the fire ought to be lit—as well as the number of days required and the measure of the weights. For if he handles all these things with foresight and reason, his intention will be fulfilled by the help of the Divinity. 

Therefore, let all haste be driven far from the craftsman, and let foresight, reason, and firm expectation be applied. Furthermore, that which most enlivens these bodies is "blood" <note>In alchemy, "blood" often refers to a red mercurial spirit or a specific vitalizing solvent rather than literal blood</note>; for it vivifies and joins them, and from all these things it creates a single body. For this reason, a gentle heat must be applied for a long time, which should remain equal throughout its designated days. For if the heat of the fire creeps into the bodies with a hasty combustion, it will consume the body itself.

<summary>Morienus instructs King Khalid on the final stabilization of the Elixir, emphasizing the need for a steady, indirect heat and the "natural affinity" between alchemical bodies. He warns that haste and excessive heat will destroy the work, requiring instead a patient, reasoned approach.</summary>

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

For if *eudica* <note>original: "eudica"; likely a corruption of the Arabic "al-tutiya" or tutty, but here defined as glass dross</note> is applied to them, it will protect the bodies themselves, once changed into earth, from all combustion. For after bodies no longer retain their souls, they are quickly consumed by fire. *Eudica* (the dross of glass) indeed suits all bodies well: for it vivifies and prepares them, and defends them from all burning. For it sends certain of them into others, and once they are sent in, it afterwards defends them from excessive heat. And when you wish to seek *eudica*, look for it in glass vessels; when you have found it, store it away; do not do anything with it until it becomes acidic. Let it not be unleavened <note>original: "azima"; referring to the state of the matter before fermentation</note>, for otherwise your intention would be utterly destroyed. The "stinking earth" <note>a term for the crude, impure base matter of the alchemical work</note> also quickly receives white sparks, and restrains the blood so that it is not ruined in the decoction. For the power of the blood and its strength is exceedingly great; for which reason the blood must be "broken" <note>tempered or diluted</note> lest it hinder or overwhelm; this breaking should be done after it has been whitened. That which remains of the colors takes on a blackness—the colors, I say, of the veins previously poured out—from a new being which indeed pertains to this Mastery <note>original: "magisterio"; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note>. If you do not see the truth at the beginning of this, it is altogether deceptive and useless. This too is the secret of this Mastery, which I have briefly gathered here into one, and having gathered it, I have explained it to you: namely, that one part of this substance converts a thousand parts of silver into the purest gold. These things, therefore, which have already been said, are sufficient for you for this Mastery. But there still remain certain things without which the Mastery cannot be completed. And it is fitting for you to know that the intention of a man seeking this divine and pure science ought to consider it nothing other than a gift of God, the Most High and Great, who entrusts it to His own; may His name be forever blessed. But you, good King, be now present with me in your whole mind, that you may hear and understand those things which I shall now tell you. King Khalid: Speak as you please, for I am present and assist you with attentive ears.

# MORIENUS THE ROMAN

...this can in no way be handled correctly. **King Khalid:** Explain these names to me. **Morienus:** I shall explain them at the end of the book, since for the present I will complete the mastery <note>original: "magisterium," referring to the completed alchemical process or "Great Work"</note> for you concerning those things whose names these are, so that the things I have already said may be proven through the actual effect of the matter itself. For the root of this science is that he who wishes to learn it must first receive its teaching from a master, and the master must frequently perform it in the presence of his disciple. There are, however, some who seek this science for a long time and yet do not find it. But you, always work in these matters as you see me work; do not seek anything else in this mastery, for if you do, you will undoubtedly wander into error. There are many obstacles in this science. For as the Wise Man says: There is a great distance between the wise and the foolish, and between the blind and those who see; nor indeed is he who has perfectly known the arrangement of this mastery through proof equal to him who still persists in searching for it through books. For books composed about this art are written under figures <note>symbolic or metaphorical language intended to hide the meaning from the uninitiated</note>, of which the greater part appears very obscure and the science complex, nor can it be understood except by its own authors; yet this is the science which, among others, ought to be most sought after, since through it we may arrive at another even more admirable science. **King Khalid:** All things that you bring forth are spoken truly, and their truth flourishes and shines forth wonderfully in its explanation.

-># ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS<-

Join them together, specifically so that in their mixing an equal weight of each is applied. Once mixed, let them be placed perfectly into a thick vessel, in a measure of approximately one pound; the mouth of which should be suitably sealed with bitumen <note>original: "bitumine"; here referring to "Philosophers' Clay," a sealant used to make vessels airtight</note>. For there are winds <note>volatile gases or spirits</note> within them which, if they are not detained in the vessel, will escape, and thus the mastery <term>magisterium: the successful completion of an alchemical process</term> will be brought to nothing. Indeed, that bitumen is what is called "Lutū" <note>Lute or sealing clay</note> in the books of the Philosophers. In this, clearly, you should add a little salt before closing it, by which it may be more strengthened and able to resist the burning of the fire for a longer time.

Then, heat the furnace, and once it is heated, let the aforementioned vessel with all that it contains be sublimated <term>sublimatio: the process of heating a substance until it vaporizes and then solidifies again</term> within it. This sublimation should take place after sunset, and let it be left there until the day cools. Afterward, draw out the vessel itself and break it open. If you find those things which you had placed inside mixed into one body in the manner of a stone: take it, grind it well, and sift it <note>original: "tantarisa"; to pass through a fine sieve</note>. 

When you have done this, take another vessel whose bottom is round, and place this material—now well-ground and well-sifted—inside, and close the mouth of the vessel on all sides with the bitumen of the Philosophers. Then, construct a "Philosophers' Furnace," in which you shall kindle the "Philosophic Fire" in the manner of the Philosophers, which should endure burning at an equal heat for a space of 21 days. 

Indeed, the Philosophic Fire is such that its matter is divided into two parts. For either its fuel shall be composed of horse dung, or of olive leaves; for there is nothing that makes a fire endure more equally in its burning than these. Therefore, when the aforementioned days have passed, draw the vessel from the furnace and dry what you find inside. 

Afterward, take one part of it and mix it with ten parts of the purified material, and again take one part of the purified and mix it similarly with a tenth part of the pure. And so on, according to this order and number, let one be added to the other so they are mixed into one. When they are mixed into one, make from it the **Elixir**: that is, disperse it, and if what remains in it is white and well-fixed <note>stable and non-volatile</note>, and you find no loss due to the scorching of the fire, you have now completed two parts of this mastery. This, therefore, is the method by which the "White" is most recently joined with the "Unclean," nor is any other method found besides this.

<margin>//</margin>Morienus said: Take the white smoke <note>likely a reference to mercury or ammonia vapors</note> and the green lion <term>Green Lion: a common alchemical term often referring to vitriol or unrefined antimony</term>, and the red Almagra <note>original: "Almagra rubeum" - a red earth or iron oxide</note>, and the "filth of the dead" <note>a cryptic term for the base matter or dregs of a previous process</note>. When it has been dried, add the Elixir to it, and finally pour over it the "water of blood" <note>likely a red-tinted solvent or mineral acid</note> until it floats above it. After three days and nights likewise, moisten it with "fetid water" <note>original: "aqua fœtida" - often referring to sulfurous water or a sharp solvent</note>, taking care that you do not diminish any of its days, nor let its fire be extinguished, nor let it grow too intense by burning, nor let its scorching be lessened by decreasing the heat. Therefore, when seventeen nights have passed, you shall open the aforesaid vessel and extract the water you find inside, and again put other fetid water back into it. This must be done for three nights, taking care that the vessel is in no way removed from its furnace; let the addition of the fetid water be done once in each of the three nights. Then, when twenty-one nights have passed, extract the vessel from the furnace and dry the Elixir that was in it. Afterward, take the white body—in which you have already fixed the white—and place it in a very small vessel, which is according to the size of the furnace of the Mastery <note>the "Mastery" refers to the completion of the alchemical Great Work</note>, which shall be done after you have constructed it. "Red smoke" is red orpiment. "White smoke" is quicksilver <note>mercury</note>; and "citrine smoke" is yellow sulfur. Behold, I now express the names of the species to you, of which three will suffice for the whole mastery: that is, white smoke, the green lion, and stinking water. # MORIENUS THE ROMAN

The precept of God cannot be avoided. For some people believe that the secret of this <term>mastery</term> <note>Latin: *magisterium*; the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> is earth, or stone, or wine, or blood, or even vinegar; and they grind and cook all these things by themselves, and extract something from their boiling, and bury what they have extracted. They do this because they believe they are acting according to their own opinion, so that their error might be further strengthened, and so they do not despair of finding what they seek.

But know that earth and stone, and all these things, are useless for the mastery and lead to a bad end. It is also fitting for you to know that the greatest efficacy of this work is weighed in its fire; for with fire the minerals are prepared, and the <term>evil souls</term> <note>Refers to volatile or impure elements that must be fixed or purified</note> are retained within their bodies. Its fire is also its entire nature, and the perfect proof of this matter. Furthermore, whatever you might do for this mastery, if you do not find <term>the One</term> <note>The principle of unity or the "All in One" central to alchemical philosophy</note> at the beginning, it is useless. For what good can be hoped for when the thing itself does not act, nor does it complete itself within the world? That is to say, so that it may be reduced into one body. If, however, you handle these things according to what we have said, your intention will be fulfilled by the help of God.

Therefore, understand well what we have said, and commit what you have understood to your memory; arrange that disposition according to its order, and study frequently within their disposition. For frequent study of it will show you a straighter path. Likewise, you should know that the greatest root of this work lies in the investigation of the <term>species</term> <note>The specific types of substances or "seeds" of metals</note> which are better for this mastery. For every mineral is of many kinds.

Regarding that which you asked about the **white smoke**, it is fitting for you to know that the **white smoke** is the <term>tincture</term> <note>The coloring principle or the agent of transformation</note>, and also the **soul** of these dissolved and even dead bodies—those bodies, namely, whose souls we have already extracted and have joined again to their bodies. For every body, when it lacks a soul, will be dark and obscure. And the **white smoke** is that which flows down into the body like a soul, so that it may utterly take away its <term>blackness</term> <note>Latin: *nigredo*; the first stage of the work, representing decay and purification</note> and its uncleanness from it, and consolidate the bodies into one, and multiply their water. For the unclean is black and very light; and therefore, when its blackness is taken away, its <term>whiteness</term> <note>Latin: *albedo*; the second stage, representing purification and enlightenment</note> is strengthened, and its water is multiplied, and its beauty will be more apparent, and the tincture will then work more effectively within it.

<summary>Morienus warns against using common substances like blood or vinegar for alchemy, emphasizing instead the role of fire and the "white smoke" (soul) in purifying the "blackness" of the material. He explains that the goal is to reunite the extracted soul with the body to achieve a state of perfected whiteness.</summary>

<keywords>Morienus the Roman, alchemy, mastery, white smoke, soul and body, nigredo, albedo, tincture, purification, chemical wedding</keywords>

# ON THE TRANSMUTATION OF METALS

What more is there to say? If all these things have been handled well, the tincture <note>A potent substance or "medicine" believed to transform base metals into gold</note> will work effectively within it, and its gold will emerge most pure and reddish-gold; indeed, you will be able to find none better or more pure than this. For this reason, therefore, this gold is accustomed to be called by some "Gold," or "Roman Ethees" <note>original: "Ethees Romanum." Likely a corruption of an Arabic term for the "hidden" or "ethereal" essence of gold</note>. I also wish you to know this: that if the white smoke were not present, the pure or useful gold of the Ethees of Alchemy could in no way be produced. This is the very head of this mastery, and, as it were, its entire direction. For if, when the Alchemy <note>Here referring to the completed alchemical substance or Elixir</note> has been finished, one part of it is placed among nine parts of silver, the whole will be converted into the purest gold. May God therefore be blessed, Amen, through all the ages of ages.
